attarissiya.s: Attarissiya was a warlord described in Hittite records as 'the man of Ahhiya' around 1400 BCE. According to the Indictment of Madduwatta, he drove the Hittite vassal Madduwatta from his land in western Anatolia and later joined him in raiding Alashiya, probably Cyprus.

achaeans-homer.s: The Achaeans are the Greeks of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey; it is the poet's most common collective name, alongside Danaans and Argives, for the army that besieged Troy. Many scholars connect the name with Ahhiyawa, a Late Bronze Age kingdom mentioned in Hittite texts and…

ahmadil-ibn-ibrahim.s: Ahmadil ibn Ibrahim was a Kurdish emir of the Rawwadid family who held Maragheh in north-western Iran under the Seljuk sultans. He was one of the leading Seljuk commanders in Azerbaijan and joined the campaign against the Crusaders in Syria in 1111.

aq-sunqur-ahmadili.s: Aq Sunqur Ahmadili was a Turkish mamluk of the Kurdish emir Ahmadil ibn Ibrahim who took control of Maragheh around 1122 and founded the Ahmadili dynasty, named after his former master. As atabeg of a Seljuk prince he took part in the succession wars of the Seljuk Sultanate of…

ahmadnagar.s: Ahmadnagar is a city in Maharashtra, western India, founded in 1494 by Ahmad Nizam Shah I as the capital of the Nizam Shahi sultanate. Its fort was defended by Chand Bibi against the Mughals in 1595 and fell to them in 1600.

aurangabad.s: Aurangabad is a city in Maharashtra, western India. Founded in 1610 by Malik Ambar as Khadki, the capital of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, it was renamed after Aurangzeb, who governed the Deccan from there and is buried nearby.

ahom-people.s: The Ahom are a people of Assam in north-eastern India, descended from Tai followers of Sukaphaa who entered the Brahmaputra valley from upper Burma in 1228 and mixed with local peoples. They founded the Ahom kingdom, which ruled Assam for about six centuries.

amur-river.s: The Amur is a major river of north-east Asia, about 2,800 kilometres long, forming much of the border between Russia and China before flowing into the Strait of Tartary opposite Sakhalin. Its valley was home to the Mohe, the Jurchens and other peoples.

abraha.s: Abraha was an Aksumite general who seized power in Himyar, in Yemen, in the 530s and ruled it, nominally as a vassal of Aksum, until about 570. He built a great church at Sanaa and repaired the Marib dam, recording his deeds in inscriptions.

akropong.s: Akropong is a town on the Akuapem ridge in south-eastern Ghana and the seat of the Okuapehene, paramount chief of the Akuapem state, since the 18th century. The Basel Mission settled there in 1835, and its seminary, founded in 1848, made the town a leading centre of education…

akuapem-twi.s: Akuapem Twi is a dialect of the Akan language spoken on the Akuapem ridge in south-eastern Ghana. In the 19th century Basel missionaries, above all Johann Gottlieb Christaller, chose it as the basis of written Twi, publishing a grammar, a dictionary and a complete Bible…

akusha.s: Akusha is a village in the mountains of central Dagestan, Russia, and the historic centre of the Dargin people. From at least the 17th century it led the Akusha-Dargo union of village communities, whose qadi served as its leading authority.

asameni.s: Asameni was a trader of the Akwamu kingdom on the Gold Coast who in 1693 led a party posing as customers that seized the Danish fort of Christiansborg at Osu, near Accra. He held it for about a year, flying his own flag and trading with European ships, before selling it back…

addac.s: Addax was king of the Alans in Hispania, who had crossed the Rhine with the Vandals and Suebi in 406 and entered Spain in 409. The Alans settled in Lusitania and Carthaginiensis.

akhmet-baitursynov.s: Akhmet Baitursynov was a Kazakh scholar, poet and politician, a founder of the Alash party and a leader of the Alash Orda government. He reformed the Arabic-based Kazakh alphabet, wrote pioneering grammars of the Kazakh language and edited the newspaper Qazaq from 1913.

alash-party.s: Alash was a Kazakh national party founded in 1917 by intellectuals including Alikhan Bukeikhanov, Akhmet Baitursynov and Mirzhakip Dulatov, and named after the legendary ancestor of the Kazakhs. It sought Kazakh autonomy within a democratic Russian federation and formed the…

amir-kabir.s: Amir Kabir (Mirza Taqi Khan Farahani) was chief minister of Iran under Naser al-Din Shah from 1848 to 1851. He reformed the finances and the army, curbed foreign influence and founded the Dar ol-Fonun, Iran's first modern college, which opened in 1851.

alawites.s: The Alawites are a religious community that emerged from Shia Islam in the 9th and 10th centuries, named after the caliph Ali and associated with the teacher Ibn Nusayr, hence the older name Nusayris. Concentrated in the coastal mountains of north-western Syria and around…

aeneas.s: Aeneas is a Trojan hero of Greek and Roman legend, son of the prince Anchises and the goddess Venus (Aphrodite). Roman tradition, given its classic form in Virgil's Aeneid, told how he escaped the fall of Troy and settled in Latium, founding Lavinium, while his son Ascanius…

amulius.s: Amulius is a legendary king of Alba Longa in Roman tradition, who seized the throne from his elder brother Numitor. To prevent rivals, he made Numitor's daughter Rhea Silvia a Vestal Virgin, and when she bore the twins Romulus and Remus he ordered them to be drowned.

ascanius.s: Ascanius, also called Iulus, is the son of Aeneas in Roman legend. Tradition held that he left Lavinium and founded Alba Longa about thirty years later, ruling as its first king.

albanian-fascist-party.s: The Albanian Fascist Party was the ruling party of Albania under Italian occupation, founded in April 1939 after Italy's invasion and modelled on Mussolini's National Fascist Party. Membership was required for many state posts, and the party was subordinate to Italian…

amago-clan.s: The Amago clan was a Japanese warrior family that rose from deputy governors of Izumo province for the Kyōgoku into one of the leading daimyō houses of western Honshu. Under Amago Tsunehisa and his grandson Haruhisa they ruled from Gassantoda Castle and contested the San'in…

amago-haruhisa.s: Amago Haruhisa was a Japanese daimyō of the Sengoku period who led the Amago clan of Izumo from 1537, succeeding his grandfather Amago Tsunehisa. He failed in an attack on Mōri Motonari at Yoshida-Kōriyama in 1540–1541 but repelled an Ōuchi siege of Gassantoda in 1543, and at…

ain.s: Ain is a department of eastern France, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, named after the river Ain, a tributary of the Rhône. It lies between the Saône and the Jura mountains and borders Switzerland near Geneva, with its prefecture at Bourg-en-Bresse.

amiens.s: Amiens is a city on the Somme in northern France, the historic capital of Picardy. As Samarobriva, 'the bridge on the Somme', it was the chief town of the Gallic Ambiani, where Julius Caesar wintered in 54 BCE, and it later took the people's name.

acarnania.s: Acarnania is a region of western Greece between the Ambracian Gulf, the Achelous river and the Ionian Sea. In antiquity its people, the Acarnanians, lived in small towns joined in a federal league centred on Stratos, and they were long allied with Athens against Corinth's…

amphilochian-argos.s: Amphilochian Argos was an ancient Greek city at the south-eastern corner of the Ambracian Gulf, in western Greece, the chief town of the Amphilochians. Legend named the hero Amphilochus as its founder.

arachthos.s: The Arachthos is a river of Epirus in north-western Greece, flowing from the Pindus mountains south past Arta into the Ambracian Gulf. Ancient Ambracia, founded by Corinthian colonists around 625 BCE, stood on its banks.

arta-greece.s: Arta is a city in Epirus, north-western Greece, on the Arachthos river near the Ambracian Gulf, standing on the site of ancient Ambracia. In the 13th century it was the capital of the Despotate of Epirus, whose rulers built Byzantine churches such as the Panagia Parigoritissa.

aunuu.s: Aunuʻu is a small volcanic island off the south-east coast of Tutuila in American Samoa. Its chiefs, together with those of Tutuila, signed the deed of cession to the United States in 1900.

amman.s: Amman is the capital and largest city of Jordan. As Rabbah, or Rabbath Ammon, it was the capital of the Iron Age kingdom of Ammon; the Ptolemies refounded it as Philadelphia, and it became a city of the Decapolis with a Roman theatre that still stands.

amman-citadel-inscription.s: The Amman Citadel Inscription is a fragmentary stone inscription in the Ammonite language, found in 1961 on the citadel hill of Amman, Jordan. Dated to the 9th century BCE, it records a building text introduced by the god Milkom.

anthela.s: Anthela was a small place near the pass of Thermopylae in central Greece, with a sanctuary of Demeter Amphictyonis. It was the original meeting place of the Delphic Amphictyony, the league of Greek peoples that later also met at Delphi, so that the council gathered at both…

altinum.s: Altinum was an ancient city of the Veneti on the edge of the Venetian lagoon, near modern Quarto d'Altino in north-eastern Italy. Under Rome it became a prosperous municipium and a junction of the Via Annia and the Via Claudia Augusta.

antenor.s: Antenor is a Trojan elder in Greek legend, an adviser of King Priam who argued for returning Helen to the Greeks. Later tradition, followed by Livy and Virgil, told how after the fall of Troy he led the Eneti from Paphlagonia to northern Italy and founded Padua.

angers.s: Angers is a city on the Maine river near the Loire in western France, the historic capital of Anjou. As Juliomagus it was the chief town of the Gallic Andecavi under Rome, later taking their name.

acanthus-greece.s: Acanthus was an ancient Greek city on the Chalcidice peninsula in northern Greece, near the isthmus of Mount Athos, founded by colonists from Andros around 655 BCE. Xerxes' army passed it in 480 BCE while digging a canal through the isthmus, and in 424 BCE it went over to the…

argilus.s: Argilus was an ancient Greek city on the coast of Thrace, west of the mouth of the Strymon in northern Greece, founded by colonists from Andros around 655 BCE. It was a neighbour and rival of Amphipolis, and in 424 BCE its people helped the Spartan Brasidas take that city.

angria.s: Angria, or Engern, was one of the three main divisions of Old Saxony, between Westphalia and Eastphalia along the middle Weser in north-western Germany, named after the ancient Angrivarii. Charlemagne conquered it in the Saxon Wars of 772–804.

agokoli.s: Agokoli is remembered in Ewe tradition as a tyrannical king of Notsie, in modern Togo. According to the story, his cruelty drove the Ewe to escape secretly from the walled town, probably in the 17th century, and to disperse and found new settlements, including the Anlo state.

anloga.s: Anloga is a town on the sandbar between the Keta lagoon and the Atlantic in the Volta Region of south-eastern Ghana. It is the traditional capital of the Anlo Ewe and the seat of their paramount ruler, the Awoamefia.

awoamefia.s: Awoamefia is the title of the paramount ruler of the Anlo Ewe of south-eastern Ghana, who resides at Anloga. Traditionally a sacred figure, the Awoamefia lived largely in seclusion and was rarely seen in public, while war leaders and lineage heads handled day-to-day affairs.

abul-fath-muhammad-ibn-annaz.s: Abu'l-Fath Muhammad ibn Annaz was a Kurdish chief of the Shadhanjan tribe who founded the Annazid dynasty. Around 990, as Buyid authority weakened, he established himself at Hulwan on the road from Baghdad to Hamadan, and he ruled the frontier lands of western Iran and eastern…

antanosy.s: The Antanosy are a Malagasy people of the Anosy region in south-eastern Madagascar, around Taolagnaro (Fort-Dauphin). From around 1500 they were ruled by the Zafiraminia, a clan claiming Muslim origins, and in 1643 French settlers founded Fort-Dauphin in their land.

antemoro.s: The Antemoro (Antaimoro) are a Malagasy people of south-eastern Madagascar, around the Matitana river and Vohipeno. Their ruling clans, who claim descent from Muslim immigrants, established a kingdom around 1500, and their scribes preserved the sorabe, Malagasy texts written…

allen-stanford.s: Allen Stanford is an American financier who built a banking and investment empire based in Antigua, where he became the largest private employer and was knighted in 2006. In 2009 US authorities charged him with running a Ponzi scheme worth about 7 billion dollars through his…

antigua-labour-party.s: The Antigua Labour Party, later renamed the Antigua and Barbuda Labour Party, grew out of the Antigua Trades and Labour Union in the 1940s. Under Vere Bird and later his son Lester Bird it dominated Antiguan politics, leading the country to independence in 1981 and governing…

alexander-iv-of-macedon.s: Alexander IV was the son of Alexander the Great and Roxane, born after his father's death in 323 BCE. He was proclaimed joint king with his uncle Philip III Arrhidaeus, but real power lay with the generals who fought over the empire.

anyi-people.s: The Anyi are an Akan people living mainly in south-eastern Côte d'Ivoire and neighbouring western Ghana. Moving westwards from the Akan heartland in the 17th and 18th centuries, they founded kingdoms such as Sanwi, Indénié and Moronou in the forest and lagoon country.

anhaica.s: Anhaica was the principal town of the Apalachee chiefdom in northern Florida, located within modern Tallahassee. Hernando de Soto's expedition seized it and spent the winter of 1539–1540 there.

aucilla-river.s: The Aucilla River flows about 140 kilometres from southern Georgia across northern Florida to the Gulf of Mexico. It marked the eastern edge of the Apalachee province in the 16th and 17th centuries.

aspavarma.s: Aspavarma was a ruler of the Apracharajas, a dynasty of Bajaur in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, in the early 1st century CE. A son of Indravarma, he is known from coins on which he calls himself strategos, a general, serving first under the Indo-Scythian king Azes…

abel-beth-maacah.s: Abel-beth-maacah was an ancient town in the far north of Israel, near Metula, identified with the mound of Tel Abel Beth Maacah. The Bible names it as a city in the land of Maacah, attacked by Ben-Hadad I of Damascus and conquered by Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria in 732 BCE.

albert-suerbeer.s: Albert Suerbeer was a German churchman who became the first archbishop of Riga. Earlier archbishop of Armagh in Ireland and papal legate for the Baltic lands and Russia, he took up the see of Riga, raised to an archbishopric in 1255, with authority over the bishoprics of…

areopagus.s: The Areopagus was the ancient council of Athens, named after the hill north-west of the Acropolis where it met. Composed of former archons, it originally had wide powers of oversight, but the reforms of Ephialtes in 462 BCE reduced it largely to a court for homicide and…

ageladas.s: Ageladas, also spelled Hageladas, was a Greek bronze sculptor of Argos active in the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE. He made statues of Olympic victors and of gods, among them a Zeus for the Messenians at Ithome.

argungu-fishing-festival.s: The Argungu Fishing Festival is an annual festival held at the Matan Fada river near Argungu in Kebbi State, north-western Nigeria. Begun in 1934 to mark the end of long hostility between the kingdom of Argungu and the Sokoto Caliphate, it culminates in a contest in which…

arjuna.s: Arjuna is a hero of the Indian epic Mahabharata, the third of the five Pandava brothers and a peerless archer. His dialogue with his charioteer Krishna before the battle of Kurukshetra forms the Bhagavad Gita.

ayas-cilicia.s: Ayas, the Laiazzo of Italian merchants, is a port on the Gulf of İskenderun in southern Turkey, now the town of Yumurtalık. In the 13th and 14th centuries it was the chief harbour of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, where Venetian and Genoese traders bought silk and spices…

anazarbus.s: Anazarbus was an ancient city of Cilicia in southern Turkey, near the Ceyhan river. Favoured by the Romans, it became the metropolis of the province of Cilicia Secunda, and in the 12th century it served as an early capital of the Rubenid Armenian lords.

alexander-tamanian.s: Alexander Tamanian was an Armenian architect trained in St Petersburg, where he worked before the Russian Revolution. Moving to Yerevan in 1923, he drew up the master plan of the modern city, with its circular and radial layout, and designed landmarks such as the Opera and…

abam.s: The Abam are an Igbo clan of modern Abia State in south-eastern Nigeria. Renowned as warriors, they served the Aro Confederacy as mercenaries in the 18th and 19th centuries, raiding communities that defied Aro authority and helping to supply captives for the slave trade.

anglo-aro-war.s: The Anglo-Aro War was a British military campaign of 1901–1902 against the Aro Confederacy in south-eastern Nigeria. Aiming to end Aro power, the slave trade and the influence of the Aro oracle, the Long Juju, columns of the Southern Nigeria Regiment advanced on Arochukwu,…

arno.s: The Arno is the chief river of Tuscany in central Italy, flowing about 240 kilometres from the Apennines past Arezzo, Florence and Pisa to the Ligurian Sea. Its valley linked Etruscan cities and later carried the trade of Florence, and its floods, notably that of 1966, have…

artuq-ibn-ekseb.s: Artuq ibn Ekseb was a Turkmen commander in the service of the Seljuks in the late 11th century. He fought in Anatolia, Syria and Mesopotamia and was appointed governor of Jerusalem by the Seljuk prince Tutush around 1086.

apasa.s: Apasa was the capital of the Bronze Age kingdom of Arzawa in western Anatolia, known from Hittite texts. It is generally identified with the site of later Ephesus, near modern Selçuk, where remains of a Late Bronze Age settlement have been found on the hill of Ayasuluk.

ark-of-the-covenant.s: The Ark of the Covenant is, in the Hebrew Bible, a gilded wooden chest holding the tablets of the Law given to Moses. Carried before the Israelites, it was captured by the Philistines and placed in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod before being returned, and David brought it to…

astrakhan.s: Astrakhan is a city on the Volga delta near the Caspian Sea, in southern Russia. Its predecessor, Hajji Tarkhan or Xacitarxan, was a trading town of the Golden Horde and from the 15th century the capital of the Astrakhan Khanate.

astorga.s: Astorga is a town in the province of León in north-western Spain. It grew from Asturica Augusta, a Roman foundation of the reign of Augustus that became the administrative centre of the gold-mining district of the north-west.

asturias.s: Asturias is an autonomous community and historic region on the Bay of Biscay coast of northern Spain, separated from the Meseta by the Cantabrian Mountains. It takes its name from the Astures, the last Iberian peoples conquered by Rome.

aeschylus.s: Aeschylus was an Athenian tragic playwright, often called the father of tragedy, who lived from about 525 to 456 BCE. He fought at Marathon and is credited with adding a second actor to the stage.

arras.s: Arras is a city in the Pas-de-Calais department of northern France and the historic capital of Artois. It began as Nemetocenna, the chief town of the Gallic Atrebates, whose name survives in Arras and Artois.

aluksne.s: Alūksne is a town in north-eastern Latvia, near the borders with Estonia and Russia, on the shore of Lake Alūksne. It lay in the land of Atzele, inhabited by Latgalians and known to Rus' sources.

aulerci.s: The Aulerci were a group of related Gallic peoples in north-western Gaul, named by Julius Caesar. Their branches were the Cenomani around Le Mans, the Diablintes around Jublains and the Eburovices around Évreux, with a fourth, the Brannovices, mentioned once.

aundh-experiment.s: The Aundh Experiment was a trial of village self-government in the princely state of Aundh, in western India, launched in 1938 by its ruler Bhawanrao Pant Pratinidhi. On the advice of Mahatma Gandhi, the raja handed most powers to elected village panchayats and a state…

auch.s: Auch is a town in Gascony, south-western France, and the capital of the Gers department. Called Elimberris by the Aquitanian Ausci and Augusta Auscorum by the Romans, it became the seat of the archbishops of Gascony in the early Middle Ages.

afar-triangle.s: The Afar Triangle is a lowland region in the Horn of Africa where Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti meet. It lies at the junction of three tectonic rifts and contains some of the lowest and hottest places on Earth, including the Danakil Depression.

alimirah-hanfare.s: Alimirah Hanfare was Sultan of Aussa, the traditional leader of the Afar people of Ethiopia, from 1944 until his death in 2011. He resisted the Derg military government after 1975 and went into exile in Saudi Arabia, while the Afar Liberation Front, led by his family, fought…

ardiaei.s: The Ardiaei were an Illyrian people of the eastern Adriatic, living around the Neretva valley in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. Their kings Agron and his widow Teuta built a powerful state whose piracy provoked the First Illyrian War with Rome in 229 BCE.

asaf-ud-daula.s: Asaf-ud-Daula was Nawab of Awadh from 1775 until his death in 1797. He moved the capital from Faizabad to Lucknow, which he transformed with monuments such as the Bara Imambara and the Rumi Darwaza, built partly as famine relief from 1784.

al-amjad-bahramshah.s: Al-Amjad Bahramshah was the Ayyubid emir of Baalbek from 1182 to 1230, son of Saladin's nephew Farrukh Shah. A minor prince who depended on the rulers of Damascus, he was known as a poet.

al-mansur-ibrahim.s: Al-Mansur Ibrahim was the Ayyubid emir of Homs from 1240 to 1246, son of al-Mujahid Shirkuh II. Allied with Damascus and the Crusaders against as-Salih Ayyub of Egypt, he commanded Syrian troops at La Forbie in 1244 and escaped the defeat.

al-awhad-ayyub.s: Al-Awhad Ayyub was an Ayyubid prince, son of al-Adil, who governed Mayyafariqin in Upper Mesopotamia for his father from about 1200. In 1207 he took Ahlat from the Shah-Armens, extending Ayyubid rule to Lake Van, and held it against Georgian attacks.

al-masud-yusuf.s: Al-Mas'ud Yusuf was the last Ayyubid ruler of Yemen, from 1215 to 1229, and a son of the Egyptian sultan al-Kamil. He also extended his authority to Mecca.

andaman-and-nicobar-islands.s: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are an archipelago in the Bay of Bengal, a union territory of India with its capital at Port Blair. The British established a penal colony there after 1857, later including the Cellular Jail.

azai-hisamasa.s: Azai Hisamasa was a Japanese daimyo of northern Ōmi province, son of Azai Sukemasa and father of Azai Nagamasa. Weaker than his father, he largely submitted to the Rokkaku clan of southern Ōmi until retainers forced him to retire in favour of Nagamasa in 1560.

azai-nagamasa.s: Azai Nagamasa was a Japanese daimyo of northern Ōmi province who led the Azai clan from 1560. He defeated the Rokkaku and married Oichi, sister of Oda Nobunaga, but in 1570 sided with the Asakura against Nobunaga.

ahmad-qavam.s: Ahmad Qavam, also known as Qavam os-Saltaneh, was an Iranian statesman who served five times as prime minister between 1921 and 1952. In 1946 he persuaded the Soviet Union to withdraw its troops from northern Iran by promising an oil concession, which the Majlis later…

ani.s: Ani is a ruined medieval city on the Turkish-Armenian border, near Kars. Made capital of Bagratid Armenia by Ashot III in 961, it grew into a great trading city known as 'the city of a thousand and one churches'.

ani-cathedral.s: Ani Cathedral is the ruined cathedral of the medieval Armenian capital Ani, in present-day eastern Turkey. Begun under King Smbat II in 989 and completed in 1001 under Gagik I by the architect Trdat, it is notable for pointed arches and clustered piers that anticipate features…

ashot-ii-of-armenia.s: Ashot II, called Yerkat, 'the Iron', was king of Bagratid Armenia from 914 to 929. Son of Smbat I, who had been executed by the Sajid emir Yusuf, he fought the Sajids and rival Armenian princes for years with Byzantine help and restored royal authority.

ayrarat.s: Ayrarat was a central province of historic Armenia, in the plain of the Aras river around Mount Ararat. It contained many of the kingdom's capitals, including Artashat, Vagharshapat and Dvin, and in the Bagratid period also Ani in its district of Shirak.

abaco-islands.s: The Abaco Islands are a chain of islands in the northern Bahamas, made up of Great Abaco, Little Abaco and many smaller cays. They were settled largely by Loyalists from the United States after the American War of Independence, and Marsh Harbour is their main town.

amadiya.s: Amadiya, or Amedi, is an ancient town in the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq, built on a flat-topped rock plateau rising sheer above a mountain valley near the Turkish border. From the late Middle Ages it was the capital of the Kurdish emirate of Bahdinan, known for its…

absheron-peninsula.s: The Absheron Peninsula is a peninsula in eastern Azerbaijan that juts some 60 kilometres into the Caspian Sea, with the capital Baku on its southern coast. Its oil seeps and wells were exploited from the Middle Ages, and in the late 19th century it became one of the world's…

austro-turkish-war-1716-1718.s: The Austro-Turkish War of 1716 to 1718 was fought between the Habsburg monarchy and the Ottoman Empire, which Austria entered in support of Venice, then at war with the Ottomans. Prince Eugene of Savoy won a decisive victory at Petrovaradin in 1716, took Temeswar the same year…

andhra-state.s: Andhra State was a state of India formed on 1 October 1953 from the Telugu-speaking northern districts of Madras State, with its capital at Kurnool. It was the first Indian state created on linguistic lines, after the death of Potti Sriramulu during a hunger strike for it in…

awami-league.s: The Awami League is a political party of Bangladesh, founded in Dhaka in 1949 as a rival to the Muslim League in East Pakistan. Under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman it campaigned for Bengali autonomy, won the 1970 general election and led the independence struggle of 1971.

al-amin.s: Al-Amin was the sixth Abbasid caliph, a son of Harun al-Rashid, who reigned from 809 to 813. His attempt to exclude his half-brother al-Ma'mun, governor of Khurasan, from the succession led to a civil war, the Fourth Fitna.

abu-rakwa.s: Abu Rakwa was an Umayyad pretender who led a major revolt against the Fatimid Caliphate from 1004 to 1006. Claiming descent from the Umayyad caliphs of Córdoba, he won over Berber and Arab tribes in Cyrenaica and defeated Fatimid armies before advancing into Egypt.

ahmad-shah-bahadur.s: Ahmad Shah Bahadur was Mughal emperor from 1748 to 1754, the son of Muhammad Shah. His reign saw the empire lose the Punjab to Ahmad Shah Durrani and suffer raids by the Marathas, while power at court lay with ministers and his mother.

alamgir-ii.s: Alamgir II was Mughal emperor from 1754 to 1759, a son of Jahandar Shah placed on the throne by the vizier Ghazi-ud-din Khan Imad-ul-Mulk. He held little real power, as Ahmad Shah Durrani sacked Delhi in 1757 and the Marathas and the vizier competed for control.

arcesilaus-ii.s: Arcesilaus II, called 'the Harsh', was the fourth king of the Battiad dynasty of Cyrene in Libya in the mid-6th century BCE. According to Herodotus, a quarrel with his brothers led them to leave Cyrene and found the city of Barca inland.

arcesilaus-iii.s: Arcesilaus III was a Battiad king of Cyrene in the later 6th century BCE, son of Battus III and Pheretime. He tried to restore the royal powers curbed by the reforms of Demonax, was driven into exile, returned with mercenaries from Samos and submitted to the Persian king…

aryandes.s: Aryandes was the Persian satrap of Egypt under Cambyses II and Darius I in the late 6th century BCE. At the request of Pheretime of Cyrene he sent an army and fleet against Barca, which fell around 515 BCE after a long siege, and many of its people were deported to Bactria.

al-marj.s: Al-Marj is a town in Cyrenaica, north-eastern Libya, on a fertile upland plain inland from the Mediterranean coast. It stands near the site of the ancient Greek city of Barca and was known as Barce under Italian rule.

aelia-capitolina.s: Aelia Capitolina was the Roman colony founded by the emperor Hadrian on the ruins of Jerusalem around 130 CE, with a temple to Jupiter Capitolinus. The plan is often seen as a cause of the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132–135, after which Jews were barred from the city.

alpheios.s: The Alpheios is the longest river of the Peloponnese in Greece, flowing about 110 km from the mountains of Arcadia westwards through Elis, past ancient Olympia, to the Ionian Sea. In Greek myth it was a river god who pursued the nymph Arethusa.

alexander-kolchak.s: Alexander Kolchak was a Russian admiral and polar explorer who commanded the Black Sea Fleet in the First World War. In November 1918 he seized power in Omsk and became Supreme Ruler of the White movement during the Russian Civil War.

almeria.s: Almería is a port city in south-eastern Andalusia, Spain, and capital of the province of the same name. It grew into a great port and naval base under the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba, which built its Alcazaba in the 10th century, and later became the capital of a taifa kingdom.

amol.s: Amol is a city in Mazandaran province, northern Iran, on the Haraz river near the Caspian coast. In the early Islamic centuries it was the chief city of Tabaristan, ruled in turn by local dynasties such as the Bavandids, the Alids and the Marashis.

anak-wungsu.s: Anak Wungsu was a king of Bali of the Warmadewa dynasty in the 11th century, the youngest son of King Udayana and Queen Mahendradatta and a younger brother of Airlangga of Java. He left many inscriptions across the island.

ammunira.s: Ammunira was the ruler of Beirut in the mid-14th century BCE, a vassal of the Egyptian pharaoh. He is known from his letters in the Amarna archive, in which he promised loyalty, reported on events in the region and sheltered Rib-Hadda of Byblos when that king was driven from…

awadh.s: Awadh, or Oudh, is a region of north-central Uttar Pradesh in India, between the Ganges and the Himalayan foothills. From the 1720s it was ruled by the Nawabs of Awadh, first as Mughal governors and then as near-independent rulers, from Faizabad and later Lucknow.

adina-mosque.s: The Adina Mosque is a ruined mosque at Pandua in the Malda district of West Bengal, India, built by Sultan Sikandar Shah of the Bengal Sultanate and completed in the 1370s. Built of brick and stone with a vast courtyard surrounded by domed aisles, it was among the largest…

achalpur.s: Achalpur, historically Ellichpur, is a town in the Amravati district of Maharashtra, India. It was the capital of Berar under the Bahmani Sultanate and the Imad Shahi sultans of Berar, who ruled from it and the nearby fortress of Gawilgarh, and it remained the seat of the…

areopolis.s: Areopolis, formerly Tsimova, is a village in the Mani peninsula of the southern Peloponnese, Greece, and was the seat of the Mavromichalis family. On 17 March 1821 Petrobey Mavromichalis raised the flag of revolt there, one of the first acts of the Greek War of Independence;…

aizpute.s: Aizpute, in German Hasenpoth, is a small town in the Kurzeme region of western Latvia. In the Middle Ages it held the cathedral of the Bishopric of Courland, and after 1559 it lay in the bishop's former lands, later the District of Pilten.

ahuni.s: Ahuni was the king of Bit-Adini, an Aramaean state on the Euphrates in northern Syria, in the 9th century BCE. He resisted the Assyrian kings Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III with the help of Carchemish and other Syrian kingdoms.

ashur-nirari-v.s: Ashur-nirari V was king of Assyria from 755 to 745 BCE, at a low point of Assyrian power, when provincial governors were largely independent. His treaty with Mati'ilu of Arpad, preserved on a clay tablet, is an important example of an Assyrian vassal treaty.

attar-shumki-i.s: Attar-shumki I was king of Arpad, the Aramaean state of Bit-Agusi in northern Syria, around 800 BCE. He led a coalition of north Syrian kings against the Assyrian king Adad-nirari III, which was defeated.

adad-nirari-ii.s: Adad-nirari II was king of Assyria from 911 to 891 BCE and is counted as the first king of the Neo-Assyrian period. He campaigned against the Aramaean states of upper Mesopotamia, collecting tribute from rulers along the Khabur, and fought Babylonia, recovering territory and…

ambigatus.s: Ambigatus was a legendary king of the Bituriges in Gaul, known from the Roman historian Livy. Livy says that in the time of Tarquinius Priscus his people held supremacy among the Celts, and that, as Gaul grew overpopulated, he sent his nephews Bellovesus and Segovesus to lead…

avaricum.s: Avaricum was the chief oppidum of the Bituriges Cubi in Gaul, on the site of modern Bourges. Protected by marshes and a timber-laced murus gallicus rampart, it was one of the largest and richest towns of Gaul.

aude-river.s: The Aude is a river in southern France, about 224 km long. It rises in the eastern Pyrenees and flows north through Quillan and Limoux to Carcassonne, then east to the Mediterranean near Narbonne.

ausonius.s: Decimus Magnus Ausonius was a Latin poet and teacher from Burdigala, modern Bordeaux. After decades teaching rhetoric there, he became tutor to the future emperor Gratian, under whom he held high office and was consul in 379.

anseung.s: Anseung was a member of the Goguryeo royal family whom Silla recognised as king of Goguryeo in 670, after the fall of Goguryeo to Silla and Tang China. Silla settled him and his followers at Geummajeo, modern Iksan, where his state was later called Bodeok.

andriamandisoarivo.s: Andriamandisoarivo was a Sakalava king of the Maroserana dynasty of Menabe in western Madagascar. Around 1690 he led his followers north and founded the kingdom of Boina on the north-west coast, taking control of the trading towns of the Antalaotra.

antalaotra.s: The Antalaotra were Muslim, Swahili-speaking merchant communities of north-western Madagascar, of mixed East African, Arab and Malagasy descent. From towns such as Mahajanga they traded with East Africa, Arabia and India, dealing in slaves, cattle and cloth.

arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington.s: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was a British general and statesman. After campaigns in India, he commanded the British and Portuguese armies in the Peninsular War from 1808, driving the French out of Portugal and Spain by 1814.

abubakar-garbai.s: Abubakar Garbai was Shehu of Borno from 1902 to 1922. After the fall of Rabih az-Zubayr he was installed by the British as ruler of the British part of Borno, and in 1907 he founded a new capital at Yerwa, which grew into the city of Maiduguri.

aspurgus.s: Aspurgus was king of the Bosporan Kingdom in the early 1st century CE, until his death in 37 or 38 CE. A client of Rome, he received Roman citizenship and founded the line of kings who took the names Tiberius Julius and ruled the kingdom for the next three centuries.

archaeanactids.s: The Archaeanactids were the first known ruling dynasty of the Bosporan Kingdom, governing the Greek cities around the Cimmerian Bosporus from Panticapaeum from about 480 BCE until 438 BCE, according to Diodorus. Little is known about them beyond their name; they were succeeded…

ahanta-people.s: The Ahanta are an Akan people of the western coast of Ghana, between the Ankobra River and Takoradi. From the 17th century their coast was lined with European trading forts, including the Brandenburg post of Gross Friedrichsburg and Dutch forts, and Ahanta rulers signed…

all-india-muslim-league.s: The All-India Muslim League was a political party founded at Dhaka in 1906 to represent the interests of Muslims in British India. Under Muhammad Ali Jinnah it adopted the Lahore Resolution of 1940 calling for separate Muslim states, and its success in the 1946 elections led…

anti-fascist-peoples-freedom-league.s: The Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League was a Burmese nationalist coalition formed during the Second World War and led by Aung San. It turned against the Japanese in 1945, negotiated independence with Britain after the war and governed the Union of Burma from 1948 under U Nu,…

adamawa-emirate.s: The Adamawa Emirate was a Fulani state founded around 1809 by Modibbo Adama during the jihad of Usman dan Fodio, as part of the Sokoto Caliphate. Centred on Yola on the Benue River, it expanded over the highlands of what are now north-eastern Nigeria and northern Cameroon.

anagarika-dharmapala.s: Anagarika Dharmapala was a Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer and a leader of the Buddhist revival in British Ceylon. In 1891 he founded the Maha Bodhi Society to restore the Buddhist site of Bodh Gaya, and he spread Buddhism abroad and promoted a Sinhalese Buddhist identity that…

aapravasi-ghat.s: Aapravasi Ghat is the former immigration depot in Port Louis, Mauritius, where indentured labourers arriving from India were received from 1849 until the early 20th century. Nearly half a million workers passed through Mauritius under the indenture system after the abolition…

adrian-pelt.s: Adrian Pelt was a Dutch journalist and international civil servant who served as United Nations Commissioner in Libya from 1950 to 1951. He guided the drafting of a federal constitution and the creation of the government that led Libya to independence as the United Kingdom of…

anegada.s: Anegada is the northernmost of the British Virgin Islands, a flat island of coral and limestone unlike the volcanic islands of the group. It is surrounded by the Horseshoe Reef, one of the largest barrier reefs in the Caribbean, which has wrecked hundreds of ships.

ashura.s: Ashura is the tenth day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. For Shia Muslims it is the day of mourning for the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, at the Battle of Karbala in 680, marked by processions, sermons and passion plays.

al-sahib-ibn-abbad.s: Al-Sahib ibn Abbad was a Persian statesman and man of letters, vizier to the Buyid rulers Mu'ayyad al-Dawla and Fakhr al-Dawla at Ray and Isfahan from 976 until his death in 995. A pupil of Ibn al-Amid, he gathered poets and scholars at his court and owned a famous library.

ahiram.s: Ahiram was a king of Byblos, known from his stone sarcophagus found in the city's royal necropolis in 1923. The sarcophagus, made for him by his son Ittobaal and usually dated to around 1000 BCE, bears one of the oldest substantial inscriptions in the Phoenician alphabet,…

agila-i.s: Agila I was king of the Visigoths in Hispania from 549 to 554. A defeat at Córdoba early in his reign and his harsh rule provoked the revolt of the noble Athanagild, who called on the Byzantine emperor Justinian for help.

athanagild.s: Athanagild was king of the Visigoths from 554 to 567. He rebelled against King Agila I and sought help from the Byzantine emperor Justinian, whose forces then seized a coastal strip of south-eastern Hispania.

agno-river.s: The Agno is a river of northern Luzon in the Philippines, rising in the Cordillera Central of Benguet and flowing south and then west across the plain of Pangasinan into the Lingayen Gulf. Its floods deposit the fertile silt that makes the province a major rice-growing area.

agoo.s: Agoo is a town in La Union province on the Lingayen Gulf in northern Luzon, Philippines. Before and during early Spanish rule it was a trading port visited by Japanese and Chinese merchants, so that the Spanish called it Puerto de Japón.

andres-malong.s: Andrés Malong was a Pangasinan chief from Binalatongan who led a revolt against Spanish rule in 1660–1661. Proclaimed king of Pangasinan by his followers, he sought to spread the uprising to Ilocos and Pampanga, but Spanish forces sent by Governor-General Manrique de Lara…

agueybana-i.s: Agüeybaná I was the paramount cacique of the Taíno of Puerto Rico when the Spanish arrived, ruling the chiefdom of Guaynía on the island's south coast. He received Juan Ponce de León peacefully in 1508 and allowed Spanish settlement.

anacaona.s: Anacaona was a Taíno noblewoman and ruler of Jaragua in western Hispaniola, the wife of Caonabo of Maguana and sister of the cacique Bohechío, whom she succeeded. Celebrated as a poet and composer of areítos, the Taíno songs and dances, she received the Spanish with hospitality.

alonso-de-ojeda.s: Alonso de Ojeda was a Spanish explorer who sailed on Columbus's second voyage in 1493. On Hispaniola he captured the Taíno cacique Caonabo by a ruse in 1495.

alsium.s: Alsium was an ancient port town on the Tyrrhenian coast of Etruria, at modern Palo Laziale near Ladispoli, west of Rome. It served as one of the harbours of the Etruscan city of Caere and became a Roman citizen colony in 247 BCE.

assynt.s: Assynt is a mountainous district on the west coast of Sutherland in the north-west Highlands of Scotland, centred on the village of Lochinver. Its isolated peaks, such as Suilven, rise from some of the oldest rocks in Europe.

argentocoxus.s: Argentocoxus was a Caledonian chieftain in northern Britain around 210 CE, known only from the history of Cassius Dio. During peace talks after the campaigns of Septimius Severus, the empress Julia Domna jested about the free ways of British women, and Argentocoxus's wife…

al-hakam-ii.s: Al-Hakam II was the second Umayyad caliph of Córdoba, reigning from 961 to 976 after his father Abd al-Rahman III. A scholar and bibliophile, he assembled a library said to hold some 400,000 volumes and enlarged the Great Mosque of Córdoba with a richly decorated mihrab.

alids.s: The Alids are the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, especially through his sons Hasan and Husayn. Many Muslims, above all the Shia, regarded them as the rightful leaders of the community, and Alid claimants led revolts against the…

al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf.s: Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf was an Umayyad general and governor, the most powerful servant of the caliphs Abd al-Malik and al-Walid I. He besieged Mecca in 692, ending the caliphate of Ibn al-Zubayr, and then governed Iraq and the east from 694 until his death in 714, crushing the…

al-mukhtar-al-thaqafi.s: Al-Mukhtar al-Thaqafi was an Arab revolutionary who seized Kufa in 685 in the name of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, a son of Ali, during the Second Fitna. He took revenge on the killers of Husayn and won support from non-Arab converts, the mawali.

anand-district.s: Anand is a district of central Gujarat, India, formed in 1997 from part of Kheda district, with its headquarters at the town of Anand. The town is famous as the home of the Amul dairy co-operative, which grew from 1946 into the centre of India's White Revolution.

atahualpa.s: Atahualpa was the last Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire before the Spanish conquest. A son of Huayna Capac, he defeated his half-brother Huáscar in the civil war of 1529–1532, but in November 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured him at Cajamarca.

azuay-province.s: Azuay is a province in the southern highlands of Ecuador, with its capital at Cuenca. Its valleys were the heartland of the Cañari people, and the Inca city of Tomebamba was built there in the 15th century.

altdorf-uri.s: Altdorf is the capital of the Swiss canton of Uri, near the southern end of Lake Lucerne on the road to the Gotthard Pass. It is the setting of the legend of William Tell, who was said to have shot an apple from his son's head in its square.

ageri.s: Ägeri is a valley in the Swiss canton of Zug around Lake Ägeri, with the municipalities of Oberägeri and Unterägeri. It was one of the three rural communes, with Menzingen and Baar, that shared government of the old canton of Zug with the town.

antigua-guatemala.s: Antigua Guatemala is a city in the central highlands of Guatemala, founded in 1543 as Santiago de los Caballeros after the destruction of the previous capital. For over two centuries it was the capital of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, rich in churches and convents.

aleijadinho.s: Aleijadinho, born Antônio Francisco Lisboa, was a sculptor and architect of colonial Minas Gerais and the leading artist of the Brazilian Baroque. The son of a Portuguese architect and an enslaved African woman, he worked on churches in Ouro Preto and other mining towns.

aimore.s: The Aimoré were Macro-Jê-speaking peoples of the Atlantic forest of eastern Brazil, in southern Bahia, Espírito Santo and Minas Gerais, later called Botocudos by the Portuguese for their lip and ear plugs. From the mid-16th century their raids devastated the captaincies of…

aspero.s: Áspero is an archaeological site at the mouth of the Supe valley on the coast of Peru, one of the earliest monumental centres of the Americas. Its platform mounds, such as the Huaca de los Ídolos, date from about 3000 BCE.

allectus.s: Allectus was a Roman usurper who ruled Britain from 293 to 296. A finance official under the breakaway emperor Carausius, he murdered him in 293, after Constantius Chlorus had taken Boulogne, and took power.

arcot.s: Arcot is a town on the Palar river in Tamil Nadu, southern India, which became the capital of the Nawabs of the Carnatic under Mughal rule. During the Carnatic Wars, Robert Clive seized it in 1751 and held it through a long siege by forces of Chanda Sahib and the French,…

avignon.s: Avignon is a city on the Rhône in Provence, southern France, the Avennio of the Cavares and of Roman Gaul. The popes resided there from 1309 to 1377, building the vast Palace of the Popes, and Pope Clement VI bought the city in 1348; it remained papal territory until France…

adomnan.s: Adomnán (c. 624–704) was abbot of Iona from 679 and the biographer of its founder, Columba.

aethelfrith-of-northumbria.s: Æthelfrith was king of Bernicia from about 593 and, from about 604, also of Deira, uniting them as the first ruler of Northumbria. He defeated Áedán mac Gabráin of Dál Riata at Degsastan in 603 and the Britons at Chester around 615, but was killed by Rædwald of East Anglia at…

aime-savoie.s: Aime is a town in the Tarentaise valley of Savoie, south-eastern France. As Axima it was the chief town of the Ceutrones, and under the emperor Claudius it became Forum Claudii Ceutronum, capital of the small Roman province of Alpes Graiae.

alpes-graiae.s: Alpes Graiae was a small province of the Roman Empire in the western Alps, covering the Tarentaise valley in modern Savoie and the approaches to the Little St Bernard Pass. Organised in the 1st century CE, probably under Claudius, it was governed by an equestrian procurator…

aosta-valley.s: The Aosta Valley is a mountainous region of north-western Italy, bordering France and Switzerland and drained by the Dora Baltea. Its passes, the Great and Little St Bernard, made it a key route across the western Alps; the Salassi held it until Rome conquered them in 25 BCE…

aosta.s: Aosta is the capital of the Aosta Valley in north-western Italy. It was founded in 25 BCE as the Roman colony of Augusta Praetoria Salassorum after the conquest of the Salassi, and preserves its Roman street grid, walls, theatre and the Arch of Augustus.

amazonas-region.s: Amazonas is a region of northern Peru on the eastern slopes of the Andes, crossed by the Marañón and Utcubamba rivers, with its capital at Chachapoyas. Its cloud forests were the home of the Chachapoya culture, whose walled site of Kuélap, the sarcophagi of Karajía and the…

alhana.s: Alhana was a Chahamana king of Naddula (Nadol) in Rajasthan in the mid-12th century, ruling as a feudatory of the Chaulukyas of Gujarat. He served in the campaigns of the Chaulukya king Kumarapala, and his inscriptions show patronage of both Shaiva and Jain religion.

ajayaraja-ii.s: Ajayaraja II was a king of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari in the early 12th century who founded the city of Ajmer, then called Ajayameru, around 1113 and made it the dynasty's capital. He fought the Paramaras of Malwa and is credited with repelling Ghaznavid raids.

ajmer.s: Ajmer is a city in central Rajasthan, India, among the Aravalli hills. Founded as Ajayameru by the Chahamana king Ajayaraja II in the early 12th century, it was the capital of Prithviraj Chauhan before the Ghurid conquest of 1192.

ana-sagar-lake.s: Ana Sagar is an artificial lake in Ajmer, Rajasthan, India, created in the mid-12th century by the Chahamana king Arnoraja, also called Anaji, after whom it is named, by damming a stream in the Aravalli hills. The Mughal emperor Jahangir laid out the Daulat Bagh gardens beside…

arnoraja.s: Arnoraja was king of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari in Rajasthan from about 1135 to 1150, ruling from Ajmer. He defeated Turkish raiders near Ajmer, fought the Chaulukyas of Gujarat, and built the Ana Sagar lake.

amyntas-iii-of-macedon.s: Amyntas III was king of Macedon from about 393 to 370 BCE and father of Philip II. His reign was beset by Illyrian invasions and rival claimants, and the Chalcidian League led by Olynthus seized much of his kingdom, including Pella, until Sparta intervened and broke the league…

amecameca.s: Amecameca is a town in the State of Mexico, at the foot of the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl. As Amaquemecan it was one of the leading altepetl of the Chalca confederation before the Aztec conquest of Chalco in the 15th century.

aihole.s: Aihole is a village in Bagalkot district of Karnataka, India, with more than a hundred temples built from the 5th to the 12th century, many under the Chalukyas of Badami. Its Meguti temple bears the Aihole inscription of 634, composed by the poet Ravikirti in praise of…

adipurana-pampa.s: The Adipurana is a Kannada epic poem by Pampa, completed in 941, telling the life of Rishabhanatha, the first Jain tirthankara. Written in the champu style mixing verse and prose, it is a founding classic of Kannada literature.

adikavi-pampa.s: Pampa, called Adikavi or 'first poet', was a 10th-century Kannada poet at the court of the Vemulavada Chalukya king Arikesari II. His two epics, the Jain Adipurana and the Vikramarjuna Vijaya, a version of the Mahabharata in which Arikesari is cast as Arjuna, were both…

ajaigarh.s: Ajaigarh is a hill fort and town in Panna district of Madhya Pradesh, India, on a flat-topped hill above the Ken river. It was one of the great strongholds of the Chandela dynasty, which held out there after losing Kalinjar in 1203, and contains Chandela temples and inscriptions.

andahuaylas.s: Andahuaylas is a town in the Apurímac region of the southern Peruvian Andes, west of Cusco on the old route to Ayacucho. Before the Incas it was the heart of the Chanka confederation, whose attack on Cusco around 1438, by Inca tradition, prompted the rise of Pachacuti.

apurimac-region.s: Apurímac is a region of the southern Peruvian Andes, with its capital at Abancay, named after the Apurímac river, whose deep canyon crosses it. Its highlands were the home of the Chanka confederation before the Inca conquest in the 15th century.

ancash-region.s: Áncash is a region of north-central Peru, stretching from the Pacific coast to the Cordillera Blanca, whose peak Huascarán is the highest in the country. Its highland valleys were home to the Chavín culture, centred on Chavín de Huántar, and later to the Recuay culture.

alonso-davila.s: Alonso Dávila, or Alonso de Ávila, was a Spanish conquistador who served under Hernán Cortés in the conquest of Mexico and then under Francisco de Montejo in the conquest of Yucatán. In 1531 he led an expedition into the Maya province of Chetumal and founded a settlement…

ardahan.s: Ardahan is a city in north-eastern Turkey, the capital of Ardahan Province, on the upper Kura river near the Georgian border. Long held by Georgian rulers and then by the Ottoman Empire, it was taken by Russia in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78.

artvin.s: Artvin is a city in north-eastern Turkey, the capital of Artvin Province, on the Çoruh river near the Black Sea and the Georgian border. Part of the medieval Georgian lands of Tao-Klarjeti, it passed to the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century and was annexed by Russia in 1878.

adyghe-khabze.s: Adyghe Khabze is the traditional unwritten code of conduct and customary law of the Circassians. It governs hospitality, honour, respect for elders, the duties between social ranks, relations between men and women, and behaviour in war and in assemblies.

assam.s: Assam is a state of north-eastern India centred on the Brahmaputra and Barak valleys, with its capital at Dispur in Guwahati. Ruled by the Ahom kingdom for about six centuries from the 13th, it was overrun by Burma in 1817–26 and ceded to the British East India Company by the…

arunachal-pradesh.s: Arunachal Pradesh is the north-easternmost state of India, in the eastern Himalayas, bordering Bhutan, China and Myanmar, with its capital at Itanagar. Home to many tribal peoples such as the Adi, Nyishi and Monpa, it was administered by the British as the North-East Frontier…

associates-of-the-swiss-confederacy.s: The Associates of the Swiss Confederacy, in German zugewandte Orte, were territories allied to the Old Swiss Confederacy without being full member cantons. They included the Abbey and City of St.

anaxagoras.s: Anaxagoras was a Greek philosopher from Clazomenae in Ionia who brought philosophy to Athens, where he lived for about 30 years in the circle of Pericles. He taught that Mind (nous) set the cosmos in order and that the Sun was a fiery stone, which led to a charge of impiety.

aba-womens-war.s: The Aba Women's War was a revolt by thousands of Igbo and Ibibio women in south-eastern Nigeria in November and December 1929. Sparked by fears that women would be taxed, it targeted the warrant chiefs appointed under British indirect rule; women gathered to 'sit on' chiefs…

ahmadu-bello.s: Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, was a Nigerian politician and leader of the Northern People's Congress. A descendant of Usman dan Fodio, he became the first premier of Northern Nigeria in 1954, held the post through independence in 1960 and pursued the modernisation and…

aden-trades-union-congress.s: The Aden Trades Union Congress was the federation of trade unions in the British colony of Aden, founded in 1956 amid the rapid growth of the port and the oil refinery. Led by Abdullah al-Asnag, it organised large strikes and became the base of Arab nationalist opposition to…

amor-de-cosmos.s: Amor De Cosmos, born William Alexander Smith in Nova Scotia, was a journalist and politician in British Columbia. He founded the newspaper British Colonist in Victoria in 1858 and campaigned for responsible government and for British Columbia to join Canada.

anthony-musgrave.s: Anthony Musgrave was a British colonial administrator born in Antigua who governed several colonies, including Newfoundland, British Columbia, Natal, South Australia, Jamaica and Queensland. As governor of British Columbia from 1869 he guided the colony's negotiations to join…

arthur-hamilton-gordon-1st-baron-stanmor.s: Arthur Hamilton-Gordon, 1st Baron Stanmore, was a British colonial governor and the youngest son of the prime minister Lord Aberdeen. As the first substantive governor of Fiji from 1875 to 1880 he ruled through the chiefs and a Great Council of Chiefs, protected Fijian land…

american-colonization-society.s: The American Colonization Society was an organisation founded in Washington in 1816 to settle free Black Americans in Africa. Its supporters ranged from opponents of slavery to slaveholders who wished to remove free Black people from the United States, and it was opposed by…

americo-liberians.s: Americo-Liberians are Liberians descended from the free and formerly enslaved African Americans who settled Liberia from 1822, together with Africans freed from slave ships. Although a small minority, they dominated the politics and economy of the country through the True Whig…

aime-cesaire.s: Aimé Césaire was a poet, playwright and politician from Martinique, one of the founders of the Négritude movement with Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon Damas. His Notebook of a Return to the Native Land (1939) and Discourse on Colonialism (1950) became classics of anti-colonial…

aboriginal-australians.s: Aboriginal Australians are the Indigenous peoples of mainland Australia and Tasmania, whose ancestors have lived on the continent for at least 50,000 years. They formed hundreds of nations with distinct languages, laws and ties to country.

auckland.s: Auckland is the largest city of New Zealand, on an isthmus between two harbours in the north of the North Island. Governor William Hobson chose the site as the colonial capital in 1840, and it remained the capital until Wellington replaced it in 1865.

annapolis-royal.s: Annapolis Royal is a town on the Annapolis Basin in western Nova Scotia, Canada. As Port-Royal it was the capital of French Acadia, and after a New England expedition captured it in 1710 it was renamed after Queen Anne.

anderson-dawson.s: Anderson Dawson was an Australian miner, trade unionist and politician who led the world's first parliamentary Labour government. As Premier of Queensland he held office for only one week, from 1 to 7 December 1899, before losing a vote in parliament.

anguilla.s: Anguilla is a low coral island in the northern Leeward Islands of the Caribbean and a British Overseas Territory. English settlers arrived from Saint Kitts in 1650, and in 1882 it was joined with Saint Kitts and Nevis in a single colony.

aboriginal-tasmanians.s: Aboriginal Tasmanians are the Indigenous people of Tasmania, isolated from the mainland when rising seas formed Bass Strait about 10,000 years ago. Numbering several thousand at British settlement in 1803, they were devastated by violence, disease and dispossession, especially…

andrew-inglis-clark.s: Andrew Inglis Clark was a Tasmanian lawyer, politician and judge, and a leading author of the Australian Constitution. As attorney-general of Tasmania he introduced the Hare–Clark system of proportional representation, and in 1891 he prepared a draft constitution that formed…

alfred-deakin.s: Alfred Deakin was an Australian lawyer and politician from Victoria, a leader of the federation movement and the second prime minister of Australia. He served three terms between 1903 and 1910 and shaped the early Commonwealth through protective tariffs, the arbitration system…

arizpe.s: Arizpe is a town in northern Sonora, Mexico, on the Sonora River, founded as a Jesuit mission in 1646. In 1776 it was made the seat of the Commandancy General of the Internal Provinces under Teodoro de Croix, briefly serving as the capital of Spain's northern frontier.

azzo-vii-deste.s: Azzo VII d'Este, called Novello, was marquis of Este and leader of the Guelph party in north-eastern Italy. With Venetian and papal help he drove the Ghibelline Salinguerra Torelli from Ferrara in 1240 and ruled the city as lord.

adda.s: The Adda is a river of Lombardy, northern Italy, about 313 km long, rising in the Alps, crossing the Valtellina and Lake Como and joining the Po near Cremona. For centuries it marked a frontier: between Milan and its eastern neighbours in the Middle Ages, and between the Duchy…

alberto-pitentino.s: Alberto Pitentino was a 12th-century engineer of Mantua who, around 1190, regulated the Mincio river with dams and embankments. His works created the four lakes that surrounded the city and protected it for centuries, and also powered mills and supported navigation.

albertino-mussato.s: Albertino Mussato was a Paduan statesman, historian and poet, an early figure of Italian humanism. His Latin tragedy Ecerinis, on the tyranny of Ezzelino III da Romano, written in the style of Seneca, warned Padua against Cangrande della Scala and earned him the poet's laurel…

assisi.s: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, central Italy, the birthplace of Saint Francis and Saint Clare. After Francis's death in 1226 the double Basilica of San Francesco was built and decorated with frescoes by Cimabue, Giotto and others, making the town one of Christianity's great…

alberico-da-romano.s: Alberico da Romano was lord of Treviso and brother of Ezzelino III da Romano, sharing in the family's domination of the March of Treviso. He ruled Treviso harshly for two decades.

alberico-i-cybo-malaspina.s: Alberico I Cybo-Malaspina was the ruler of Massa and Carrara, inheriting the Malaspina lands through his mother Ricciarda. He was made prince of Massa by the emperor in 1568 and ruled for nearly sixty years, rebuilding Massa with a new planned town centre and expanding the…

abraham-lincoln.s: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States, from 1861 until his assassination in 1865. His election as a Republican opposed to the expansion of slavery led Southern states to secede, and he led the Union through the Civil War.

army-of-northern-virginia.s: The Army of Northern Virginia was the main Confederate army in the eastern theatre of the American Civil War. Commanded by Robert E.

ariege-department.s: Ariège is a department of south-western France in the central Pyrenees, created in 1790 from the County of Foix and the Couserans, with its prefecture at Foix. Named after the river Ariège, it is mountainous and thinly populated, and its castles such as Montségur are…

ariege-river.s: The Ariège is a river of south-western France, about 163 km long, rising in the Pyrenees near the border with Andorra and flowing north past Foix and Pamiers to join the Garonne just south of Toulouse. The medieval County of Foix grew up around the castle above its valley.

alcoy.s: Alcoy is an industrial town in the province of Alicante in the Valencian Community, Spain, in a mountain valley of the Serpis river. Iberian settlements such as La Serreta stood nearby.

alicante.s: Alicante is a port city on the Mediterranean coast of south-eastern Spain, capital of the province of the same name in the Valencian Community. Near the Roman town of Lucentum, it was held by the Moors until 1248, when Castile took it, and passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1296.

albert-henry.s: Albert Henry was a Cook Islands politician, founder of the Cook Islands Party and the first premier from 1965, when the islands became self-governing in free association with New Zealand. In 1978 a court found that his party had flown in voters from New Zealand with public…

aitutaki.s: Aitutaki is an island in the southern Cook Islands, made up of a volcanic island and a ring of reef islets enclosing a large lagoon. Reached by William Bligh on the Bounty in 1789, it was the first of the Cook Islands to accept Christian missionaries, in 1821.

anglo-normans.s: The Anglo-Normans were the medieval descendants of the Normans who ruled England after the conquest of 1066, together with the French-speaking aristocracy they formed there. From 1169 Anglo-Norman lords, invited by the deposed Leinster king Diarmait Mac Murchada, invaded…

acrocorinth.s: Acrocorinth is the steep rock, about 575 metres high, that rises above ancient Corinth in southern Greece. It served as the city's acropolis, with a temple of Aphrodite on its summit, and as one of the strongest fortresses in Greece, controlling the Isthmus of Corinth.

an-account-of-corsica.s: An Account of Corsica is a book by the Scottish writer James Boswell, published in 1768, describing the island and his visit in 1765 to Pasquale Paoli, leader of the Corsican Republic. Its portrait of Paoli as a heroic patriot made him famous across Britain and Europe and won…

angouleme-cathedral.s: Angoulême Cathedral, dedicated to Saint Peter (Saint-Pierre), is the cathedral of Angoulême in western France. Rebuilt in the first half of the 12th century under Bishop Girard II, it is a leading example of the Romanesque churches of south-western France roofed with a row of…

aznar-galindez-i.s: Aznar Galíndez I was the first known count of Aragon, ruling the small county around Jaca in the central Pyrenees in the early 9th century under Frankish protection. Around 820 he was driven out by his son-in-law García the Bad, who was allied with the rulers of Pamplona, and…

adela-of-normandy.s: Adela of Normandy was a daughter of William the Conqueror who married Stephen-Henry, Count of Blois, and governed his lands while he was on the First Crusade and after his death in 1102. A patron of churches and poets, she was among the most capable rulers of her time.

adalulf-count-of-boulogne.s: Adalulf was count of Boulogne in the early 10th century, a younger son of Baldwin II of Flanders and Ælfthryth, daughter of Alfred the Great. He held Boulogne and Thérouanne from his father's death in 918 until his own in 933, and was also lay abbot of Saint-Bertin.

anthony-ii-count-of-delmenhorst.s: Anthony II was count of Delmenhorst, a younger son of Count Anthony I of Oldenburg. After a long dispute with his elder brother John VII of Oldenburg over the inheritance, he obtained Delmenhorst as a separate county, founding a branch line of the House of Oldenburg.

alfonso-ii-count-of-provence.s: Alfonso II was count of Provence from 1196 to 1209, a younger son of Alfonso II of Aragon, who left him the county. In 1193 he married Garsenda, granddaughter and heiress of William IV of Forcalquier, which reunited Forcalquier with Provence when William died in 1209.

aare.s: The Aare is the longest river lying entirely within Switzerland, flowing nearly 300 km from the Bernese Alps through Lake Brienz and Lake Thun, past Bern, Solothurn and Aarau, to join the Rhine at Koblenz on the German border. Duke Berthold V of Zähringen founded Bern on a…

aargau.s: The Aargau is a region of northern Switzerland on the lower Aare, Reuss and Limmat, today a canton with its capital at Aarau. It was the cradle of the Habsburg dynasty, whose ancestral castle stands near Brugg, until the Swiss Confederates, led by Bern, conquered it in 1415.

ashkelon.s: Ashkelon is a city on the Mediterranean coast of southern Israel and one of the oldest seaports of the Levant. A Philistine city in the Iron Age, it later flourished under Hellenistic, Roman and Islamic rule.

alexandra-feodorovna-alix-of-hesse.s: Alexandra Feodorovna (1872–1918), born Princess Alix of Hesse and by Rhine, was the last Empress of Russia as wife of Tsar Nicholas II. A granddaughter of Queen Victoria, she married Nicholas in 1894.

auxerre.s: Auxerre is a city in Burgundy, central France, on the Yonne, prefecture of the Yonne department. The Roman Autessiodurum, it became an important bishopric associated with Saint Germanus of Auxerre, whose abbey survives.

anton-gunther-count-of-oldenburg.s: Anton Günther was Count of Oldenburg from 1603 until his death in 1667, and from 1647 also of Delmenhorst. Through careful diplomacy and payments to commanders he kept his county out of the fighting of the Thirty Years' War, and he won the lucrative Weser toll at Elsfleth.

arnau-mir-de-tost.s: Arnau Mir de Tost was a Catalan frontier lord who led the conquest and resettlement of lands taken from the Muslim taifas in the 11th century. After capturing Àger in 1034 he built a large lordship around it, later the Viscounty of Àger, and founded the canonry of Sant Pere…

angouleme.s: Angoulême is a city in south-western France on a hill above the Charente, capital of the Charente department. From 866 it was the seat of counts descended from Vulgrin I, later the Taillefer line and the Lusignans, and it passed to the French crown in 1308.

amfissa.s: Amfissa is a town in Phocis, central Greece, below Mount Parnassus near Delphi. In the Middle Ages it was known as Salona, and from 1205 its castle on the ancient acropolis was the seat of a Frankish lordship, the County of Salona, held by the Autremencourt and Fadrique…

amadeus-vi-count-of-savoy.s: Amadeus VI, known as the Green Count from the colour he wore at tournaments, ruled Savoy from 1343 to 1383. He expanded his lands in Piedmont, Bresse and the Vaud and founded the Order of the Collar.

ainsa.s: Aínsa is a small town in the province of Huesca, Aragon, at the meeting of the Cinca and Ara rivers. Its walled medieval centre, castle and Romanesque church of Santa María stand on a hill above the rivers.

albi.s: Albi is a city on the Tarn in southern France, capital of the Tarn department. Its name was applied to the Cathars, called Albigensians, and to the crusade launched against them in 1209.

andreas-hofer.s: Andreas Hofer was a Tyrolean innkeeper who led the uprising of 1809 against Bavarian and French rule in Tyrol. His peasant militia won several battles at Bergisel near Innsbruck, and he governed Tyrol for some months, but after Austria made peace the revolt collapsed.

abraham-roentgen.s: Abraham Roentgen was a German cabinetmaker who set up a furniture workshop at Neuwied on the Rhine in 1750. Trained in the Netherlands and London, he made fine marquetry furniture with hidden mechanical fittings for princely clients.

achterhoek.s: The Achterhoek ('back corner') is a rural region in the east of the Dutch province of Gelderland, bordering Germany. Historically part of the County of Zutphen, it is a land of farms, woods and small towns such as Doetinchem, Winterswijk and Groenlo, and its fortified towns…

arnulf-de-montgomery.s: Arnulf de Montgomery was an Anglo-Norman nobleman, a younger son of Roger of Montgomery, Earl of Shrewsbury. During the Norman invasion of south-west Wales in 1093 he built the first castle at Pembroke, which held out against Welsh counter-attacks.

ardnamurchan.s: Ardnamurchan is a rugged peninsula in Lochaber, in the western Highlands of Scotland. Its tip, Ardnamurchan Point, is the most westerly point of the British mainland.

alcmaeon-of-croton.s: Alcmaeon of Croton was a Greek physician and natural philosopher of around 500 BCE, associated with the Pythagoreans. He is said to have carried out early dissections, identified the brain as the seat of thought and perception, and explained health as a balance of opposing…

aricia.s: Aricia was an ancient Latin town in the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, near modern Ariccia. Close to the sanctuary of Diana at Lake Nemi, it was a meeting place of the Latin League.

aristodemus-of-cumae.s: Aristodemus, called Malakos, was tyrant of Cumae in Campania in the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE. After defeating the Etruscans at Aricia around 504 BCE, he seized power at Cumae with popular support, gave refuge to the exiled Roman king Tarquinius Superbus, and was…

apuole.s: Apuolė is a hillfort in north-western Lithuania, in the historical land of the Curonians. Rimbert's Life of Ansgar records that the Swedish king Olof besieged the fortified town of Apulia there in 854 and forced its defenders to pay tribute, making it the earliest place in…

aina-mahal.s: The Aina Mahal ('hall of mirrors') is an 18th-century palace in Bhuj, Gujarat, India, built for Rao Lakhpatji of Cutch. It was designed by Ramsinh Malam, a local craftsman who had learned European crafts during years abroad, and is known for its mirrored hall, Venetian glass…

acajutla.s: Acajutla is a port town on the Pacific coast of western El Salvador and the country's main seaport. In June 1524 the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Alvarado fought the Pipil there in the first major battle of the Spanish conquest of El Salvador; Alvarado won but was badly…

antiguo-cuscatlan.s: Antiguo Cuscatlán is a city in the La Libertad department of El Salvador, on the south-western edge of the capital, San Salvador. It takes its name from Cuzcatlan, the most powerful lordship of the Pipil before the Spanish conquest, whose centre lay nearby.

aliaga.s: Aliağa is a town and district on the Aegean coast of İzmir Province, western Turkey. It lies near the ruins of ancient Cyme, the leading city of Aeolis, and today is a centre of heavy industry, with an oil refinery, a petrochemical complex and one of the world's largest…

alentejo.s: The Alentejo is a region of southern Portugal between the Tagus and the Algarve, a land of plains, cork oaks, olive groves and wheat fields. Inhabited in antiquity by peoples such as the Cynetes and Celtici, it was part of Roman Lusitania and later of al-Andalus, and was taken…

alcibiades.s: Alcibiades was an Athenian statesman and general and an associate of Socrates. He promoted the Sicilian Expedition of 415 BCE, deserted to Sparta when accused of sacrilege, and later returned to lead the Athenian fleet to victories such as Cyzicus in 410 BCE.

alexander-dubcek.s: Alexander Dubček was a Slovak politician who became first secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia in January 1968. His Prague Spring reforms, promising 'socialism with a human face', eased censorship and encouraged open debate until the Warsaw Pact invasion of…

ards-peninsula.s: The Ards Peninsula is a low, fertile peninsula in County Down, Northern Ireland, between Strangford Lough and the Irish Sea. In the early Middle Ages it belonged to the lands of the Dál Fiatach, and it later passed to the Anglo-Normans and, in the early 17th century, to…

ayrshire.s: Ayrshire is a historic county in south-west Scotland, on the Firth of Clyde, divided into the districts of Carrick, Kyle and Cunninghame. Inhabited in Roman times by the Damnonii, it later formed part of the British kingdom of Strathclyde.

ahwa.s: Ahwa is a small town in the hills of southern Gujarat, India, the headquarters of the Dang district. Each year before Holi it hosts the Dang Darbar, a festival at which the descendants of the Bhil chiefs of the Dangs receive the political pensions first paid by the British for…

accra.s: Accra is the capital of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea. It grew from towns of the Ga people, and in the 17th century the Dutch, English and Danes built forts there: Ussher Fort, James Fort and Christiansborg.

amasya.s: Amasya is a city in northern Anatolia, Turkey, in the narrow gorge of the Yeşilırmak river. As ancient Amaseia it was a capital of the kings of Pontus, whose rock tombs line the cliffs, and the birthplace of the geographer Strabo.

aizu.s: Aizu is the western part of Fukushima Prefecture in northern Japan, a mountain basin centred on the castle town of Aizuwakamatsu. It was fought over by the Ashina, Date and other clans in the 16th century and in the Edo period formed a strong domain loyal to the Tokugawa shoguns.

apulia.s: Apulia (Puglia) is the region in the south-east of Italy that forms the heel of the peninsula, with its capital at Bari. In antiquity it was home to the Iapygian peoples, the Daunians, Peucetians and Messapians, before Roman conquest.

artemis.s: Artemis was the Greek goddess of hunting, the wilderness, wild animals and childbirth, daughter of Zeus and Leto and twin of Apollo, born, according to myth, on the island of Delos. She was worshipped throughout the Greek world, and her temple at Ephesus was counted among the…

aristides.s: Aristides, called the Just, was an Athenian statesman and general. He fought at Marathon in 490 BCE, was ostracised in 482 after opposing Themistocles, and was recalled to command at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479.

andetrium.s: Andetrium was a hill fortress of the Delmatae near Muć, north-east of Salona in modern Croatia. In the last stage of the Great Illyrian Revolt in 9 CE it was the final stronghold of the rebel leader Bato, and Tiberius took it after a hard siege.

aulus-gabinius.s: Aulus Gabinius was a Roman politician and general. As tribune in 67 BCE he passed the Gabinian law giving Pompey sweeping command against the pirates, and he was consul in 58 BCE.

alcmaeonidae.s: The Alcmaeonids were a powerful noble family of ancient Athens. They were accused of sacrilege for killing followers of Cylon in a sanctuary around 632 BCE, and spent periods in exile.

anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1814.s: The Convention of London, also called the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814, was signed on 13 August 1814 by Britain and the Netherlands. Britain returned most of the Dutch colonies it had taken in the Napoleonic Wars, including Java, but kept the Cape Colony and the South American…

august-revolution.s: The August Revolution was the seizure of power across Vietnam by the Viet Minh in August 1945, after Japan's surrender at the end of the Second World War. Uprisings took Hanoi on 19 August, Hue and Saigon soon after, and Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated on 30 August.

ain-i-akbari.s: The Ain-i-Akbari is a detailed account of the administration of the Mughal Empire under Akbar, written by his minister Abu'l-Fazl and completed around 1598 as the third volume of his Akbarnama. It describes the court, army, revenue system and provinces, with statistics on…

anum-muttabbil.s: Anum-muttabbil was a ruler of the Mesopotamian city of Der, east of the Tigris, around the start of the 2nd millennium BCE. In an inscription he claimed to have struck down the heads of Anshan, Elam and Shimashki, a boast that shows Der acting as an independent power on the…

aetolia.s: Aetolia is a mountainous region of west-central Greece, north of the Gulf of Corinth, between Acarnania and the Achelous to the west and Phocis and Locris to the east. In the Hellenistic period its people formed the Aetolian League, a strong federal state.

angelokastron.s: Angelokastron is a Byzantine castle on a hill near Agrinio in Aetolia-Acarnania, western Greece. It probably takes its name from the Angelos family who ruled the Despotate of Epirus.

anna-of-savoy.s: Anna of Savoy was a Byzantine empress, wife of Andronikos III Palaiologos. After her husband's death in 1341 she acted as regent for their young son John V and led the regency government against John Kantakouzenos in the civil war of 1341–1347, seeking help from Serbs,…

anna-of-east-anglia.s: Anna was king of the East Angles from about 636 until 654, a devout Christian ruler remembered for his saintly daughters. He gave refuge to King Cenwalh of Wessex and was killed in battle at Bulcamp by Penda of Mercia.

anna-of-kashin.s: Anna of Kashin was a Russian princess, wife of Grand Prince Mikhail of Tver, who was executed at the court of the Golden Horde in 1318. Two of her sons were also killed by the Horde.

anna-of-russia.s: Anna Ioannovna was Empress of Russia from 1730 to 1740, a niece of Peter the Great. Before her accession she was duchess of Courland, having married its duke, who died in 1711.

angelos-dynasty.s: The Angelos family ruled the Byzantine Empire from 1185 to 1204 through the emperors Isaac II, Alexios III and Alexios IV. Their reign saw the loss of Bulgaria and Cyprus and ended with the Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople in 1204.

amoghapasa.s: Amoghapasa is a form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara in Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism, whose name refers to his unfailing noose for saving beings. He was especially honoured in Java and Sumatra in the 13th and 14th centuries.

alaouite-dynasty.s: The Alaouite dynasty is the ruling house of Morocco, a sharifian family claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hasan. Settled in the Tafilalt oasis since the 13th century, it rose to power from the 1630s, and Mawlay al-Rashid reunited the country in…

ahlat.s: Ahlat is a town on the north-western shore of Lake Van in eastern Turkey, known in medieval sources as Khilat. Held by Armenian, Arab and Kurdish rulers, it became the capital of the Shah-Armens, a Turkish dynasty that ruled from 1100 to 1207, and then passed to the Ayyubids,…
