artuqid-dynasty.s: The Artuqid dynasty was a Turkoman dynasty that ruled parts of Upper Mesopotamia and eastern Anatolia from the early 12th to the early 15th century. Founded by the sons of Artuq ibn Ekseb, a Seljuk commander, it divided into branches at Hasankeyf and Amid, at Mardin and at…

aegidius.s: Aegidius was a Roman general who commanded in northern Gaul from about 457 until his death in 464 or 465. Appointed by Emperor Majorian, he refused to accept Majorian's murder in 461 and ruled the region around Soissons independently of the Italian court, defeating the…

antonio-guzman-fernandez.s: Antonio Guzmán Fernández was President of the Dominican Republic from 1978 to 1982 for the Dominican Revolutionary Party. His election victory over Joaquín Balaguer in 1978, upheld after United States pressure stopped the army from halting the count, brought the country's…

azov.s: Azov is a town in Rostov oblast, southern Russia, on the Don near the Sea of Azov. On the site of the medieval Italian trading post of Tana, it was an Ottoman fortress from 1475.

afrikan-bogaevsky.s: Afrikan Bogaevsky was a Russian general and Don Cossack leader who served as ataman of the Don from February 1919 to 1920. A veteran of the Volunteer Army's Ice March of 1918, he succeeded Pyotr Krasnov and placed the Don army under Anton Denikin's Armed Forces of South Russia.

alexey-kaledin.s: Alexey Kaledin was a Russian cavalry general and the first elected ataman of the Don Cossacks after the February Revolution of 1917. A successful army commander in the First World War, he refused to recognise the Bolshevik seizure of power and gave refuge to the Volunteer Army…

alfred-saker.s: Alfred Saker was an English Baptist missionary who worked on Fernando Po and the Cameroon coast from 1844. He founded the mission at Douala, translated the Bible into the Duala language and in 1858 founded the settlement of Victoria, now Limbe, after the Spanish authorities…

adalrich-duke-of-alsace.s: Adalrich, also called Eticho, was Duke of Alsace in the later 7th century and founder of the Etichonid family. A powerful noble in Merovingian politics, he endowed monasteries in Alsace.

ananuri.s: Ananuri is a castle complex on the Aragvi river in Georgia, about 70 kilometres north of Tbilisi on the Georgian Military Road. It was the seat of the dukes of Aragvi, and its walls enclose two churches, the larger of which, the Church of the Mother of God, was built in 1689.

agilolfings.s: The Agilolfings were a noble family that ruled the Duchy of Bavaria from about 555 to 788 and also provided kings of the Lombards. Recognised by the Frankish kings from Garibald I onwards, the dukes governed almost as kings, issued the Lex Baiuvariorum and founded bishoprics…

agnes-bernauer.s: Agnes Bernauer was the daughter of an Augsburg barber-surgeon who became the wife, probably by secret marriage, of Albert, heir to the Duchy of Bavaria-Munich. His father, Duke Ernest, saw the match as a threat to the dynasty; while Albert was away he had her condemned, partly…

alter-hof.s: The Alter Hof is the former residence of the Wittelsbach dukes in the old town of Munich, built from the mid-13th century. Emperor Louis IV the Bavarian made it the first permanent imperial residence of the Holy Roman Empire.

arechis-i-of-benevento.s: Arechis I was Duke of Benevento from 591 to 641, appointed after the death of Zotto, the first duke. During his fifty-year rule he extended the Lombard duchy over most of southern Italy, taking Capua and sacking Crotone, though he could not capture Naples.

anne-of-france.s: Anne of France was the eldest daughter of King Louis XI. With her husband Peter of Beaujeu, later Duke of Bourbon, she governed France during the minority of her brother Charles VIII from 1483, defeating the princes' revolt known as the Mad War and arranging his marriage to…

antonio-da-sangallo-the-younger.s: Antonio da Sangallo the Younger was a Florentine architect of the High Renaissance, active mainly in Rome. He designed the Palazzo Farnese for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, later Pope Paul III, served as chief architect of St Peter's Basilica and built fortifications for the…

addizione-erculea.s: The Addizione Erculea was a planned extension of Ferrara begun in 1492 for Duke Ercole I d'Este and designed by the architect Biagio Rossetti. It roughly doubled the city's area with broad straight streets, new walls and palaces such as the Palazzo dei Diamanti, and is often…

adalbert-of-babenberg.s: Adalbert of Babenberg was a Franconian count of the Popponid family, the elder Babenbergs. His feud with the rival Conradines for dominance in Franconia culminated in 906, when Conrad the Elder was killed in battle at Fritzlar.

ahtum.s: Ahtum, or Ajtony, was an early 11th-century ruler of the region between the Mureș and the lower Danube, known from the Legend of Saint Gerard. Baptised in the Orthodox rite at Vidin, he grew rich by taxing the salt carried on the Mureș and defied King Stephen I of Hungary,…

arnhem.s: Arnhem is a city in the eastern Netherlands on the Nederrijn, capital of the province of Gelderland. It received town rights in 1233 and was the chief town of one of the four quarters of the Duchy of Guelders.

adam-olearius.s: Adam Olearius was a German scholar in the service of Duke Frederick III of Holstein-Gottorp. He was secretary of the duke's embassy to Muscovy and Safavid Persia from 1635 to 1639, and his account of the journey became a widely read description of both countries.

arlon.s: Arlon is a town in south-eastern Belgium, the capital of the province of Luxembourg, close to the border with the Grand Duchy. It grew from the Roman settlement of Orolaunum on the road from Reims to Trier.

andernach.s: Andernach is a town in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, on the left bank of the Rhine north-west of Koblenz. Founded as a Roman fort, Antunnacum, it is one of the oldest towns in Germany.

august-hermann-francke.s: August Hermann Francke (1663–1727) was a German Lutheran clergyman, theologian and educator, a leader of Pietism. As professor at the University of Halle and pastor at Glaucha, he founded in 1698 the Francke Foundations, a complex of orphanage, schools, printing house and…

andrea-mantegna.s: Andrea Mantegna (c. 1431–1506) was an Italian painter of the early Renaissance, trained in Padua.

apuan-alps.s: The Apuan Alps are a mountain range in north-western Tuscany, Italy, running parallel to the coast between the valleys of the Serchio and the Magra. Their marble, quarried around Carrara since Roman times, includes the white statuary marble used by Michelangelo and many other…

archduke-ferdinand-karl-of-austria.s: Archduke Ferdinand Karl (1754–1806) was a son of Maria Theresa and Emperor Francis I. His marriage in 1771 to Maria Beatrice d'Este, heiress of Modena and of Massa and Carrara, founded the House of Austria-Este.

adolphus-frederick-iii-duke-of-mecklenbu.n: Adolphus Frederick III, Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz
adolphus-frederick-iii-duke-of-mecklenbu.s: Adolphus Frederick III (1686–1752) was Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz from 1708, the second ruler of the duchy created by the partition of Mecklenburg in 1701. After the old residence at Strelitz burned down in 1712, he founded the planned town of Neustrelitz in 1733 around a…

agnes-of-merania.s: Agnes of Merania (d. 1201) was queen of France as the third wife of Philip II Augustus, and a daughter of Berthold IV, Duke of Merania.

anselm-of-canterbury.s: Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109) was an Italian-born monk, abbot of Bec in Normandy and from 1093 Archbishop of Canterbury.

anklam.s: Anklam is a town in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Germany, on the Peene river near the Szczecin Lagoon. A member of the Hanseatic League from the late 13th century, it was Swedish from 1648 until 1720, when it passed to Prussia.

albert-frederick-duke-of-prussia.s: Albert Frederick (1553–1618) was Duke of Prussia from 1568, the son and successor of Albert, the first duke. Mentally ill from his youth, he was unable to rule, and his Hohenzollern relatives of Brandenburg-Ansbach and then the electors of Brandenburg governed as regents.

amadeus-v-count-of-savoy.s: Amadeus V, called the Great, was Count of Savoy from 1285 until his death in 1323. He extended Savoyard rule, gaining Bresse through his marriage to Sibylle of Baugé, and in 1294 settled his nephew Philip with the family's lands in Piedmont, the origin of the Savoy-Achaea line.

altenburg-castle.s: Altenburg Castle is a palace complex on a rock above the town of Altenburg in Thuringia, Germany. It was the residence of the dukes of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg and, from 1826, of Saxe-Altenburg.

adolf-william-duke-of-saxe-eisenach.s: Adolf William was a son of Duke William of Saxe-Weimar who received Eisenach as his own duchy when his father's lands were divided in 1662. He ruled it until his death in 1668.

anna-amalia-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel.s: Anna Amalia of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel was Duchess of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach and regent for her son Charles Augustus from 1758 to 1775. A niece of Frederick the Great and a composer herself, she invited Christoph Martin Wieland to Weimar as tutor and made her court a centre of…

abel-king-of-denmark.s: Abel was King of Denmark from 1250 to 1252 and before that Duke of Schleswig. A son of Valdemar II, he quarrelled with his brother King Eric IV, and when Eric was murdered in 1250 Abel was suspected of the crime.

abbey-of-saint-martin-of-tours.s: The Abbey of Saint-Martin of Tours grew up around the tomb of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, who died in 397, and became one of the greatest pilgrimage churches of Frankish Gaul. Alcuin was its abbot from 796 to 804, and later the Robertian dukes, including Hugh Capet, held it…

arnstadt.s: Arnstadt is a town in Thuringia, Germany, south of Erfurt, first recorded in 704 and regarded as the oldest town in Thuringia. It was a residence of the counts of Schwarzburg and of the princes of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen.

alahis.s: Alahis was a Lombard Duke of Trent, and later of Brescia, who rebelled against King Cunipert. In about 688 he seized the royal capital Pavia while Cunipert fled, but his harsh rule turned many Lombards against him.

arnsberg.s: Arnsberg is a town on the Ruhr river in the Sauerland, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It was the seat of the counts of Arnsberg until 1368, when the county was sold to the Archbishop of Cologne, and then the capital of the Duchy of Westphalia, where its estates met.

arak-iran.s: Arak is a city in western Iran and the capital of Markazi Province. It was founded in the early nineteenth century under the Qajars as Soltanabad and renamed Arak in the 1930s.

ali-bey-of-dulkadir.s: Şehsuvaroğlu Ali Bey was the last ruler of the Dulkadirid beylik in south-eastern Anatolia. The son of Şehsuvar Bey, he was installed by Sultan Selim I in 1515 after the Ottomans killed his uncle Alaüddevle, and he helped the Ottomans in their conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate.

armorica.s: Armorica was the ancient name for the north-western part of Gaul between the Seine and the Loire, including the peninsula of modern Brittany. Its Gallic peoples, among them the Veneti and Osismii, traded across the Channel with Britain and were conquered by Julius Caesar in 56…

albert-eckhout.s: Albert Eckhout was a Dutch painter from Groningen who worked in Dutch Brazil from 1637 to 1644 in the household of Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen. He painted life-size portraits of Indigenous, African and mixed-descent inhabitants of Brazil, as well as still lifes of tropical…

afrikaans.s: Afrikaans is a West Germanic language that developed at the Cape of Good Hope from the Dutch spoken by settlers of the Dutch East India Company, with influence from Malay, Portuguese, Khoekhoe and other languages. It was recognised as an official language of South Africa in…

amursana.s: Amursana was an Oirat prince of the Khoit tribe who took part in the succession struggles of the Dzungar Khanate in the 1750s. After falling out with Dawachi, the khan he had helped to power, he submitted to the Qing in 1754 and guided their armies into Dzungaria.

askeaton.s: Askeaton is a town on the River Deel in County Limerick, Ireland. Its castle, on a rock island in the river, was begun in the late 12th century and became a principal seat of the FitzGerald earls of Desmond, who also founded a Franciscan friary nearby in the 14th century.

association-of-southeast-asian-nations.s: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is a regional organisation founded in Bangkok in August 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. It later admitted Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia, and Timor-Leste became its eleventh…

ambiorix.s: Ambiorix was a king of the Eburones, a Belgic people between the Meuse and the Rhine, who ruled jointly with Catuvolcus. In 54 BCE he lured a Roman force of a legion and a half under Sabinus and Cotta out of its winter camp at Atuatuca and destroyed it, one of the heaviest…

atuatuca.s: Atuatuca was a stronghold in the territory of the Eburones in northern Gaul, described by Julius Caesar. Roman troops under Sabinus and Cotta wintered there in 54 BCE before being ambushed and destroyed by Ambiorix, and Quintus Cicero held it with a garrison the following year.

arabah.s: The Arabah is the long desert valley running south from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba, now forming part of the border between Israel and Jordan. Rich in copper ores at Faynan and Timna, it was an important mining area in the Bronze and Iron Ages, and the land of Edom lay…

alake-of-egbaland.s: The Alake of Egbaland is the paramount traditional ruler of the Egba, a Yoruba people whose capital is Abeokuta in south-western Nigeria. The title was originally that of the ruler of Ake, one of the old Egba townships; after the founding of Abeokuta the Alake became, from…

alzey.s: Alzey is a town in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, in the hills of Rhenish Hesse south-west of Mainz. It grew around a Staufer castle and from the 13th century was a centre of power of the counts palatine of the Rhine, with a castle and administrative district.

act-of-settlement-1701.s: The Act of Settlement 1701 is an Act of the Parliament of England that settled the succession to the English and Irish crowns on Sophia, Electress of Hanover, and her Protestant descendants, excluding Catholics. Passed after the death of Princess Anne's last surviving child,…

aschaffenburg.s: Aschaffenburg is a city on the Main in Lower Franconia, Bavaria, south-east of Frankfurt. For centuries it was the second residence of the archbishop-electors of Mainz, who built the Renaissance Johannisburg Palace there in 1605–1614.

ancient-olympic-games.s: The ancient Olympic Games were a religious and athletic festival held every four years at Olympia in honour of Zeus, traditionally from 776 BCE. Free Greek men competed in running, wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon and chariot races, and a sacred truce protected travellers to…

atar.s: Atar is a town in central Mauritania and the capital of the Adrar region. An oasis of date palms on caravan routes across the western Sahara, it became the main centre of the Emirate of Adrar.

abha.s: Abha is the capital of the Asir region in south-western Saudi Arabia, standing about 2,200 metres up in the Sarawat mountains. In the 19th century it was the seat of the Al Aidh emirs of Asir until an Ottoman army took it in 1871–1872, and it was incorporated into the Saudi…

asir.s: Asir is a mountainous region of south-western Arabia between the Hejaz and Yemen, now a province of Saudi Arabia with its capital at Abha. Its highlands catch monsoon rains and support terraced farming.

ahmad-khani.s: Ahmad Khani was a Kurdish poet, scholar and mystic from the Hakkari region who settled at Bayazid and wrote in Kurmanji Kurdish. His verse epic Mem and Zin, completed in 1692, retells a tragic love story set at the court of the emirate of Bohtan at Cizre.

aleg.s: Aleg is a town in south-western Mauritania and the capital of the Brakna region, on the road between Nouakchott and the Senegal River valley, beside a seasonal lake. It lies in the former lands of the Emirate of Brakna, whose emirs dominated the area until French colonial rule…

arthur-conolly.s: Arthur Conolly was a British intelligence officer and traveller in the East India Company's army who is credited with coining the phrase 'the Great Game' for the Anglo-Russian rivalry in Central Asia. In 1841 he went to Bukhara to try to free his colleague Charles Stoddart,…

al-hakam-i.s: Al-Hakam I was the Umayyad emir of Córdoba from 796 to 822. His reign was marked by harsh repression of internal opposition, including a massacre of notables at Toledo in 797 and the crushing of the Revolt of the Arrabal in Córdoba in 818, after which the rebellious suburb was…

abdullah-ibn-saud.s: Abdullah ibn Saud was the last ruler of the Emirate of Diriyah, the first Saudi state, from 1814 to 1818. He faced the Ottoman-Egyptian invasion launched by Muhammad Ali of Egypt and led by Ibrahim Pasha, which overran Najd and besieged Diriyah.

at-turaif.s: At-Turaif is the historic citadel district of Diriyah, near Riyadh, which served as the seat of the first Saudi state in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Its mud-brick palaces, mosques and houses are a leading example of the Najdi architectural style.

alhambra.s: The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex on the Sabika hill above Granada, in southern Spain. Begun by the Nasrid founder Muhammad I in the 13th century, its finest palaces, including the Court of the Lions, were built under Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century,…

arjona.s: Arjona is a town in the province of Jaén in Andalusia, southern Spain. It is known as the birthplace of Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Ahmar, who proclaimed himself ruler there in 1232 and went on to found the Nasrid Emirate of Granada.

al-hoceima.s: Al Hoceima is a port city on the Mediterranean coast of northern Morocco, in the Rif. It lies near the site of Nekor, capital of an early Islamic emirate.

abe-clan-of-mutsu.s: The Abe clan of Mutsu was a powerful family in northern Honshu in the 11th century, holding the six districts of the Kitakami basin on behalf of the court. Their leaders Abe no Yoritoki and his son Sadato fought the provincial governor Minamoto no Yoriyoshi in the Former Nine…

ainu.s: The Ainu are an indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, with their own language, religion and culture centred on hunting, fishing and trade. From the 15th century they came under growing pressure from Japanese settlers, and after 1869 Hokkaido was…

artemis-of-ephesus.s: Artemis of Ephesus was the form of the goddess Artemis worshipped at Ephesus, in western Asia Minor, where she was the city's protector. Her cult statue, hung with rounded ornaments whose meaning is debated, differed from the Greek huntress and drew on older Anatolian traditions.

androclus.s: Androclus was the legendary founder of Ephesus, said to be a son of King Codrus of Athens who led Ionian settlers across the Aegean. According to Strabo and Pausanias, an oracle told him to found a city where a fish and a boar would show him, and he drove out the local Carians…

asclepius.s: Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine, a son of Apollo, whose symbol was a staff with a serpent coiled around it. His main sanctuary at Epidaurus attracted the sick, who slept in its halls hoping for healing dreams, and his cult spread across the Greek world.

aeacidae.s: The Aeacidae were the royal house of the Molossians and the Kingdom of Epirus, who claimed descent from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles and grandson of Aeacus. Its members included Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, and Pyrrhus, who fought Rome in the 3rd century BCE.

abbeville.s: Abbeville is a town in the Somme department of northern France, on the River Somme. In the Middle Ages it was the capital of the County of Ponthieu and a prosperous cloth town, with the Gothic church of Saint-Vulfran.

alulim.s: Alulim is the first king named in the Sumerian King List, which states that after kingship descended from heaven it was at Eridu, where Alulim reigned for 28,800 years. He is a legendary figure belonging to the list's mythical era before the flood.

amharic.s: Amharic is a Semitic language of Ethiopia, written in the Ge'ez script, and the working language of the Ethiopian federal government. It was the language of the court and administration of the Ethiopian Empire from the Middle Ages.

aksehir.s: Akşehir is a town in Konya Province in central Turkey, at the foot of the Sultan Mountains, ancient Philomelium. Under the Seljuks and the Anatolian beyliks it was an important stop on the road between Konya and western Anatolia, and it passed to the Ottomans in the 14th century.

aras-river.s: The Aras, ancient Araxes, is a river of the South Caucasus, about 1,070 kilometres long, which rises in eastern Turkey and joins the Kura in Azerbaijan. Its fertile valley was the heartland of ancient Armenia, where the capitals Artaxata and Armavir stood.

ager-faliscus.s: The Ager Faliscus was the territory of the Falisci, an Italic people of southern Etruria living north of Rome between the Tiber and the Monti Cimini. The Falisci spoke Faliscan, a language closely related to Latin, but shared much of their material culture with the Etruscans.

andres-guazurary.s: Andrés Guazurary, known as Andresito, was a Guaraní leader from the former Jesuit missions who was adopted by José Gervasio Artigas and became commander of the province of Misiones in the Federal League from 1815. He led Guaraní forces against Paraguay, Buenos Aires and the…

anschluss.s: The Anschluss was the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in March 1938. After Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg called a referendum on independence, Hitler forced his resignation, and German troops crossed the border on 12 March to an enthusiastic reception from many Austrians.

aulus-cornelius-cossus.s: Aulus Cornelius Cossus was a Roman commander of the 5th century BCE who killed Lars Tolumnius, king of Veii, in single combat during the war over Fidenae. He dedicated the king's armour in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius as the spolia opima, the second Roman after Romulus said…

apepi.s: Apepi was a Hyksos king of the Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt who ruled from Avaris in the eastern Delta for some forty years in the 16th century BCE, the best-attested ruler of his line. The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was copied in the 33rd year of his reign.

artibonite.s: The Artibonite is the longest river of Hispaniola, rising in the Dominican Republic and flowing about 320 km west through Haiti to the Gulf of Gonâve. Its broad valley is Haiti's main rice-growing region, and it gives its name to the Artibonite department, whose capital is…

al-julanda-ibn-masud.s: Al-Julanda ibn Mas'ud was the first Ibadi imam of Oman, elected around 750 by the Ibadi scholars and leaders after the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate. His imamate was short: in 752 an army sent by the new Abbasid Caliphate defeated and killed him, ending the first Ibadi state…

agustin-de-iturbide.s: Agustín de Iturbide was a Mexican royalist officer who changed sides in 1821 and, with the insurgent Vicente Guerrero, issued the Plan of Iguala, which brought Mexico independence from Spain. In May 1822 he was proclaimed Emperor Agustín I of the First Mexican Empire, but…

alvars.s: The Alvars were twelve Tamil poet-saints devoted to Vishnu who lived in south India between about the 6th and 9th centuries, among them the woman poet Andal. Their emotional hymns of devotion, composed in Tamil and sung in temples, were gathered by Nathamuni in the 10th…

andriscus.s: Andriscus was a pretender who claimed to be Philip, son of Perseus, the last king of Macedon. In 149 BCE, two decades after Rome had abolished the Macedonian monarchy and divided the country into four republics, he seized power as king and reunited Macedon.

avaris.s: Avaris was an ancient city in the north-eastern Nile Delta, at the modern site of Tell el-Dab'a. From the late Middle Kingdom a large population of Levantine origin settled there, and it became the seat of the Fourteenth Dynasty and then the capital of the Hyksos kings of the…

abbey-of-saint-medard.s: The Abbey of Saint-Médard was a Benedictine monastery at Soissons in northern France, founded in the 6th century over the tomb of Saint Médard, bishop of Noyon. King Chlothar I was buried there in 561, as was his son Sigebert I, and it became one of the richest abbeys of…

arbogast.s: Arbogast was a Frankish general in the Roman army who became the dominant figure at the western court of the young emperor Valentinian II. After Valentinian's death in 392 he raised the rhetorician Eugenius as emperor, but their army was defeated by Theodosius I at the Battle…

altona.s: Altona is a district of Hamburg on the north bank of the Elbe, which grew in the 16th century as a fishing and trading settlement beside the city under the counts of Holstein-Pinneberg. Passing to the Danish crown in 1640, it received town rights in 1664 and became the second…

archbishopric-of-hamburg-bremen.s: The Archbishopric of Hamburg-Bremen was the see formed in the 9th century when the mission archbishopric of Hamburg, founded for Ansgar in the 830s, was united with the bishopric of Bremen after Vikings sacked Hamburg in 845. Its archbishops led the Christian mission to…

augusta-vindelicorum.s: Augusta Vindelicorum was the Roman town that became Augsburg, which grew from a military base set up after the Roman conquest of the Alpine region in 15 BCE. Named after Augustus and the Vindelici people, it became the capital of the province of Raetia and a station on the Via…

ambrosius-blarer.s: Ambrosius Blarer was a Protestant reformer from Constance who left his monastery in 1522 and led the Reformation in his home city. He also helped to reform Ulm, Esslingen, Isny and the Duchy of Württemberg, and wrote many hymns.

albrecht-durer.s: Albrecht Dürer was a painter, printmaker and theorist from Nuremberg, the leading artist of the German Renaissance. His woodcuts and engravings, such as the Apocalypse series, Melencolia I and the Rhinoceros, spread his fame across Europe, and his journeys to Italy brought…

achalm.s: The Achalm is a hill of 707 metres on the edge of the Swabian Jura above Reutlingen in Baden-Württemberg. A castle built on it in the 11th century was the seat of the counts of Achalm, who founded Zwiefalten Abbey in 1089, and it later passed to the Hohenstaufen and then to…

arae-flaviae.s: Arae Flaviae was a Roman town on the upper Neckar on the site of present-day Rottweil, founded around 73 CE under the Flavian emperors, from whom it took its name. It grew out of a series of military camps and became a municipium, the only Roman town in what is now…

albert-alcibiades-margrave-of-brandenbur.s: Albert Alcibiades was Margrave of Brandenburg-Kulmbach from 1541 to 1554, a soldier notorious for plunder. In the Second Margrave War he ravaged Franconia, extorting money from the bishoprics of Bamberg and Würzburg and attacking Nuremberg, until he was defeated at…

albert-einstein.s: Albert Einstein was a German-born physicist, born in Ulm, whose theories of special and general relativity transformed physics. In 1905, while working at the Swiss patent office in Bern, he published papers on relativity, light quanta and Brownian motion, and he received the…

autonomist-party-fiume.s: The Autonomist Party was a political party of Fiume, now Rijeka, founded in 1896, which defended the city's self-government against Hungarian centralism and later against annexation by Italy or Yugoslavia. Led after 1918 by Riccardo Zanella, it won the elections of April 1921…

agios-kirykos.s: Agios Kirykos is the main town and port of the Greek island of Ikaria in the eastern Aegean. In July 1912 it was the seat of the provisional government of the short-lived Free State of Icaria, set up after the islanders expelled the Ottoman garrison, before the island joined…

alfred-meyer.s: Alfred Meyer was a Nazi Party official who was Gauleiter of Westphalia-North and from 1933 Reich governor of Lippe and Schaumburg-Lippe. From 1941 he was also deputy to Alfred Rosenberg in the Reich Ministry for the Occupied Eastern Territories, and he attended the Wannsee…

arado-flugzeugwerke.s: Arado Flugzeugwerke was a German aircraft maker founded in 1925 at Warnemünde near Rostock. It built trainers and seaplanes and, in the Second World War, the Arado Ar 234, the first operational jet bomber, before it was dissolved at the end of the war.

armistice-of-mudros.s: The Armistice of Mudros, signed on 30 October 1918 aboard HMS Agamemnon in Mudros harbour on the island of Lemnos, ended fighting between the Ottoman Empire and the Allies in the First World War. It opened the Dardanelles, demobilised the Ottoman army and allowed the Allies to…

alfred-amedee-dodds.s: Alfred-Amédée Dodds was a French general of mixed African and European descent, born at Saint-Louis in Senegal. He commanded the French expedition of 1892 in the Second Franco-Dahomean War, defeating the army of King Béhanzin and taking the capital Abomey; Béhanzin surrendered…

austral-islands.s: The Austral Islands are the southernmost island group of French Polynesia in the South Pacific, including Rurutu, Tubuai, Rimatara, Raivavae and Rapa. Their chiefs came under Tahitian influence in the 19th century, and France annexed the islands one by one between 1880 and 1901.

alfred-dreyfus.s: Alfred Dreyfus was a French artillery officer from a Jewish Alsatian family. In 1894 he was falsely convicted of passing military secrets to Germany and sent to the penal colony on Devil's Island in French Guiana.

ariane-rocket-family.s: Ariane is a series of European civilian launch vehicles developed for the European Space Agency, first flown in 1979. All Ariane rockets lift off from the Guiana Space Centre at Kourou in French Guiana, close to the equator.

abidjan.s: Abidjan is the largest city and economic capital of Ivory Coast, on the Ébrié Lagoon. A small village chosen as a railway terminus, it became the capital of the French colony in 1934, and the opening of the Vridi canal around 1950 made it a deep-water port.

african-agricultural-union.s: The African Agricultural Union (Syndicat Agricole Africain) was an association of African planters in the Ivory Coast founded in 1944 by Félix Houphouët-Boigny. It campaigned against forced labour, which favoured European planters, and against the unequal treatment of African…

arthur-verdier.s: Arthur Verdier was a French merchant and shipowner from La Rochelle whose trading house worked on the Ivory Coast from the 1860s. When France withdrew its garrisons from the coast after the Franco-Prussian War, his company kept up the French presence, and he was named French…

abd-al-hafid-of-morocco.s: Abd al-Hafid was sultan of Morocco of the Alaouite dynasty from 1908 to 1912. He rebelled against his brother Abd al-Aziz, whose concessions to European powers were unpopular, and was proclaimed sultan in 1907–1908.

agadir-crisis.s: The Agadir Crisis, or Second Moroccan Crisis, began in July 1911 when Germany sent the gunboat Panther to the Moroccan port of Agadir in protest against the French occupation of Fez. Britain backed France, and in November 1911 Germany accepted a French protectorate over…

antillean-creole.s: Antillean Creole is a French-based creole language spoken in the Lesser Antilles, including Martinique, Guadeloupe, Dominica and Saint Lucia, where it is called Kwéyòl. It arose among enslaved Africans and French colonists on the plantations of the 17th and 18th centuries,…

aurich.s: Aurich is a town in East Frisia in Lower Saxony, north-west Germany. The nearby Upstalsboom was a meeting place of the medieval Frisian communities, and from the 16th century Aurich was the residence of the Cirksena counts and princes of East Frisia.

aldgisl.s: Aldgisl was a king of the Frisians in the late 7th century, the first whose name is reliably known. In 678–679 he gave shelter to the English bishop Wilfrid of York, who preached to the Frisians on his way to Rome, and he reportedly refused a Frankish demand to hand Wilfrid over.

angkor-borei.s: Angkor Borei is a town and archaeological site in Takeo province in southern Cambodia, near the Vietnamese border. Excavations have revealed brick walls, canals linking it to the port of Oc Eo, and occupation from the late 1st millennium BCE, and many scholars see it as a…

ayawaso.s: Ayawaso was the inland capital of the Ga kingdom on the Accra plains of present-day Ghana. Europeans called it Great Accra to distinguish it from the coastal town of Small Accra, where they traded with the Ga.

amyntas-of-galatia.s: Amyntas was the last king of Galatia in central Anatolia, ruling from 36 to 25 BCE. A former secretary of the Galatian king Deiotarus, he was made king by Mark Antony, went over to Octavian before Actium, and extended his rule over Pisidia, Lycaonia and parts of Cilicia.

ankara.s: Ankara, the ancient Ancyra, is the capital of Turkey, on the central Anatolian plateau. Galatian Celts settled there in the 3rd century BCE, and it became the capital of the Roman province of Galatia, where the Temple of Augustus preserves the best surviving copy of the Res…

attalus-i.s: Attalus I Soter ruled Pergamon from 241 to 197 BCE. After defeating the Galatians, he took the title of king, the first of his dynasty to do so, and celebrated the victory with monuments that included statues of dying Gauls.

aquae-flaviae.s: Aquae Flaviae was a Roman town in Gallaecia on the site of modern Chaves in northern Portugal. Founded under the Flavian emperors in the 1st century CE at hot springs on the Tâmega river, it is known for its Roman bridge, the Ponte de Trajano.

astana-gede.s: Astana Gede is a sacred site at Kawali in Ciamis Regency, West Java, Indonesia, associated with the Sundanese kingdom of Galuh. It holds the Kawali inscriptions, 14th-century stones in Old Sundanese that name Prabu Raja Wastu, who fortified the royal town of Kawali and urged…

alaknanda.s: The Alaknanda is a Himalayan river in Uttarakhand, India, and one of the two headstreams of the Ganges. Rising near Badrinath, it flows through Garhwal past Srinagar and joins the Bhagirathi at Devprayag to form the Ganges.

arawakan-languages.s: The Arawakan languages are a family of languages of South America and the Caribbean, spoken from the Andes and Amazonia to the Antilles. Before the Spanish conquest they included Taíno in the Greater Antilles and the Island Carib language of the Lesser Antilles, ancestor of…

azores.s: The Azores are an archipelago of nine volcanic islands in the North Atlantic, about 1,400 kilometres west of mainland Portugal. Settled by the Portuguese from the 1430s, they served as a waystation for ships returning from the Americas and Asia.

amasra.s: Amasra is a small port town on the Black Sea coast of Turkey, in Bartın Province. The ancient Amastris, it was a Byzantine port before Genoese merchants made it one of their trading stations in the 13th and 14th centuries, building walls whose remains survive.

albert-hahl.s: Albert Hahl was a German colonial administrator, governor of German New Guinea from 1902 to 1914. He extended administration through appointed village headmen, the luluai, and a head tax that pushed men into plantation labour, and he moved the capital to Rabaul in 1910.

angaur.s: Angaur is a small island in the south of Palau in the western Pacific. Under German rule phosphate was mined there from 1909, a business continued by the Japanese after they seized the islands in 1914.

adolf-luderitz.s: Adolf Lüderitz was a Bremen merchant whose purchase of the bay of Angra Pequena and its hinterland in 1883 led Germany to proclaim a protectorate over South West Africa in 1884. His land deals with the Nama chief Joseph Fredericks were notoriously one-sided, measured in German…

ahmedi.s: Ahmedi was an Anatolian Turkish poet who wrote at the courts of the Germiyanid beys and later of the Ottoman prince Süleyman Çelebi. His İskendername, a long verse romance on Alexander the Great, includes a section on Ottoman history that is among the earliest Ottoman chronicles.

alasehir.s: Alaşehir is a town in Manisa Province in western Turkey. As Philadelphia, founded by the Attalid kings of Pergamon in the 2nd century BCE, it was one of the seven churches of Asia named in the Book of Revelation.

agatharchides.s: Agatharchides of Cnidus was a Greek historian and geographer of the 2nd century BCE who worked in Ptolemaic Alexandria. His work On the Erythraean Sea, preserved in excerpts by Photius and Diodorus, describes the peoples and trade of the Red Sea and Arabia, including the…

absalom.s: Absalom is the third son of King David in the Hebrew Bible, born to Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur. After killing his half-brother Amnon he fled to Geshur, and later he led a revolt that drove David from Jerusalem.

anastasius-i-dicorus.s: Anastasius I was emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire from 491 to 518. A palace official chosen by the widowed empress Ariadne, he reformed the coinage and taxation, leaving a large surplus in the treasury, and fought a war with Persia from 502 to 506.

azd.s: The Azd were a major group of Arab tribes originating in South Arabia. After migrations that tradition links with the collapse of the Marib dam, branches settled across Arabia: the Ghassanids in Syria, the Aws and Khazraj in Medina, and others in Oman, where the Azd became…

al-nabigha-al-dhubyani.s: Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani was a pre-Islamic Arab poet of the 6th century, counted in some collections among the poets of the Mu'allaqat. He lived for long periods at the courts of the Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III at al-Hira and of the Ghassanid rulers, writing praise poems and…

arthur-grimble.s: Arthur Grimble was a British colonial administrator who served in the Gilbert and Ellice Islands from 1914 and became its resident commissioner in 1926, later governing the Seychelles and the Windward Islands. He recorded Gilbertese traditions and customs, and his humorous…

achimota-school.s: Achimota School is a boarding school near Accra, Ghana, founded in the 1920s by Governor Gordon Guggisberg, the Reverend Alexander Fraser and James Kwegyir Aggrey and opened in 1927 as the Prince of Wales College. Co-educational from the start, it trained much of the Gold…

ambrose.s: Ambrose was bishop of Milan from 374 and one of the four original Doctors of the Latin Church. A Roman governor chosen bishop by popular acclaim, he opposed the Arians, defended the Church's independence from emperors, made Theodosius I do penance after the massacre at…

astrakhan-khanate.s: The Astrakhan Khanate was a Tatar state on the lower Volga, centred on the city of Astrakhan, that emerged from the break-up of the Golden Horde in the fifteenth century. It controlled trade routes between Russia, Persia and Central Asia until Ivan IV of Russia conquered it in…

arrow-cross-party.s: The Arrow Cross Party was a Hungarian fascist and antisemitic party led by Ferenc Szálasi, which grew from his movement founded in 1935. In October 1944 Germany installed it in power after Regent Miklós Horthy tried to leave the war.

alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca.s: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca was a Spanish explorer, one of four survivors of the Narváez expedition to Florida of 1527, who wandered for eight years across what is now the south-western United States and northern Mexico; his account is a key source on its peoples. As governor…

asuncion.s: Asunción is the capital and largest city of Paraguay, on the east bank of the Paraguay river. Founded by Juan de Salazar in 1537, it was for decades the centre of Spanish settlement in the Río de la Plata region, and from it Buenos Aires was refounded in 1580.

adolphe-grand-duke-of-luxembourg.s: Adolphe was the last Duke of Nassau, from 1839 to 1866, and Grand Duke of Luxembourg from 1890 to 1905. He lost his duchy when he sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War and Prussia annexed it in 1866.

antoni-radziwill.s: Prince Antoni Radziwiłł was a Polish-Lithuanian aristocrat, composer and patron of the arts who married Princess Louise of Prussia. From 1815 to 1831 he served as the Prussian king's governor of the Grand Duchy of Posen, mediating between the Polish nobility and the Prussian…

anna-maria-luisa-de-medici.s: Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici, Electress Palatine, was the last member of the ruling Medici family of Tuscany. Daughter of Grand Duke Cosimo III and widow of the Elector Palatine Johann Wilhelm, she returned to Florence in 1717.

afanasy-nikitin.s: Afanasy Nikitin was a merchant of Tver who travelled through Persia to India between about 1466 and 1472, one of the first Europeans to describe the country. His travel notes, A Journey Beyond Three Seas, record life in the Bahmani Sultanate, where he stayed at Bidar.

amapala.s: Amapala is a port town on El Tigre island in the Gulf of Fonseca, Honduras. For a long time Honduras's main Pacific port, it was the meeting place of the Diet of the Greater Republic of Central America in the 1890s, when Honduras, Nicaragua and El Salvador briefly joined in a…

ai-khanoum.s: Ai-Khanoum is the site of a Hellenistic city at the meeting of the Amu Darya and Kokcha rivers in northern Afghanistan, probably founded in the early Seleucid period around 300 BCE. Excavated by French archaeologists from 1964 to 1978, it revealed a theatre, gymnasium, palace…

alatheus.s: Alatheus was a chieftain of the Greuthungi Goths who, with Saphrax, acted as guardian of the boy-king Vithericus after the Huns overran their people around 375. In 376 they crossed the Danube into the Roman Empire without permission and joined the Tervingi under Fritigern.

andersen-air-force-base.s: Andersen Air Force Base is a United States Air Force base in the north of Guam, built after American forces retook the island from Japan in 1944. It served as a base for B-29 raids on Japan in 1945 and for B-52 bombers in the Vietnam War, and remains one of the main US…

antonio-de-andrade.s: António de Andrade was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary and explorer who in 1624 crossed the Himalaya from India and became one of the first Europeans to enter Tibet. Welcomed by the king of Guge, he founded a mission and built a church at Tsaparang in 1626.

atisha.s: Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana was a Buddhist teacher from Bengal who taught at the monasteries of the Pala Empire, including Vikramashila. Invited by the rulers of Guge, he arrived in western Tibet in 1042 and spent the rest of his life in Tibet, writing the Lamp for the Path to…

ahmedabad.s: Ahmedabad is the largest city of Gujarat in western India, on the Sabarmati river. It was founded in 1411 by Ahmad Shah I of the Gujarat Sultanate as his capital and became famous for its mosques, stepwells and textile trade.

aksu.s: Aksu is an oasis city in the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region of China, on the northern rim of the Tarim Basin at the foot of the Tian Shan. A station on the northern Silk Road since ancient times, it was ruled by Turkic and Mongol powers, including Moghulistan and the Yarkent…

abu-hafs-umar-i.s: Abu Hafs Umar I was the Hafsid sultan of Tunis from 1284 to 1295, a son of Abu Zakariya Yahya I. He took power after overthrowing the usurper Ibn Abi Umara, but his nephew Abu Zakariya set up a rival Hafsid state at Béjaïa in 1285 that refused to recognise him.

abu-ishaq-ibrahim-i.s: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim I was Hafsid sultan of Ifriqiya from 1279 to 1283, a son of Abu Zakariya Yahya I and brother of al-Mustansir. With help from the Crown of Aragon he overthrew his nephew Yahya II al-Wathiq.

al-mustansir-i.s: Al-Mustansir I was the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad from 1226 to 1242, one of the last before the Mongol conquest. He strengthened the caliphate's small state in Iraq, annexed Erbil in 1233 on the death of its ruler Gökböri, and founded the Mustansiriya, a college in Baghdad that…

abu-amr-uthman.s: Abu Amr Uthman was the Hafsid sultan of Ifriqiya from 1435 to 1488, one of the longest reigns of the dynasty. He continued the restoration begun by his grandfather Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz II, keeping the Arab tribes in check and holding Tunis, Constantine and Béjaïa together.

al-zaytuna-mosque.s: The Al-Zaytuna Mosque is the great mosque of the medina of Tunis, founded in the early 8th century and largely rebuilt under the Aghlabids in the 9th century. For centuries it was also one of the leading centres of learning in the Islamic world, teaching Maliki law and the…

artemisia-i-of-caria.s: Artemisia I was the queen of Halicarnassus in Caria in the early 5th century BCE, ruling as a vassal of the Achaemenid Empire after the death of her husband. Herodotus, himself from Halicarnassus, describes how she commanded five ships in Xerxes' invasion of Greece and fought…

abu-firas-al-hamdani.s: Abu Firas al-Hamdani was an Arab poet and warrior, a cousin of Sayf al-Dawla, the Hamdanid emir of Aleppo. He served as governor of Manbij and fought in the wars against Byzantium, during which he was captured and spent several years as a prisoner in Constantinople.

al-farabi.s: Al-Farabi was a philosopher of the Islamic world, born in Central Asia, who worked in Baghdad and spent his last years at the court of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo and in Damascus, where he died around 950. Called the 'Second Teacher' after Aristotle, he wrote commentaries on Greek…

abul-hayja-abdallah-ibn-hamdan.s: Abu'l-Hayja Abdallah ibn Hamdan was an Arab commander of the Banu Taghlib who laid the foundations of the Hamdanid dynasty's power. Appointed governor of Mosul by the Abbasid caliph in 905, he held the post for much of the following years and became a leading figure at the…

al-nasir-ibn-alnas.s: Al-Nasir ibn Alnas was the Hammadid ruler of the central Maghreb from 1062 to 1088, under whom the dynasty reached its height. Pressed by the Banu Hilal Arab tribes in the interior, he founded a new capital on the coast at Béjaïa, which he called al-Nasiriyya, and developed it…

ali-ibn-daud.s: Ali ibn Daud was the emir of Harar who in 1647 founded an independent dynasty in the walled city, after the leadership of the Adal state had moved to Aussa. His descendants ruled Harar and its farmlands, surrounded by Oromo-settled countryside, until the Egyptian occupation of…

angelina-river.s: The Angelina River is a river of East Texas in the United States that flows south-east through the Piney Woods to join the Neches River. It is named after Angelina, a Hasinai woman who worked as an interpreter for Spanish missionaries in the early 18th century.

arkansas.s: Arkansas is a state of the south-central United States, west of the Mississippi River, with its capital at Little Rock. Its south-west was part of the homeland of the Caddo, and the region passed between France and Spain before the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

aristobulus-ii.s: Aristobulus II was Hasmonean king and high priest of Judaea from 67 to 63 BCE, a younger son of Alexander Jannaeus and Salome Alexandra. His civil war with his elder brother Hyrcanus II drew in Pompey, who took Jerusalem in 63 BCE and led him captive to Rome.

anjar.s: Anjar is a town in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, known for the ruins of an Umayyad palace city built in the early 8th century, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The modern town was founded in 1939 by Armenian refugees from Musa Dagh, who left their villages when the Sanjak of…

arinna.s: Arinna was a Hittite holy city in central Anatolia, a short distance from the capital Hattusa, whose exact site has not been identified. It was the cult centre of the sun goddess of Arinna, the chief goddess of the Hittite state and patron of its kings, a deity inherited from…

afrasiyab-of-basra.s: Afrasiyab was the founder of a hereditary dynasty of pashas who ruled Basra in southern Iraq under nominal Ottoman sovereignty. A local official of uncertain origin, he bought the governorship from the Ottoman governor in 1596 and passed it to his son Ali Pasha in 1624.

ada-of-caria.s: Ada was a member of the Hecatomnid dynasty of Caria, a daughter of Hecatomnus, who ruled as satrap with her brother and husband Idrieus and alone after his death in 344 BCE. Her younger brother Pixodarus drove her out around 340 BCE, leaving her only the fortress of Alinda.

aarau.s: Aarau is the capital of the Swiss canton of Aargau, on the River Aare. Founded by the counts of Kyburg in the 13th century, it came under Bernese rule in 1415.

agen.s: Agen is a city in south-western France on the Garonne, capital of the Lot-et-Garonne department. As Aginnum it was the chief town of the Gallic Nitiobroges, and in 107 BCE the Tigurini defeated a Roman army in its region.

aventicum.s: Aventicum was the capital of the Helvetii under Roman rule, on the site of the modern town of Avenches in western Switzerland, near Lake Murten. Raised to a colony by Vespasian, it had walls more than 5 km long, an amphitheatre, a theatre and temples, and perhaps some 20,000…

alba-helviorum.s: Alba Helviorum was the Roman town of the Helvii in southern Gaul, at the modern village of Alba-la-Romaine in the Ardèche. Excavations have revealed a theatre, temples and a forum.

ardeche.s: The Ardèche is a department of south-eastern France on the right bank of the Rhône, named after the river Ardèche, known for its gorges. It largely corresponds to the old province of Vivarais, the land of the Gallic Helvii in antiquity.

amastris-queen.s: Amastris was a Persian princess, niece of Darius III, who married Craterus and then Dionysius, tyrant of Heraclea Pontica. After his death around 305 BCE she ruled Heraclea as regent for their sons, married the Macedonian king Lysimachus and founded the city of Amastris on the…

anagni.s: Anagni, ancient Anagnia, is a hill town in the Sacco valley south-east of Rome and was the leading city of the Hernici. Rome punished it after its revolt of 306 BCE.

alatri.s: Alatri, ancient Aletrium, is a hill town of the Hernici in southern Lazio, Italy, famous for its acropolis enclosed by massive polygonal walls of the pre-Roman period. Loyal to Rome during the Hernican revolt of 306 BCE, it remained an allied city with its own laws before…

anandapala.s: Anandapala was a king of the Hindu Shahi dynasty, which ruled lands from the Indus to the Punjab, and succeeded his father Jayapala around 1002. He continued the resistance to Mahmud of Ghazni, who defeated him in a great battle in 1008 and seized much of his realm.

abgaal.s: The Abgaal are a major Somali clan of the Hawiye clan family, belonging to its Hiraab branch and living mainly in and around Mogadishu and the middle Shabelle region. In the late 17th century they took part in the revolt that ended the Ajuran Sultanate's control of the coast…

aomori-prefecture.s: Aomori Prefecture is the northernmost prefecture of Honshu, Japan, with its capital at Aomori, facing Hokkaido across the Tsugaru Strait. It was formed in 1871 from the Hirosaki domain of the Tsugaru and part of the lands of their old rivals, the Nanbu.

asano-clan.s: The Asano clan was a Japanese warrior family that rose through its ties with Toyotomi Hideyoshi, whose wife Nene had been adopted into the family. From 1619 its main line ruled the Hiroshima domain until 1871, while a branch held Akō, whose lord's forced suicide in 1701 led to…

abellinum.s: Abellinum was an ancient town of the Hirpini in Campania, southern Italy, at modern Atripalda, next to Avellino, which takes its name from it. It became a Roman colony, and its remains include walls, houses and an early Christian cemetery.

aeclanum.s: Aeclanum was the main town of the Hirpini in the southern Apennines, near modern Mirabella Eclano in Campania. Sulla captured and sacked it in 89 BCE during the Social War, after which it became a Roman municipium on the Via Appia.

aquileia.s: Aquileia is a town near the head of the Adriatic in north-eastern Italy, founded as a Latin colony in 181 BCE to guard the north-eastern approaches to Italy. It became one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire and a major church centre, with fine floor mosaics in its…

ambon-island.s: Ambon Island is an island in the Maluku archipelago of eastern Indonesia, home to the city of Ambon, capital of Maluku province. Valued for cloves, it drew the Portuguese in the 16th century and was taken by the Dutch East India Company in 1605, which made it the centre of its…

ashraf-hotak.s: Ashraf Hotak was an Afghan ruler of the Hotak dynasty who reigned as shah in Persia from 1725, after deposing his cousin Mahmud Hotak. He made peace with the Ottomans, but Nader, fighting for the Safavid Tahmasp II, defeated him at Damghan and Murche-Khort in 1729 and drove…

aster-revolution.s: The Aster Revolution was the uprising in Budapest of 28-31 October 1918, as Austria-Hungary collapsed at the end of the First World War. Soldiers and civilians wearing asters as their emblem forced the appointment of Count Mihály Károlyi as prime minister on 31 October, the…

arad-romania.s: Arad is a city in western Romania on the Mureș river, part of the Kingdom of Hungary until 1920. After the defeat of the Hungarian revolution of 1848-1849, thirteen Hungarian generals were executed there by the Austrians on 6 October 1849.

asaf-jah-i.s: Asaf Jah I, born Qamar-ud-din Khan and titled Nizam-ul-Mulk, was a Mughal noble who founded Hyderabad State. Viceroy of the Deccan, he defeated the governor Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda in 1724 and made himself effectively independent while still acknowledging the Mughal emperor.

aragon-river.s: The Aragón is a river of northern Spain that rises in the central Pyrenees near the Somport pass, flows past Jaca and joins the Ebro in Navarre. Its upper valley was the home of the Iacetani in antiquity, and in the 9th century it gave its name to the County of Aragon, from…

aughnanure-castle.s: Aughnanure Castle is a six-storey tower house near Oughterard, County Galway, Ireland, built by the O'Flaherty lords of Iar Connacht in the 15th or 16th century. Standing on a rocky islet beside Lough Corrib, it is surrounded by a fortified bawn.

abu-hamza-al-mukhtar-ibn-awf.s: Abu Hamza al-Mukhtar ibn Awf was an Ibadi Kharijite leader and the general of Abd Allah ibn Yahya, the imam proclaimed in Hadramawt in 746. In 747 he marched north, defeated a Medinan army at Qudayd and occupied Mecca and Medina, where his sermons were long remembered.

abd-al-malik-ibn-atiyya.s: Abd al-Malik ibn Atiyya was an Umayyad general sent by the caliph Marwan II with Syrian troops against the Ibadi rebels who had seized Mecca and Medina in 747. He defeated their commander Abu Hamza in the Hejaz and then advanced into Yemen, where the Ibadi imam Abd Allah ibn…

althing.s: The Althing is the parliament of Iceland, founded around 930 as an open-air general assembly at Þingvellir. In the Icelandic Commonwealth it made law and settled disputes, with a law-speaker who recited the laws.

antedios.s: Antedios is the name of a ruler of the Iceni, an Iron Age people of East Anglia, known from silver coins inscribed with his name. He probably ruled in the early 1st century CE, before the Roman conquest of 43.

abhai-singh-of-marwar.s: Abhai Singh was the Rathore maharaja of Marwar, ruling from Jodhpur from 1724 to 1749. He came to the throne after the murder of his father, Ajit Singh, and served the Mughals as governor of Gujarat in the 1730s.

al-hasan-ibn-kannun.s: Al-Hasan ibn Kannun was the last Idrisid ruler in Morocco, holding territory in the north of the country in the mid-10th century between the Fatimids and the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba. He surrendered to the Cordoban general Ghalib in 974 and was taken to Córdoba and then…

ahmad-ibn-idris.s: Ahmad ibn Idris al-Fasi was a Moroccan Sufi teacher whose reformist teaching stressed the direct study of the Quran and hadith. He taught at Fez, Mecca and finally Sabya in the Asir region of Arabia, where he died.

ait-ba-amran.s: The Ait Ba Amran are a Berber tribal confederation of south-western Morocco, living in the hinterland of Sidi Ifni. They lived under Spanish colonial rule after Spain occupied Ifni in 1934.

awujale.s: The Awujale is the title of the paramount ruler of the Ijebu Kingdom, a Yoruba state in south-western Nigeria with its seat at Ijebu-Ode. The king traditionally governed together with the Osugbo council of elders and the town chiefs, and the office survived the British…

ajibogun.s: Ajibogun, also called Obokun, is the legendary founder of the Ijesha Kingdom, centred on Ilesa in south-western Nigeria. Ijesha tradition makes him a son of Oduduwa who fetched sea water to cure his father's blindness and was rewarded with a crown and the right to found a…

andhra-ikshvakus.s: The Andhra Ikshvakus were a dynasty that ruled the lower Krishna valley in present-day Andhra Pradesh, India, in the 3rd and early 4th centuries CE, after the fall of the Satavahanas. Claiming descent from the legendary solar dynasty of Ikshvaku, they ruled from their capital…

adam-baldridge.s: Adam Baldridge was an English former pirate who from 1691 ran a fortified trading post on Île Sainte-Marie off the north-east coast of Madagascar. Backed by New York merchants, notably Frederick Philipse, he sold supplies, liquor and arms to pirates operating in the Indian…

ambodifotatra.s: Ambodifotatra is the main town of Île Sainte-Marie, or Nosy Boraha, an island off the north-east coast of Madagascar. France reoccupied the island in 1818 and built a base there for trade and for its claims on Madagascar.

aetolians.s: The Aetolians were the ancient Greek inhabitants of Aetolia, a mountainous region north of the Gulf of Corinth. Organised from the 4th century BCE in the Aetolian League, they became a leading military power, controlled Delphi and fought Macedon and the Achaean League.

aussa.s: Aussa is an oasis region in the lower valley of the Awash river in the Afar lowlands of north-eastern Ethiopia, watered by the river before it ends in a chain of lakes. In 1577 the imams of Adal moved their seat there from Harar, founding the Imamate of Aussa.

adelindis-of-buchau.s: Adelindis was a Frankish noblewoman who, according to tradition, founded the convent of Buchau on the Federsee in upper Swabia around 770 and became its first abbess. Venerated locally as a saint, she is linked by legend to the family of Hildegard, wife of Charlemagne.

altfrid.s: Altfrid was bishop of Hildesheim from 851 until his death in 874 and is venerated as a saint. A churchman from the Saxon nobility and an adviser to the East Frankish king Louis the German, he founded Essen Abbey as a community of canonesses around 845 to 852.

akim-oda.s: Akim Oda is a town in the Eastern Region of Ghana, in the valley of the Birim river. It became the capital of the Akan state of Akyem Kotoku in the 19th century and remains the seat of its paramount chief, the Kotokuhene.

anna-ii-abbess-of-quedlinburg.s: Anna II of Stolberg was princess-abbess of Quedlinburg from 1516, when she was elected as a girl, until her death in 1574. In 1539 she introduced the Lutheran Reformation in the abbey and town, turning Quedlinburg into a Protestant foundation for noblewomen while keeping its…

appenzell-wars.s: The Appenzell Wars were a series of conflicts from 1401 to 1429 in which the people of Appenzell, in north-eastern Switzerland, threw off the rule of the prince-abbots of Saint Gall. With help from Schwyz they defeated the abbey's forces and its Habsburg allies at Vögelinsegg…

ansfried-of-utrecht.s: Ansfried was a count in the Low Countries who served Emperor Otto III before becoming bishop of Utrecht in 995. Around 990 he and his wife Hilsondis founded the convent of Thorn, near the Meuse, with their daughter Benedicta as its first abbess.

antialcidas.s: Antialcidas was an Indo-Greek king who ruled from Taxila in the late 2nd century BCE. He is known from his coins and from the Heliodorus pillar at Vidisha in central India, set up by his Greek ambassador Heliodorus, who called himself a devotee of Vasudeva.

abdagases-i.s: Abdagases I was an Indo-Parthian king of the 1st century CE, a nephew of Gondophares according to his coins. He ruled in the Punjab and Gandhara after his uncle, as the kingdom broke up among several successors.

acts-of-thomas.s: The Acts of Thomas is an early 3rd-century Christian text, probably written in Syriac at Edessa, telling of the mission of the Apostle Thomas to India. It describes him being sold as a carpenter to an envoy of King Gudnaphar, a name that matches the Indo-Parthian king…

apollonius-of-tyana.s: Apollonius of Tyana was a Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and wandering teacher from Cappadocia in the 1st century CE. His life is known chiefly from a biography by Philostratus, written over a century later, which credits him with miracles and travels to Babylon and India,…

azes-i.s: Azes I was an Indo-Scythian king of north-western India in the 1st century BCE who ruled over Gandhara and the Punjab. He is widely thought to have founded the Azes era, which began in about 57 BCE and was used in later inscriptions, though its exact start is debated.

assiniboine.s: The Assiniboine, or Nakoda, are a Siouan-speaking Indigenous people of the northern Great Plains, in present-day Saskatchewan, Alberta, Montana and North Dakota. Having separated from the Yanktonai Dakota, they became close allies of the Cree in the fur trade and in wars with…

al-qaeda.s: Al-Qaeda is a Sunni jihadist organisation founded in 1988 by Osama bin Laden and other veterans of the war against the Soviets in Afghanistan. Based in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan in the late 1990s, it carried out the attacks of 11 September 2001, which led to the United States…

abdullah-abdullah.s: Abdullah Abdullah is an Afghan politician and former ophthalmologist who was an adviser to the commander Ahmad Shah Massoud. He served as foreign minister after 2001 and ran for president in 2009, 2014 and 2019.

abdul-rashid-dostum.s: Abdul Rashid Dostum is an Afghan Uzbek militia leader and politician from the north of the country. He commanded a militia for the communist government, then switched sides in 1992, helping to bring down President Najibullah, and fought in the civil wars from his base at…

ahmad-shah-massoud.s: Ahmad Shah Massoud was an Afghan mujahideen commander of the Jamiat-e Islami, known as the Lion of Panjshir for defending the Panjshir valley against Soviet offensives in the 1980s. He was defence minister of the Islamic State of Afghanistan from 1992 and later led the…

agordat.s: Agordat is a town in western Eritrea on the Barka River. Italian forces defeated the Mahdists of Sudan there in 1890 and 1893, and the Italian railway from Massawa through Asmara and Keren was extended to it in the 1920s.

asmara.s: Asmara is the capital of Eritrea, on the highland plateau at about 2,300 metres. A village grew into a city after the Italians made it the capital of their colony in the 1890s, and in the 1930s it was rebuilt with modernist and Art Deco buildings.

alessandro-pirzio-biroli.s: Alessandro Pirzio Biroli was an Italian army general. He commanded troops in the Italian conquest of Ethiopia in 1935–36 and was governor of Amhara.

alceste-de-ambris.s: Alceste De Ambris was an Italian revolutionary syndicalist and trade union organiser. He campaigned for Italy's entry into the First World War and in 1920 drafted with Gabriele D'Annunzio the Charter of Carnaro, the constitution of the regency at Fiume.

azawagh.s: The Azawagh is a dry basin and a fossil river valley in the southern Sahara and Sahel, mainly in north-western Niger with parts in Mali and Algeria. It is grazing land of Tuareg and Fulani herders and gives its name to a breed of sighthound.

albert-kwok.s: Albert Kwok was a Chinese resistance leader in North Borneo during the Japanese occupation. He organised the Kinabalu Guerrillas and led the Jesselton Revolt of October 1943, in which rebels attacked Japanese posts in Jesselton, now Kota Kinabalu.

abul-futuh-al-hasan-ibn-jafar.s: Abu'l-Futuh al-Hasan ibn Ja'far was Sharif of Mecca from about 994 to 1039. In 1011, encouraged by the Jarrahid chief Mufarrij ibn Daghfal, he was proclaimed caliph at Ramla in Palestine in opposition to the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim.

al-fadl.s: Al Fadl was an Arab Bedouin tribe of the Syrian desert, descended from the Tayy and the Jarrahid family. Under the Mamluk Sultanate its chiefs, notably the Al Muhanna line, held the office of amir al-arab, commander of the Bedouin, guarding desert routes and frontiers.

atala-mosque.s: The Atala Mosque is a mosque in Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh, India, begun in the late 14th century and completed in 1408 under Ibrahim Shah Sharqi. Built on the site of a temple of the goddess Atala Devi, it has a massive arched gateway screen in front of its prayer hall, the…

abbey-of-saint-victor-marseille.s: The Abbey of Saint-Victor in Marseille, France, was founded around 415 by John Cassian near the tomb of the martyr Victor. Rebuilt after Saracen raids, it became one of the most powerful monasteries of southern France in the 11th century, with dependent priories across…

adelasia-of-torres.s: Adelasia of Torres was judge, or ruler, of the Judicate of Logudoro in northern Sardinia from 1236 until her death in 1259. Her first husband, Ubaldo Visconti, also ruled Gallura; in 1238 she married Enzo, son of Emperor Frederick II, who took the title King of Sardinia.

anita-garibaldi.s: Anita Garibaldi, born Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro in Santa Catarina, Brazil, was the companion and later wife of Giuseppe Garibaldi. She met him at Laguna in 1839 and fought beside him in the Ragamuffin War, in Uruguay and in the defence of the Roman Republic in 1849.

alimuly.s: The Alimuly are one of the three main tribal groupings of the Junior Zhuz, the western branch of the Kazakh people, made up of six clans. Their pastures lay in the steppes of western Kazakhstan around the Syr Darya and the Aral Sea, and they took part in the region's conflicts…

aitakkama.s: Aitakkama was king of Kadesh in western Syria during the Amarna period in the 14th century BCE. Letters from Egyptian vassals in the Amarna archive accuse him of going over to the Hittite Empire and raiding neighbours loyal to Egypt.

arjunawiwaha.s: The Arjunawiwaha, "Arjuna's Wedding", is an Old Javanese poem (kakawin) written around 1030 by Mpu Kanwa at the court of King Airlangga in East Java. Based on an episode of the Mahabharata, it tells of Arjuna's penance, his resistance to temptation and his victory over a demon…

abarkuh.s: Abarkuh is a town in Yazd Province in central Iran, on old routes between Yazd, Shiraz and Isfahan. In the 11th century it was granted with Yazd to the Kakuyid prince Faramurz by the Seljuks, and it later belonged to the atabegs of Yazd.

abonnema.s: Abonnema is a town in Rivers State in the Niger Delta of Nigeria. It was founded in the early 1880s by Kalabari people who left their old capital, Elem Kalabari, after a civil war and rivalry with the Bonny Kingdom.

amanyanabo.s: Amanyanabo, meaning owner of the town, is the title of the traditional rulers of the Ijaw city-states of the eastern Niger Delta, such as Kalabari, Bonny, Nembe and Okrika. The Amanyanabo ruled with the heads of the trading houses that dominated the slave and later palm-oil…

accuta-vikkanta.s: Accuta Vikkanta was a king of the Kalabhra family in the Kaveri region of southern India, known from the Pali writings of the Buddhist scholar Buddhadatta in the 5th century. Buddhadatta describes him as ruling the Chola country while Buddhist monasteries flourished there.

ashikaga-mitsukane.s: Ashikaga Mitsukane was the third Kamakura kubo, the shogunate's governor-general of the Kanto, from 1398 to 1409. Like his father Ujimitsu he resented the authority of the shogun in Kyoto and was suspected of plotting with the rebel Ouchi Yoshihiro in 1399.

ashikaga-ujimitsu.s: Ashikaga Ujimitsu was the second Kamakura kubo, the shogunate's governor-general of the Kanto, from 1367 to 1398. He suppressed revolts by Kanto warrior families and enlarged the authority of his office, but was suspected of ambitions to replace his cousin, the shogun Ashikaga…

ashikaga-yoshinori.s: Ashikaga Yoshinori was the sixth shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate, ruling from 1429 to 1441. Chosen by lot from among the sons of Yoshimitsu, he governed autocratically, crushed the Kamakura kubo Ashikaga Mochiuji in the Eikyo Rebellion and punished opponents harshly.

aspasioi.s: The Aspasioi were a people of the hill valleys north-east of the Kabul river, in the region of the Kunar and Bajaur, whom Alexander the Great fought in 327 BCE. Arrian describes fierce resistance in which Alexander was wounded and large herds of cattle were captured.

assakenoi.s: The Assakenoi were a people of the Swat and Buner valleys in what is now northern Pakistan, whom Alexander the Great fought in 327 BCE. Their capital, Massaga, fell after a hard siege in which their queen Cleophis surrendered, and fugitives held out on the rock of Aornos.

agastya.s: Agastya is a revered sage of Hindu tradition, credited with hymns of the Rigveda and celebrated in the Ramayana and the Puranas. Legend says he crossed the Vindhya mountains to bring Vedic learning to the south, and Tamil tradition counts him as the father of Tamil grammar.

aliyu-babba.s: Aliyu Babba was Emir of Kano in northern Nigeria from 1894 to 1903. He came to power after winning a civil war over the succession, and ruled as a vassal of the Sokoto Caliphate.

annals-of-the-kaqchikels.s: The Annals of the Kaqchikels is a chronicle written in the Kaqchikel Maya language in Latin script by members of the Xajil family in the late 16th century. It traces the history of the Kaqchikel people from their origin myths and migrations to the founding of Iximche, the…

aktekke-mosque.s: The Aktekke Mosque is a 14th-century mosque in Karaman, central Anatolia, built under the Karamanid ruler Alaeddin Bey on the site of an earlier dervish lodge. It is linked to the family of the poet Rumi, whose mother is traditionally said to be buried there, and is also known…

ali-mirza-karkiya.s: Ali Mirza Karkiya was a ruler of the Karkiya dynasty of Zaydi sayyids in eastern Gilan, on Iran's Caspian coast, with his seat at Lahijan. From 1494 to 1499 he sheltered the young Ismail, heir of the Safavid order, against the Aq Qoyunlu.

avantivarman.s: Avantivarman was king of Kashmir from 855 to 883 and founder of the Utpala dynasty, which replaced the Karkota line. His reign was remembered as a time of recovery: his engineer Suyya drained marshes and regulated the Jhelum to win new farmland, and he founded the town of…

agum-ii.s: Agum II, also called Agum-kakrime, was an early Kassite king of Babylonia in the 16th century BCE. He is known from an inscription, preserved in a later copy, claiming that he brought back the statue of Marduk to Babylon after it had been carried off, apparently after the…

alexander-burnes.s: Alexander Burnes was a Scottish officer and explorer in the service of the East India Company. His journey through Afghanistan to Bukhara in 1831–1833, described in his best-selling Travels into Bokhara, made him famous.

azare.s: Azare is a town in Bauchi State in northern Nigeria. It became the seat of the Katagum Emirate, founded during the Fulani jihad of the early 19th century, and the Emir of Katagum still lives there.

askot.s: Askot is a small town in Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand, India, near the borders with Nepal and Tibet. After the Katyuri kingdom broke up, a branch of the Katyuri dynasty, the Rajwars, ruled the surrounding estate from Askot for centuries under the Chand kings and later…

almaty.s: Almaty is the largest city of Kazakhstan, at the foot of the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains in the south-east of the country. Founded as the Russian fort of Verny in 1854, it was renamed Alma-Ata in 1921 and became capital of the Kazakh republic in 1929.

ahmad-yasawi.s: Ahmad Yasawi was a Turkic Sufi poet and teacher of the 12th century, based at the town of Yasi, now Turkistan, in southern Kazakhstan. His order, the Yasawiyya, and his Turkic devotional verse spread Islam among the nomads of the steppe.

astana.s: Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan, on the Ishim River in the north of the country. Founded as the Russian fort of Akmolinsk in 1830, it was renamed Tselinograd during the Virgin Lands campaign and became the capital in 1997.

astana-cemetery.s: The Astana Cemetery is an ancient burial ground near the ruins of Gaochang, east of Turpan in Xinjiang, China. Its tombs, used from about the 3rd to the 8th century, have preserved silk, figurines, paintings and thousands of paper documents, many reused to make burial garments.

abdullah-mukarram-shah.s: Abdullah Mukarram Shah was sultan of Kedah on the Malay Peninsula from 1778 to 1797. Seeking protection against Siam and Burma, he allowed Francis Light of the British East India Company to occupy Penang in 1786.

alor-setar.s: Alor Setar is the capital of the state of Kedah in north-western Peninsular Malaysia, on the Kedah River amid the rice plains of the north. It became the royal seat of the sultans of Kedah in the 18th century and remains the home of the state's ruler.

anglo-siamese-treaty-of-1909.s: The Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 was an agreement signed in Bangkok by which Siam transferred its claims over the northern Malay states of Kedah, Kelantan, Terengganu and Perlis to Britain. In return Britain gave up most of its extraterritorial rights in Siam and provided a…

ati-atihan-festival.s: The Ati-Atihan is a festival held each January in Kalibo, Aklan, on the island of Panay in the Philippines, in honour of the Santo Niño. Participants paint their faces black and dance in the streets in costume.

aghoreshwara-temple.s: The Aghoreshwara Temple is a stone temple to Shiva at Ikkeri in the Shimoga district of Karnataka, India. It was built by the Keladi Nayakas when Ikkeri was their capital in the 16th century, and combines Hoysala, Vijayanagara and other styles.

ahaggar-mountains.s: The Ahaggar, or Hoggar, Mountains are a highland of volcanic peaks and plateaus in southern Algeria, in the central Sahara. They are the homeland of the Kel Ahaggar Tuareg, and Tamanrasset is the main town.

air-mountains.s: The Aïr Mountains are a massif of granite and volcanic highlands in northern Niger, in the Sahara. They are the homeland of Tuareg groups such as the Kel Ewey, and the Sultanate of Agadez lies on their southern edge.

ayia-irini-kea.s: Ayia Irini is a Bronze Age settlement on a small peninsula in the bay of Agios Nikolaos on the island of Kea, in the Cyclades, Greece. Occupied from about the 4th millennium BCE, it was a fortified town with strong Minoan and later Mycenaean links.

arabshahid-dynasty.s: The Arabshahids were a Chinggisid dynasty descended from Shiban that ruled Khwarazm, the Khanate of Khiva, from 1511. Founded by the brothers Ilbars and Balbars, it ruled first from Urgench and from the 17th century from Khiva.

ahar-iran.s: Ahar is a city in East Azerbaijan province of north-western Iran, north-east of Tabriz, the main town of the Qaradagh or Arasbaran region. It is known for the shrine of the 13th-century Sufi Sheikh Shihab al-Din Ahari, a complex enlarged under the Safavids.

abbas-mirza.s: Abbas Mirza was the crown prince of Qajar Iran and governor of Azerbaijan, based at Tabriz. He commanded Iranian armies in the Russo-Persian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828, which ended with the loss of the South Caucasus in the treaties of Gulistan and Turkmenchay.

asirgarh-fort.s: Asirgarh is a hill fortress in Burhanpur district of Madhya Pradesh, India, commanding the pass between the Narmada and Tapti valleys and long called the key to the Deccan. The Faruqi rulers of Khandesh held it from the early 15th century.

ahmed-urabi.s: Ahmed Urabi was an Egyptian army officer who led a nationalist movement against the Khedive Tewfik and European control of Egypt's finances. Of peasant origin, he opposed the dominance of Turco-Circassian officers and became minister of war in 1882.

anton-denikin.s: Anton Denikin was a Russian general and a leading commander of the White movement in the Russian Civil War. As head of the Armed Forces of South Russia he advanced on Moscow in 1919, taking much of Ukraine, but was defeated by the Red Army near Oryol and driven back to Crimea.

alfred-meyer-waldeck.s: Alfred Meyer-Waldeck was a German naval officer and the last governor of the Kiautschou Bay concession in China, from 1911. When Japan, supported by British troops, attacked in 1914, he defended Tsingtao through the siege until he surrendered on 7 November 1914.

aranuka.s: Aranuka is a small atoll in the central Gilbert Islands of Kiribati, near Abemama, made up of two main islets around a lagoon. In the 19th century the rulers of Abemama, Tem Baiteke and his son Tem Binoka, brought it under their kingdom, which was absorbed into the British…

armagh.s: Armagh is a city in County Armagh, Northern Ireland, near the ancient royal site of Emain Macha, Navan Fort. By tradition Saint Patrick founded his principal church there in the 5th century, and it became the seat of the primate of all Ireland, a role now held by both the…

atbara-river.s: The Atbara is a river of north-eastern Africa, about 800 kilometres long, which rises in the Ethiopian Highlands near Lake Tana and joins the Nile at the town of Atbara in Sudan, the Nile's last tributary. It floods in summer and shrinks to pools in the dry season.

achaea.s: Achaea is a region in the northern Peloponnese of Greece, along the southern shore of the Gulf of Corinth, with its chief city at Patras. In antiquity it held twelve small cities whose federation, the Achaean League, became a leading power in Greece in the 3rd century BCE.

aja-people.s: The Aja are a Gbe-speaking people of southern Benin and Togo, related to the Fon and Ewe. Their traditional centre was Tado, near the Mono river in Togo, from which migrants are said to have founded Allada, and the royal houses of Dahomey and Porto-Novo in turn traced their…

awraba.s: The Awraba were a Berber tribal confederation of north-western Africa. In the 7th century their leader Kusaila, a Christian, led resistance to the Arab conquest and defeated and killed the Arab commander Uqba ibn Nafi in 683.

abu-al-muhajir-dinar.s: Abu al-Muhajir Dinar was an Umayyad commander and governor of Ifriqiya from about 674 to 681. A freedman client of the governor of Egypt, he replaced Uqba ibn Nafi and sought alliance with the Berbers, winning over the Awraba chief Kusaila, who converted to Islam.

ankole-agreement.s: The Ankole Agreement was signed in 1901 between Britain and the king and chiefs of Ankole in present-day south-western Uganda. Modelled on the Buganda Agreement of 1900, it confirmed the mugabe and his chiefs under British protection, fixed the kingdom's boundaries and added…

arles.s: Arles is a city on the Rhône in Provence, southern France, near the head of the river's delta. As Roman Arelate it was a leading city of Gaul, with an amphitheatre and theatre that still stand, and an imperial residence in the 4th century.

artaxiad-dynasty.s: The Artaxiad dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Armenia from about 189 BCE to the early 1st century CE. Its founder, Artaxias I, a former Seleucid governor, declared independence after Antiochus III's defeat at Magnesia and built a new capital at Artaxata.
