artaxata.s: Artaxata was the capital of ancient Armenia, founded by Artaxias I in the early 2nd century BCE on the Araxes river, near the modern town of Artashat. Ancient writers say Hannibal advised on its site.

armavir-ancient-city.s: Armavir was an ancient city in the Ararat plain of Armenia, near the Araxes river. It grew on the site of the Urartian fortress of Argishtihinili, founded in the 8th century BCE, and became the capital of the Orontid kings of Armenia before they moved to Yervandashat.

artaxias-i.s: Artaxias I was the founder of the Artaxiad dynasty of Armenia. A general serving the Seleucid king Antiochus III, he declared himself king after the Seleucid defeat at the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE and united the Armenian-speaking lands, setting boundary stones that still…

amynander.s: Amynander was king of the Athamanians in the mountains of north-western Greece around the end of the 3rd and start of the 2nd century BCE. He joined Rome against Philip V of Macedon in the Second Macedonian War and acted as an intermediary, then sided with Antiochus III in 191…

athamanians.s: The Athamanians were an ancient people of the Pindus mountains in north-western Greece, living around the upper Achelous between Epirus, Thessaly and Aetolia. Usually counted among the Epirote tribes, they were ruled by their own kings and formed a small independent kingdom in…

atholl.s: Atholl is a historic district of the central Highlands of Scotland, in northern Perthshire, covering the valleys of the Tay, Tummel and Garry. Its name, recorded as Athfotla, is usually interpreted as 'New Ireland'.

amadou-bamba.s: Amadou Bamba was a Senegalese Sufi teacher and founder of the Mouride brotherhood. Preaching work, prayer and non-violent devotion, he founded the holy city of Touba in 1887 and drew large numbers of followers, which alarmed the French colonial authorities, who exiled him to…

akenzua-ii.s: Akenzua II was the Oba of Benin in southern Nigeria from 1933 until his death in 1978. The son of Eweka II, he continued his father's revival of the monarchy and its court institutions after the British conquest of 1897, and he took part in Nigerian regional politics in the…

avranchin.s: The Avranchin is the historic district around Avranches in south-western Normandy, France, facing Mont-Saint-Michel across the bay. In 867 Charles the Bald granted it with the Cotentin to the Breton king Salomon, but in 933 it passed to William Longsword of Normandy, fixing…

aethelflaed.s: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, was the eldest daughter of Alfred the Great and ruled English Mercia from the death of her husband Æthelred in 911 until her own death in 918. Working with her brother Edward the Elder, she built fortified burhs and led campaigns that recovered…

aleksandar-stamboliyski.s: Aleksandar Stamboliyski was a Bulgarian politician who led the Bulgarian Agrarian National Union and served as prime minister from 1919 to 1923. He had opposed Bulgaria's entry into the First World War, signed the Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine and carried out land reform and…

archelaus-of-cappadocia.s: Archelaus was the last king of Cappadocia, installed by Mark Antony in 36 BCE. A loyal client of Rome, he also received parts of Cilicia and Lesser Armenia from Augustus.

archelaus-i-of-macedon.s: Archelaus I was king of Macedon from about 413 to 399 BCE. He built roads and fortresses, strengthened the army and moved the royal seat from Aegae to Pella.

ariarathes-i-of-cappadocia.s: Ariarathes I was the Persian satrap of Cappadocia who kept control of the region after Alexander the Great conquered the Achaemenid Empire. In 322 BCE the regent Perdiccas invaded Cappadocia to install Eumenes, defeated Ariarathes and had him executed.

ariarathes-v-of-cappadocia.s: Ariarathes V Eusebes Philopator was king of Cappadocia from about 163 to 130 BCE. Educated in Greek culture, he was honoured at Athens and admired by philosophers of his time.

ariarathes-ii-of-cappadocia.s: Ariarathes II was the adopted son of the satrap Ariarathes I, who restored his family's rule in Cappadocia after his father's execution in 322 BCE. Around 301 BCE, with Armenian help, he drove out the Macedonian governor and re-established an independent principality in the…

ariarathid-dynasty.s: The Ariarathid dynasty ruled Cappadocia in central Anatolia from the late 4th century BCE until about 96 BCE. Of Persian origin, its kings, most of them named Ariarathes, mixed Iranian traditions with Greek culture and allied with Rome from the 2nd century BCE.

ariobarzanes-i-of-cappadocia.s: Ariobarzanes I Philoromaios was king of Cappadocia from about 95 to 63 BCE, chosen with Roman approval after the Ariarathid line ended. He was repeatedly driven out by Mithridates VI of Pontus and his ally Tigranes of Armenia and restored by Roman commanders, among them Sulla…

antalas.s: Antalas was a Berber chief who ruled a principality around Capsa (Gafsa) in southern Byzacena, in present-day Tunisia, in the 6th century. Around 530 he defeated a Vandal army sent by King Hilderic.

attambelos-vii.s: Attambelos VII was king of Characene, the trading kingdom at the head of the Persian Gulf, in the early 2nd century CE. When the Roman emperor Trajan advanced down the Tigris to the Gulf in 116 CE, Attambelos received him and submitted.

appuashu.s: Appuashu was king of Pirindu, a kingdom in the rugged west of Cilicia in southern Anatolia, in the 6th century BCE. A Babylonian chronicle relates that in 557 BCE Neriglissar of Babylon defeated him, pursued him through the mountains and captured his cities, including Ura and…

aberlemno.s: Aberlemno is a village in Angus, eastern Scotland, known for its group of Pictish carved stones. They include a symbol stone with the Pictish serpent and a churchyard cross-slab of the 8th century whose battle scene is often linked with the Pictish victory over the…

argonauts.s: The Argonauts were the band of heroes in Greek mythology who sailed with Jason on the ship Argo to Colchis, on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, to fetch the Golden Fleece. With the help of the Colchian princess Medea they took the fleece from King Aeetes.

antiochus-i-theos-of-commagene.s: Antiochus I Theos was king of Commagene from about 70 to 38 BCE. Claiming descent from both the Persian Achaemenids and the Seleucids, he created a royal cult that merged Greek and Persian gods with himself, and built the great tomb sanctuary on Mount Nemrut.

anglo-mysore-wars.s: The Anglo-Mysore Wars were four wars fought between the kingdom of Mysore and the British East India Company and its allies between 1767 and 1799. Under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan, Mysore was among the Company's strongest opponents in India.

arch-of-augustus-susa.s: The Arch of Augustus at Susa in Piedmont, Italy, was built in 9–8 BCE by Marcus Julius Cottius to mark his alliance with Augustus. Its inscription names Cottius as prefect and lists the Alpine peoples he governed.

ayarmaca.s: The Ayarmaca were an Andean people whose lordship, centred north-west of Cusco in Peru, was one of the main rivals of the early Inca kingdom. Inca traditions recorded by the Spanish tell of wars, captures and royal marriages between the two, and archaeology suggests they…

aimery-of-cyprus.s: Aimery of Lusignan was the first king of Cyprus and later also king of Jerusalem. He succeeded his brother Guy as ruler of Cyprus in 1194, obtained a royal crown from the Emperor Henry VI and was crowned king in 1197.

apries.s: Apries was a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty of Egypt, reigning from 589 to 570 BCE. He intervened in the Levant against Babylon and sent an army against the Greek colony of Cyrene, whose defeat at Irasa around 570 BCE provoked a mutiny.

apama-wife-of-magas.s: Apama was a daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus I who married Magas, ruler of Cyrene, and drew him into the Seleucid alliance against Ptolemy II. After Magas died, around 250 BCE, she opposed the planned marriage of their daughter Berenice to the future Ptolemy III and…

autonomist-party-dalmatia.s: The Autonomist Party was a political party in the Austrian Kingdom of Dalmatia, founded in the 1860s, that opposed union with Croatia and defended Dalmatia's separate status and the place of Italian language and culture. Supported mainly by Italian-speaking townspeople and…

al-khuraybah.s: Al-Khuraybah is an archaeological site in the AlUla valley of north-western Saudi Arabia, identified as ancient Dedan, the seat of the kingdoms of Dedan and Lihyan. Excavations have uncovered a sanctuary with a large stone basin and monumental statues of kings, and the nearby…

alula.s: AlUla is an oasis town in Medina Province, north-western Saudi Arabia, on the ancient incense route. Its valley was the seat of the kingdoms of Dedan and Lihyan in the 1st millennium BCE, and nearby lies Hegra, the Nabataean city that became Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage…

alhfrith.s: Alhfrith was a son of King Oswiu of Northumbria who ruled Deira as sub-king under his father from about 655. He married Cyneburh, a daughter of Penda of Mercia, and supported the Roman party at the Synod of Whitby in 664 as a patron of Wilfrid.

amlaib-conung.s: Amlaíb Conung was a Viking leader who, according to the Irish annals, arrived in Ireland in 853 and ruled the Norse of Dublin with Ímar. He raided widely in Ireland and northern Britain and in 870 took Dumbarton Rock, the fortress of Strathclyde, together with Ímar.

aldhelm.s: Aldhelm was an Anglo-Saxon scholar, poet and churchman, abbot of Malmesbury and from 705 the first bishop of Sherborne. Writing in an elaborate Latin style, he produced riddles, verse and a treatise on virginity, and he urged King Geraint of Dumnonia to adopt the Roman…

ardudwy.s: Ardudwy is a historic district of Merioneth in north-west Wales, a coastal strip between the Mawddach estuary and the Dwyryd beneath the Rhinog mountains. With Eifionydd it formed the early kingdom of Dunoding and later part of Gwynedd.

asser.s: Asser was a Welsh monk from St Davids who became an adviser to Alfred the Great of Wessex and later bishop of Sherborne. In 893 he wrote a Latin Life of King Alfred, the main source for Alfred's reign, which also records the submission of several south Welsh kings to Alfred in…

aethelthryth.s: Æthelthryth, also known as Etheldreda or Audrey, was an East Anglian princess, a daughter of King Anna. Twice married, the second time to Ecgfrith of Northumbria, she left her husband to become a nun and in 673 founded a double monastery at Ely, where she was abbess until her…

abdeen-palace.s: Abdeen Palace is a royal palace in central Cairo, built for Khedive Ismail and completed in 1874, and the main residence of Egypt's rulers until 1952. On 4 February 1942 British tanks surrounded it while Ambassador Miles Lampson forced King Farouk to appoint a Wafd government…

anglo-egyptian-treaty-of-1936.s: The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936 was an agreement between the United Kingdom and the Kingdom of Egypt. Britain recognised Egypt's independence and withdrew from most of the country, but kept a garrison of 10,000 troops in the Suez Canal Zone and the right to defend Egypt in war.

angles.s: The Angles were a Germanic people from the Anglia peninsula, in what is now Schleswig-Holstein, recorded by Tacitus in the 1st century. From the 5th century many settled in Britain, where they founded the kingdoms of East Anglia, Mercia, Deira and Bernicia, the last two later…

ariconium.s: Ariconium was a Romano-British town near Weston-under-Penyard, east of Ross-on-Wye in Herefordshire, England. It was a centre of iron-working that used ore from the Forest of Dean, and it gave its name to the post-Roman Welsh kingdom of Ergyng, later the English district of…

aescwine-of-essex.s: Æscwine is the traditional founder of the East Saxon royal line, placed by later sources in 527. Nothing certain is known of him, but the genealogies of the kings of Essex begin with him, and most of his descendants bore names beginning with S.

alagakkonara-family.s: The Alagakkonara, or Alakeshvara, were a powerful family of ministers in 14th- and early 15th-century Sri Lanka, of south Indian origin. Under the weak kings of Gampola they held real power, built the fortress of Kotte near Colombo and resisted the expansion of the Jaffna…

antonio-cecchi.s: Antonio Cecchi was an Italian explorer and colonial official. On an expedition to the Gibe region of south-western Ethiopia he and Giovanni Chiarini were held captive in the kingdom of Gera from 1879, where Chiarini died, until Cecchi's release in 1880.

ayung-river.s: The Ayung is the longest river on Bali, Indonesia, flowing south from the central highlands past Ubud to the sea near Sanur. Its deep gorge and terraced valleys lie on the western side of the old kingdom of Gianyar, and it is now known for its rice terraces and river rafting.

alkalawa.s: Alkalawa was the capital of the Hausa kingdom of Gobir, in what is now north-western Nigeria, from the 18th century. Its capture in 1808 by the forces of Usman dan Fodio, in which King Yunfa was killed, marked the defeat of Gobir in the Fulani jihad.

aneirin.s: Aneirin was a British poet of the late 6th century, named in the Historia Brittonum among the early poets of the Britons. He is credited with Y Gododdin, a series of elegies for the warriors of the kingdom of Gododdin who fell at the Battle of Catraeth, preserved in the…

andre-alvares-de-almada.s: André Álvares de Almada was a Cape Verdean trader and writer of Portuguese descent. His Brief Treatise on the Rivers of Guinea of 1594 describes the peoples, kingdoms and markets of the coast between the Senegal River and Sierra Leone, and is one of the main sources for the…

ambrosius-aurelianus.s: Ambrosius Aurelianus was a Romano-British war leader of the 5th century who, according to Gildas, rallied the Britons against the Anglo-Saxon invaders after the end of Roman rule. The Historia Brittonum made him a rival and successor of Vortigern, and in Geoffrey of Monmouth…

aberffraw.s: Aberffraw is a village on the south-west coast of Anglesey that served as the chief royal seat of the kings and princes of Gwynedd in the Middle Ages. Llywelyn the Great used the title 'Prince of Aberffraw and Lord of Snowdon' from about 1230.

acts-of-the-apostles.s: The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament, written by the author of the Gospel of Luke, probably late in the 1st century CE. It tells of the early Christian community in Jerusalem and the missions of Peter and Paul across the eastern Mediterranean to Rome.

andrew-ii-of-hungary.s: Andrew II was king of Hungary from 1205, of the Árpád dynasty. He led the Fifth Crusade to the Holy Land in 1217–1218 and spent heavily on wars in Galicia, granting away royal estates to his supporters.

auschwitz-concentration-camp.s: Auschwitz was the largest Nazi German concentration and extermination camp, built from 1940 near the Polish town of Oświęcim, which the Germans called Auschwitz. About 1.1 million people were murdered there, around a million of them Jews, most in the gas chambers of Auschwitz…

annals-of-inisfallen.s: The Annals of Inisfallen are a chronicle of medieval Irish history, preserved in a manuscript written largely in the late 11th century and continued by later hands into the 14th. They are associated with the monastery on Inisfallen in Lough Leane near Killarney and are a key…

austrian-littoral.s: The Austrian Littoral was a crown land of the Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary on the northern Adriatic, formed in 1849 from the coastal parts of the Kingdom of Illyria. It comprised the free city of Trieste, the Margraviate of Istria and the County of Gorizia and Gradisca,…

anglo-iraqi-war.s: The Anglo-Iraqi War was a British campaign in May 1941 against the government of Rashid Ali al-Gaylani, which had seized power in Iraq in a pro-Axis coup in April. After Iraqi forces besieged the RAF base at Habbaniya, British and Commonwealth troops relieved it and advanced…

abd-al-ilah.s: Abd al-Ilah was regent of Iraq from 1939 to 1953 for his young nephew King Faisal II, and remained crown prince and a dominant influence afterwards. A member of the Hashemite family and a firm ally of Britain, he fled Rashid Ali's coup in 1941 and returned with British troops.

amos-prophet.s: Amos was a Hebrew prophet of the 8th century BCE, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who preached in the northern Kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam II. The biblical Book of Amos records his attacks on the luxury of Samaria, the oppression of the poor and empty ritual, and his…

agostino-depretis.s: Agostino Depretis was an Italian statesman who served as prime minister several times between 1876 and 1887, leading the parliamentary Left after the fall of the Right in 1876. He became known for trasformismo, the practice of building majorities by absorbing deputies from the…

advocate-of-the-holy-sepulchre.s: Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre was the title taken by Godfrey of Bouillon after the crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, when he declined to be called king. According to tradition he refused to wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn a crown of thorns.

al-ashraf-khalil.s: Al-Ashraf Khalil was the Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria from 1290, son of Qalawun. In 1291 he besieged and stormed Acre, the last major stronghold of the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, and the remaining Frankish towns on the coast were abandoned within months.

aghsartan-i-of-kakheti.s: Aghsartan I was king of Kakheti and Hereti in eastern Georgia from 1058 to 1084. Faced with the Seljuk invasions, he submitted to Sultan Alp Arslan in 1068 and outwardly converted to Islam to keep his throne, while competing with the kings of Georgia for border lands.

aghsartan-ii-of-kakheti.s: Aghsartan II was the last king of Kakheti and Hereti in eastern Georgia, a vassal of the Seljuks. In 1104 nobles of Hereti seized him and handed him over to King David IV the Builder, who annexed his kingdom to the Kingdom of Georgia, a major step in David's unification of the…

allat.s: Allat was a pre-Islamic Arabian goddess worshipped widely across Arabia and the Syrian desert, from Ta'if to Palmyra and Hatra. In Palmyra she was identified with Athena, and in Mecca she was one of the three goddesses named in the Qur'an together with al-Uzza and Manat.

amnon-ben-tor.s: Amnon Ben-Tor is an Israeli archaeologist and professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who has directed renewed excavations at Tel Hazor since 1990. His work there uncovered Bronze Age palaces, statues and cuneiform tablets, and he has argued that the Canaanite city was…

amlapura.s: Amlapura is a town in eastern Bali, Indonesia, and the capital of Karangasem Regency. It was the seat of the rajas of Karangasem, who in the 18th century also ruled western Lombok, and the last kings built its palace, the Puri Agung Karangasem, and the nearby water palaces of…

abas-i-of-armenia.s: Abas I was king of Bagratid Armenia from about 929 to 953. Ruling from Kars, he restored order after the wars of the early 10th century, repelled an attack by the king of Abkhazia, and built the Church of the Holy Apostles at Kars.

ajatashatru.s: Ajatashatru was a king of Magadha in eastern India in the 5th century BCE, the son and successor of Bimbisara of the Haryanka dynasty. He conquered Kosala and the Vajji confederacy, fortified Pataligrama, the future Pataliputra, and made Magadha the leading power of the Ganges…

aethelberht-of-kent.s: Æthelberht was king of Kent from about 589 to 616 and the first English king to accept Christianity. Married to the Frankish Christian princess Bertha, he welcomed Augustine's mission from Pope Gregory I in 597 and gave it Canterbury as its base.

augustine-of-canterbury.s: Augustine of Canterbury was a monk from Rome sent by Pope Gregory I to convert the Anglo-Saxons. Landing in Kent in 597, he baptised King Æthelberht and became the first archbishop of Canterbury, founding the cathedral and the monastery later named after him.

augustine-of-hippo.s: Augustine of Hippo was a Christian theologian and bishop from Roman North Africa, born at Thagaste in Numidia. After teaching rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and Milan, he converted to Christianity in 386 and became bishop of Hippo Regius in 395, where he wrote against the…

ayaz-kala.s: Ayaz-Kala is a group of fortresses on and around a hill at the edge of the Kyzylkum Desert in Karakalpakstan, north-western Uzbekistan. Built mainly between the 4th century BCE and the 7th century CE, they guarded the irrigated lands of ancient Khwarazm against nomads, and the…

al-harith-ibn-amr.s: al-Harith ibn Amr was the most powerful king of Kinda in central Arabia in the early 6th century. He extended Kindite rule over the tribes of Najd and, according to Arab tradition, was installed at al-Hira by the Sasanian king Kavad I in place of the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III.

astarte.s: Astarte was a major goddess of the ancient Levant, worshipped by Phoenicians, Canaanites and others as a deity of love, fertility and war. Known in Phoenician as Ashtart and related to the Mesopotamian Ishtar, she had great temples at Sidon, Tyre and Kition in Cyprus, and the…

andreas-victor-michiels.s: Andreas Victor Michiels was a Dutch general who served in the Dutch East Indies. He led campaigns in western Sumatra in the 1830s and 1840s and commanded the third Dutch military expedition to Bali in 1849, which took Jagaraga in Buleleng.

anathapindika.s: Anathapindika, whose personal name was Sudatta, was a wealthy merchant of Shravasti in Kosala and the Buddha's foremost lay supporter. According to Buddhist tradition he bought the Jetavana grove from Prince Jeta by covering its ground with gold coins and built a monastery…

ayodhya.s: Ayodhya is a city on the Sarayu River in Uttar Pradesh, India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace and capital of Rama in the Ramayana. Associated with the ancient kingdom of Kosala and the nearby city of Saketa, it is also sacred to Jains as the birthplace of several…

anxi-protectorate.s: The Anxi Protectorate, or Protectorate General to Pacify the West, was the Tang dynasty's military government for the Tarim Basin and the lands farther west. Founded in 640 at Jiaohe after the conquest of Gaochang, it moved to Kucha in 648 and oversaw the Four Garrisons of Anxi.

alchi-monastery.s: Alchi Monastery is a Buddhist temple complex beside the Indus in Ladakh, India, traditionally attributed to the translator Rinchen Zangpo but built mainly between the late 11th and early 13th centuries. Its temples, including the three-storeyed Sumtsek, keep some of the finest…

akitoye.s: Akitoye was Oba of Lagos from 1841 to 1845 and again from 1851 to 1853. Driven out by his nephew Kosoko in 1845, he sought British support, and in 1851 a British naval force bombarded Lagos, removed Kosoko and restored him.

awori.s: The Awori are a Yoruba subgroup of the coastal lagoons of south-western Nigeria, in present-day Lagos and Ogun states. According to tradition they came from Ile-Ife and founded settlements including Isheri, Otta and Lagos, which they called Eko.

aoife-macmurrough.s: Aoife MacMurrough was the daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, king of Leinster. Under the agreement that brought Anglo-Norman help to her father, she married Richard de Clare, known as Strongbow, at Waterford in 1170, and through her Strongbow claimed the succession to Leinster.

alfonso-v-of-leon.s: Alfonso V was king of León from 999 to 1028, coming to the throne as a child after the death of his father Bermudo II. He rebuilt the city of León after the raids of Almanzor and in 1017 granted it a fuero, one of the earliest Spanish codes of municipal law.

alyattes.s: Alyattes was king of Lydia from around 610 to 560 BCE, of the Mermnad dynasty, and father of Croesus. He expelled the Cimmerians from Anatolia, destroyed Smyrna, and fought a long war with the Median Empire that ended after the solar eclipse of 585 BCE with the Halys river as…

agathocles-son-of-lysimachus.s: Agathocles was the eldest son of Lysimachus, king of Thrace, Macedon and western Asia Minor, and a successful commander for his father. Around 283 BCE Lysimachus had him executed on a charge of treason, reportedly at the instigation of his stepmother Arsinoe II.

aigai.s: Aigai, or Aegae, was the first capital and royal burial place of the Kingdom of Macedon, at modern Vergina in northern Greece. Excavations by Manolis Andronikos in 1977 uncovered royal tombs, one widely attributed to Philip II, who was assassinated in the city's theatre in 336…

argead-dynasty.s: The Argead dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Macedon from around the 7th century BCE until about 310 BCE. Its kings claimed descent from Temenos of Argos and through him from Heracles, a claim that allowed Alexander I to compete at the Olympic Games.

al-jawf-yemen.s: Al-Jawf is a region of northern Yemen, a broad desert valley north-east of Sanaa and north of Marib, now a governorate. In the 1st millennium BCE it held the city-states of the Kingdom of Ma'in, including Qarnawu and Yathill (Baraqish), which grew rich on the incense trade.

anglo-manipur-war.s: The Anglo-Manipur War was a brief conflict in 1891 between the British Empire and the Kingdom of Manipur. After a palace coup by Tikendrajit Singh, a British attempt to arrest him led to the killing of the Chief Commissioner of Assam, James Quinton, and other officials at Imphal.

anglo-portuguese-treaty-of-1891.s: The Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1891, signed in Lisbon on 11 June 1891, fixed the borders between Portugal's colonies of Mozambique and Angola and the British spheres in central Africa. It followed the British Ultimatum of 1890, which had forced Portugal to abandon its claim to…

aedemon.s: Aedemon was a freedman of King Ptolemy of Mauretania who led a revolt after the emperor Caligula had Ptolemy executed in 40 CE. Roman forces under Suetonius Paulinus and Hosidius Geta put down the rising in 41–42 CE, after which Claudius annexed the kingdom and divided it into…

afon-mawddach.s: The Mawddach is a river of Gwynedd in north-west Wales that flows from the hills north of Dolgellau into Cardigan Bay at Barmouth through a wide, wooded estuary. The estuary is crossed by Barmouth Bridge, a timber railway viaduct opened in 1867.

aethelred-lord-of-the-mercians.s: Æthelred was the ruler of English Mercia from about 881 until his death in 911, after the Danes had taken the eastern half of the kingdom. He accepted the overlordship of Alfred the Great of Wessex, married Alfred's daughter Æthelflæd and led Mercian forces against the Vikings.

angus-of-moray.s: Angus was mormaer of Moray and a grandson, through his mother, of King Lulach. In 1130, while King David I was in England, he invaded the kingdom with Malcolm, son of Alexander I, but was defeated and killed at Stracathro in Angus.

annals-of-loch-ce.s: The Annals of Loch Cé are an Irish chronicle in Irish and Latin covering events from 1014 to 1590, chiefly in Connacht. They were compiled in the 1580s for Brian MacDermot, lord of Moylurg, whose seat was an island fortress on Lough Key in County Roscommon.

abba-el-i.s: Abba-El I was king of Yamhad, with its capital at Aleppo, in the 18th century BCE. After putting down a revolt in the city of Irridu, he destroyed it and gave his brother Yarim-Lim the city of Alalakh in exchange, creating a dependent kingdom there.

amuq-valley.s: The Amuq Valley is a fertile plain in Hatay province, southern Turkey, around the lower Orontes near Antakya. It was densely settled from the Neolithic onwards, and its mounds include Alalakh, capital of the Bronze Age kingdom of Mukish, and Tell Tayinat, capital of the Iron…

alalakh.s: Alalakh is a Bronze Age city mound at Tell Atchana near Antakya in southern Turkey, in the Amuq plain. It was the capital of the kingdom of Mukish, under Yamhad in the 18th century BCE and later under Mitanni and the Hittites.

agamemnon.s: Agamemnon is the legendary king of Mycenae who, in Homer's Iliad, led the Greek army against Troy. Son of Atreus and brother of Menelaus, he sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia for a fair wind and on his return was murdered by his wife Clytemnestra, a story dramatised by Aeschylus.

argolid.s: The Argolid is the plain and peninsula in the north-eastern Peloponnese of Greece around the Gulf of Argolis. In the Bronze Age it held the Mycenaean centres of Mycenae and Tiryns, and in classical times the cities of Argos, Epidaurus, Troezen and Hermione.

aguascalientes.s: Aguascalientes is one of the smallest states of Mexico, in the centre-north of the country, with its capital at the city of the same name, founded in 1575 as a waystation on the silver road. In colonial times it belonged to New Galicia and later to the intendancy of Zacatecas.

albreda.s: Albreda is a village on the north bank of the Gambia River in The Gambia, near James Island. From the late 17th century it was a French trading post that competed with the English fort on James Island for the trade of the kingdom of Niumi, including the slave trade.

anambra-river.s: The Anambra River, also called the Omambala, is a river of south-eastern Nigeria that flows into the Niger near Onitsha. Its valley is the setting of Nri traditions, which say the culture hero Eri descended from the sky near its banks.

anambra-state.s: Anambra State is a state of south-eastern Nigeria, created in 1976 and named after the Anambra River, with its capital at Awka and its largest commercial centre at Onitsha. Its population is overwhelmingly Igbo.

anglo-norman-invasion-of-ireland.s: The Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland began in 1169, when Norman knights from Wales landed to support the deposed king of Leinster, Diarmait Mac Murchada. Led from 1170 by Richard de Clare, known as Strongbow, they took Waterford and Dublin, and in 1171 King Henry II of England…

aghaboe.s: Aghaboe is a village in County Laois, Ireland, and the site of a monastery founded by Saint Canice in the 6th century. It became the chief church of the kingdom of Osraige and the first seat of the diocese of Ossory, before the see moved to Kilkenny in the late 12th century.

apollo.s: Apollo is a major god of Greek and Roman religion, son of Zeus and Leto and twin brother of Artemis. He was god of prophecy, music, healing, archery and light, and his oracles at Delphi, Didyma and Claros were consulted by cities and kings across the Greek world.

audoleon.s: Audoleon was king of Paeonia from about 315 to 285 BCE, son of King Patraos. He issued silver coins showing Apollo and a horseman, and with help from Cassander he repelled an attack by the Autariatae.

attalid-dynasty.s: The Attalid dynasty ruled the Hellenistic kingdom of Pergamon in western Asia Minor from 282 to 133 BCE. Founded by Philetaerus and named after his father Attalus, it included Eumenes I, Attalus I and Eumenes II.

aleksander-kakowski.s: Aleksander Kakowski was a Polish Catholic prelate, Archbishop of Warsaw from 1913 and a cardinal from 1919. In 1917–18 he was one of the three members of the Regency Council of the German- and Austrian-sponsored Kingdom of Poland, which in November 1918 handed power to Józef…

agudas.s: The Agudás are the descendants of Afro-Brazilians, many of them freed slaves, and Brazilian traders who settled on the coast of present-day Benin, Togo and Nigeria in the 19th century. They brought Catholicism, Islam, Portuguese surnames and Brazilian-style architecture to…

amm.s: Amm was the national god of the ancient South Arabian kingdom of Qataban in Yemen, often thought to be a moon god. The Qatabanians called themselves the 'children of Amm', and his temples stood in the capital, Timna, and other towns.

avarua.s: Avarua is the capital of the Cook Islands, on the north coast of Rarotonga. It grew around the London Missionary Society station and the seat of the Makea ariki, whose leading title holder was regarded by Europeans as the island's monarch.

annales-cambriae.s: The Annales Cambriae, or Welsh Annals, are a set of Latin chronicles compiled in Wales, the oldest version probably at St Davids in the 10th century. They record events from the mid-5th century onwards, including the battles of Badon and Camlann, the deaths of kings and the…

almaqah.s: Almaqah was the chief god of the ancient South Arabian kingdom of Saba, worshipped as the national deity of the Sabaeans. His main sanctuary was the Awwam Temple near Marib, and his cult also spread to Dʿmt in the Ethiopian highlands, where the Great Temple of Yeha honoured him.

awwam-temple.s: The Awwam Temple, known in Arabic as Mahram Bilqis, is the great sanctuary of the god Almaqah near Marib in Yemen. Built and enlarged from the early 1st millennium BCE, it has an oval walled enclosure and a monumental pillared hall, and its walls carry hundreds of Sabaean…

ajax-the-great.s: Ajax the Great is a hero of Greek mythology, son of Telamon king of Salamis, who fights in the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad as the mightiest Greek warrior after Achilles. After losing the contest for Achilles' armour to Odysseus he took his own life, a story told in Sophocles'…

ajax-the-lesser.s: Ajax the Lesser is a hero of Greek mythology, son of Oileus and leader of the Locrians in the Trojan War. During the sack of Troy he dragged Cassandra from the statue of Athena, a sacrilege for which the goddess wrecked him on his way home.

albert-steinberger.s: Albert Barnes Steinberger was an American adventurer who became premier of Samoa. Sent to the islands on a special mission by the United States government in 1873, he returned in 1875 and drew up a constitution under which Malietoa Laupepa was king and he himself premier.

apia.s: Apia is the capital and largest town of Samoa, on the north coast of Upolu. It grew in the 19th century as the main harbour and trading post of the islands, where German, British and American interests competed, and in March 1889 a hurricane wrecked the German and American…

aby-lagoon.s: Aby Lagoon is a lagoon in south-eastern Ivory Coast, near the border with Ghana, linked to the Gulf of Guinea near Assinie. Its shores were settled by the Agni of the kingdom of Sanwi, whose capital Krinjabo lay nearby, and by the older Ehotile and Essouma peoples.

assinie.s: Assinie is a coastal town in south-eastern Ivory Coast, on the sandbar between the Aby lagoon and the Gulf of Guinea. It was an early trading place where Europeans exchanged guns, cloth and spirits for gold and ivory, and the French briefly held a fort there in the early 18th…

ankober.s: Ankober is a town in the highlands of North Shewa in central Ethiopia, on the edge of the escarpment above the Afar lowlands. From the 18th century it was the capital of the rulers of Shewa, and under Sahle Selassie in the 19th century it received British and French diplomatic…

antipope-anacletus-ii.s: Anacletus II, born Pietro Pierleoni, was an antipope from 1130 to 1138. Elected by a majority of the cardinals in a disputed election against Innocent II, he held Rome but was rejected by most of Europe, led by Bernard of Clairvaux.

aristocyprus.s: Aristocyprus was king of Soloi in Cyprus in the early 5th century BCE, son of Philocyprus. He joined the Cypriot revolt against Persia led by Onesilus of Salamis and was killed in the battle near Salamis in 497 BCE.

amanuban.s: Amanuban was a traditional Atoni kingdom in the interior of West Timor, Indonesia, centred on Niki Niki. Long recognised as one of the larger domains of the island, its rulers resisted Dutch control until the early 20th century.

atoni.s: The Atoni, or Atoin Meto, are the largest people of West Timor, Indonesia, speaking the Uab Meto language. Traditionally they lived in dispersed hamlets in the mountains, growing maize and rice, and were organised in domains under rulers with ritual and political roles, such…

adolfo-suarez.s: Adolfo Suárez was a Spanish politician who as prime minister from 1976 to 1981 led the transition from Franco's dictatorship to democracy. Appointed by King Juan Carlos I, he pushed through the Law for Political Reform, legalised political parties including the Communists, won…

aethelwealh-of-sussex.s: Æthelwealh was king of the South Saxons in the later 7th century and the first Christian king of Sussex. Baptised in Mercia with King Wulfhere as his sponsor, he received the Isle of Wight and the Meon valley from him, and gave Wilfrid land at Selsey to found a monastery.

abel-aubert-du-petit-thouars.s: Abel Aubert du Petit-Thouars was a French naval officer who extended French power in the Pacific. In 1842 he took possession of the Marquesas Islands and imposed a French protectorate on Tahiti under Queen Pōmare IV, and in 1843 he declared Tahiti annexed, a step disavowed by…

anuradhapura.s: Anuradhapura is a city in north-central Sri Lanka that was the island's first great capital, from about the 4th century BCE until the 11th century CE. The chronicles credit its founding to King Pandukabhaya, and it grew into a centre of Theravada Buddhism with vast stupas such…

ambhi.s: Ambhi was the king of Taxila in north-western India in the late 4th century BCE, known to the Greeks as Taxiles and also as Omphis. A rival of the neighbouring Paurava king Porus, he submitted to Alexander the Great in 326 BCE and supplied troops and elephants for the campaign…

annaly.s: Annaly was a medieval Irish lordship in the northern part of Tethba, roughly the area of modern County Longford. From the 11th and 12th centuries it was ruled by the Uí Fergail, later known as the O'Farrells, who kept it largely free of the Anglo-Norman lords of Meath.

ardagh-county-longford.s: Ardagh is a village in County Longford, Ireland, whose church is traditionally said to have been founded by Saint Mel, a disciple of Saint Patrick, in the 5th century. It became the seat of the medieval diocese of Ardagh, and the ruins of a small early stone church survive there.

arris.s: Arris is a town in the Aurès mountains of north-eastern Algeria, in Batna Province. A Latin inscription found there commemorates the Berber ruler Masties, who claimed to have been duke and emperor and to have kept faith with both Romans and Moors.

apahida.s: Apahida is a village near Cluj-Napoca in Transylvania, Romania, known for princely graves of the late 5th century. Finds made in 1889 and 1968 included gold jewellery, garnet-inlaid fittings and horse harness, buried with members of the Gepid elite after the collapse of Hunnic…

ardaric.s: Ardaric was king of the Gepids in the mid 5th century and, according to Jordanes, one of Attila's most trusted subject rulers. After Attila's death in 453 he led the revolt of the subject peoples against his sons and won the Battle of Nedao in 454.

attila.s: Attila was ruler of the Huns from 434, at first jointly with his brother Bleda, and sole ruler from about 445 until his death in 453. From the Hungarian plain he dominated many Germanic and steppe peoples, extracted heavy tribute from the Eastern Roman Empire and ravaged the…

artanuji.s: Artanuji is a medieval fortress town in the historic Georgian region of Klarjeti, today Ardanuç in Artvin Province, north-eastern Turkey. Traditionally founded by King Vakhtang Gorgasali, it was rebuilt in the early 9th century by the Bagratid prince Ashot I and became the…

arwald.s: Arwald was the last king of the Isle of Wight and the last pagan king in Anglo-Saxon England. In 686 Caedwalla of Wessex conquered the island and killed him, and, as Bede records, his two young brothers were baptised and then executed.

aistulf.s: Aistulf was king of the Lombards from 749 to 756, previously duke of Friuli. In 751 he captured Ravenna, ending the Byzantine Exarchate, and then threatened Rome, which led Pope Stephen II to seek help from the Frankish king Pepin the Short.

alhflaed.s: Alhflæd was a daughter of King Oswiu of Northumbria who married Peada, ruler of the Middle Angles, around 653, on condition that he accept baptism. The marriage brought Northumbrian missionaries into Mercian lands.

altava.s: Altava was a Roman town in Mauretania Caesariensis, today Ouled Mimoun near Tlemcen in north-western Algeria. An inscription there dated 508 names Masuna as king of the peoples of the Moors and Romans, the main evidence for a Romano-Berber kingdom in the region.

andeca.s: Andeca was the last ruler of the Suebic kingdom in Gallaecia. In 584 he overthrew the young king Eboric, son of Miro, and married Miro's widow.

amalaberga.s: Amalaberga was a niece of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, the daughter of his sister Amalafrida. Around 510 she married Herminafrid, king of the Thuringians, linking Thuringia to Theodoric's alliance system.

anglicanism.s: Anglicanism is the Christian tradition that grew from the Church of England after its break with Rome under Henry VIII in the 1530s. It combines Catholic church order with Protestant teaching, expressed in the Book of Common Prayer.

abbey-of-saint-maurice-dagaune.s: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune is a monastery in the Rhône valley of the Swiss canton of Valais, built at the traditional site of the martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion. Refounded in 515 by the Burgundian king Sigismund, it is one of the oldest continuously…

argishti-i.s: Argishti I was king of Urartu from about 786 to 764 BCE, the son and successor of Menua. His annals, carved in the rock of Van, record campaigns north into Transcaucasia and against the Assyrians.

amelia-tokagahahau.s: Amelia Tokagahahau Aliki was Queen of Uvea, on Wallis Island in the Pacific, from 1869 until her death in 1895. A Catholic ruler closely allied with the Marist missionaries, she governed with a code of laws drawn up under their influence.

anouvong.s: Anouvong was the last king of Vientiane, ruling from 1805 as a vassal of Siam. He built Wat Si Saket and other monuments and sought to restore Lao independence.

anandachandra-inscription.s: The Anandachandra inscription is a Sanskrit inscription on a stone pillar now at the Shitthaung temple at Mrauk U in Rakhine State, Myanmar. Carved for King Anandachandra of Waithali around 729 CE, it lists the kings of his Chandra dynasty and records his gifts to Buddhist…

adana.s: Adana is a city of southern Turkey on the Seyhan river in the Cilician plain, one of the largest cities in the country. Hittite texts of the 2nd millennium BCE name it Adaniya, a town of the kingdom of Kizzuwatna.

ashikaga-masatomo.s: Ashikaga Masatomo was a half-brother of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, sent in 1457 to replace the rebellious Kamakura kubo Ashikaga Shigeuji as shogunal deputy in the Kantō. Unable to enter Kamakura, he settled at Horigoe in Izu province and became known as the Horigoe kubo.

ashikaga-masauji.s: Ashikaga Masauji was the second Koga kubo, ruling from 1497 as head of the eastern branch of the Ashikaga at Koga in Shimōsa province, Japan. His long reign was troubled by quarrels with his son Takamoto and his younger son Yoshiaki, who set up a rival seat at Oyumi, while the…

ashikaga-takamoto.s: Ashikaga Takamoto was the third Koga kubo, the head of the eastern branch of the Ashikaga at Koga in the Kantō region of Japan. He fought his father Masauji for control of the line before succeeding him around 1512.

ashikaga-haruuji.s: Ashikaga Haruuji was the fourth Koga kubo, head of the eastern branch of the Ashikaga in the Kantō region of Japan. At first allied with the Later Hōjō, who helped him destroy his uncle Yoshiaki in 1538, he married a daughter of Hōjō Ujitsuna.

abu-bakr-atiku.s: Abu Bakr Atiku was the second caliph of Sokoto, ruling from 1837 to 1842. A son of Usman dan Fodio, the founder of the caliphate, he succeeded his brother Muhammad Bello and was known for his strict religious policy.

asclepieion-of-kos.s: The Asclepieion of Kos was a healing sanctuary of the god Asclepius on terraces above the town of Kos in the Dodecanese. Built from the 4th century BCE, after the Coans founded their new capital in 366 BCE, it combined temples, porticoes and rooms for the sick, and was…

aurel-stein.s: Aurel Stein was a Hungarian-born British archaeologist and explorer who led four expeditions to Central Asia between 1900 and 1930. He excavated sites along the southern Silk Road, including Niya, Loulan and Dunhuang, where he acquired thousands of manuscripts, among them the…

alexei-kulabukhov.s: Alexei Kulabukhov was an Orthodox priest and member of the Kuban Rada during the Russian Civil War, a supporter of Kuban autonomy and closer ties with Ukraine. In 1919 he was among the Kuban delegates in Paris who signed a treaty of friendship with the Mountainous Republic of…

akita.s: Akita is the capital of Akita Prefecture in northern Honshu, Japan, on the Sea of Japan coast. It grew around Kubota Castle, built by Satake Yoshinobu in 1604 as the seat of the Kubota domain, and took the name Akita after the abolition of the domains in 1871.

akita-prefecture.s: Akita Prefecture is a prefecture in the Tohoku region of northern Honshu, Japan, on the Sea of Japan, with its capital at Akita. It was formed in 1871 from the Kubota domain and neighbouring lands after the abolition of the han system, and covers most of the former province of…

almora.s: Almora is a hill town in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand, India, on a ridge at about 1,600 metres. It became the capital of the Chand rajas of Kumaon around 1563, was taken by the Gorkhas of Nepal in 1790, and passed to the British after the Anglo-Nepalese War in 1815.

akhnoor.s: Akhnoor is a town on the Chenab River in the Jammu district of Jammu and Kashmir, India, about 30 kilometres north-west of Jammu. It has an old fort on the riverbank, and the nearby site of Manda is the northernmost known settlement of the Indus Valley Civilisation.

amoghabhuti.s: Amoghabhuti was a king of the Kunindas, a people of the Himalayan foothills, who reigned around the 1st century BCE. He is known from his silver coins, modelled on Indo-Greek drachms, which carry legends in Brahmi and Kharoshthi and show a deer and a goddess.

anoia.s: Anoia is a comarca, or county, in central Catalonia, Spain, with its capital at Igualada, named after the Anoia river that crosses it. Its towns grew on leather tanning, textiles and paper-making, with Capellades long known for its paper mills.

al-ahsa-oasis.s: Al-Ahsa is a large oasis in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, about 60 kilometres inland from the Persian Gulf, and one of the largest date-palm oases in the world. Its towns, chief among them Hofuf, were held by the Ottomans from the mid-16th century, by the Banu Khalid…

al-numan-iii-ibn-al-mundhir.s: Al-Nu'man III ibn al-Mundhir was the last Lakhmid king of al-Hira, reigning from about 582 until 602 as a client of the Sasanian Empire. A Christian of the Church of the East and a patron of poets such as al-Nabigha, he fell out with Khosrow II, who had him imprisoned and put…

al-masudi.s: Al-Masudi was an Arab historian and geographer from Baghdad, often called the Herodotus of the Arabs. He travelled widely through Persia, India, the Caspian lands, East Africa and Syria, and his Meadows of Gold, completed in the 940s, combines world history with descriptions…

adamawa-plateau.s: The Adamawa Plateau is an upland region of central Cameroon extending into Nigeria and the Central African Republic, rising to over 1,000 metres between the southern forests and the northern savannas. It takes its name from Modibo Adama, the Fulani leader who conquered much of…

agathias.s: Agathias was a Byzantine historian and poet of the 6th century, born at Myrina in Asia Minor and trained as a lawyer in Constantinople. His Histories continue Procopius's account of Justinian's reign for the years 552 to 559, covering the wars in Italy and Lazica and the…

atharvaveda.s: The Atharvaveda is the fourth of the Vedas, the sacred texts of Hinduism, compiled around 1000 BCE or somewhat later. Besides hymns, it contains spells and charms for healing, protection, love and harming enemies, as well as speculation on the cosmos, giving a picture of…

aceh.s: Aceh is the northernmost province of Indonesia, at the tip of Sumatra, with its capital at Banda Aceh. From the 16th century it was the seat of the Aceh Sultanate, a leading Muslim power of the Strait of Malacca, which resisted the Dutch in the long Aceh War from 1873.

amalie-elisabeth-of-hanau-munzenberg.s: Amalie Elisabeth of Hanau-Münzenberg was the wife of Landgrave William V of Hesse-Kassel and regent for her son William VI from 1637 to 1650. During the Thirty Years' War she kept Hesse-Kassel in alliance with France and Sweden, held its army together and won the Hessian War…

anah.s: Anah is a town on the Euphrates in western Iraq, known in ancient sources as Anat. In the early 1st millennium BCE it was the centre of the land of Suhu, whose governors ruled from an island in the river.

azizi-mosque.s: The Azizi Mosque is a mosque at Tanjung Pura in Langkat Regency, North Sumatra, Indonesia, built from 1899 to 1902 by Sultan Abdul Aziz of Langkat. Its design mixes Malay, Middle Eastern and Indian elements, with a tall minaret.

amir-hamzah.s: Amir Hamzah was an Indonesian poet and a member of the royal family of the Langkat Sultanate in North Sumatra. His collections Nyanyi Sunyi and Buah Rindu, written in Malay in the 1930s, made him the leading poet of the Pujangga Baru generation.

aleuadae.s: The Aleuadae were an aristocratic family of Larissa in Thessaly, claiming descent from Heracles through their ancestor Aleuas. They often led the Thessalian League in the Archaic and Classical periods.

adityasena.s: Adityasena was a king of the Later Gupta dynasty of Magadha in the second half of the 7th century. After the death of Harsha he restored his family's power in Magadha, took the title of maharajadhiraja and is said to have performed the horse sacrifice.

aphsad-inscription.s: The Aphsad inscription is a Sanskrit stone inscription of the 7th century found at Aphsad, near Nawada in Bihar, India. It records King Adityasena's building of a temple and lists the kings of the Later Gupta dynasty from Krishnagupta onwards, with their wars against the…

agios-nikolaos.s: Agios Nikolaos is a town on the Gulf of Mirabello in eastern Crete, Greece, and the capital of the regional unit of Lasithi. It stands on the site of Lato pros Kamara, the harbour of the ancient city of Lato, and takes its name from a Byzantine church of Saint Nicholas.

augusts-voss.s: Augusts Voss was a Soviet Latvian politician who served as first secretary of the Communist Party of Latvia from 1966 to 1984. Raised in Russia, he followed the line of his predecessor Arvīds Pelše, promoting industrial growth and the use of Russian.

aristobulus-of-chalcis.s: Aristobulus of Chalcis was a Herodian prince, a great-grandson of Herod the Great and son of Herod of Chalcis. In the mid-50s CE the emperor Nero made him king of Lesser Armenia, and from 57 he also ruled Chalcis in Syria.

aristobulus-i.s: Aristobulus I was a ruler of the Hasmonean dynasty of Judaea, the eldest son of John Hyrcanus. According to Josephus he was the first of the Hasmoneans to take the title of king alongside the high priesthood.

apollo-grannus.s: Apollo Grannus was a Gallo-Roman healing god, the Celtic deity Grannus identified with the Roman Apollo and worshipped especially at springs. His cult was strong in eastern Gaul and the Rhineland, and his greatest sanctuary was at Grand in the Vosges, where a large mosaic and…

amshuvarman.s: Amshuvarman was a ruler of Nepal in the Licchavi period, first a powerful minister under King Shivadeva I and then holder of royal titles. His inscriptions show a well-organised administration, and he built the Kailashakuta palace in the Kathmandu Valley.

apuani.s: The Apuani were a Ligurian people of the mountains of north-western Tuscany, between the Magra and Serchio valleys, where the Apuan Alps keep their name. They resisted Rome stubbornly in the early 2nd century BCE until, in 180 BCE, the consuls deported about 40,000 of them…

andre-massena.s: André Masséna was a French general of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, made a Marshal of the Empire in 1804. He won the Second Battle of Zurich in 1799, held besieged Genoa for two months in 1800, and fought at Aspern-Essling and Wagram in 1809.

antaeus.s: Antaeus was a giant of Greek mythology, a son of Poseidon and Gaia, who lived in Libya and forced travellers to wrestle with him, killing them. He drew his strength from contact with the earth, his mother, and Heracles defeated him by lifting him off the ground and crushing him.

albarracin.s: Albarracín is a small walled town in the province of Teruel, Aragon, eastern Spain, on a rock above the Guadalaviar river. In the 11th century it was the seat of the Banu Razin taifa, and from 1170 it was an independent Christian lordship of the Azagra family until Peter III…

apollonia-illyria.s: Apollonia was an ancient Greek city in Illyria, near modern Fier in Albania, founded around 600 BCE by colonists from Corinth and Corcyra. It prospered from trade with the Illyrian interior, became an ally of Rome in 229 BCE and stood at the western end of the Via Egnatia.

apollonia-cyrenaica.s: Apollonia was the ancient port of Cyrene in eastern Libya, at modern Marsa Susa. It grew from Cyrene's harbour into one of the five cities of the Pentapolis of Cyrenaica, and in late Roman and Byzantine times, renamed Sozousa, it became the leading city of the province.

arsuf.s: Arsuf is the site of an ancient and medieval town on the Mediterranean coast north of modern Herzliya, Israel, known in antiquity as Apollonia. Taken by the crusaders in 1101, it was the seat of a lordship of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and in 1191 Richard I defeated Saladin…

aldus-manutius.s: Aldus Manutius was an Italian humanist and printer who founded the Aldine Press in Venice in the 1490s. He published the first printed editions of many Greek classics, introduced italic type and the small portable octavo book, and helped make Venice the leading centre of…

andronikos-iii-palaiologos.s: Andronikos III Palaiologos was Byzantine emperor from 1328 to 1341, after deposing his grandfather Andronikos II in a long civil war. With his chief minister John Kantakouzenos he recovered Chios from the Genoese Zaccaria in 1329 and annexed Thessaly and Epirus, but lost most…

aodh-buidhe-oneill.s: Aodh Buidhe O'Neill was a king of Tír Eoghain in Ulster in the 13th century, who ruled with the backing of the Anglo-Norman earls of Ulster and was killed in 1283. His descendants, the Clann Aodha Buidhe, moved east across the River Bann in the 14th century and founded the…

area-of-outstanding-natural-beauty.s: An Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) is a protected landscape designation in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, created under the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949. The Gower peninsula in south Wales was the first area to be designated, in 1956.

al-karak.s: Al-Karak is a town in central Jordan, east of the Dead Sea, dominated by Kerak Castle. The castle was begun in 1142 by Payen the Butler and became the centre of the crusader lordship of Oultrejordain, controlling routes between Syria, Egypt and Arabia.

altmuhl.s: The Altmühl is a river in Bavaria, Germany, a left tributary of the Danube about 220 kilometres long. It flows through Franconia past Treuchtlingen, Pappenheim and Eichstätt in a winding limestone valley, now the Altmühl Valley Nature Park, and joins the Danube at Kelheim.

altenburg.s: Altenburg is a city in eastern Thuringia, Germany, south of Leipzig. An imperial castle and town in the Middle Ages, it was the centre of the Pleissenland, the imperial territory later absorbed by the Wettins.

ahwar.s: Ahwar is a town on the coastal plain of Abyan Governorate in southern Yemen, near the Gulf of Aden. It was the seat of the Lower Aulaqi Sultanate, a small state under the British Aden Protectorate that joined the Federation of South Arabia before being absorbed into South…

anubanini.s: Anubanini was a king of the Lullubi, a mountain people of the Zagros, in the late third millennium BCE. He is known from a rock relief at Sar-e Pol-e Zahab in western Iran, showing him standing over defeated enemies before the goddess Inanna (Ishtar), in a style copying…

alexandropolis-thrace.s: Alexandropolis was a city founded around 340 BCE by the young Alexander the Great in the land of the Maedi, a Thracian people of the Strymon valley. According to Plutarch, Alexander, left as regent while Philip II besieged Byzantium, defeated the rebellious Maedi, took their…

aba-island.s: Aba Island is an island in the White Nile south of Khartoum in Sudan. In 1881 the Sufi teacher Muhammad Ahmad, living there, declared himself the Mahdi and defeated the first government force sent against him, beginning the Mahdist uprising.

abdallahi-ibn-muhammad.s: Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, known as the Khalifa, was ruler of the Mahdist State in Sudan from 1885 to 1898. A Baggara Arab from Darfur, he was the Mahdi's chief lieutenant and succeeded him on his death, ruling from Omdurman.

ansar-sudan.s: The Ansar ('helpers') were the followers of Muhammad Ahmad, the Mahdi of Sudan, who rose against Turco-Egyptian rule in 1881. They destroyed Hicks Pasha's army in 1883, took Khartoum in 1885 and formed the army of the Mahdist State until its defeat in 1898.

allauddin-khan.s: Allauddin Khan was an Indian sarod player and composer, one of the most influential teachers of Hindustani classical music in the 20th century. As court musician to the Maharaja of Maihar from 1918 he founded the Maihar gharana, and his pupils included Ravi Shankar, his son…

alula-somalia.s: Alula is a coastal town in the far north-east of Somalia, near Cape Guardafui on the Gulf of Aden, in the region of Puntland. In the 19th century it was one of the seats of the boqors (kings) of the Majeerteen Sultanate, which accepted an Italian protectorate in 1889 and was…

alcazaba-of-malaga.s: The Alcazaba of Málaga is a Moorish fortress-palace on a hill above the port of Málaga in southern Spain, built mainly in the 11th century and enlarged under the Nasrids. It stands above remains of the Phoenician and Roman town, beside a Roman theatre, and is linked by walls…

alcazaba-of-almeria.s: The Alcazaba of Almería is a fortified complex on a hill above Almería in southern Spain, founded under the Córdoban caliph Abd al-Rahman III in the 10th century. The taifa ruler al-Mutasim enlarged it in the 11th century with palaces and gardens, and after the Christian…

adham-khan.s: Adham Khan was a Mughal general, son of the emperor Akbar's wet-nurse Maham Anga. In 1561 he defeated Baz Bahadur, the last sultan of Malwa, at Sarangpur, but his cruelty and seizure of the spoils angered Akbar.

ali-riza-pasha-al-laz.s: Ali Rıza Pasha, known as al-Laz, was an Ottoman governor who ended Mamluk rule in Iraq. Sent from Aleppo in 1831, he reached Baghdad after plague and floods had crippled the city and deposed its last Mamluk governor, Dawud Pasha.

abu-nasr-mansur.s: Abu Nasr Mansur ibn Iraq was a Persian mathematician and astronomer, a prince of the Afrighid dynasty of Khwarazm. He worked at the court of the Ma'munid Khwarazmshahs at Gurganj, where he taught al-Biruni, and later followed him to the court of Mahmud of Ghazni.

anglo-iraqi-treaty-1930.s: The Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 1930 was an alliance signed between Britain and the Kingdom of Iraq, then under a League of Nations mandate. It provided for Iraqi independence once Iraq joined the League, which happened in 1932, but kept close British influence, including air bases…

assassination-of-abraham-lincoln.s: The assassination of Abraham Lincoln took place on 14 April 1865, five days after the surrender of the main Confederate army, when the actor and Confederate sympathiser John Wilkes Booth shot the president at Ford's Theatre in Washington; Lincoln died the next morning. It was…

ataturks-reforms.s: Atatürk's reforms were the political, legal, cultural and social changes carried out in Turkey under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk between 1923 and 1938 to build a secular, national and modern state in place of the Ottoman Empire. They included the abolition of the caliphate in 1924,…

aswan-high-dam.s: The Aswan High Dam is a rock-fill dam across the Nile at Aswan in southern Egypt, built between 1960 and 1970 with Soviet finance and engineering after the United States and Britain withdrew their offer of support in 1956. It ended the annual Nile flood, provided water for…

ajbar-sen.s: Ajbar Sen was a raja of Mandi, a hill state in the western Himalaya in present-day Himachal Pradesh, India. In 1527 he founded the town of Mandi on the Beas river as his new capital, and tradition credits him with building its Bhutnath temple.

alise-sainte-reine.s: Alise-Sainte-Reine is a village in the Côte-d'Or department of Burgundy, France, below Mont Auxois, the site of the Gallic oppidum of Alesia. Excavations ordered by Napoleon III in the 1860s confirmed it as the place where Julius Caesar besieged Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, and a…

auxois.s: The Auxois is a hilly farming region in the north-west of the Côte-d'Or department in Burgundy, France, whose chief town is Semur-en-Auxois. Its name derives from Alesia, the Gallic stronghold on Mont Auxois.

ahsheri.s: Ahsheri was a king of Mannaea, south of Lake Urmia in north-western Iran, in the first half of the 7th century BCE. Assyrian records state that he raided Assyrian territory and was defeated around 660 BCE by an army of Ashurbanipal, which took several of his towns.

aisso.s: Aissó, or Aizo, was a Gothic noble of the Spanish March who rebelled against Frankish rule in 826. With support from the Emirate of Córdoba he seized strongholds in the region of Osona and ravaged the area around Barcelona and Girona.

almanzor.s: Almanzor (al-Mansur, 'the Victorious'), born Muhammad ibn Abi Amir, was the hajib (chief minister) and real ruler of the Caliphate of Córdoba from 978, governing for the young caliph Hisham II. He led dozens of campaigns against the Christian north, sacking Barcelona in 985…

avar-ring.s: The Avar Ring was the fortified central residence of the khagans of the Avar Khaganate in the Pannonian plain, where they kept the treasure gathered from Byzantine tribute and plunder. Frankish forces led by Eric of Friuli captured it in 795, and Pepin of Italy destroyed it in…

anscar-i-of-ivrea.s: Anscar I was a Burgundian noble who supported Guy of Spoleto's bid for the crowns of France and Italy in 888. Guy rewarded him with a march around Ivrea in north-western Italy, guarding the Alpine passes.

anscarids.s: The Anscarids were a dynasty descended from Anscar I, margrave of Ivrea in north-western Italy in the late 9th century. Its Italian line produced Berengar II and Adalbert, kings of Italy in the 950s, while a Burgundian branch became counts of Burgundy.

arduinici.s: The Arduinici were a noble family of Piedmont descended from Arduin Glaber, who received Turin and the Susa valley around 941 and drove Arab raiders from the Alpine passes. They held the March of Turin for about 150 years.

aleramo.s: Aleramo was a nobleman in northern Italy, of Frankish descent, who in 967 was confirmed by Emperor Otto I as margrave of lands in the hills south of the Po between Turin and the Ligurian coast. He founded the Aleramici dynasty, from which descended the marquises of Montferrat,…

abalgamash.s: Abalgamash was a king of Marhashi, a land east of Elam in south-eastern Iran, in the 23rd century BCE. Inscriptions of Rimush, king of Akkad, record that he defeated Abalgamash and his allies in a great battle and brought back booty, including stone vessels, which he dedicated…

abu-inan-faris.s: Abu Inan Faris was sultan of the Marinid dynasty of Morocco from 1348 to 1358. He seized power from his father Abu al-Hasan, conquered the Zayyanid kingdom of Tlemcen in 1352 and briefly took Tunis in 1357.

al-attarine-madrasa.s: The al-Attarine Madrasa is a college for Islamic studies in Fez, Morocco, next to the Qarawiyyin Mosque, built from 1323 to 1325 by the Marinid sultan Abu Said Uthman II. It takes its name from the nearby spice market.

abd-al-haqq-ii.s: Abd al-Haqq II was the last Marinid sultan of Morocco, proclaimed as a baby in 1420 and kept under the control of Wattasid regents for most of his reign. In 1459 he tried to free himself by massacring the Wattasids, but his government grew unpopular, and he was killed in a…

angitia.s: Angitia was an Italic goddess of healing and of snakes, worshipped especially by the Marsi around the Fucine Lake in central Italy. Her sacred grove, the Lucus Angitiae, stood near modern Luco dei Marsi.

abu-ali-al-hasan-ibn-marwan.s: Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn Marwan was the founder of Marwanid rule in Diyar Bakr, in what is now south-eastern Turkey. A nephew of the Kurdish chief Badh, he took over his uncle's lands after Badh was killed in 990 and defeated the Hamdanids.

anne-hutchinson.s: Anne Hutchinson was an English-born Puritan spiritual adviser in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Her religious meetings in Boston and her teaching on grace led to the Antinomian Controversy, and in 1638 she was tried and banished.

antibes.s: Antibes is a town on the French Riviera between Cannes and Nice. It began as Antipolis, a Greek trading settlement founded by Massalia, facing the Ligurian peoples of the hills behind it.

antonio-vicente-da-cruz.s: António Vicente da Cruz, known as Bonga, was a member of the Afro-Portuguese Da Cruz family who ruled Massangano on the Zambezi in present-day Mozambique in the mid-nineteenth century. With Chikunda soldiers based in stockaded forts, he controlled river traffic and destroyed…

amangkurat-i.s: Amangkurat I was ruler of the Mataram Sultanate in Java from 1646 to 1677, son of Sultan Agung. He centralised power harshly, killing many nobles and religious leaders, moved the court to Plered and made agreements with the Dutch East India Company.

airlangga.s: Airlangga was a Javanese king who founded the kingdom of Kahuripan in East Java. Born in Bali around 1002, son of King Udayana and the Javanese princess Mahendradatta, he married into the court of Dharmawangsa of Medang and survived its destruction in 1016.

adur-gushnasp.s: Adur Gushnasp was one of the three great sacred fires of Zoroastrian Iran, associated with the warrior class and the kings. Under the Sasanians it was kept in the temple complex at Takht-e Soleyman in north-western Iran, where kings went on pilgrimage after their accession.

artavasdes-i-of-media-atropatene.s: Artavasdes I was king of Media Atropatene in north-western Iran in the first century BCE. Allied with Parthia, he helped defeat Mark Antony's campaign of 36 BCE, when Antony's siege train was destroyed and his siege of Phraaspa failed.

atropates.s: Atropates was a Persian noble who served as satrap of Media under the Achaemenid king Darius III and fought at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. Alexander the Great later restored him as satrap, and after Alexander's death he made the northern part of Media an independent kingdom, Media…

arslantepe.s: Arslantepe is an archaeological mound near Malatya in eastern Turkey, the site of ancient Melid. Settled from at least the fifth millennium BCE, it held a palace complex of the late fourth millennium with some of the oldest known swords.

andriandahifotsy.s: Andriandahifotsy was a king of the Sakalava in western Madagascar in the second half of the seventeenth century, of the Maroserana dynasty. Remembered as a great conqueror, he used firearms acquired from European traders to defeat neighbouring rulers and built up the kingdom…

ahmad-shah-of-divrigi.s: Ahmad Shah was the Mengujekid ruler of Divriği in eastern Anatolia in the early thirteenth century, under the overlordship of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. In 1228–1229 he and his wife Turan Malik founded the Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği, whose carved stone portals are…

ambohimanga.s: Ambohimanga is a fortified royal hill town about 20 kilometres north-east of Antananarivo in the highlands of Madagascar. It was the seat of Andrianampoinimerina, who began reuniting the Merina kingdom there around 1787, and remained a sacred city of the Merina monarchy, with…

andriamanelo.s: Andriamanelo was a Merina king of the central highlands of Madagascar, traditionally dated to the mid-sixteenth century. Royal tradition credits him with subduing the earlier Vazimba inhabitants with iron-tipped spears, founding the line of Merina kings and building fortified…

andrianampoinimerina.s: Andrianampoinimerina was king of Imerina in the central highlands of Madagascar from around 1787 to 1810. Starting from Ambohimanga, he reunited the divided Merina chiefdoms, made Antananarivo his capital, expanded irrigated rice farming and organised forced labour, and…

antananarivo.s: Antananarivo is the capital and largest city of Madagascar, in the central highlands. Traditionally said to have been taken by the Merina king Andrianjaka in the early seventeenth century, it became the capital of the reunited Merina kingdom under Andrianampoinimerina and the…

archidamus-iii.s: Archidamus III was king of Sparta from about 360 to 338 BCE, son of Agesilaus II. He defended Sparta against Epaminondas in 362 BCE and fought in the Third Sacred War.

artas.s: Artas was a Messapian ruler in south-eastern Italy in the late fifth century BCE. According to Thucydides, in 413 BCE he renewed an old friendship with Athens and supplied 150 Messapian javelin-men to the Athenian expedition to Sicily under Demosthenes.

arcadian-gate.s: The Arcadian Gate is the monumental northern gateway of ancient Messene in the south-western Peloponnese, built when the city was founded under Theban protection in 369 BCE. A double gate with a circular inner courtyard, it carried the road towards Arcadia and Megalopolis and…

aristomenes.s: Aristomenes is the legendary hero of the Messenians, said to have led their revolt against Sparta in the Second Messenian War in the 7th century BCE. According to the account preserved by Pausanias, he won early victories, held out for years in the mountain stronghold of Eira…

arion-of-methymna.s: Arion of Methymna was a Greek lyric poet and lyre-player from Methymna on Lesbos, active in the late 7th century BCE, chiefly at the court of the tyrant Periander of Corinth. Ancient writers credited him with giving the dithyramb, a choral song for Dionysus, its literary form.

andre-matsoua.s: André Matsoua was a Congolese activist from the Lari people near Brazzaville who challenged French colonial rule in Middle Congo. In 1926 in Paris he founded the Amicale, an association of Africans from French Equatorial Africa that campaigned against forced labour and unequal…

abilmambet.s: Abilmambet was a Kazakh khan of the Middle Juz from about 1739 until his death in 1771, residing at Turkestan. His position was largely nominal, and real power lay with the sultan Ablai, who led the struggle against the Dzungars.

argyn.s: The Argyn are one of the largest tribes of the Middle Juz of the Kazakhs, living mainly in central, northern and eastern Kazakhstan. Their name is recorded among the tribes of the Golden Horde before the formation of the Kazakh Khanate in the 15th century, and they formed a…

amenemhat-i.s: Amenemhat I was the founder of Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty, reigning for about thirty years from around 1985 BCE. Probably the vizier of the same name who served Mentuhotep IV, he moved the royal residence from Thebes to a new city, Itjtawy, near Lisht, and reorganised the provinces.

anaximander.s: Anaximander of Miletus was a Greek philosopher of the 6th century BCE and a pupil of Thales in the Milesian school. He held that the origin of all things was the apeiron, 'the boundless', an indefinite substance from which opposites separate.

anaximenes.s: Anaximenes of Miletus was a Greek philosopher of the 6th century BCE, the third member of the Milesian school after Thales and Anaximander. He held that air was the underlying substance of all things, turning into fire when rarefied and into wind, water, earth and stone when…

azaz.s: Azaz is a town in north-western Syria, north of Aleppo near the Turkish border. In 1030 the Mirdasid emir of Aleppo defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos III Argyros near it, and its castle was later fought over by Byzantines, Crusaders of the County of Edessa and Muslim…

ashikaga-yoshiteru.s: Ashikaga Yoshiteru was the thirteenth shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate, holding the office from 1546 to 1565. For much of his rule he was overshadowed or driven from Kyoto by Miyoshi Nagayoshi, while trying to restore shogunal authority by mediating between daimyo and studying…

awa-province-tokushima.s: Awa was an old province of Japan in the east of the island of Shikoku, corresponding to present-day Tokushima Prefecture. In the 16th century it was the home base of the Miyoshi clan, retainers of the Hosokawa who rose to dominate Kyoto.

ahab.s: Ahab was king of Israel in the 9th century BCE, the son of Omri, reigning from Samaria roughly between 871 and 852 BCE. He married the Phoenician princess Jezebel, and the Hebrew Bible condemns him for promoting the worship of Baal.

arnon.s: The Arnon, now Wadi Mujib, is a river in Jordan that flows through a deep gorge into the Dead Sea from the east. In antiquity it formed the traditional northern boundary of Moab, though Moabite kings often held land beyond it, and the Mesha Stele records the building of a road…

akwesasne.s: Akwesasne is a Mohawk community on the St Lawrence river that straddles the border between Canada and the United States, divided among Quebec, Ontario and New York State. It grew from a Catholic mission settlement founded in the mid-18th century by Mohawks from Kahnawake.

alabama.s: Alabama is a state in the south-eastern United States, stretching from the Tennessee River valley to the Gulf of Mexico at Mobile. It was home to Mississippian chiefdoms such as Moundville and later to the Muscogee, Choctaw and Chickasaw, most of whom were forcibly removed in…

alaol.s: Alaol was a Bengali poet of the 17th century who lived at the court of Mrauk U in Arakan. Captured by Portuguese pirates as a young man, he served the kingdom's Muslim ministers, who commissioned his works.

anabaptism.s: Anabaptism is a radical Protestant movement that arose in Zürich in 1525 and spread through Germany, the Netherlands and Moravia. Anabaptists rejected infant baptism, baptising only adult believers, and generally sought to separate the church from the state; Catholics and…

ammaedara.s: Ammaedara was a Roman town in the west of present-day Tunisia, at modern Haïdra near the Algerian border. It was the first base of the Third Augustan legion in Africa, set on the lands of the Musulamii, and became a colony of veterans when the legion moved to Theveste under…

argo.s: In Greek mythology, the Argo was the ship on which Jason and the Argonauts sailed from Iolkos in Thessaly to Colchis on the Black Sea in search of the Golden Fleece. It was said to have been built by Argus with the help of Athena and to carry a speaking timber from the oak of…

athinkhaya.s: Athinkhaya was the eldest of the three brothers who founded the Myinsaing regime in central Burma in the late 13th century. Commanders under the last Pagan kings, he and his brothers Yazathingyan and Thihathu governed the Kyaukse district, overthrew King Kyawswa in 1297 and…

alcaeus.s: Alcaeus was a Greek lyric poet of Mytilene on Lesbos and a contemporary of Sappho. An aristocrat, he took part in the city's factional struggles against the tyrants Melanchrus, Myrsilus and Pittacus and spent years in exile.

artaxerxes-i.s: Artaxerxes I was king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 465 to 424 BCE, the son of Xerxes I. He put down a revolt in Egypt supported by Athens, and his reign saw the end of open war with the Greeks, traditionally through the Peace of Callias.

al-khazneh.s: Al-Khazneh, 'the Treasury', is a monumental facade carved into the sandstone cliff at the end of the Siq gorge in Petra, Jordan. Built probably in the 1st century CE, perhaps as the tomb of the Nabataean king Aretas IV, it combines Hellenistic columns and sculpture with…

aretas-i.s: Aretas I is the earliest known king of the Nabataeans, mentioned in the Second Book of Maccabees as 'tyrant of the Arabs' in about 169 BCE, when the deposed Jewish high priest Jason sought refuge with him. An inscription found at Elusa in the Negev may also refer to him.

arabia-petraea.s: Arabia Petraea was a province of the Roman Empire formed in 106 CE when Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom. It covered southern Syria, Jordan, the Negev and the Sinai, with its capital at Bostra.

akali-movement.s: The Akali movement was a campaign by Sikh reformers in the Punjab from 1920 to 1925 to take control of gurdwaras, Sikh shrines, from hereditary custodians backed by the British. Through mass non-violent protests, or morchas, its volunteers won the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925,…

azariqa.s: The Azariqa were the most militant faction of the Kharijites, named after their leader Nafi ibn al-Azraq, who broke away at Basra around 684. They declared Muslims who did not join them unbelievers and held that their women and children could lawfully be killed.

aj-wosal-chan-kinich.s: Aj Wosal Chan K'inich was a king of the Maya city of Naranjo in present-day Guatemala, who came to the throne as a child in 546 and reigned for about seventy years. His accession was overseen by the Kaanul dynasty, then the leading Maya power, which made Naranjo its client.

awjila.s: Awjila is an oasis town in the Libyan Desert of eastern Libya, some 250 km inland from the Gulf of Sirte. Herodotus mentions it as Augila, where the Nasamones went each summer to harvest dates.

antoine-simon-le-page-du-pratz.s: Antoine-Simon Le Page du Pratz was a French settler, engineer and naturalist who lived in Louisiana from 1718 to 1734, part of that time near the Natchez. His Histoire de la Louisiane, published in 1758, describes the colony's natural history and Natchez society, including the…

anapa.s: Anapa is a resort town on the Black Sea coast of Krasnodar Krai in southern Russia, near the Taman Peninsula. Near the site of the ancient Greek colony of Gorgippia, it became an Ottoman fortress in the 1780s and a key base for trade and contacts with the Circassians.

ariadne.s: Ariadne is a figure of Greek mythology, daughter of King Minos of Crete, who gave Theseus the thread that guided him out of the Labyrinth after he killed the Minotaur. Abandoned by Theseus on the island of Naxos, she was found there by the god Dionysus, who made her his wife.

amuntai.s: Amuntai is a town in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, the capital of Hulu Sungai Utara Regency, near the meeting of the Tabalong and Balangan rivers. According to the Hikayat Banjar it was the seat of the early Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Negara Dipa, and the ruins of the Candi…

akassa-raid.s: The Akassa raid was an attack on 29 January 1895 by warriors of the Nembe kingdom of Brass, led by King Frederick William Koko, on the Royal Niger Company's depot at Akassa in the Niger delta. Protesting the company's exclusion of Nembe traders from the Niger markets, they…

act-of-free-choice.s: The Act of Free Choice was the process in July and August 1969 by which Indonesia sought to confirm its sovereignty over West New Guinea under the New York Agreement of 1962. Instead of a general vote, 1,025 selected representatives voted unanimously, under Indonesian military…
