atai.s: Ataï was a Kanak high chief from the region of La Foa in New Caledonia who led the great revolt of 1878 against French colonial land seizures. The rising killed more than 100 settlers and soldiers, and French forces with Kanak auxiliaries suppressed it harshly.

antioquia-department.s: Antioquia is a department of north-western Colombia in the Central and Western Cordilleras; its capital is Medellín. In the colonial era it was a major source of gold, worked by enslaved Africans and free prospectors.

albany-new-york.s: Albany is the capital of the state of New York, on the west bank of the Hudson River. It grew from the Dutch fur-trading post of Fort Orange, built in 1624 near an earlier post of 1614, and the village of Beverwijck.

anzus.s: ANZUS is the security treaty signed by Australia, New Zealand and the United States in San Francisco on 1 September 1951, each pledging to act against a common danger in the Pacific. It became the basis of Australian defence policy.

apamea-syria.s: Apamea was an ancient city on the Orontes river in western Syria, founded around 300 BCE by Seleucus I and named after his wife Apama. It was the military base of the Seleucid kingdom, where its war elephants were kept, and later a large Roman city with a colonnaded street…

al-kahf-castle.s: Al-Kahf Castle is a ruined medieval fortress in the coastal mountains of western Syria, near Qadmus in Tartus governorate, built on a rocky spur and reached through a passage cut into the rock. The Nizari Ismailis acquired it in the 1130s, and it is said to have been an early…

anantapur.s: Anantapur is a city in the Rayalaseema region of southern Andhra Pradesh, India, and the headquarters of Anantapur district. It grew around a large reservoir built in the 14th century under the Vijayanagara Empire.

andhra-pradesh.s: Andhra Pradesh is a state on the south-eastern coast of India, inhabited mainly by Telugu speakers, with its capital at Amaravati. It was created in 1953 as Andhra State, the first Indian state formed on linguistic lines, and enlarged in 1956 with the Telugu districts of…

altmark.s: The Altmark, 'old march', is a historical region in the north of Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, west of the Elbe, with towns such as Stendal, Salzwedel and Tangermünde. It was the remnant of the Northern March held by the margraves after the Slav rising of 983, and from it Albert the…

ayushiridara.s: Ayushiridara, known as Biligtü Khan, was the son of Toghon Temür, the last Yuan emperor of China, and ruled the Northern Yuan in Mongolia from 1370 to 1378. Driven from China by the Ming, he re-established the court at Karakorum and still claimed to rule all China, and his…

aethelred-the-unready.s: Æthelred the Unready was king of the English from 978 to 1016, apart from a brief exile in 1013–1014; his nickname means 'poorly advised'. His reign saw renewed Viking attacks, which he tried to buy off with heavy payments of tribute, and the massacre of Danes on St Brice's…

apache.s: The Apache are a group of culturally related Indigenous peoples of the American Southwest and northern Mexico, speaking Southern Athabaskan languages. Arriving from the north by about 1500, they include the Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan and Western Apache.

adherbal.s: Adherbal was a king of Numidia, the elder son of Micipsa, who shared the kingdom from 118 BCE with his brother Hiempsal and his adoptive brother Jugurtha. After Hiempsal's murder he fled to Rome, which divided Numidia between him and Jugurtha.

achilles.s: Achilles is the greatest Greek warrior of the Trojan War in Greek legend and the central figure of Homer's Iliad. The son of the hero Peleus and the sea-nymph Thetis, he killed the Trojan prince Hector and was himself killed by an arrow of Paris.

antera-duke.s: Antera Duke was an Efik slave trader of Duke Town in Old Calabar, in present-day south-eastern Nigeria, in the late 18th century. His diary, kept in trade English from 1785 to 1788, records dealings with European ships, the Ekpe society, funerals and daily life in the town.

asparuh-of-bulgaria.s: Asparuh was the founder of the First Bulgarian Empire on the lower Danube. A son of Kubrat of Old Great Bulgaria, he led part of the Bulgars west after the Khazars broke up his father's realm, defeated a Byzantine army under Constantine IV at Ongal in 680 and won a treaty…

abdul-ghafur-muhiuddin-shah.s: Abdul Ghafur Muhiuddin Shah was sultan of Pahang, on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, from 1592 to 1614. His reign is associated with the Pahang legal code, the Hukum Kanun Pahang, and with trade and alliance with the Dutch, who were then contesting the region with the…

appellate-division-of-the-supreme-court-.n: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of South Africa
appellate-division-of-the-supreme-court-.s: The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of South Africa was the country's highest court of appeal from the creation of the Union in 1910. Seated in Bloemfontein, it made that city South Africa's judicial capital.

abul-fazl-ibn-mubarak.s: Abu'l-Fazl ibn Mubarak was the vizier, historian and close adviser of the Mughal emperor Akbar. He wrote the Akbarnama, a history of Akbar's reign, with the Ain-i-Akbari, a detailed account of the empire's administration, and championed Akbar's policy of universal tolerance.

arcadia.s: Arcadia is a mountainous region of the central Peloponnese in Greece. In antiquity it was divided among city-states such as Tegea, Mantinea and Orchomenus, which formed an Arcadian League after Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE and founded Megalopolis as a federal capital.

anglesey.s: Anglesey, in Welsh Ynys Môn and in Latin Mona, is the largest island off Wales, separated from the mainland by the Menai Strait. A centre of the druids, it was attacked by the Romans in 60 CE and conquered by Agricola in 77, and its fertile farmland later made it the granary…

abgar-v.s: Abgar V was a king of Osroene who ruled from Edessa in the early 1st century CE. Christian tradition, recorded by Eusebius, claims that he exchanged letters with Jesus and was healed by the disciple Addai, and the later legend of the Image of Edessa grew from this story.

amalasuntha.s: Amalasuntha was the daughter of Theodoric the Great and ruled the Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy as regent for her son Athalaric from 526. Educated in Latin and Greek, she favoured friendship with the Byzantine court, which angered Gothic nobles.

aichi-prefecture.s: Aichi Prefecture is a prefecture in central Honshu, Japan, with its capital at Nagoya. It was formed in 1871–1872 from the old provinces of Owari and Mikawa, the homelands of Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

aegitna.s: Aegitna was an ancient port on the coast of southern Gaul, in the territory of the Ligurian Oxybii, known chiefly from the historian Polybius. In 154 BCE the Oxybii attacked Roman envoys landing there, and a Roman army under the consul Quintus Opimius then defeated them and…

aceh-river.s: The Aceh River, in Indonesian Krueng Aceh, flows north through the province of Aceh at the northern tip of Sumatra and reaches the sea at Banda Aceh. Its valley, Aceh Besar, was the heartland of the Aceh Sultanate, whose capital stood near the river mouth from the 16th century.

alauddin-al-kahar.s: Alauddin al-Kahar was sultan of Aceh from about 1537 to 1571 and made it a regional power. He sought military aid from the Ottoman Empire, which sent gunners and cannon in the 1560s, and repeatedly attacked Portuguese Malacca as well as Johor and the Batak lands.

acts-of-the-scillitan-martyrs.s: The Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs is a short Latin record of the trial at Carthage on 17 July 180 of twelve Christians from the town of Scilli in Roman North Africa. Refusing to swear by the emperor's genius, they were condemned and beheaded on the order of the proconsul…

african-red-slip-ware.s: African Red Slip ware is a class of fine red-gloss pottery made in the Roman province of Africa, chiefly in modern Tunisia, from the late 1st to the 7th century CE. Mass-produced and widely exported, its plates and bowls became the dominant tableware across the Mediterranean…

apuleius.s: Apuleius was a Latin writer, orator and Platonist philosopher from Madauros in Roman North Africa. His novel the Metamorphoses, also called The Golden Ass, tells of a man turned into a donkey and is the only Latin novel to survive complete.

aspar.s: Flavius Ardabur Aspar was an Eastern Roman general of Alan descent who dominated the court at Constantinople for much of the mid-fifth century. Consul in 434 and long a senior commander, he helped place the emperors Marcian in 450 and Leo I in 457 on the throne, but as an…

arrian.s: Arrian of Nicomedia was a Greek historian, philosopher and Roman official of the second century CE. A pupil of Epictetus, whose teachings he recorded in the Discourses and the Enchiridion, he governed Cappadocia under Hadrian and repelled an invasion by the Alans around 135.

agri-decumates.s: The Agri Decumates were a region of the Roman Empire between the upper Rhine and the upper Danube, roughly the Black Forest and Swabian Jura in present-day south-west Germany. Occupied under the Flavian emperors and enclosed by the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, it was given up…

asinius-quadratus.s: Asinius Quadratus was a Roman historian of the third century CE who wrote in Greek. His works, a history of Rome from its foundation to the reign of Severus Alexander and a history of Parthia, survive only in fragments.

almoravid-qubba.s: The Almoravid Qubba, also known as the Qubba Ba'adiyyin, is a small domed pavilion in Marrakesh, Morocco, built in the early twelfth century under the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf, probably as an ablutions building for his great mosque. Uncovered in 1952, it is the only…

andorra-la-vella.s: Andorra la Vella is the capital and largest town of Andorra, in the Pyrenees at the meeting of branches of the Valira river. At about 1,023 metres above sea level it is the highest capital city in Europe.

aratus-of-soli.s: Aratus of Soli was a Greek poet from Cilicia who lived at the Macedonian court of Antigonus II Gonatas. His Phaenomena, a didactic poem describing the constellations and weather signs, became one of the most widely read works of ancient literature, translated into Latin by…

abu-bakr-tihrani.s: Abu Bakr Tihrani was a fifteenth-century Persian historian at the court of the Aq Qoyunlu. Commissioned by Uzun Hasan, he wrote the Kitab-i Diyarbakriyya, a chronicle of the Bayandur dynasty and its rise among the Turkmen tribes of eastern Anatolia, which traces the rulers'…

alvand-beg.s: Alvand Beg was an Aq Qoyunlu ruler, a grandson of Uzun Hasan, who held Azerbaijan and Diyarbakır at the end of the fifteenth century while his cousin Murad ruled central Iran. In 1501 he was defeated by the young Safavid leader Ismail at the Battle of Sharur, which opened…

ambrogio-contarini.s: Ambrogio Contarini was a Venetian merchant and diplomat sent in 1474 as ambassador to the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan, to seek an alliance against the Ottoman Empire. He travelled through Poland, the Crimea and Georgia to Tabriz and returned by way of Muscovy, where he met…

ara-general-belgrano.s: ARA General Belgrano was an Argentine light cruiser, built in the United States as USS Phoenix, which survived the attack on Pearl Harbor and was sold to Argentina in 1951. During the Falklands War it was torpedoed by the British submarine HMS Conqueror on 2 May 1982, with the…

alberto-fernandez.s: Alberto Fernández is an Argentine Peronist lawyer and politician who served as chief of cabinet under Néstor Kirchner and as president from 2019 to 2023, with Cristina Fernández de Kirchner as vice-president. His term was dominated by the COVID-19 pandemic, a restructuring of…

asantemanhyiamu.s: The Asantemanhyiamu was the national assembly of the Asante kingdom, in which the Asantehene met the paramount chiefs of the member states of the union. It gathered in Kumasi, notably at the annual Odwira festival, to hear disputes, approve major decisions such as war, and…

austen-henry-layard.s: Austen Henry Layard was a British archaeologist and diplomat who excavated the Assyrian capitals of Nimrud and Nineveh between 1845 and 1851, sending colossal winged bulls and palace reliefs to the British Museum. His book Nineveh and Its Remains (1849) was a best-seller.

aristion.s: Aristion was an Athenian philosopher who seized power as tyrant of Athens and brought the city to the side of Mithridates VI of Pontus against Rome in the First Mithridatic War. The Roman general Sulla besieged Athens and Piraeus, stormed the city on 1 March 86 BCE, and had…

aristophanes.s: Aristophanes was an Athenian comic playwright, the chief representative of Old Comedy, whose eleven surviving plays include The Clouds, The Birds, Lysistrata and The Frogs. Written largely during the Peloponnesian War, they mocked politicians such as Cleon, intellectuals…

acropolis-of-athens.s: The Acropolis of Athens is the rocky citadel above the city, occupied since the Neolithic and the site of a fortified Mycenaean palace in the Late Bronze Age. After the Persians sacked it in 480 BCE it was rebuilt under Pericles with the Parthenon, the Propylaea, the…

alexander-von-bach.s: Alexander von Bach was an Austrian lawyer and statesman who served as minister of the interior from 1849 to 1859. He gave his name to the decade of neo-absolutism that followed the revolutions of 1848, the 'Bach system' of centralised bureaucratic rule, German as the language…

alfred-i-prince-of-windisch-gratz.s: Alfred, Prince of Windisch-Grätz, was an Austrian field marshal who led the counter-revolution of 1848. He crushed the Prague uprising in June and retook Vienna from the revolutionaries in October 1848, then advanced into Hungary, but after defeats by the Hungarian army he was…

austrian-lloyd.s: The Austrian Lloyd was a shipping and insurance company founded in Trieste in 1833, which began steamship services in 1836 and became the largest shipping line of the Habsburg monarchy. Its ships linked Trieste with the Levant, Egypt and, after the opening of the Suez Canal,…

austro-slavism.s: Austro-Slavism was a political programme of the Slav peoples of the Austrian Empire, especially the Czechs, which sought equal rights and autonomy for them within a federal Habsburg state rather than independence or union with Russia. Its leading advocate, the historian…

archduke-franz-ferdinand-of-austria.s: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was the nephew of Emperor Franz Joseph I and heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne from 1896. He favoured army reform and greater rights for the empire's Slav peoples, and his morganatic marriage to Sophie Chotek strained relations at court.

armistice-of-villa-giusti.s: The Armistice of Villa Giusti was signed on 3 November 1918 at a villa near Padua by Austria-Hungary and Italy on behalf of the Allies, and took effect the next day. Coming after the Italian victory at Vittorio Veneto, it ended the war on the Italian front while the Habsburg…

asin-of-baekje.s: Asin was the seventeenth king of Baekje, reigning from 392 to 405. Early in his reign Goguryeo under Gwanggaeto the Great captured many Baekje fortresses, and in 396 Asin was forced to submit, as recorded on Gwanggaeto's stele.

asuka-dera.s: Asuka-dera is a Buddhist temple in Asuka, Nara Prefecture, and one of the oldest in Japan. It was founded by Soga no Umako and completed around 596, built with the help of craftsmen, tile-makers and monks sent from Baekje.

afaqis.s: The Afaqis, meaning "people of the horizons", were the immigrant nobles of the Bahmani Sultanate and its successor states in the Deccan, mostly Persians, Arabs and Central Asians who came by sea from the fourteenth century onwards. Their rivalry with the Deccanis, Muslims long…

ala-ud-din-ahmad-shah.s: Ala-ud-Din Ahmad Shah was a sultan of the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan, reigning from 1436 to 1458 at Bidar. He fought Vijayanagara and neighbouring sultanates, and his reign kept the kingdom large and wealthy.

ashtur.s: Ashtur is a village near Bidar in Karnataka, India, site of the tombs of the Bahmani sultans who ruled from Bidar after the 1420s. The domed tombs, among them that of Ahmad Shah I Wali, whose interior is covered in painted and gilded decoration, show strong Iranian influence.

alexander-coutanche.s: Alexander Coutanche was Bailiff of Jersey from 1935 to 1961. During the German occupation of 1940–1945 he remained at the head of the island's government, dealing with the occupying authorities to protect the population while carrying out their orders.

akufuna-tatila.s: Akufuna Tatila was briefly Litunga, king of the Lozi of Barotseland, in 1884–1885. He was installed by a rebellion of leading councillors who drove Lubosi, later known as Lewanika, from the throne.

afzal-khan-general.s: Afzal Khan was a leading general of the Bijapur Sultanate under Ali Adil Shah II. In 1659 he was sent with a large army to destroy the rising power of Shivaji, and at a meeting arranged below the fort of Pratapgad he was killed by the Maratha leader, whose troops then routed…

ali-adil-shah-i.s: Ali Adil Shah I was the fifth Adil Shahi sultan of Bijapur, ruling from 1558 to 1580. He joined the alliance of Deccan sultanates that crushed the Vijayanagara Empire at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, but his long siege of Portuguese Goa in 1570–1571 failed.

ali-adil-shah-ii.s: Ali Adil Shah II ruled the Bijapur Sultanate from 1656 to 1672. His reign opened with a Mughal invasion under Aurangzeb and saw the rise of Shivaji, who killed the Bijapuri general Afzal Khan in 1659 and carved a Maratha state out of Bijapur's western lands.

asar-mahal.s: The Asar Mahal is a palace hall in Bijapur, in present-day Karnataka, built around 1646 by Sultan Muhammad Adil Shah, reputedly as a hall of justice. It later housed relics believed to be hairs from the beard of the Prophet Muhammad, from which it takes its name.

acraephia.s: Acraephia was an ancient city of Boeotia in central Greece, on the eastern shore of Lake Copais below Mount Ptoon. It controlled the nearby sanctuary of Apollo Ptoios, an oracle whose dedications include many archaic kouroi statues.

ascra.s: Ascra was a village of ancient Boeotia on the slopes of Mount Helicon, near Thespiae. It is known almost entirely as the home of the poet Hesiod, whose father settled there after leaving Cyme in Aeolis; in the Works and Days Hesiod describes it as bad in winter, hard in summer…

asander-bosporan-king.s: Asander was ruler of the Bosporan Kingdom from 47 BCE until about 17 BCE. Left in charge of the Bosporus by Pharnaces II, he rebelled against him, and after Pharnaces' defeat by Julius Caesar at Zela he fought and killed him and seized power, marrying Pharnaces' daughter…

abdul-hakkul-mubin.s: Abdul Hakkul Mubin was the thirteenth sultan of Brunei, who seized the throne in 1660 after killing Sultan Muhammad Ali. His usurpation provoked a long civil war with Muhyiddin, who was proclaimed sultan in the capital.

abu-kalijar.s: Abu Kalijar was a Buyid ruler who governed Fars and Khuzistan from 1024 and also Iraq from 1044 until his death in 1048. One of the last capable members of the dynasty, he reunited much of its southern territory, but his reign was troubled by quarrels with his relatives and by…

abu-mansur-fulad-sutun.s: Abu Mansur Fulad Sutun was the last Buyid ruler of Fars, a son of Abu Kalijar. After his father's death in 1048 he struggled against his brothers and the advancing Seljuks to hold Fars and its capital Shiraz.

andromeda-galaxy.s: The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light years away, and the most distant object easily visible to the naked eye. The Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi gave one of the earliest recorded descriptions of it, as a…

al-shaykh-al-mufid.s: Al-Shaykh al-Mufid was a Twelver Shia theologian and jurist of Baghdad and the leading Shia scholar of the Buyid period. He defended Shia doctrine in debates with Sunni and Mu'tazili opponents, adopting rational methods in theology, and his Kitab al-Irshad on the lives of the…

al-sharif-al-murtada.s: Al-Sharif al-Murtada was a Twelver Shia theologian, jurist and poet of Baghdad, a descendant of the Prophet through the Imam Musa al-Kazim and brother of al-Sharif al-Radi. He succeeded al-Shaykh al-Mufid as the leading Shia scholar of the city and led the Talibid descendants…

al-sharif-al-radi.s: Al-Sharif al-Radi was a poet and scholar of Baghdad, a descendant of the Prophet and brother of al-Sharif al-Murtada. He headed the Talibid descendants of Ali under the Buyids and was among the leading Arabic poets of his time.

al-muti.s: Al-Muti was the Abbasid caliph from 946 to 974, placed on the throne by the Buyid ruler Mu'izz al-Dawla after the blinding and deposition of al-Mustakfi. Throughout his reign real power in Baghdad lay with the Buyid emirs, and the caliph was reduced to a figurehead who…

al-malik-al-rahim.s: Al-Malik al-Rahim was the last Buyid ruler of Iraq, succeeding his father Abu Kalijar in 1048. Unable to control his Turkish troops or his brothers, he lost authority to the military commander al-Basasiri.

abdi-ashirta.s: Abdi-Ashirta was the ruler of Amurru, a land in the mountains and coast of present-day northern Lebanon and western Syria, in the fourteenth century BCE. Nominally a vassal of Egypt, he seized neighbouring towns and threatened Byblos, whose king Rib-Hadda denounced him…

abibaal.s: Abibaal was a king of Byblos in the tenth century BCE. He is known from a Phoenician inscription on a statue of the pharaoh Shoshenq I, which he dedicated to the Baalat Gebal, the goddess of Byblos.

abishemu-i.s: Abishemu I was a ruler of Byblos in the Middle Bronze Age, contemporary with the pharaoh Amenemhat III of Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty. His rock-cut tomb in the royal necropolis of Byblos contained Egyptian gifts, among them an obsidian vase inscribed with Amenemhat III's name.

adonis.s: Adonis was a figure of Greek myth, a beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite who was killed by a boar and mourned each year in the festival of the Adonia. His name derives from the Semitic word adon, 'lord', and his cult had Near Eastern roots.

aziru.s: Aziru was the ruler of Amurru in the fourteenth century BCE and the son of Abdi-Ashirta. Continuing his father's expansion, he took towns on the Levantine coast and isolated Byblos, as the Amarna letters of its king Rib-Hadda record.

aristophanes-of-byzantium.s: Aristophanes of Byzantium was a Greek scholar and grammarian who became head of the Library of Alexandria around 195 BCE. He produced critical editions of Homer, Hesiod, Pindar and other poets, compiled lexicons and is credited with introducing the system of accent marks used…

al-zahrawi.s: Al-Zahrawi, known in Latin as Abulcasis, was a physician of al-Andalus who worked at Córdoba and is regarded as one of the greatest surgeons of the medieval world. His medical encyclopedia, the Kitab al-Tasrif, ends with a treatise on surgery describing operations and…

ali-ibn-hammud-al-nasir.s: Ali ibn Hammud al-Nasir was a commander of Idrisid descent who seized Córdoba in 1016 during the Fitna of al-Andalus and proclaimed himself caliph, the first non-Umayyad to hold the title in al-Andalus. Founder of the Hammudid dynasty, he ruled until 1018, when he was murdered…

abd-al-rahman-sanchuelo.s: Abd al-Rahman Sanchuelo was a son of Almanzor by a daughter of King Sancho II of Pamplona, hence his nickname 'Little Sancho'. He succeeded his brother Abd al-Malik as hajib of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1008 and persuaded Hisham II to name him heir to the caliphate.

alice-munro.s: Alice Munro was a Canadian writer of short stories, most of them set in small-town Ontario. Her collections, including Lives of Girls and Women, The Moons of Jupiter and Runaway, are known for their compressed treatment of whole lives and shifts in time.

albert-ii-duke-of-austria.s: Albert II, called the Lame or the Wise, was a Habsburg duke of Austria from 1330 to 1358. He added Carinthia and Carniola to the family's lands in 1335 and governed through a long period of peace in Austria.

afrikaner-bond.s: The Afrikaner Bond was a political organisation founded in 1880 to promote the interests of Afrikaners in southern Africa. In the Cape Colony, under Jan Hofmeyr, it became the main party of Dutch-speaking farmers and supported Cecil Rhodes's ministry from 1890 until the…

abul-abbas.s: Abul-Abbas was an Asian elephant sent by the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid to Charlemagne. Escorted by the Jewish envoy Isaac, it arrived at Aachen in 802 after a journey through North Africa and Italy.

artsakh-historical-province.s: Artsakh was a province of ancient Armenia, corresponding broadly to the highlands of Nagorno-Karabakh. After the partition of Armenia between Rome and Persia around 387 it passed with neighbouring Utik to Caucasian Albania, but its population remained closely tied to Armenian…

adolf-schulten.s: Adolf Schulten was a German historian and archaeologist of ancient Spain. From 1905 he excavated at Numantia, uncovering the Celtiberian town and the ring of camps and walls built by Scipio Aemilianus for the siege of 134–133 BCE, which he published in a multi-volume study.

arevaci.s: The Arevaci were the most powerful Celtiberian people, living in the upper Douro valley around the modern province of Soria in Spain. Their towns included Numantia, Termes, Uxama and Clunia.

alghu.s: Alghu was khan of the Chagatai Khanate from 1260 to 1266, a grandson of Chagatai Khan. Installed by Ariq Böke during the Toluid civil war, he soon turned against him, seized Transoxiana and Khwarazm and took control of their revenues.

amel-marduk.s: Amel-Marduk was king of Babylon from 562 to 560 BCE, the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar II. The Hebrew Bible, which calls him Evil-merodach, records that he released the exiled Judean king Jehoiachin from prison.

avanijanashraya-pulakeshin.s: Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin was a prince of the Gujarat branch of the Chalukyas of Badami, who governed southern Gujarat as a vassal of Vikramaditya II. His Navsari copper-plate grant of 739 records that he defeated an Arab army raiding from Sindh, a victory for which the…

archermus.s: Archermus was a Greek sculptor of Chios active in the mid-sixth century BCE, from a family of sculptors that included his sons Bupalus and Athenis. Ancient writers credited him with being the first to represent the goddess Nike with wings.

atarneus.s: Atarneus was an ancient Greek town on the coast of Mysia in north-western Asia Minor, opposite Lesbos. According to Herodotus the Persians gave its district to Chios in return for surrendering the Lydian rebel Pactyes.

advance-australia-fair.s: Advance Australia Fair is the national anthem of Australia, written by Peter Dodds McCormick and first performed in Sydney in 1878. After being chosen in a national poll in 1977, it was proclaimed the national anthem in 1984, replacing God Save the Queen, which remained the…

anthony-albanese.s: Anthony Albanese is an Australian politician who became prime minister in May 2022 at the head of a Labor government. Member of parliament for the Sydney seat of Grayndler since 1996, he held ministerial posts in the Rudd and Gillard governments and became Labor leader in 2019.

australian-and-new-zealand-army-corps.n: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
australian-and-new-zealand-army-corps.s: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps was a First World War army corps formed in Egypt in December 1914 under the British general William Birdwood. Its landing at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915 and the costly campaign that followed made the 'Anzac' tradition a foundation of…

anzac-day.s: Anzac Day, 25 April, is the national day of remembrance in Australia and New Zealand, marking the anniversary of the landing of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps at Gallipoli in 1915. First observed in 1916, it now commemorates all who served and died in military…

asia-pacific-economic-cooperation.s: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation is an intergovernmental forum of 21 Pacific Rim economies founded in Canberra in 1989 at the initiative of the Australian prime minister Bob Hawke. It promotes free trade and economic integration in the region through annual leaders' meetings…

aukus.s: AUKUS is a security partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States announced in September 2021. Its main element provides for Australia to acquire nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines, first by purchase from the United States and then of a…

australia-act-1986.s: The Australia Act 1986 comprises matching laws of the Australian and British parliaments that took effect on 3 March 1986. They ended the British Parliament's power to legislate for Australia and its states, removed remaining British involvement in state government and…

australian-labor-party.s: The Australian Labor Party is Australia's oldest political party, formed in the 1890s by the trade union movement in the colonies and organised federally from 1901. In 1904 Chris Watson led the world's first national labour government.

anglo-belgian-india-rubber-company.s: The Anglo-Belgian India Rubber Company, known as ABIR, was a company founded in 1892 that received a concession for rubber in the Lopori and Maringa basins of the Congo Free State, where the state held a large share. It enforced rubber quotas through armed sentries,…

alice-seeley-harris.s: Alice Seeley Harris was an English Baptist missionary in the Congo Free State whose photographs of mutilated Congolese, taken from 1904 at the Baringa mission, became key evidence in the campaign against Leopold II's regime. With her husband John Harris she showed them at…

arthur-conan-doyle.s: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle was a Scottish writer and physician, creator of the detective Sherlock Holmes. He was also active in public causes, and in 1909 published The Crime of the Congo, a summary of the evidence of atrocities in the Congo Free State written in support of the…

aelfthryth-countess-of-flanders.s: Ælfthryth was a daughter of Alfred the Great, king of Wessex, and the wife of Baldwin II, Count of Flanders, whom she married in the 890s. The marriage linked the young Flemish principality to the West Saxon royal house, and through her son Arnulf I she was an ancestor of the…

antoine-watteau.s: Antoine Watteau was a French painter born in Valenciennes, which had become French only a few years earlier. Working in Paris, he created the fête galante, scenes of elegantly dressed figures at leisure in parkland, and his Pilgrimage to Cythera was accepted by the Royal…

arnulf-iii-count-of-flanders.s: Arnulf III was count of Flanders from 1070 to 1071, succeeding his father Baldwin VI as a boy under the regency of his mother Richilde. His uncle Robert the Frisian challenged them, and Arnulf was killed at the Battle of Cassel on 22 February 1071.

adhemar-of-le-puy.s: Adhemar of Le Puy, also called Adhemar of Monteil, was bishop of Le Puy and the papal legate appointed by Pope Urban II to the First Crusade. He travelled with the army of Raymond of Saint-Gilles, count of Toulouse, and acted as spiritual leader and mediator among the crusade…

agenais.s: The Agenais is a historical region of south-western France around Agen, on the Garonne, corresponding roughly to the modern Lot-et-Garonne department. Part of the duchy of Aquitaine, it was given by Richard I of England as the dowry of his sister Joan on her marriage to…

albigeois.s: The Albigeois is a historical region of southern France around Albi, on the Tarn, corresponding largely to the modern Tarn department. Its viscounts, the Trencavels, held it under the counts of Toulouse.

amaury-vi-of-montfort.s: Amaury de Montfort was the eldest son of Simon de Montfort, leader of the Albigensian Crusade. After his father was killed at Toulouse in 1218 he inherited his conquests in the south but could not hold them against the counts of Toulouse and ceded his rights to King Louis VIII.

archive-of-the-crown-of-aragon.n: Archive of the Crown of Aragon
archive-of-the-crown-of-aragon.s: The Archive of the Crown of Aragon in Barcelona is one of the oldest and richest archives in Europe. It grew from the royal archive organised by King James II in 1318 and holds records of the counts of Barcelona and kings of Aragon from the ninth century onwards, with…

alfonsine-tables.s: The Alfonsine Tables were astronomical tables for calculating the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, compiled in Toledo under Alfonso X of Castile by the Jewish scholars Isaac ibn Sid and Judah ben Moses. Spread in Latin versions from Paris and first printed in 1483, they…

alfonso-xi-of-castile.s: Alfonso XI was king of Castile and León from 1312 to 1350. After a long minority he restored royal authority, and in 1340, with Afonso IV of Portugal, he defeated the Marinids and Granada at the Battle of Río Salado.

antonio-de-nebrija.s: Antonio de Nebrija was a Castilian humanist who taught at the universities of Salamanca and Alcalá. His Gramática de la lengua castellana of 1492, presented to Isabella I, was the first printed grammar of a modern European vernacular.

andrej-hlinka.s: Andrej Hlinka was a Slovak Catholic priest and politician who led the Slovak People's Party, which became known as Hlinka's Slovak People's Party. He supported the union with the Czechs in 1918 but then campaigned for Slovak autonomy against Prague's centralism.

aed-find.s: Áed Find was a king of Dál Riata of the Cenél nGabráin, whose death the Irish annals record in 778. In 768 he fought the Pictish king Ciniod in Fortriu, and he is credited with restoring a measure of Dál Riata's independence after a period of Pictish overlordship.

aed-mac-ainmuirech.s: Áed mac Ainmuirech was a king of the Cenél Conaill of the northern Uí Néill and high king of Ireland in the late sixth century. According to Adomnán he met Áedán mac Gabráin of Dál Riata in the presence of Columba at the Convention of Druim Cett.

alam-khan-lodi.s: Alam Khan Lodi was a son of Bahlul Lodi and uncle of Ibrahim Lodi, the last sultan of Delhi. Claiming the throne for himself, he joined Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, in inviting Babur to intervene against Ibrahim in the 1520s.

alai-darwaza.s: The Alai Darwaza is a domed gateway in the Qutb Minar complex in Delhi, built in 1311 by Alauddin Khalji as the southern entrance to the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque. Faced with red sandstone and white marble, it was the first building in India with true arches and a true dome built…

amir-khusrau.s: Amir Khusrau was a poet and musician of the Delhi Sultanate who served several sultans and was a disciple of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya. He wrote mainly in Persian, including historical poems on the Khalji sultans, but also verse in Hindavi.

apology-of-socrates.s: The Apology of Socrates is Plato's version of the speech Socrates gave in his own defence at his trial in Athens in 399 BCE on charges of impiety and corrupting the young. In it Socrates explains his questioning of others as a response to the Delphic oracle's answer that no…

aetolian-league.s: The Aetolian League was a federation of the cities and tribes of Aetolia in west-central Greece that became a leading power in the third century BCE. It dominated Delphi and the Amphictyony after defending the sanctuary against the Gauls in 279 BCE.

alvsborg.s: Älvsborg was a Swedish fortress at the mouth of the Göta älv river, near present-day Gothenburg, guarding Sweden's only outlet to the North Sea. Denmark-Norway captured it twice and returned it for large ransoms, after the Treaty of Stettin in 1570 and the Treaty of Knäred in…

aali.s: A'ali is a village in central Bahrain known for its burial mounds, among them the large royal tombs of the Early Dilmun period, built around 2050–1750 BCE and the largest in the island's mound fields. Excavations there show the wealth of Dilmun's ruling class.

ahlamu.s: The Ahlamu were nomadic groups of Syria and Mesopotamia named in cuneiform sources from the 14th century BCE, including the Amarna letters and Kassite letters from Nippur. Assyrian kings fought them along the Euphrates, and from the time of Tiglath-pileser I they were linked…

acfred-duke-of-aquitaine.s: Acfred was duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne from 926 until his death in 927, succeeding his brother William II. A nephew of William the Pious through his mother, he was the last ruler of the Auvergnat line of dukes.

abbey-of-saint-martial-limoges.s: The Abbey of Saint Martial was a Benedictine monastery in Limoges, founded in 848 around the tomb of Saint Martial, the first bishop of the city. From the tenth to the twelfth century it was among the great abbeys of southern France, known for its library and its manuscripts…

agilulf.s: Agilulf was king of the Lombards in Italy from 590 to 616. Duke of Turin, he became king by marrying Theodelinda, widow of King Authari, and consolidated Lombard rule, fighting the Byzantine exarchate of Ravenna and making peace with Pope Gregory the Great.

arnulf-duke-of-bavaria.s: Arnulf, called the Bad, was duke of Bavaria from 907 to 937, the son of Margrave Luitpold, who had fallen against the Magyars at Pressburg. He defended Bavaria against Magyar raids and made it a powerful stem duchy, and in 919 some Bavarians proclaimed him king before he…

authari.s: Authari was king of the Lombards from 584 to 590, chosen after a ten-year interregnum during which the dukes had ruled without a king. He restored royal power, defended Lombard Italy against Frankish and Byzantine attacks and in 589 married Theodelinda, daughter of the…

affligem-abbey.s: Affligem Abbey is a Benedictine monastery in Flemish Brabant, Belgium, founded around 1062 by a group of repentant knights and richly endowed by the counts of Louvain, later dukes of Brabant. It became one of the most powerful abbeys of the duchy and a centre of monastic…

antoine-duke-of-brabant.s: Antoine of Burgundy was duke of Brabant and Limburg from 1406 until 1415, a younger son of Philip the Bold of Burgundy. His great-aunt Duchess Joanna made him her heir, and he governed Brabant from 1404 and recovered Antwerp for the duchy.

alain-bouchart.s: Alain Bouchart was a Breton lawyer and chronicler who served Duke Francis II and Duchess Anne of Brittany. His Grandes Croniques de Bretaigne, printed in Paris in 1514, told the history of Brittany from its legendary origins and presented it as an ancient kingdom equal to France.

alan-rufus.s: Alan Rufus (Alan the Red) was a Breton nobleman, a kinsman of the dukes of Brittany, who served William the Conqueror and was rewarded with vast estates in England. As lord of the Honour of Richmond in Yorkshire he built Richmond Castle and became one of the richest men in the…

arthur-iii-duke-of-brittany.s: Arthur III, known before his accession as Arthur de Richemont, was constable of France from 1425 and duke of Brittany from 1457 to 1458. A son of Duke John IV, he was wounded and captured at Agincourt in 1415, later served Charles VII and reformed the royal army.

antoine-martin-chaumont-de-la-galaiziere.s: Antoine-Martin Chaumont de La Galaizière was a French administrator who governed Lorraine as chancellor for Stanisław Leszczyński from 1737 to 1766. Under the secret Declaration of Meudon of 1736 Stanisław left real power to him, and he prepared the duchy's absorption into…

adda-river.s: The Adda is a river of northern Italy, about 313 km long, which rises in the Alps, flows through the Valtellina and Lake Como and joins the Po near Cremona. From the fifteenth century it marked much of the frontier between the Duchy of Milan and the mainland territories of…

alessandro-manzoni.s: Alessandro Manzoni was an Italian novelist and poet from Milan. His historical novel The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), set in Spanish-ruled Lombardy in 1628–1630 and describing the plague of 1630, appeared in its final form in 1840–1842 and became a founding work of modern…

arthur-i-duke-of-brittany.s: Arthur of Brittany was the posthumous son of Geoffrey, son of Henry II of England, and Constance, duchess of Brittany. On the death of Richard I in 1199 he claimed the Angevin inheritance against his uncle John, with the support of Philip II of France.

abbey-of-saint-etienne-caen.s: The Abbey of Saint-Étienne, known as the Abbaye aux Hommes, is a former Benedictine abbey in Caen founded by William the Conqueror around 1063, with Lanfranc as its first abbot. Its church, consecrated in 1077, is a major example of Norman Romanesque architecture.

armistice-of-cherasco.s: The Armistice of Cherasco was signed on 28 April 1796 between Napoleon Bonaparte and the Kingdom of Sardinia of Victor Amadeus III, after a two-week French campaign in Piedmont. It took the kingdom out of the War of the First Coalition and handed key fortresses and free…

albert-ii-of-belgium.s: Albert II is a former King of the Belgians, who reigned from 1993 to 2013. A younger son of Leopold III, he succeeded his brother Baudouin, who died without children, shortly after constitutional reform had made Belgium a federal state.

alidius-tjarda-van-starkenborgh-stachouw.s: Alidius Tjarda van Starkenborgh Stachouwer was governor-general of the Dutch East Indies from 1936, the last before the Japanese conquest. A conservative diplomat, he presided over a colony that rejected nationalist demands for autonomy such as the Soetardjo petition of 1936.

antonie-van-leeuwenhoek.s: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch draper and self-taught scientist of Delft. Using small single-lens microscopes of his own making, he was the first to observe and describe bacteria and protozoa, and he studied sperm cells and the flow of blood in capillaries, reporting his…

anthonie-heinsius.s: Anthonie Heinsius was Grand Pensionary of Holland from 1689 until his death in 1720 and a close ally of the stadtholder and English king William III. After William's death in 1702 he directed Dutch policy in the War of the Spanish Succession, working with the Duke of…

altishahr.s: Altishahr ('six cities') is a historical name for the oasis region of the western and southern Tarim Basin, in present-day Xinjiang, which included Kashgar, Yarkand, Khotan, Aksu and other cities. Its Turkic-speaking Muslim population lived from irrigated farming and caravan…

admonitions-of-the-instructress-to-the-c.n: Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies
admonitions-of-the-instructress-to-the-c.s: The Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies is a Chinese handscroll painting illustrating a moralising text written by Zhang Hua in 292 for women of the imperial court. Traditionally attributed to the Eastern Jin painter Gu Kaizhi, the surviving scroll in the…

abarsal.s: Abarsal was an ancient city-state of the twenty-fourth century BCE known from the archives of Ebla in Syria. A treaty between Ebla and Abarsal, preserved on a clay tablet, is one of the oldest known international agreements, setting out rules on boundaries, trade and the…

arrukum.s: Arrukum was a vizier of the kingdom of Ebla in Syria in the twenty-fourth century BCE, the first of three high officials, followed by Ibrium and Ibrium's son Ibbi-Zikir, who appear in the palace archives as the most powerful figures after the king. The tablets show these…

aten.s: The Aten was the disc of the sun worshipped as a god in ancient Egypt, depicted as a sun whose rays end in human hands. Already honoured under Amenhotep III, it was raised by his son Akhenaten in the fourteenth century BCE above all other gods, whose cults, especially that of…

ashur-nadin-shumi.s: Ashur-nadin-shumi was the eldest son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib, who installed him as king of Babylon in 700 BCE. In 694 BCE, while Sennacherib campaigned against Elam, Babylonians handed him over to the Elamites, who carried him off; he was never heard of again and was…

albert-iii-elector-of-saxony.s: Albert III was Duke of Saxe-Wittenberg and Elector of Saxony from 1419 to 1422, the last elector of the Ascanian line. He died childless in 1422, reportedly after a fire at a hunting lodge, and Emperor Sigismund then granted the electorate in 1423 to Frederick the Warlike,…

albertine-line.s: The Albertine line is the younger branch of the house of Wettin, founded by Duke Albert III of Saxony when he and his brother Ernest divided their lands by the Division of Leipzig in 1485. It held Meissen with Dresden and Leipzig, and in 1547 it gained the electoral title from…

annaberg-buchholz.s: Annaberg-Buchholz is a town in the Ore Mountains of Saxony, Germany. Annaberg was founded in 1496 after rich silver strikes and quickly became one of the largest towns in Saxony; its late Gothic hall church of St Anne is among the finest in the region, and the arithmetic…

arch-marshal-of-the-holy-roman-empire.n: Arch-Marshal of the Holy Roman Empire
arch-marshal-of-the-holy-roman-empire.s: The Arch-Marshal (Erzmarschall) was one of the ceremonial high offices of the Holy Roman Empire attached to the electoral dignity. Confirmed for the electors of Saxony by the Golden Bull of 1356, it gave them the duty of carrying the imperial sword at coronations and keeping…

abbas-ibn-firnas.s: Abbas ibn Firnas was an Andalusi polymath of Berber descent at the court of the Umayyad emirs of Córdoba in the ninth century. A poet, astronomer and inventor, he is credited with a method of cutting rock crystal and with a planetarium-like device, and according to a later…

al-ala-ibn-mughith.s: Al-Ala ibn Mughith was an Arab leader in al-Andalus who in 763 raised the black banner of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur against the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman I, gathering support in the south-west of the peninsula. Abd al-Rahman besieged and defeated him near Carmona and…

abencerrajes.s: The Abencerrajes (Banu Sarraj) were a noble family of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada who were influential at court in the fifteenth century. They acted as kingmakers in the civil wars among Nasrid claimants, notably supporting Muhammad IX, and their rivalries with other clans…

albaicin.s: The Albaicín is the old Moorish quarter of Granada, Spain, on a hill facing the Alhambra across the valley of the Darro. Its steep, narrow streets, walled houses with gardens and former mosques, many turned into churches, preserve the street plan of Nasrid Granada.

alcazar-of-seville.s: The Alcázar of Seville is a royal palace in Seville, Spain, developed from an Islamic fortress of the Abbadid and Almohad periods. After the Castilian conquest of 1248 the kings rebuilt it, and Peter I's palace of the 1360s, decorated by Muslim craftsmen from Granada and…

alhama-de-granada.s: Alhama de Granada is a town in the province of Granada, Spain, known since Roman and Moorish times for its hot springs. A Nasrid stronghold guarding the road to Granada, it was taken by a Castilian surprise attack in February 1482, in reply to the Nasrid seizure of Zahara,…

alpujarras.s: The Alpujarras is a mountainous region on the southern slopes of the Sierra Nevada in the provinces of Granada and Almería, Spain. Under the Nasrids it was a densely settled land of terraced, irrigated farms and silk production.

antequera.s: Antequera is a town in the province of Málaga, Spain, at a crossing of the routes between Seville, Granada and Málaga. A frontier stronghold of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, it was taken after a long siege in 1410 by the regent Ferdinand of Castile, later Ferdinand I of…

archidona.s: Archidona is a town in the province of Málaga in Andalusia, Spain, below a hill crowned by the remains of a Moorish fortress. Under the Nasrid Emirate of Granada it was an important frontier stronghold on the north-western approaches to Granada, and it fell to Castilian forces…

abu-al-hasan-ali-of-granada.s: Abu al-Hasan Ali, known to the Castilians as Muley Hacén, was Nasrid emir of Granada from 1464 to 1482 and again in 1483–1485. His seizure of the Castilian town of Zahara in 1481 provoked the Granada War.

alexios-ii-of-trebizond.s: Alexios II was Emperor of Trebizond from 1297 to 1330, the son of John II and Eudokia Palaiologina. His long reign was a time of prosperity, when Trebizond flourished as a terminus of the trade route from Tabriz under Ilkhanid overlordship, with Genoese and Venetian merchants…

attalus-ii-philadelphus.s: Attalus II Philadelphus was King of Pergamon from 159 to 138 BCE, succeeding his brother Eumenes II. A loyal ally of Rome, he fought in its wars in Greece and Asia Minor, founded the city of Attalia (modern Antalya), rebuilt the harbour of Ephesus and gave Athens the Stoa of…

asia-roman-province.s: Asia was a Roman province in western Anatolia, formed from the Kingdom of Pergamon, which Attalus III bequeathed to Rome in 133 BCE. Organised by 129 BCE, it was among the richest provinces of the empire, with cities such as Ephesus, its leading city and the governor's seat,…

alptakin.s: Alptakin was a Turkish military commander who had served the Buyids in Iraq before seizing Damascus in 975 and resisting the Fatimid advance into Syria. Allied with the Qarmatians, he was defeated by the Fatimid caliph al-Aziz near Ramla in 978 and captured.

al-mustali.s: Al-Musta'li (1074–1101) was the ninth Fatimid caliph, ruling from 1094 to 1101. A younger son of al-Mustansir, he was placed on the throne by the vizier al-Afdal in preference to his elder brother Nizar, splitting the Ismaili movement into Musta'li and Nizari branches.

aelia-eudoxia.s: Aelia Eudoxia (died 404) was the wife of the eastern Roman emperor Arcadius, whom she married in 395. The daughter of the Frankish general Bauto, she was proclaimed augusta in 400 and became a powerful figure at the court in Constantinople.

amsivarii.s: The Amsivarii were a Germanic people living near the river Ems in north-western Germany in the 1st century CE. Driven from their lands in 58 CE, they sought Roman permission to settle on the lower Rhine and were refused.

ascaric.s: Ascaric was a Frankish king who, with Merogaisus, led raids across the lower Rhine into Roman territory at the start of the 4th century. Both were captured by Constantine the Great, then ruling in Gaul, and thrown to wild beasts in the arena at Trier around 306.

adolf-iii-of-holstein.s: Adolf III (1160–1225) was count of Holstein and Stormarn from the house of Schauenburg. Around 1188 he granted merchants land to found a new town beside the old cathedral settlement of Hamburg, the origin of the city's commercial growth, and obtained privileges for its trade.

albert-ballin.s: Albert Ballin (1857–1918) was a German shipping magnate who directed the Hamburg America Line (HAPAG) from 1899. Under him it became the largest shipping company in the world, carrying millions of emigrants and pioneering luxury cruises.

alster.s: The Alster is a river in northern Germany that rises in Schleswig-Holstein and flows into the Elbe at Hamburg. In the city it was dammed in the Middle Ages to drive mills, forming the two lakes of the Inner and Outer Alster that are central to Hamburg's townscape.

ag-weser.s: AG Weser was a shipbuilding company in Bremen, established under that name in 1872 and one of Germany's largest yards. It built liners, warships and many U-boats in both world wars, and from 1926 formed the core of the Deschimag group.

abdelhamid-ben-badis.s: Abdelhamid Ben Badis (1889–1940) was an Algerian Muslim scholar from Constantine and the leading figure of Islamic reform in colonial Algeria. In 1931 he founded the Association of Algerian Muslim Ulama, which set up schools teaching Arabic and Islam and opposed assimilation…

armee-d-afrique.s: The Armée d'Afrique was the part of the French army stationed in North Africa from the conquest of Algeria in 1830 until 1962. It included units recruited largely from Europeans, such as the Zouaves, the Chasseurs d'Afrique and the Foreign Legion, and from North Africans, such…

aimable-pelissier.s: Aimable Pélissier (1794–1864) was a French general who served for many years in the conquest of Algeria. In 1845 his troops asphyxiated hundreds of members of the Ouled Riah tribe sheltering in caves in the Dahra by lighting fires at the entrances, an act that caused outrage…

albert-camus.s: Albert Camus (1913–1960) was a French writer and philosopher born in Algeria to a poor settler family. His novels The Stranger and The Plague, both set in Algeria, and his essay The Myth of Sisyphus made him a leading figure of post-war literature, and he won the Nobel Prize…

arab-bureaux.s: The Arab Bureaux were French army offices created in 1844 to administer the Muslim population of the military territories of Algeria. Staffed by officers who learned Arabic and local customs, they collected taxes, settled disputes and gathered intelligence through local chiefs.

assia-djebar.s: Assia Djebar (1936–2015) was an Algerian novelist, historian and film-maker, the pen name of Fatima-Zohra Imalayène. Writing in French, she explored the lives of Algerian women and the memory of colonial conquest and war in novels such as Fantasia: An Algerian Cavalcade.

albert-sarraut.s: Albert Sarraut was a French Radical politician who served twice as governor-general of French Indochina, in 1911–1914 and 1917–1919, promising Franco-Vietnamese collaboration and expanding education. He was later Minister of the Colonies, where he promoted a programme of…

adlan-i.s: Adlan I was a sultan of the Funj Sultanate of Sennar in the early seventeenth century. When the Abdallab ruler Ajib, the Funj's most powerful vassal, rebelled, Adlan defeated and killed him at Karkoj on the Blue Nile around 1611, reasserting Sennar's supremacy over the…

alodia.s: Alodia, or Alwa, was the southernmost of the medieval Christian kingdoms of Nubia, centred on the central Sudan with its capital at Soba, near the confluence of the Blue and White Niles. Converted to Christianity in the sixth century, it was described by Arab writers as larger…

agisymba.s: Agisymba was a land in the interior of Africa south of the Sahara, known from Ptolemy's Geography, which drew on the earlier geographer Marinus of Tyre. According to that account, the Roman Julius Maternus reached it with the king of the Garamantes after four months' travel in…

archduke-john-of-austria.s: Archduke John of Austria was a Habsburg prince, son of Emperor Leopold II, who commanded Austrian armies against Napoleon and was a popular patron of Styria. His liberal reputation and marriage to a postmaster's daughter made him acceptable to the Frankfurt Parliament, which…

august-von-kotzebue.s: August von Kotzebue was a German playwright and writer, one of the most performed dramatists of his time, who also served the Russian government. His mockery of liberal and nationalist student movements made him a hated figure, and in March 1819 he was murdered in Mannheim by…

aeg.s: AEG, the Allgemeine Elektricitäts-Gesellschaft, was a German electrical company founded in Berlin in 1883 by Emil Rathenau to exploit Edison's patents. It grew into one of the largest electrical firms in the world, building power stations, electric railways and appliances, and…

anti-socialist-laws.s: The Anti-Socialist Laws were a German law passed in October 1878 at Otto von Bismarck's urging after two attempts on the life of Wilhelm I. It banned socialist and social democratic organisations, meetings and publications, although Social Democrats could still stand for the…

al-yaqubi.s: Al-Ya'qubi was an Arab historian and geographer of the Abbasid period who died in the late ninth century. He wrote a universal history and the Book of Countries, a geography based on his own travels and inquiries, which describes cities, routes and peoples from Central Asia to…

abul-fazl-bayhaqi.s: Abu'l-Fazl Bayhaqi was a Persian secretary in the chancery of the Ghaznavid sultans and a historian. His multi-volume history of the dynasty, of which the part on the reign of Mas'ud I survives as the Tarikh-i Bayhaqi, describes court life, politics and personalities in vivid…

ahmad-ibn-hasan-maymandi.s: Ahmad ibn Hasan Maymandi was a Persian administrator who served as vizier to the Ghaznavid sultan Mahmud of Ghazni from about 1013 to 1024. He promoted Persian instead of Arabic as the language of the chancery.

alp-tegin.s: Alp Tegin was a Turkic slave commander of the Samanid dynasty who rose to command the army of Khurasan. After a failed attempt to influence the Samanid succession, he withdrew to Ghazni in eastern Afghanistan in 962, took the town from its local ruler and held it as a nearly…

al-qanun-al-masudi.s: The Qanun al-Mas'udi is an encyclopaedic treatise on astronomy, mathematics and geography written in Arabic by al-Biruni and dedicated to the Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud I in the 1030s. It covers chronology, trigonometry, the motions of the sun, moon and planets and the…

anak-tomb-no-3.s: Anak Tomb No. 3 is a painted tomb near Anak in South Hwanghae Province, North Korea, dated by an ink inscription to 357 CE.

andong.s: Andong is a city in North Gyeongsang province in south-eastern South Korea, on the upper Nakdong River. In 1361, when Red Turban rebels from China took the Goryeo capital Kaegyong, King Gongmin took refuge there.

an-hyang.s: An Hyang was a Korean scholar-official of the Goryeo period who introduced Neo-Confucianism to Korea. Having encountered the works of Zhu Xi in the Yuan capital, he brought them back and promoted their study, reviving the state academy.

admirable-congress.s: The Admirable Congress was the constituent congress of Gran Colombia that met in Bogotá from January to May 1830, presided over by Antonio José de Sucre. It drafted a new constitution and accepted the resignation of Simón Bolívar as president.

adam-opel.s: Adam Opel was a German industrialist who founded the company that bears his name. Trained as a locksmith, he began making sewing machines at Rüsselsheim in the Grand Duchy of Hesse in 1862 and later added bicycles.

alexander-jagiellon.s: Alexander Jagiellon was grand duke of Lithuania from 1492 and king of Poland from 1501 until his death in 1506, a son of Casimir IV. He married Helena, daughter of Ivan III of Moscow, but could not prevent Muscovite conquests, including the defeat at Vedrosha in 1500.

arbed.s: ARBED was a Luxembourg steel company formed in 1911 by the merger of several ironworks and steelworks. Using the minette iron ore of southern Luxembourg, it became one of Europe's leading steel producers and the country's largest employer, with plants in Luxembourg, Germany,…

arcelor.s: Arcelor was a steel company formed in 2002 by the merger of ARBED of Luxembourg, Usinor of France and Aceralia of Spain, with its headquarters in Luxembourg. It was the world's largest steel producer by turnover.

arcelormittal.s: ArcelorMittal is a multinational steel and mining company formed in 2006 when Mittal Steel took over Arcelor. Headquartered in Luxembourg, it is one of the largest steel producers in the world, with plants in Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia.

andrei-rublev.s: Andrei Rublev was the most celebrated Russian icon painter of the Middle Ages, a monk associated with the Trinity Monastery of Sergius of Radonezh and the Andronikov Monastery in Moscow. He worked with Theophanes the Greek on the Annunciation Cathedral in the Moscow Kremlin…

accademia-del-cimento.s: The Accademia del Cimento was a scientific society founded in Florence in 1657 by Grand Duke Ferdinando II and his brother Leopoldo de' Medici, followers of Galileo. One of the first academies devoted to experiment, it carried out tests on air pressure, heat, freezing and the…

arcetri.s: Arcetri is a hilly district on the southern edge of Florence. Galileo Galilei moved there in 1631, to his villa Il Gioiello near the convent where his daughter was a nun, and after his condemnation by the Inquisition in 1633 he lived there under house arrest until his death in…

accademia-della-crusca.s: The Accademia della Crusca is a Florentine academy founded in the early 1580s to study and preserve the Italian language. Its name, meaning 'bran', refers to sifting good language from bad.

aryabhatiya.s: The Aryabhatiya is a Sanskrit astronomical and mathematical treatise composed by Aryabhata in 499 CE. In 121 verses it covers arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy, gives an approximation of pi of 3.1416 and proposes that the Earth rotates on its axis.

aulikara-dynasty.s: The Aulikara dynasty ruled the region of Dashapura, modern Mandsaur in western Malwa, in the fifth and sixth centuries CE, at first as subordinates of the Gupta Empire. Its most famous king, Yashodharman, claimed victory over the Huna ruler Mihirakula around 528 and boasted in…

agnikula.s: Agnikula, the 'fire lineage', is a legend of origin claimed by four Rajput clans: the Pratiharas, Paramaras, Chaulukyas and Chahamanas. In its developed form, found in bardic literature such as the Prithviraj Raso, the sage Vashistha created heroes from a sacrificial fire on…

ayudha-dynasty.s: The Ayudha dynasty ruled Kannauj in the late eighth and early ninth centuries CE, when the city was the prize of the tripartite struggle between the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas. Its kings Indrayudha and Chakrayudha were largely puppets of their more powerful neighbours:…

anna-of-bohemia-and-hungary.s: Anna of Bohemia and Hungary was the daughter of King Vladislaus II and sister of Louis II, and the wife of Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, the future Emperor Ferdinand I, whom she married in 1521 under a Habsburg–Jagiellonian double marriage treaty. When Louis II died at Mohács…

aulic-war-council.s: The Aulic War Council, or Hofkriegsrat, was the central military administration of the Habsburg Monarchy, established in Vienna in 1556. It oversaw the army, fortresses, supply and the Military Frontier against the Ottomans, and for long periods also conducted relations with…

abu-al-abbas-ahmad-ii.s: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad II was a Hafsid sultan who ruled from Tunis from 1370 to 1394. Already ruler of Constantine and Bejaia, he took Tunis in 1370 and spent his reign reuniting the dynasty's lands, subduing Arab tribes and rebellious towns in the south.

abu-faris-abd-al-aziz-ii.s: Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz II was a Hafsid sultan who ruled from Tunis from 1394 to 1434, one of the longest and most successful reigns of the dynasty. He restored central authority over Ifriqiya, imposed his overlordship on Tlemcen, and waged naval and corsair warfare against…

abu-al-hasan-ali-ibn-othman.s: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Othman was the Marinid sultan of Morocco from 1331 to 1348 and the dynasty's most ambitious ruler. He conquered Tlemcen in 1337 but was defeated by Castile and Portugal at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340.

abd-al-wahid-ben-messaoud.s: Abd al-Wahid ben Messaoud was a Moroccan envoy of the Saadi sultan Ahmad al-Mansur who led an embassy to the court of Elizabeth I of England in 1600. During his six months in London he proposed a joint Anglo-Moroccan attack on Spain, a plan that came to nothing.

anglo-hanseatic-war.s: The Anglo-Hanseatic War was a conflict between England and the Hanseatic League, fought mainly at sea by privateers, after Hanseatic merchants in London were arrested and fined in 1468. Danzig captains such as Paul Beneke raided English shipping, and Edward IV, needing peace,…

al-iklil.s: Al-Iklil, "the Crown", is a ten-volume work on the history, genealogies, antiquities and castles of south Arabia by the Yemeni scholar al-Hasan al-Hamdani, who died around 945. Only four volumes survive.

avitus.s: Avitus was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became Western Roman emperor in 455 with the backing of the Visigothic king Theodoric II. In his name Theodoric crushed the Suebi in Hispania in 456.

a-coruna.s: A Coruña is a port city in Galicia, north-western Spain, on the Atlantic coast. Its Roman lighthouse, the Tower of Hercules, still in use, is a World Heritage Site.

anwaruddin-khan.s: Anwaruddin Khan was Nawab of the Carnatic, ruling from Arcot, from 1744 to 1749, installed by Asaf Jah I, the Nizam of Hyderabad. In 1746 his large army was routed by a small French force at the Adyar river, an early sign of the superiority of European-trained troops.

asaf-jahi-dynasty.s: The Asaf Jahi dynasty ruled Hyderabad State in the Deccan from 1724 to 1948 under the title of Nizam. It was founded by the Mughal noble Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, Asaf Jah I, and its seven rulers became the foremost princes of British India after accepting a subsidiary alliance…

all-india-majlis-e-ittehadul-muslimeen.s: The Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen is a political party founded in Hyderabad State in 1927 to promote the interests of Muslims and the Nizam's rule. Under Qasim Razvi in 1946–1948 it opposed accession to India and organised the Razakar militia.

antisuyu.s: Antisuyu was the north-eastern quarter of the Inca Empire, covering the eastern slopes of the Andes and the edge of the Amazonian forest beyond Cusco. Its name is often thought to be the origin of the word Andes.

algonquin-people.s: The Algonquin are an Indigenous people of the Ottawa River valley in present-day Quebec and Ontario, whose name was later given to the wider Algonquian language family. Hunters and fur traders, they allied with Samuel de Champlain and the Huron against the Mohawk in 1609,…

abdul-jalil-iv-of-johor.s: Abdul Jalil IV was sultan of Johor from 1699 to 1718 and the first ruler of its Bendahara dynasty. As bendahara, the chief minister, he took the throne after the murder of Sultan Mahmud Shah II ended the old Malacca royal line.

alvise-cadamosto.s: Alvise Cadamosto was a Venetian merchant and navigator who sailed for Prince Henry of Portugal along the coast of West Africa in 1455 and 1456. He explored the Senegal and Gambia rivers and visited the court of the ruler of Cayor, then part of the Jolof realm.

andong-kim-clan.s: The Andong Kim clan was a Korean aristocratic lineage that dominated the government of Joseon for most of the first half of the nineteenth century. After the death of King Jeongjo in 1800, its leader Kim Jo-sun married his daughter to the boy king Sunjo, and the clan used its…

annals-of-the-joseon-dynasty.s: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (Joseon Wangjo Sillok) are the official chronicles of the reigns of Joseon kings from Taejo to Cheoljong, covering 1392 to 1863 in 1,893 volumes. Each reign's annals were compiled after the king's death from the daily notes of court historians,…

ahmad-ibn-furtu.s: Ahmad ibn Furtu was the chief imam and chronicler of Mai Idris Alooma of the Bornu Empire in the late sixteenth century. He wrote two Arabic accounts of the ruler's campaigns, the Book of the Bornu Wars and the Book of the Kanem Wars.

ali-tegin.s: Ali Tegin was a prince of the Kara-Khanid dynasty who ruled Bukhara and much of Transoxiana from about 1020 until his death in 1034. He fought rival members of his family and the Ghaznavids, and in 1025 Mahmud of Ghazni joined the eastern khan Yusuf Qadir Khan against him,…

abul-khayr-khan.s: Abu'l-Khayr Khan was a Shibanid descendant of Genghis Khan who ruled the nomadic Uzbeks of the steppe east of the Ural River from 1428 until his death. He united many tribes, took towns on the Syr Darya and raided Transoxiana, but after a defeat by the Oirats in 1457 his…

abylai-khan.s: Abylai Khan was a Kazakh ruler of the Middle Juz and a hero of the wars against the Dzungars, during which he was for a time held prisoner by them. After the Qing destroyed the Dzungar state in the 1750s, he balanced skilfully between Russia and China, acknowledging both, and…

aiteke-bi.s: Aiteke Bi was a Kazakh judge and orator of the Junior Juz, one of the three biys traditionally credited with drafting the law code Zhety Zhargy ('Seven Charters') under Tauke Khan, together with Tole Bi of the Senior Juz and Kazybek Bi of the Middle Juz. As a biy he settled…

asan-kaigy.s: Asan Kaigy was a semi-legendary poet and thinker of the fifteenth century, remembered as the first great zhyrau, or poet-adviser, of the Kazakhs and an adviser to Kazakh khans. In tradition he searched the steppe on a swift camel for Zheruiyk, a promised land of plenty where…

arsiyah.s: The Arsiyah were the Muslim guard of the Khazar rulers, a standing force of mercenaries said to have come from Khwarazm and stationed at the capital, Itil. The tenth-century historian al-Masudi describes them as several thousand mounted archers who served on condition that…

anna-of-kiev.s: Anna of Kiev was a daughter of Yaroslav the Wise who became queen of France as the wife of Henry I, whom she married in 1051. She was the mother of Philip I and acted with him in government during his minority after Henry's death in 1060.

ankole-watusi.s: The Ankole-Watusi is a breed of cattle known for its enormous horns, developed in the United States in the twentieth century from long-horned Sanga cattle of east-central Africa. Its ancestors include the Ankole cattle of the Bahima herders of Nkore in Uganda and the…

antonio-perez.s: Antonio Pérez was secretary of state to Philip II of Spain. Implicated in the murder of Juan de Escobedo, secretary of Don John of Austria, in 1578, he was arrested and in 1590 escaped to Aragon, where he claimed the protection of the Justicia.

adoptionism.s: Adoptionism is the Christian doctrine that Jesus, in his human nature, was the adopted rather than the natural Son of God. In late eighth-century Spain it was taught by Archbishop Elipandus of Toledo and Bishop Felix of Urgell, and attacked by Beatus of Liébana and Alcuin.

alte-pinakothek.s: The Alte Pinakothek is an art museum in Munich, commissioned by Ludwig I of Bavaria and built by Leo von Klenze, which opened in 1836. One of the first large public picture galleries in Europe, it houses the Old Master paintings of the Wittelsbach collections, from the…

anif-declaration.s: The Anif Declaration was issued on 12 November 1918 by Ludwig III of Bavaria at Anif Palace near Salzburg, where he had fled after Kurt Eisner proclaimed a republic in Munich. In it the king released his officials, officers and soldiers from their oath of loyalty, without…

adolphe-sax.s: Adolphe Sax was a Belgian instrument maker, born in Dinant, who invented the saxophone, patented in Paris in 1846. Working mainly in Paris, he also developed the saxhorn family of brass instruments, which were widely adopted by military bands.

atomium.s: The Atomium is a monument in Brussels built for the 1958 world's fair, Expo 58. Designed by the engineer André Waterkeyn with the architects André and Jean Polak, it represents an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times, with nine steel spheres joined by tubes and standing…

andrew-cohen.s: Andrew Cohen was a British colonial administrator who served as Governor of Uganda from 1952 to 1957. A reformer who favoured a unitary, self-governing Uganda, he deported Kabaka Mutesa II of Buganda to Britain in 1953 after the kabaka refused to cooperate and demanded…

apolo-kagwa.s: Apolo Kagwa was katikkiro, or chief minister, of Buganda from 1889 to 1926. A leader of the Protestant party in the religious wars, he headed the regency for the infant Kabaka Daudi Chwa II and negotiated the Buganda Agreement of 1900 with Sir Harry Johnston, which secured…

almagest.s: The Almagest is the astronomical treatise of Claudius Ptolemy, written in Greek in Alexandria around 150 CE. It set out the geocentric model of the universe and tables of planetary movements that remained the basis of astronomy until the work of Copernicus.

adandozan.s: Adandozan was king of Dahomey from 1797 to 1818. His reign coincided with a decline in the Atlantic slave trade and with continued tribute to Oyo.

agoli-agbo.s: Agoli-agbo was the last king of Dahomey, installed by the French in 1894 after the defeat and surrender of his brother Behanzin. He ruled a reduced kingdom around Abomey under French protection, without an army or foreign policy of its own.

akaba.s: Akaba was king of Dahomey from about 1685, succeeding Houegbadja. He extended the kingdom's territory on the Abomey plateau through wars with its neighbours.

abomey.s: Abomey is a town in southern Benin, the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey from the seventeenth century until 1894. Each king built his own palace there, and the Royal Palaces of Abomey, with their painted clay bas-reliefs recording the kingdom's history, were made a UNESCO…

aggersborg.s: Aggersborg is the largest of the Viking-age ring fortresses of Denmark, on the north shore of the Limfjord in northern Jutland. Built around 980, probably under Harald Bluetooth, it had a circular rampart about 240 metres across, divided by two streets into quarters filled…

albert-king-of-sweden.s: Albert, King of Sweden, also known as Albert of Mecklenburg, reigned from 1364 to 1389, after Swedish nobles deposed Magnus Eriksson and offered him the crown. His reliance on German advisers made him unpopular, and the nobles turned to Margaret I of Denmark and Norway, whose…

act-of-supremacy-1534.s: The Act of Supremacy 1534 was a law passed by the English Parliament declaring Henry VIII and his successors the Supreme Head of the Church of England. It completed the break with the papacy that followed the king's wish to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.

academie-francaise.s: The Académie française is the French institution responsible for the French language, founded in 1635 by Cardinal Richelieu under Louis XIII. Its forty members, known as the immortals, prepare the official dictionary of the language and rule on its usage.

adalbero-of-reims.s: Adalbero was Archbishop of Reims from 969 until his death in 989. After the death of the last Carolingian king, Louis V, in 987, he led the assembly of nobles and bishops that elected Hugh Capet as king of the Franks instead of the Carolingian claimant Charles of Lorraine, and…

alexis-de-tocqueville.s: Alexis de Tocqueville was a French political thinker, historian and politician. His Democracy in America (1835–1840), based on a journey through the United States, analysed the strengths and dangers of democratic society.

arsen-iqaltoeli.s: Arsen Iqaltoeli was a Georgian theologian, translator and hymnographer of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Trained at the Mangana monastery in Constantinople, he became an adviser to King David IV and taught at the Gelati and Iqalto academies.

arghun.s: Arghun was the fourth Mongol Ilkhan of Iran, reigning from 1284 to 1291. He came to power by overthrowing his uncle Tekuder, and he sent several embassies to the pope and the kings of Europe seeking an alliance against the Mamluks of Egypt.

adam-ferguson.s: Adam Ferguson was a Scottish philosopher and historian of the Scottish Enlightenment, professor at the University of Edinburgh. His Essay on the History of Civil Society of 1767 traced how societies develop from rude to commercial stages and warned that commerce and the…

adam-smith.s: Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher and economist of the Scottish Enlightenment. After The Theory of Moral Sentiments of 1759 he wrote An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, which argued that the division of labour and free markets…

alien-act-1705.s: The Alien Act 1705 was a law of the English Parliament designed to force Scotland into negotiations for union. It threatened that Scots in England would be treated as foreigners and that the main Scottish exports to England would be banned unless Scotland accepted the…

act-of-security-1704.s: The Act of Security 1704 was a law of the Parliament of Scotland that reserved its right to choose a different successor to Queen Anne from the one chosen by England, unless Scotland received guarantees of its religion, freedom and trade. It also allowed the arming of the…

alexander-of-greece.s: Alexander was king of Greece from 1917 to 1920. He was put on the throne in place of his father Constantine I, whom the Allies and Eleftherios Venizelos forced into exile for his neutral stance in the First World War, and he had little political power.

alexandros-papagos.s: Alexandros Papagos was a Greek field marshal and politician. As commander-in-chief he led the Greek army that drove back the Italian invasion of 1940–1941, and in 1949 he directed the final defeat of the communists in the Greek Civil War.

aberconwy-abbey.s: Aberconwy Abbey was a Cistercian monastery in north Wales, founded in 1186 and patronised by the princes of Gwynedd. Llywelyn the Great was buried there in 1240.

aelfgar-earl-of-mercia.s: Ælfgar was an Anglo-Saxon nobleman, son of Earl Leofric and Lady Godiva, who became Earl of East Anglia and later Earl of Mercia. Outlawed in 1055, he allied with the Welsh king Gruffudd ap Llywelyn, who married his daughter, and together they sacked Hereford.

anarawd-ap-rhodri.s: Anarawd ap Rhodri was king of Gwynedd from 878 until his death in 916, the eldest son of Rhodri the Great. In 881 he defeated the Mercians at the mouth of the Conwy, a battle the Welsh annals called vengeance for Rhodri.

admonitions-of-saint-stephen.s: The Admonitions of Saint Stephen are a Latin mirror for princes addressed by Stephen I of Hungary to his son Emeric, probably written in the 1010s or 1020s. In ten short chapters they urge the heir to keep the Catholic faith, honour the clergy and nobles, and welcome foreign…

amadeus-aba.s: Amadeus Aba was a Hungarian baron of the Aba kindred and one of the great oligarchs who ruled provinces almost independently around 1300. From the 1290s he controlled much of north-eastern Hungary, including the area around Kassa (Košice), and served several times as palatine.

andrew-i-of-hungary.s: Andrew I was king of Hungary from 1046 to 1060. A member of the Árpád dynasty who had lived in exile in Kievan Rus', he returned during the pagan uprising of 1046 that overthrew Peter Orseolo, and he restored Christianity.

albert-ii-of-germany.s: Albert II of Habsburg was duke of Austria from 1404 and, as son-in-law of Emperor Sigismund, became king of Hungary and of Bohemia in 1437–1438 and king of the Romans in 1438. He died in 1439 returning from a campaign against the Ottomans, and his posthumous son Ladislaus V…

armaztsikhe.s: Armaztsikhe is the ruined acropolis of ancient Iberia on the heights of Bagineti, above the Mtkvari river opposite Mtskheta in Georgia. Excavations since the 1930s have revealed fortification walls, a palace complex, baths and rich burials of the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

artoces.s: Artoces was king of Caucasian Iberia in the first century BCE. In 65 BCE, when Pompey pursued Mithridates VI of Pontus into the Caucasus, Artoces resisted and was defeated in battles on the Mtkvari (Kura) and Aragvi rivers, after which he submitted and gave his children as…

asomtavruli.s: Asomtavruli is the oldest form of the Georgian alphabet, written with rounded letters. Its earliest dated inscriptions, from the Bolnisi Sioni church and the Georgian monastery at Bir el Qutt near Bethlehem, belong to the fifth century.

alexander-ii-of-imereti.s: Alexander II was king of Imereti in western Georgia from 1484 to 1510, son of Bagrat II of Imereti. He held the kingdom against rivals and was recognised as overlord by the princes of Mingrelia, Guria and Abkhazia, though his attempts to take Kartli failed.
