archil-of-imereti.s: Archil was a Georgian prince of the Kakhetian Bagrationi line who reigned several times as king of Imereti between 1661 and 1698, and also for a time as king of Kakheti. Repeatedly deposed through Ottoman and local intrigues, he settled in Russia in 1699 and died in Moscow.

act-of-settlement-1662.s: The Act of Settlement 1662 was a law of the Irish Parliament that set out the terms for redistributing land in Ireland after the Restoration of Charles II. It largely confirmed Cromwellian soldiers and adventurers in the lands confiscated from Catholics after the rising of…

anthony-st-leger.s: Sir Anthony St Leger was an English administrator who served three times as lord deputy of Ireland between 1540 and 1556. He secured the Crown of Ireland Act of 1541, which made Henry VIII king of Ireland, and pursued the policy of surrender and regrant, persuading Gaelic and…

adad-nirari-iii.s: Adad-nirari III was king of Assyria from about 811 to 783 BCE, succeeding his father Shamshi-Adad V while young, possibly under the influence of his mother Sammuramat. His campaigns to the west weakened Aram-Damascus, and a stele from Tell al-Rimah records tribute from Joash…

amaziah-of-judah.s: Amaziah was king of Judah in the early eighth century BCE, the son of Joash of Judah. According to the Books of Kings he defeated the Edomites but then challenged Jehoash of Israel, who defeated and captured him at Beth-shemesh, broke down part of the walls of Jerusalem and…

armando-diaz.s: Armando Diaz was an Italian general who became chief of staff of the army in November 1917, after the defeat at Caporetto. He rebuilt morale, held the line of the Piave in 1918 and directed the victory of Vittorio Veneto that ended the war on the Italian front.

armistice-of-cassibile.s: The Armistice of Cassibile was the armistice between Italy and the Allies, signed secretly on 3 September 1943 at an Allied camp near Cassibile in Sicily and announced on 8 September. Italy surrendered unconditionally, and Germany at once occupied the centre and north of the…

assizes-of-jerusalem.s: The Assizes of Jerusalem are a collection of medieval legal treatises setting out the laws and customs of the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Cyprus. The most important were written in the 13th century by jurists such as Philip of Novara and John of Ibelin,…

atlit-castle.s: Atlit Castle, known to the crusaders as Château Pèlerin (Pilgrims' Castle), was a fortress built by the Knights Templar from 1218 on a promontory of the Mediterranean coast south of Haifa, in present-day Israel. It withstood a siege by the Mamluk sultan Baybars in 1265 and was…

ahaz.s: Ahaz was king of Judah in the second half of the 8th century BCE. When Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel attacked him in the Syro-Ephraimite War, he appealed to Tiglath-pileser III and became an Assyrian vassal, a submission recorded in Assyrian inscriptions under his full…

ahaziah-of-judah.s: Ahaziah was king of Judah for about a year around 842–841 BCE, the son of Jehoram and Athaliah. While visiting his uncle Joram of Israel at Jezreel, he was killed in Jehu's coup, although the Tel Dan Stele, probably set up by Hazael of Damascus, claims these deaths for the…

amon-of-judah.s: Amon was king of Judah for about two years in the mid-7th century BCE, the son and successor of Manasseh. The Bible says he continued his father's religious policies and was murdered by his own servants in the palace.

asherah.s: Asherah was a mother goddess of the ancient Levant, known from Ugaritic texts as the consort of the god El. Hebrew inscriptions of the 8th century BCE from Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom invoke Yahweh and his Asherah, suggesting that many Israelites and Judahites…

athaliah.s: Athaliah was queen of Judah for about six years in the 9th century BCE, the only woman to rule either Hebrew kingdom in her own right. A daughter of the house of Omri, she married Jehoram of Judah, and after her son Ahaziah was killed in Jehu's coup she seized power and killed…

azekah.s: Azekah was an ancient fortified town in the Shephelah, the low hills of Judah, at Tel Azekah in present-day Israel. It overlooked the Elah valley, the setting of the biblical story of David and Goliath.

ardys-of-lydia.s: Ardys was king of Lydia in the mid-7th century BCE, the son and successor of Gyges of the Mermnad dynasty. Early in his reign the Cimmerians sacked Sardis except for its citadel, and he sent an embassy to the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal.

aryenis.s: Aryenis was a Lydian princess of the 6th century BCE, daughter of King Alyattes and sister of Croesus. According to Herodotus she was married to Astyages, son of the Median king Cyaxares, to seal the peace that ended the war between Lydia and Media in 585 BCE.

ajivika.s: Ajivika was an ascetic religious movement of ancient India, led in the 5th century BCE by Makkhali Gosala, a contemporary and rival of the Buddha and Mahavira. Its followers held a strict determinism, believing that fate (niyati) governs everything.

aelfwynn.s: Ælfwynn was the daughter of Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, and her husband Æthelred, and briefly ruled Mercia after her mother's death in June 918. In December of that year her uncle, Edward the Elder of Wessex, removed her to Wessex and took direct control of Mercia, ending…

aethelberht-ii-of-east-anglia.s: Æthelberht II was king of East Anglia in the late 8th century, known from a few coins and later accounts. In 794 he was beheaded on the orders of Offa of Mercia, according to tradition after coming to Offa's court to seek the hand of his daughter.

aethelswith.s: Æthelswith was the daughter of King Æthelwulf of Wessex and sister of Alfred the Great. In 853 she married King Burgred of Mercia, sealing the alliance between the two kingdoms.

all-saints-church-brixworth.s: All Saints' Church in Brixworth, Northamptonshire, is one of the largest and best-preserved Anglo-Saxon churches in England. Built probably in the late 7th or 8th century, partly with reused Roman bricks and tiles, it was a basilica with side chambers and later gained a ring…

andrew-duke-of-calabria.s: Andrew, Duke of Calabria (1327–1345), was a Hungarian prince of the Angevin house, younger son of Charles I of Hungary and brother of Louis the Great. Married as a child to his cousin Joanna I of Naples, he was denied the crown by her party and was murdered at Aversa in…

antonio-beccadelli.s: Antonio Beccadelli (1394–1471), called Panormita after his native Palermo, was an Italian humanist and poet. His Latin epigrams, the Hermaphroditus (1425), made him famous and notorious.

antonio-genovesi.s: Antonio Genovesi (1713–1769) was a Neapolitan philosopher and economist and a leading figure of the Italian Enlightenment. In 1754 he took up the chair of commerce and mechanics at the University of Naples, one of the first chairs of political economy in Europe.

army-of-the-holy-faith.s: The Army of the Holy Faith (Sanfedisti) was the peasant army raised in Calabria in 1799 by Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo to restore the Bourbon king Ferdinand IV. Marching north with popular and clerical support, it retook Naples in June 1799 and destroyed the French-backed…

aishwarya-of-nepal.s: Aishwarya (1949–2001) was queen of Nepal as the wife of King Birendra, whom she married in 1970. A member of the Rana family, she was regarded as an influential figure at court and wrote poetry under a pen name.

amar-singh-thapa.s: Amar Singh Thapa (1751–1816) was a Gorkhali general who led Nepal's westward expansion. He commanded in Kumaon and Garhwal and besieged the fortress of Kangra from 1806 until he was forced back by the Sikhs of Ranjit Singh.

abercorn.s: Abercorn is a village on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth in West Lothian, Scotland. In 681 it became the seat of a Northumbrian bishopric for the Picts under Bishop Trumwine, marking the northern limit of Northumbrian power.

aelfwine-of-deira.s: Ælfwine of Deira (c. 661–679) was a younger brother of King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, who made him sub-king of Deira.

aella-of-northumbria.s: Ælla (died 867) was king of Northumbria in the 860s, having displaced King Osberht. When the Great Heathen Army seized York in 866, the rival kings made peace and attacked the city together in March 867, but both were killed.

aethelred-of-mercia.s: Æthelred was king of Mercia from 675 to 704, a son of Penda. In 679 he defeated Ecgfrith of Northumbria at the Battle of the Trent, recovering the province of Lindsey for Mercia permanently.

alhred-of-northumbria.s: Alhred was king of Northumbria from 765 to 774, during a period of rapid royal turnover. With his queen Osgifu he supported the Anglo-Saxon mission on the Continent, writing to Lul, archbishop of Mainz.

aelfgifu-of-northampton.s: Ælfgifu of Northampton (c. 990–after 1036) was the first wife of Cnut the Great and mother of Harold Harefoot, king of England.

akershus-fortress.s: Akershus Fortress is a medieval castle and fortress on the harbour of Oslo, begun around 1299 under King Haakon V, who moved the centre of royal government to Oslo. Christian IV rebuilt it as a Renaissance palace in the seventeenth century.

asiatic-vespers.s: The Asiatic Vespers was the massacre of Romans and Italians in the province of Asia and neighbouring regions ordered by Mithridates VI of Pontus in 88 BCE, during the First Mithridatic War. Ancient writers put the number of dead at 80,000 or more.

aguas-livres-aqueduct.s: The Águas Livres Aqueduct is a stone aqueduct that brought water to Lisbon, begun in 1731 under King John V and paid for largely by a tax on the city's residents. Its main arches over the Alcântara valley, completed by 1748, are among the tallest stone arches ever built.

antonio-prior-of-crato.s: António, Prior of Crato, was an illegitimate grandson of King Manuel I of Portugal and a claimant to the throne after the death of Cardinal-King Henry in 1580. Proclaimed king in Lisbon, he was defeated by the Duke of Alba at Alcântara in August 1580, and Philip II of Spain…

august-von-gneisenau.s: August Neidhardt von Gneisenau was a Prussian field marshal and military reformer. After defending Kolberg in 1807 he worked with Scharnhorst to rebuild the Prussian army after its defeat by Napoleon.

alexis-kagame.s: Alexis Kagame was a Rwandan Catholic priest, philosopher, historian and poet. Given access to the royal court's ritual specialists, he recorded the dynastic poems, genealogies and esoteric code of the Rwandan kingship, publishing them from the 1940s onwards.

arabia-felix.s: Arabia Felix ('Fortunate Arabia') was the Greek and Roman name for the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula, roughly modern Yemen. Its rainfall, farming and above all its trade in frankincense and myrrh gave it a reputation for fabulous wealth.

athtar.s: Athtar (ʿAthtar) was a god of ancient South Arabia identified with the planet Venus, the male counterpart of the Mesopotamian Ishtar and the Levantine Astarte. In Sabaean and other South Arabian inscriptions he is often named first among the gods, and he was associated with…

alfonso-iv-of-aragon.s: Alfonso IV, 'the Benign', was king of Aragon from 1327 to 1336. As heir, in 1323–1324 he led the expedition that took Sardinia from Pisa, besieging Villa di Chiesa (Iglesias) and winning at Lucocisterna, which made the Kingdom of Sardinia a reality within the Crown of Aragon.

armistice-of-villafranca.s: The Armistice of Villafranca was agreed on 11 July 1859 by Napoleon III and Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria after the battles of Magenta and Solferino. Austria gave up most of Lombardy, which passed through France to the Kingdom of Sardinia, but kept Venetia.

aberdeen.s: Aberdeen is a city and port in north-east Scotland, between the mouths of the rivers Dee and Don. A royal burgh from the twelfth century, it traded wool, hides and fish with the Low Countries and the Baltic, and its first university college, King's College, was founded in 1495.

acts-of-union-1800.s: The Acts of Union 1800 were parallel acts of the Parliament of Great Britain and the Parliament of Ireland that united the two kingdoms as the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1 January 1801. Passed after the Irish rebellion of 1798, with heavy use of patronage…

alexander-iii-of-scotland.s: Alexander III was King of Scots from 1249 to 1286. After the Battle of Largs in 1263 he gained the Western Isles and the Isle of Man from Norway by the Treaty of Perth of 1266, and his reign of peace with England and growing trade was later remembered as a golden age.

alexander-iii-of-imereti.s: Alexander III was King of Imereti in western Georgia from 1639 to 1660. Much of his reign was spent in conflict with Levan II Dadiani, the powerful prince of Mingrelia, and he sought the protection of Russia against his rivals and the Ottomans.

alnwick.s: Alnwick is a market town in Northumberland in north-east England, dominated by Alnwick Castle, the seat of the Percy family since 1309. It lay on the invasion route between Scotland and England, and two Scottish kings met disaster there: Malcolm III was killed nearby in 1093,…

auld-alliance.s: The Auld Alliance was the alliance between Scotland and France against England, first sealed by a treaty of 1295 between John Balliol and Philip IV and renewed by most later Scottish kings. It drew Scotland into repeated wars with England, including the invasion that ended at…

aeneid.s: The Aeneid is a Latin epic poem in twelve books by Virgil, written between about 29 and 19 BCE. It tells how the Trojan hero Aeneas escaped the fall of Troy and travelled to Italy, where his descendants would found Rome, and it served as a national epic for the Augustan regime.

assizes-of-ariano.s: The Assizes of Ariano are a collection of laws issued by Roger II of Sicily, traditionally at an assembly in Ariano in 1140. Drawing on Roman and canon law, they set out the authority of the king over his new kingdom, protected the church and the weak, and punished treason,…

augusta-sicily.s: Augusta is a port town on the east coast of Sicily, between Catania and Syracuse, founded by the emperor Frederick II in 1232. Off its coast on 22 April 1676 a French fleet fought a Spanish and Dutch fleet during the revolt of Messina, and the Dutch admiral Michiel de Ruyter…

alfred-nobel.s: Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer and industrialist who invented dynamite, patented in 1867, and other explosives, building an international business in explosives and armaments. In his will he left most of his fortune to found prizes for physics, chemistry,…

anders-celsius.s: Anders Celsius was a Swedish astronomer and professor at Uppsala University. He took part in the French expedition to Lapland in 1736–1737 that confirmed the flattening of the Earth at the poles, and founded the Uppsala observatory.

arboga.s: Arboga is a small town in Västmanland in central Sweden, a medieval trading centre for the iron of the Bergslagen mining district. The meeting held there in 1435 during Engelbrekt's revolt, attended by nobles, clergy, burghers and peasants, is conventionally regarded as the…

aachen-cathedral.s: Aachen Cathedral, in western Germany, has as its core the octagonal Palatine Chapel built for Charlemagne around 796–805, where he was buried in 814. From 936 to 1531 it was the coronation church of German kings, and a Gothic choir was added in the fourteenth and fifteenth…

admonitio-generalis.s: The Admonitio generalis is a capitulary issued by Charlemagne in 789, one of the main texts of the Carolingian reforms. In over eighty chapters, drawing on church law and probably drafted with the help of Alcuin, it called for the correction of the clergy and people, the…

abraham-kuyper.s: Abraham Kuyper was a Dutch Reformed theologian, journalist and politician. He founded the Anti-Revolutionary Party in 1879, the first modern Dutch political party, and the Free University of Amsterdam in 1880, and served as prime minister from 1901 to 1905.

anti-revolutionary-party.s: The Anti-Revolutionary Party was a Dutch Protestant political party founded in 1879 by Abraham Kuyper, the first national mass party in the Netherlands. Rejecting the principles of the French Revolution, it fought for state funding of religious schools, won in 1917, and took…

afsluitdijk.s: The Afsluitdijk is a dam about 32 kilometres long in the northern Netherlands, completed in 1932 as the central work of the Zuiderzee Works. It closed off the Zuiderzee from the Wadden Sea, turning it into the freshwater IJsselmeer, protecting the surrounding coasts from…

anne-frank.s: Anne Frank was a German-born Jewish girl whose family fled to Amsterdam and, from 1942, hid from the Nazi occupiers in a secret annex behind her father's business. During two years in hiding she kept a diary.

arthur-seyss-inquart.s: Arthur Seyss-Inquart was an Austrian Nazi politician who briefly served as Chancellor of Austria during its annexation by Germany in March 1938. From 1940 to 1945 he was Reichskommissar of the occupied Netherlands, where he oversaw the deportation of Dutch Jews, forced labour…

aed-mac-boanta.s: Áed mac Boanta was a king of Dál Riata in the early ninth century, probably ruling under the dominance of the Pictish kings of Fortriu. In 839 he was killed together with the Pictish king Eóganán son of Óengus and many others in a great Viking victory over the men of Fortriu,…

annals-of-ulster.s: The Annals of Ulster are a chronicle of Irish history from the fifth century to the sixteenth, compiled in the late fifteenth century for Cathal Óg Mac Maghnusa on Belle Isle in Lough Erne from much older annal collections. Their year-by-year entries, many contemporary from…

auisle.s: Auisle was a Viking leader in Ireland in the 860s, who with Amlaíb (Olaf) ruled the Norse of Dublin and is described in Irish sources as Amlaíb's brother. In 866 Olaf and Auisle plundered the whole of Pictland and took hostages, weakening the Pictish kingdom.

ammishtamru-i.s: Ammishtamru I was king of Ugarit in the fourteenth century BCE, during the Amarna period. A letter from him to the Egyptian pharaoh survives among the Amarna letters, showing Ugarit's close ties with Egypt before the Hittite advance into northern Syria.

ammishtamru-ii.s: Ammishtamru II was king of Ugarit in the thirteenth century BCE, ruling as a vassal of the Hittite Empire at the height of the city's prosperity. His divorce from a princess of Amurru, a daughter of King Benteshina, became an international affair settled by verdicts of the…

arhalba.s: Arhalba was king of Ugarit for a short reign in the late fourteenth century BCE, succeeding his father Niqmaddu II. He ruled as a vassal of the Hittite Empire, and after his brief reign his brother Niqmepa was placed on the throne by the Hittite king Mursili II, who also…

amarna-period.s: The Amarna Period is the late Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the mid-fourteenth century BCE, named after Amarna (Akhetaten), the new capital built by the pharaoh Akhenaten for the cult of the sun disc Aten. Its archive of clay tablets, the Amarna letters, preserves Egypt's…

arame-of-urartu.s: Arame was the first known king of Urartu, ruling in the mid-ninth century BCE. He is known only from Assyrian sources: the annals of Shalmaneser III record campaigns against him from 859 BCE and the sack of his royal city Arzashkun in 856 BCE.

argishti-ii.s: Argishti II was king of Urartu from about 714 to 685 BCE, succeeding his father Rusa I after Sargon II of Assyria's devastating campaign of 714 BCE. He restored royal authority and campaigned to the east, leaving inscriptions as far as the region of Lake Urmia and the Ararat…

argishtihinili.s: Argishtihinili was a Urartian city founded by Argishti I around 776 BCE on the Ararat plain, near modern Armavir in Armenia. Built on two fortified hills, it became a major administrative and agricultural centre irrigated by royal canals.

arzashkun.s: Arzashkun was the royal city of the early Urartian king Arame in the ninth century BCE and one of the earliest named centres of the Urartian kingdom. It is known only from Assyrian records: the annals of Shalmaneser III describe its capture and burning in 856 BCE.

ashur-god.s: Ashur was the chief god of the Assyrians, originally the deity of the city of Ashur on the Tigris, with which he shared his name. As Assyria grew into an empire he became the supreme god of the state, and kings presented their wars as campaigns on his behalf; Sargon II's…

ayanis.s: Ayanis is the site of a Urartian fortress on the eastern shore of Lake Van in eastern Turkey, founded by Rusa II in the seventh century BCE and known in antiquity as Rusahinili Eiduru-kai. Excavations since 1989 have uncovered a temple of the god Haldi with inlaid stone walls,…

aethelbald-of-mercia.s: Æthelbald was king of Mercia from 716 to 757 and the dominant ruler of southern England for much of his reign. Bede counted all the English kingdoms south of the Humber as subject to him by 731, and a charter of 736 styles him king of Britain.

aethelred-i-of-wessex.s: Æthelred I was king of Wessex from 865 to 871, the fourth son of Æthelwulf to reign. His reign saw the arrival of the Great Heathen Army, and in 871, the year of battles, he and his younger brother Alfred fought the Danes repeatedly, winning at Ashdown.

aethelwold-aetheling.s: Æthelwold was a West Saxon prince, the son of King Æthelred I and cousin of Edward the Elder. On the death of Alfred the Great in 899 he seized Wimborne and Christchurch to claim the throne, then fled to the Danes of Northumbria, who accepted him as king.

aethelwulf-of-wessex.s: Æthelwulf was king of Wessex from 839 to 858, the son of Ecgberht. He and his son Æthelbald won a great victory over the Vikings at Aclea in 851, and in 855 he made a pilgrimage to Rome with his youngest son Alfred, marrying the Frankish princess Judith on his return.

anglo-saxon-chronicle.s: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a collection of annals in Old English recording the history of the English from the Roman period to the twelfth century. First compiled in Wessex in the late ninth century, during the reign of Alfred the Great, it was copied and continued in…

athelney.s: Athelney is a low hill rising above the marshes of the Somerset Levels in south-west England. Alfred the Great took refuge there after the Danish attack on Chippenham in January 878, building a fort from which he harassed the enemy before his victory at Edington.

ante-trumbic.s: Ante Trumbić was a Croatian politician from Split who led the Yugoslav Committee, the exile body of South Slav politicians from Austria-Hungary, during the First World War. In 1917 he signed the Corfu Declaration with the Serbian prime minister Nikola Pašić, agreeing on a…

amnisos.s: Amnisos is an ancient harbour site on the north coast of Crete, east of Heraklion, that served as a port of Knossos. Excavations revealed a Minoan villa with frescoes of lilies, and the nearby cave of Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, is mentioned in Homer's Odyssey.

amarapura.s: Amarapura is a former royal capital of Burma, now part of the city of Mandalay. It was founded by King Bodawpaya in 1783 and served as capital from 1783 to 1821 and again from 1842 until 1859, when Mindon moved the court to Mandalay.

anglo-burmese-wars.s: The Anglo-Burmese Wars were three wars fought between British India and the Konbaung kingdom of Burma in the nineteenth century. The First (1824–1826) cost Burma Arakan, Tenasserim and its claims to Assam and Manipur; the Second (1852–1853) gave Britain Lower Burma; and the…

alaungpaya.s: Alaungpaya was the founder of the Konbaung dynasty of Burma, reigning from 1752 to 1760. Born Aung Zeya, a headman of the village of Moksobo, he resisted the Restored Hanthawaddy kingdom after its capture of Ava, made Moksobo his capital as Shwebo and reunified Burma within a…

alvaro-i-of-kongo.s: Álvaro I was king of Kongo from 1568 to 1587. Early in his reign invaders known as the Jaga overran the kingdom and drove him from his capital, São Salvador, to an island in the Congo River, and he was restored in the early 1570s with the help of Portuguese troops sent from…

ashvaghosha.s: Ashvaghosha was an Indian Buddhist philosopher, dramatist and poet, regarded as one of the first great masters of classical Sanskrit poetry. His Buddhacarita, an epic life of the Buddha, and the Saundarananda are the best-known works attributed to him.

amanirenas.s: Amanirenas was a ruling queen, or kandake, of the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë. Around 25 BCE her armies attacked Roman Egypt, sacking Syene and carrying off statues of Augustus, one of whose bronze heads was buried at Meroë.

amanishakheto.s: Amanishakheto was a ruling queen, or kandake, of the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë in the late 1st century BCE. She is known from inscriptions and building work at several sites, and from her pyramid at Meroë, where in 1834 the Italian adventurer Giuseppe Ferlini found a treasure…

alexandre-de-rhodes.s: Alexandre de Rhodes was a Jesuit missionary from Avignon who worked in Cochinchina and in Tonkin from 1627 to 1630, winning many converts before his expulsion. Building on the work of Portuguese missionaries, he published in Rome in 1651 a Vietnamese–Portuguese–Latin…

allen-yancy.s: Allen Yancy was vice-president of Liberia from 1928 to 1930 under President Charles D. B.

alcantara-bridge.s: The Alcántara Bridge is a Roman stone arch bridge over the Tagus at Alcántara in Extremadura, Spain. Built under Trajan in about 104–106 CE by the architect Gaius Julius Lacer, it was paid for by communities of Lusitania named in its inscription.

aljustrel.s: Aljustrel is a town in the Beja district of the Alentejo in southern Portugal, in the Iberian Pyrite Belt. Its copper and silver deposits were worked in Roman times at the mining district of Vipasca, where bronze tablets preserving imperial mining regulations were found in…

asturia.s: Asturia was the Roman name for the lands of the Astures in north-western Hispania, covering modern Asturias, the province of León and neighbouring areas. Conquered in Augustus' Cantabrian Wars of 29–19 BCE, it was soon attached to the province of Hispania Tarraconensis, with…

aqueduct-of-los-milagros.s: The Aqueduct of Los Milagros is a Roman aqueduct at Mérida in Spain, ancient Emerita Augusta, capital of Lusitania. It carried water from the Proserpina reservoir to the city, and a stretch of some 800 metres of its granite and brick piers still stands, up to about 25 metres…

abdallah-barshambu.s: Abdallah Barshambu was a king of Makuria in Nubia, a member of the royal house who had become a Muslim while living at the Mamluk court in Cairo. The Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad placed him on the throne in 1317, and an Arabic inscription records the conversion of the…

abdallah-ibn-sad-ibn-abi-sarh.n: Abdallah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh
abdallah-ibn-sad-ibn-abi-sarh.s: Abdallah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh was an Arab commander and governor of Egypt from about 645 to 656 under the caliph Uthman, his foster-brother. In 652 he besieged Old Dongola, capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, but could not take it and concluded the Baqt, a treaty that…

aidhab.s: Aidhab was a medieval port on the African coast of the Red Sea, in the Halaib region on the modern border of Egypt and Sudan. From the 10th to the 14th century it was a major harbour for pilgrims crossing to Jeddah and for the spice trade between Egypt, Yemen and India, linked…

akhmim.s: Akhmim is a town on the east bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, in Sohag Governorate. Called Panopolis by the Greeks, it was a cult centre of the god Min and in late antiquity a centre of textile production and Christian monasticism.

abdullah-ahmad-badawi.s: Abdullah Ahmad Badawi was the fifth prime minister of Malaysia, from 2003 to 2009, succeeding Mahathir Mohamad. He promised to fight corruption, promoted 'Islam Hadhari', a moderate approach to Islam, and won a landslide in 2004, but the Barisan Nasional lost its two-thirds…

abdul-razak-hussein.s: Abdul Razak Hussein, known as Tun Abdul Razak, was the second prime minister of Malaysia, from 1970 until his death in 1976. After the race riots of 13 May 1969 he headed the National Operations Council that governed during the emergency, then launched the New Economic Policy…

abu-ishaq-al-sahili.s: Abu Ishaq al-Sahili was an Andalusi poet from Granada who accompanied Mansa Musa back from Mecca to the Mali Empire in the 1320s. Tradition credits him with designing buildings for the mansa, including a royal audience chamber and the Djinguereber Mosque at Timbuktu.

al-maqrizi.s: Al-Maqrizi was an Egyptian historian of the Mamluk period and a pupil of Ibn Khaldun, who held posts in Cairo including that of market inspector. His Khitat, a topographical history of Cairo and Egypt, and his chronicles of the Fatimid, Ayyubid and Mamluk dynasties are among…

attock.s: Attock is a town in Punjab, Pakistan, on the Indus near its junction with the Kabul River. Its fort, built by the Mughal emperor Akbar in 1581–1583, guarded the main crossing of the Indus on the road between Kabul and Lahore.

archdiocese-of-olomouc.s: The Archdiocese of Olomouc is a Catholic see in Moravia, in the Czech Republic, established as a bishopric in 1063 and raised to an archbishopric in 1777. Its bishops were among the greatest landowners of Moravia and led German colonisation in the 13th century, notably under…

abu-kamal.s: Abu Kamal (al-Bukamal) is a town in eastern Syria, in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, on the Euphrates at the border with Iraq, opposite al-Qa'im. The ruins of ancient Mari at Tell Hariri lie a few kilometres to the north-west.

andre-parrot.s: André Parrot was a French archaeologist who directed the excavation of Mari at Tell Hariri in Syria from 1933 until 1974. His team uncovered the palace of Zimri-Lim, temples, statues and some 20,000 cuneiform tablets of the royal archives of Mari.

amangkurat-ii.s: Amangkurat II was ruler of Mataram from 1677 to 1703, the son of Amangkurat I. To defeat the Trunajaya rebellion he allied with the Dutch East India Company, granting it ports, trade monopolies and payment of its costs.

amangkurat-iii.s: Amangkurat III, also called Sunan Mas, was ruler of Mataram from 1703 to 1705. The Dutch East India Company backed his uncle Pangeran Puger, who took the throne as Pakubuwana I, in the First Javanese War of Succession.

amangkurat-iv.s: Amangkurat IV was ruler of Mataram from 1719 to 1726, succeeding his father Pakubuwana I. His accession led to the Second Javanese War of Succession, in which his brothers and uncles rebelled and were defeated with the help of the Dutch East India Company by 1723.

alexander-ii-of-epirus.s: Alexander II of Epirus was king of Epirus from 272 BCE, the son and successor of Pyrrhus. He fought Antigonus II Gonatas for Macedonia and was briefly driven from his own kingdom before regaining it.

andriamasinavalona.s: Andriamasinavalona was a king of Imerina in the central highlands of Madagascar who ruled around 1675–1710. He extended the kingdom to its largest size before the nineteenth century but divided it among his sons, leading to nearly a century of rivalry and war between four…

andrianjaka.s: Andrianjaka was a king of Imerina in the central highlands of Madagascar in the early seventeenth century, the son of Ralambo. Tradition credits him with capturing the hill of Analamanga, which he renamed Antananarivo and made the royal seat, and with acquiring firearms.

antsiranana.s: Antsiranana, formerly Diego Suarez, is a port city at the northern tip of Madagascar, on one of the world's largest natural harbours. France obtained it by the treaty of 1885 that ended the Franco-Hova War and made it a naval base.

adolfo-lopez-mateos.s: Adolfo López Mateos was president of Mexico from 1958 to 1964 for the Institutional Revolutionary Party. His government nationalised the electricity industry in 1960, expanded land distribution, social security and free school textbooks, and crushed the railway workers' strike…

alfonso-garcia-robles.s: Alfonso García Robles was a Mexican diplomat who led the negotiations for the Treaty of Tlatelolco of 1967, which made Latin America a nuclear-weapon-free zone. He later served as foreign minister and as Mexico's representative to the Committee on Disarmament in Geneva.

alvaro-obregon.s: Álvaro Obregón was a Mexican general and president from 1920 to 1924. A leading Constitutionalist commander in the Mexican Revolution, he defeated Pancho Villa at the battles of Celaya in 1915 and came to power through the Agua Prieta revolt of 1920.

andres-manuel-lopez-obrador.s: Andrés Manuel López Obrador is a Mexican politician who was president from 2018 to 2024. A former head of government of Mexico City and twice a losing presidential candidate, he founded the Morena party and won a landslide in 2018 on promises to fight corruption and poverty.

amenemhat-ii.s: Amenemhat II was the third king of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt, reigning for more than thirty years around the turn of the twentieth and nineteenth centuries BCE. His reign was largely peaceful and prosperous, with expeditions to Sinai and Punt and contacts with the Levant…

amenemhat-iv.s: Amenemhat IV was the penultimate king of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt, reigning for about nine years in the late nineteenth century BCE. He continued the works of Amenemhat III, completing the temple at Medinet Madi in the Faiyum, and sent expeditions to the turquoise mines of…

antiochus-ii-theos.s: Antiochus II Theos was king of the Seleucid Empire from 261 to 246 BCE. He fought the Second Syrian War against Ptolemy II of Egypt, which ended with his marriage to Ptolemy's daughter Berenice, and recovered cities in Asia Minor and Thrace.

ashvins.s: The Ashvins, also called the Nasatyas, are twin horsemen gods of the Rigveda, associated with dawn, healing and rescue. They are invoked as the Nasatyas, with Mitra, Varuna and Indra, in a treaty of the 14th century BCE between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza of…

arakan-rohingya-salvation-army.s: The Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army is a Rohingya insurgent group in Rakhine State, Myanmar. Its attacks on police posts in October 2016 and August 2017 were followed by military 'clearance operations' in which thousands of Rohingya were killed and more than 700,000 fled to…

aung-san-suu-kyi.s: Aung San Suu Kyi is a Burmese politician, daughter of the independence leader Aung San, who led the democracy movement against military rule from 1988. Her National League for Democracy won the 1990 election, which the junta ignored, and she spent about fifteen of the…

albert-speer.s: Albert Speer was a German architect and Nazi politician who became Hitler's favourite architect and, from 1942, Minister of Armaments and War Production. By rationalising industry and using forced labour he raised arms output to a peak in 1944.

anglo-german-naval-agreement.s: The Anglo-German Naval Agreement, signed in London on 18 June 1935, allowed Nazi Germany to build a navy of up to 35 per cent of the Royal Navy's surface tonnage and 45 per cent of its submarine tonnage. By accepting a breach of the Treaty of Versailles without consulting…

antoine-de-lamothe-cadillac.s: Antoine de Lamothe Cadillac was a French adventurer and colonial officer in North America. After commanding the post at Michilimackinac, he founded Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit on the Detroit River in 1701, the origin of the city of Detroit.

alexander-von-humboldt.s: Alexander von Humboldt was a Prussian naturalist, geographer and explorer. From 1799 to 1804 he travelled through Spanish America with the botanist Aimé Bonpland, and his Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain described Mexico's population, mines and economy.

andres-de-urdaneta.s: Andrés de Urdaneta was a Spanish navigator and Augustinian friar. Sailing with the expedition of Miguel López de Legazpi to the Philippines in 1565, he found the return route across the Pacific to Mexico by sailing north to catch the westerly winds, a route known as the…

all-blacks.s: The All Blacks are New Zealand's national rugby union team, named for their black kit and known for performing the haka before matches. Since their first international tour in 1884 they have become one of the most successful teams in any sport, winning the Rugby World Cup in…

aulus-postumius-albinus.s: Aulus Postumius Albinus was a Roman commander in the Jugurthine War. Left in charge of the army in Numidia by his brother, the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus, he marched on the royal treasury town of Suthul in the winter of 110–109 BCE, but Jugurtha surprised his camp and…

amadocus-i.s: Amadocus I, often identified with the Medocus mentioned by Xenophon, was a king of the Odrysian Thracians in the late fifth and early fourth centuries BCE. After the reign of Seuthes I he ruled the interior of the kingdom, while Seuthes II held the lands towards the Propontis.

amadocus-ii.s: Amadocus II was one of the three kings among whom the Odrysian Kingdom was divided after the murder of Cotys I in 360 BCE, ruling the central part between his rivals Cersobleptes in the east and Berisades in the west. Athens and Philip II of Macedon played the three rulers…

ares.s: Ares was the Greek god of war, a son of Zeus and Hera, identified by the Romans with Mars. Greek writers often placed his home in Thrace, and Herodotus reported that the Thracians worshipped gods he equated with Ares, Dionysus and Artemis.

albrecht-von-haller.s: Albrecht von Haller was a Swiss physiologist, anatomist, botanist and poet from Bern, often called the father of modern physiology for his experiments on the irritability of muscles and the sensibility of nerves. He taught at the University of Göttingen from 1736 to 1753.

abraham-davel.s: Abraham Davel was a Vaudois soldier and militia major who tried to free Vaud from the rule of Bern. On 31 March 1723 he led his militia into Lausanne and called on the city council to proclaim Vaud's independence, but the council betrayed him.

atiba-atobatele.s: Atiba Atobatele was Alaafin of Oyo from about 1837 to 1859. After the abandonment of Oyo-Ile he established the capital of a reduced kingdom at New Oyo, the present city of Oyo, farther south.

alaungsithu.s: Alaungsithu, also known as Sithu I, was king of Pagan from about 1112 to 1167 and the grandson and successor of Kyansittha. His long reign was a period of internal peace and prosperity, during which he travelled widely in his realm, is credited with standardising weights and…

appar.s: Appar, also called Tirunavukkarasar, was a Tamil Shaiva poet-saint of the seventh century and one of the most revered of the 63 Nayanars. Born a Shaiva, he became a Jain monk before returning to the worship of Shiva, and tradition holds that he converted the Pallava king…

ashvatthama.s: Ashvatthama is a warrior in the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata, the son of the teacher Drona, who fights for the Kauravas in the war at Kurukshetra. After the war he kills the sleeping sons of the Pandavas in a night raid and is cursed to wander the earth.

apostolic-camera.s: The Apostolic Camera was the central financial office of the papacy, which from the eleventh century collected the revenues of the Holy See and, in the Papal States, administered taxes, customs, mints and state property. Headed by the cardinal camerlengo, it also acquired…

andragoras.s: Andragoras was the Seleucid governor of the satrapy of Parthia in north-eastern Iran who declared himself independent around 245 BCE and issued his own coins. Around 238 BCE he was overthrown and killed by Arsaces I, leader of the Parni, whose seizure of Parthia began the…

anti-rightist-campaign.s: The Anti-Rightist Campaign was a political purge in the People's Republic of China launched in 1957, after the Hundred Flowers movement had invited intellectuals to criticise the Communist Party. More than half a million people, many of them intellectuals and officials, were…

andre-gretry.s: André-Ernest-Modeste Grétry was a composer from Liège who made his career in Paris and became the leading composer of French opéra comique in the late eighteenth century. His works included Zémire et Azor and Richard Cœur-de-lion (1784), and he was honoured by both the old…

alghero.s: Alghero is a port on the north-west coast of Sardinia, Italy. Taken by the Crown of Aragon in 1354 and resettled with Catalans, it has kept a Catalan dialect, still spoken by part of its population, and Catalan Gothic buildings.

aragonese-crusade.s: The Aragonese Crusade was a crusade declared by Pope Martin IV against King Peter III of Aragon, who had taken Sicily after the Sicilian Vespers. Philip III of France invaded Catalonia in 1285 and took Girona, but disease and the destruction of his fleet by Roger of Lauria…

anton-florian-prince-of-liechtenstein.s: Anton Florian was prince of Liechtenstein from 1718 to 1721. A courtier and diplomat who had been tutor to the future Emperor Charles VI, he obtained from Charles in 1719 the union of Vaduz and Schellenberg as the Imperial Principality of Liechtenstein, the state that still…

alois-hereditary-prince-of-liechtenstein.s: Alois is the eldest son and heir of Prince Hans-Adam II of Liechtenstein. Since August 2004 he has exercised the day-to-day duties of head of state as his father's representative, while Hans-Adam remains the sovereign prince.

alexandru-lapusneanu.s: Alexandru Lăpușneanu was prince of Moldavia from 1552 to 1561 and again from 1564 to 1568. Known for his cruelty towards the boyars, he moved the capital from Suceava to Iași and founded the Slatina Monastery.

arbore-church.s: Arbore Church is a church in Suceava County, Romania, built in 1503 by the Moldavian boyar Luca Arbore. Its outer walls were painted with frescoes in 1541, and it is one of the painted churches of northern Moldavia on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

anglo-persian-agreement.s: The Anglo-Persian Agreement was a treaty negotiated in August 1919 between Britain, led by Lord Curzon, and the government of Vosuq od-Dowleh in Qajar Iran. It would have given Britain control of Iran's army and finances through advisers in return for a loan, amounting to a…

abu-ubayda-ibn-al-jarrah.s: Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah was an early companion of Muhammad and one of the leading commanders of the Rashidun conquest of Syria. He commanded the Arab armies, with Khalid ibn al-Walid, at the Battle of the Yarmuk in 636, and as governor of Syria received the surrender of…

amoghavarsha-iii.s: Amoghavarsha III, also called Baddega, was Rashtrakuta emperor of the Deccan from about 936 to 939. A son of Indra III and uncle of Govinda IV, he was placed on the throne by nobles and feudatories, backed by the Chalukyas of Vemulavada, after Govinda IV's unpopular reign…

ananda-mahidol.s: Ananda Mahidol, Rama VIII, was king of Siam, later Thailand, from 1935 to 1946. He came to the throne aged nine after the abdication of his uncle Prajadhipok and spent most of his reign at school in Switzerland while regents governed.

abraham-duquesne.s: Abraham Duquesne was a French naval commander, a Protestant from Dieppe, who became one of Louis XIV's leading admirals. In 1676 he defeated a Dutch-Spanish fleet under Michiel de Ruyter at the Battle of Augusta off Sicily.

andres-bello.s: Andrés Bello was a Venezuelan-born scholar, poet and jurist who settled in Chile in 1829. He became the first rector of the University of Chile, wrote an influential grammar of the Spanish language and drafted the Chilean Civil Code of 1855, which was adopted or adapted by…

arica.s: Arica is a port city in the far north of Chile, near the border with Peru. Long part of Peru and an outlet for silver and trade from Bolivia, it was occupied by Chile during the War of the Pacific after the storming of the Morro de Arica in 1880.

army-of-the-andes.s: The Army of the Andes was the force raised by José de San Martín in Mendoza, in the province of Cuyo, between 1814 and 1817. In January and February 1817 it crossed the Andes in several columns and defeated the royalists at Chacabuco, and in 1818 it won the Battle of Maipú,…

arturo-prat.s: Arturo Prat was a Chilean naval officer and lawyer who commanded the old corvette Esmeralda at the Battle of Iquique on 21 May 1879, during the War of the Pacific. When the Peruvian ironclad Huáscar rammed his ship, he leapt aboard the enemy vessel and was killed.

afro-ecuadorians.s: Afro-Ecuadorians are Ecuadorians of African descent, most of them descendants of enslaved Africans brought to the colony from the sixteenth century and of the free maroon communities of Esmeraldas. They are concentrated in the coastal province of Esmeraldas and the Chota…

arturo-araujo.s: Arturo Araujo was a Salvadoran landowner and engineer who won the free presidential election of 1931 with the support of labour and peasant groups. He took office in March 1931, but his government was overwhelmed by the collapse of coffee prices in the Great Depression.

atlacatl-battalion.s: The Atlacatl Battalion was a rapid-response counter-insurgency unit of the Salvadoran army, created in 1981 and trained by United States advisers. During the civil war it carried out some of the worst atrocities, including the El Mozote massacre of December 1981 and the murder…

alexander-stubb.s: Alexander Stubb is a Finnish politician of the National Coalition Party who served as foreign minister, prime minister in 2014–2015 and finance minister. After several years in academic and European posts, he won the presidential election of 2024 and took office as president…

alvar-aalto.s: Alvar Aalto was a Finnish architect and designer, one of the leading figures of modern architecture. His buildings, such as the Paimio Sanatorium, the Villa Mairea and Finlandia Hall in Helsinki, combined modernist forms with natural materials and attention to human needs.

arctic-ocean.s: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's oceans, surrounding the North Pole and bordered by Europe, Asia and North America. Much of it is covered by sea ice for most of the year.

acciaiuoli-family.s: The Acciaiuoli were a Florentine family of merchant-bankers who rose to prominence in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Their company, one of the great firms of the age alongside those of the Bardi and Peruzzi, traded and lent across Europe and served the papacy and the…

arte-di-calimala.s: The Arte di Calimala was the guild of cloth merchants of Florence, named after the street where its members had their shops. The first in prestige of the city's seven major guilds, it imported woollen cloth from northern Europe, finished and dyed it, and sold it across the…

arezzo.s: Arezzo is a city in eastern Tuscany, Italy, standing on a hill above the upper valleys of the Arno and Tiber. An important Etruscan centre and later a Roman town known for its red-glazed pottery, it was a Ghibelline rival of Florence in the Middle Ages until its defeat at…

arte-della-lana.s: The Arte della Lana was the wool guild of Florence, one of the city's seven major guilds. Its members organised the manufacture of woollen cloth from imported English and later Spanish wool, employing thousands of wage workers in spinning, weaving and finishing, which made…

alta-verapaz.s: Alta Verapaz is a department of northern Guatemala with its capital at Cobán, a region of humid highlands and forests inhabited largely by Q'eqchi' Maya. From the late nineteenth century German immigrant planters developed coffee estates there, worked by indigenous labour…

alvaro-arzu.s: Álvaro Arzú (1946–2018) was a Guatemalan politician who served as president from 1996 to 2000 and for several terms as mayor of Guatemala City. His government concluded the peace negotiations with the guerrilla coalition URNG, signing the final agreement that ended the 36-year…

amatitlan.s: Amatitlán is a town in the department of Guatemala on the shore of Lake Amatitlán, south of Guatemala City. In the nineteenth century its surroundings, together with those of Antigua, were the main centre of cochineal production, the red dye that was Guatemala's chief export…

african-americans.s: African Americans are Americans of wholly or partly sub-Saharan African descent, most of them descendants of people enslaved in what became the United States from the seventeenth century until abolition in 1865. In the nineteenth century some free African Americans emigrated…

atal-bihari-vajpayee.s: Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1924–2018) was an Indian statesman and poet, a founder of the Bharatiya Janata Party and prime minister briefly in 1996 and from 1998 to 2004. His government carried out nuclear tests in 1998 and fought the Kargil War with Pakistan in 1999, while also…

aizsargi.s: The Aizsargi (Defenders) were a Latvian volunteer paramilitary home guard founded in March 1919, during the War of Independence, to protect local communities and support the army. With tens of thousands of members, they became an important prop of Kārlis Ulmanis, who relied on…

andrievs-niedra.s: Andrievs Niedra was a Latvian Lutheran pastor and writer who headed a pro-German puppet government installed after the German coup at Liepāja in April 1919, in opposition to the national government of Kārlis Ulmanis. His government collapsed after the defeat of the German…

act-of-independence-of-lithuania.s: The Act of Independence of Lithuania was signed in Vilnius on 16 February 1918 by the twenty members of the Council of Lithuania, chaired by Antanas Smetona. It proclaimed an independent, democratic Lithuanian state with Vilnius as its capital, severing all earlier ties with…

augustinas-voldemaras.s: Augustinas Voldemaras was a Lithuanian historian and politician who became the first prime minister of independent Lithuania in November 1918. After the military coup of December 1926 he again became prime minister, ruling alongside President Antanas Smetona, until Smetona…

arnoldo-aleman.s: Arnoldo Alemán is a Nicaraguan Liberal politician who was mayor of Managua and then president of Nicaragua from 1997 to 2002. His power-sharing pact with Daniel Ortega's Sandinistas divided state institutions between their two parties and lowered the threshold for winning the…

anastasio-somoza-garcia.s: Anastasio Somoza García was a Nicaraguan officer and dictator who, as director of the US-trained National Guard, had Augusto César Sandino murdered in 1934 and became president in 1937. He ruled Nicaragua directly or through puppet presidents until he was shot by the poet…

anastasio-somoza-debayle.s: Anastasio Somoza Debayle was the last of the Somoza family dictators of Nicaragua, commanding the National Guard and serving as president in 1967–1972 and 1974–1979. His regime's corruption, notably the misuse of aid after the Managua earthquake of 1972, and the murder of…

augusto-cesar-sandino.s: Augusto César Sandino was a Nicaraguan revolutionary who led a guerrilla war against the United States Marines occupying Nicaragua from 1927 to 1933, after rejecting the American-brokered peace that ended the Constitutionalist War. Operating from the northern mountains of Las…

azul-ruben-dario.s: Azul is a collection of short stories and poems by the Nicaraguan poet Rubén Darío, published in Valparaíso, Chile, in 1888. Its refined language, rich imagery and musical verse, drawing on French Parnassian and Symbolist models, made it the founding work of modernismo, the…

accessory-transit-company.s: The Accessory Transit Company was an American firm founded by Cornelius Vanderbilt that from 1851 carried travellers bound for California across Nicaragua, by steamboat up the San Juan River and across Lake Nicaragua, then by stagecoach to the Pacific port of San Juan del Sur.…

abimael-guzman.s: Abimael Guzmán was a Peruvian philosophy professor who founded and led the Maoist Shining Path, known to his followers as Chairman Gonzalo. From the University of Huamanga in Ayacucho he prepared an armed struggle, launched in May 1980, that brought Peru close to collapse and…

afro-peruvians.s: Afro-Peruvians are Peruvians of African descent, mainly descendants of enslaved people brought to work on coastal estates and in the cities under Spanish colonial rule. Slavery was abolished in 1854 under Ramón Castilla.

alan-garcia.s: Alan García was a Peruvian politician of APRA who was president of Peru from 1985 to 1990 and from 2006 to 2011. His first government, populist and unorthodox, ended in hyperinflation, economic collapse and the growth of the Shining Path insurgency.

andres-avelino-caceres.s: Andrés Avelino Cáceres was a Peruvian general who led guerrilla resistance against the Chilean occupation in the central highlands during the War of the Pacific, earning the name the Wizard of the Andes. He was president of Peru from 1886 to 1890 and from 1894 to 1895,…

american-popular-revolutionary-alliance.s: The American Popular Revolutionary Alliance (APRA) is a Peruvian political party founded by Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre in Mexico in 1924 as an anti-imperialist movement for Latin America, and organised in Peru in 1930. Peru's first mass party, it was repeatedly banned and…

aristocratic-republic.s: The Aristocratic Republic is the name given by the historian Jorge Basadre to the period of Peruvian history from 1895 to 1919, when governments dominated by the Civilista Party and the coastal landowning and financial oligarchy ruled through regular, restricted elections. It…

augusto-b-leguia.s: Augusto B. Leguía was a Peruvian businessman and politician who was president of Peru from 1908 to 1912 and again from 1919 to 1930.

a-theology-of-liberation.s: A Theology of Liberation is a book by the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez, published in Lima in 1971 as Teología de la liberación and in English in 1973. It interpreted Christian faith from the standpoint of the poor of Latin America and called on the church to commit itself…

abdirahman-ahmed-ali-tuur.s: Abdirahman Ahmed Ali Tuur was a Somali politician and chairman of the Somali National Movement (SNM). After the fall of Siad Barre he presided over the declaration of Somaliland's independence at Burao in May 1991 and became its first president.

abdirahman-mohamed-abdullahi.s: Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Irro, is a Somaliland politician and diplomat who became president of Somaliland in December 2024. A former speaker of the House of Representatives and leader of the Waddani party, he defeated the incumbent Muse Bihi Abdi in the election…

ahmed-mohamed-mohamoud.s: Ahmed Mohamed Mohamoud, known as Silanyo, is a Somaliland politician who was chairman of the Somali National Movement in the 1980s and president of Somaliland from 2010 to 2017. He founded the Kulmiye party and defeated the incumbent Dahir Riyale Kahin in the 2010 election, a…

al-shabaab.s: Al-Shabaab is a jihadist militant group in Somalia that grew out of the youth wing of the Islamic Courts Union in 2006. It controlled much of southern Somalia from about 2008 to 2011 and formally joined al-Qaeda in 2012.

apartheid.s: Apartheid (Afrikaans for "separateness") was the system of institutionalised racial segregation and white minority rule imposed in South Africa by the National Party government from 1948 until the early 1990s. Laws classified the population by race, reserved land, jobs and…

armscor.s: Armscor, the Armaments Corporation of South Africa, is the state arms procurement agency established in 1968 to make South Africa self-sufficient in weapons under the United Nations arms embargo. Through its subsidiaries it built a large domestic arms industry, producing…

agnello-participazio.s: Agnello Participazio was Doge of Venice from 811 to 827. Elected after the Frankish attack on the lagoon by Pepin of Italy, he moved the seat of government from Malamocco to the more defensible Rialto islands, the core of the later city of Venice.

andrea-palladio.s: Andrea Palladio was an architect of the Venetian Republic, active mainly in Vicenza and Venice. His villas on the Venetian mainland, his palaces in Vicenza and his Venetian churches, San Giorgio Maggiore and the Redentore, applied the forms of ancient Roman architecture with…

antonio-vivaldi.s: Antonio Vivaldi was a Venetian composer, violinist and priest, one of the leading composers of the Baroque. For much of his career he taught and wrote music for the girls' orchestra of the Ospedale della Pietà in Venice.

abdullah-ibn-husayn-al-ahmar.s: Abdullah ibn Husayn al-Ahmar was paramount sheikh of the Hashid tribal confederation, the most powerful tribal leader in Yemen. A supporter of the republic in the civil war of the 1960s, he founded the Islamist Islah party in 1990 and was speaker of parliament from 1993 until…

ahmed-ali-abdullah-saleh.s: Ahmed Ali Abdullah Saleh is the eldest son of the Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh. He commanded the Republican Guard and special forces, the best-equipped units of the army, and was widely seen as his father's intended successor.

ali-mohsen-al-ahmar.s: Ali Mohsen al-Ahmar is a Yemeni general, for decades one of the most powerful military commanders under President Ali Abdullah Saleh, from the same Sanhan tribe. He led campaigns in the 1994 civil war and against the Houthis.

al-qaeda-in-the-arabian-peninsula.s: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) is a jihadist group formed in January 2009 by the merger of al-Qaeda's Saudi and Yemeni branches, based in Yemen. It plotted attacks on Western aircraft and in 2011–2012 and 2015–2016 held towns in southern Yemen, including the port of…

al-islah-yemen.s: Al-Islah, the Yemeni Congregation for Reform, is the main Islamist party of Yemen, founded in 1990 after unification. It joined Muslim Brotherhood activists with tribal leaders, led by the Hashid sheikh Abdullah ibn Husayn al-Ahmar.

aeschines.s: Aeschines was an Athenian orator and statesman, the chief political opponent of Demosthenes. He favoured peace with Philip II of Macedon and served on the embassies that negotiated the Peace of Philocrates in 346 BCE.

apollonius-molon.s: Apollonius Molon was a Greek rhetorician from Alabanda in Caria who taught on Rhodes in the early first century BCE. He visited Rome as an ambassador of Rhodes in 81 BCE, and among his pupils were Cicero, who studied with him on Rhodes in 78 BCE, and Julius Caesar.

anglo-saxons.s: The Anglo-Saxons were the Germanic-speaking peoples, chiefly Angles, Saxons and Jutes, who settled in Britain from the fifth century after the end of Roman rule, and their descendants. They founded kingdoms such as Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria and Kent, converted to…

antoninus-pius.s: Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from 138 to 161, adopted heir of Hadrian and adoptive father of Marcus Aurelius. His long reign was among the most peaceful in Roman history; he never left Italy as emperor.

attacotti.s: The Attacotti were a people who raided Roman Britain in the fourth century, named by Ammianus Marcellinus with the Picts, Scotti and Saxons in the "barbarian conspiracy" of 367. Their origin is uncertain; they may have come from Ireland or the western or northern isles of…

aurelius-achilleus.s: Aurelius Achilleus was a leader of the revolt against Diocletian in Roman Egypt in 297–298. He served as corrector under the usurper Domitius Domitianus and, after Domitianus died, led the resistance in Alexandria.

aelius-gallus.s: Aelius Gallus was the second Roman prefect of Egypt, appointed by Augustus. In 26–25 BCE he led an expedition into Arabia Felix, modern Yemen, aimed at the rich kingdoms of the incense trade.

ammonius-saccas.s: Ammonius Saccas was a Greek philosopher who taught in Alexandria in the first half of the third century CE. He left no writings, but his pupils included Plotinus, who studied with him for about eleven years, and probably the Christian theologian Origen.

antinoopolis.s: Antinoopolis was a city founded by the emperor Hadrian in 130 CE on the east bank of the Nile in Middle Egypt, near the place where his favourite Antinous had drowned. Settled with Greek colonists and given special privileges, it later became a capital of the Thebaid.

antinous.s: Antinous was a young Greek from Bithynia who became the favourite of the emperor Hadrian. He drowned in the Nile in 130 CE during Hadrian's tour of Egypt, in circumstances that remain unclear.

apion-family.s: The Apion family were a dynasty of great landowners in Byzantine Egypt, based at Oxyrhynchus, from the fifth to the early seventh century. Members held high offices in Constantinople, among them Flavius Apion II, consul in 539.

arius.s: Arius was a Christian priest of Alexandria whose teaching that the Son was created by God the Father, and subordinate to him, caused a long controversy in the church. The Council of Nicaea condemned his views in 325, but Arianism remained influential for decades and was…

augustal-prefect.s: The Augustal prefect (praefectus augustalis) was the title of the governor of Egypt in the late Roman Empire. When a separate diocese of Egypt was created, probably around 381, its head took this title and ranked above the governors of the smaller Egyptian provinces.

avidius-cassius.s: Gaius Avidius Cassius was a Roman general born in Syria. He commanded in Lucius Verus's Parthian war, capturing Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 165, and was later given authority over the eastern provinces.

anthony-the-great.s: Anthony the Great was an Egyptian Christian who gave away his property and withdrew into the desert as a hermit in the late third century. Disciples gathered around him, and he is regarded as a founder of Christian monasticism.

annales-ennius.s: The Annales was an epic poem in Latin hexameters by Quintus Ennius, written in the early second century BCE. In eighteen books it told the history of Rome from the flight of Aeneas from Troy to the poet's own day.

appian-way.s: The Appian Way (Via Appia) was a Roman road begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, first from Rome to Capua and later extended to Brundisium on the Adriatic. Built to move armies during the Samnite Wars, it became one of the main arteries of Roman Italy.

akademgorodok.s: Akademgorodok is a scientific town near Novosibirsk in Siberia, founded in 1957 as the centre of the new Siberian Branch of the USSR Academy of Sciences. Built in forest beside the Ob reservoir, it housed dozens of research institutes and Novosibirsk State University.

all-russian-congress-of-soviets.s: The All-Russian Congress of Soviets was the supreme body of power in Soviet Russia from 1917 until the late 1930s. Its Second Congress, meeting in Petrograd during the October Revolution of 1917, approved the Bolshevik seizure of power, set up the Council of People's…

all-russian-central-executive-committee.s: The All-Russian Central Executive Committee was the standing body of the All-Russian Congress of Soviets, exercising legislative power between its sessions from 1917 to 1937. Chaired briefly by Lev Kamenev, then by Yakov Sverdlov and, from 1919, Mikhail Kalinin, it was…

amami-oshima.s: Amami Ōshima is the largest of the Amami Islands, between Kyushu and Okinawa, and is now part of Kagoshima Prefecture in Japan. It was brought under the Ryukyu Kingdom in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

amawari.s: Amawari was lord of Katsuren Castle on Okinawa in the mid-fifteenth century and a powerful rival of the Ryukyuan royal court. In 1458 he persuaded King Shō Taikyū that his rival Gosamaru was planning rebellion, and Gosamaru was destroyed.

ahmad-al-araj.s: Ahmad al-Araj was the first Saadi sultan of Morocco. With his brother Muhammad al-Shaykh he carried the Saadi movement northwards from the Sous and took Marrakesh in about 1524 or 1525, ruling there as sultan.

abd-al-aziz-al-fishtali.s: Abd al-Aziz al-Fishtali was a Moroccan scholar, poet and court historian of the Saadi sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, in whose chancery he served as a leading secretary. His chronicle Manahil al-Safa celebrated al-Mansur's reign, including the conquest of Songhai in 1591, and is a…

agadir.s: Agadir is a city on the Atlantic coast of southern Morocco. The Portuguese built a fortress there in 1505, known as Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué, which the Saadi ruler Muhammad al-Shaykh captured in 1541, a victory that led Portugal to abandon several other Moroccan ports.

abdallah-al-ghalib.s: Abdallah al-Ghalib was sultan of Morocco from 1557 to 1574, the son and successor of Muhammad al-Shaykh in the Saadi dynasty. He defeated an Ottoman army from Algiers at Wadi al-Laban near Fez in 1558 and kept Morocco independent of the Ottomans.

aldy-bel-culture.s: The Aldy-Bel culture is an early Iron Age archaeological culture of Tuva in southern Siberia, dated to about the seventh and sixth centuries BCE and counted among the early Scythian-type cultures of the steppe. Its best-known monument is the royal kurgan Arzhan 2, whose…

alexandria-eschate.s: Alexandria Eschate, 'Alexandria the Furthest', was a city founded by Alexander the Great in 329 BCE on the Syr Darya (Jaxartes) at the entrance to the Fergana Valley, at or near modern Khujand in Tajikistan. Intended as a frontier stronghold against the Saka nomads beyond the…

andronovo-culture.s: The Andronovo culture is a group of related Bronze Age cultures that spread across the steppes of southern Siberia, Kazakhstan and western Central Asia from about 2000 to 1150 BCE. Its people herded cattle, sheep and horses, used spoke-wheeled chariots and mined copper and tin.

apadana.s: The Apadana is the great audience hall of Persepolis, begun by Darius I around 515 BCE and completed under Xerxes I. Its roof rested on seventy-two stone columns about 20 metres high.

arzhan-kurgans.s: The Arzhan kurgans are royal burial mounds in the Uyuk valley of Tuva, in southern Siberia. Arzhan 1, of the late ninth or eighth century BCE, is one of the earliest known Scythian-type elite burials, with well over a hundred sacrificed horses.

aesop.s: Aesop was a Greek storyteller to whom a large collection of fables, the Aesopica, is attributed. According to Herodotus he was a slave of a Samian named Iadmon and lived in the sixth century BCE; later traditions made him a native of Phrygia or Thrace and told of his death at…

ameinocles.s: Ameinocles was a Corinthian shipbuilder named by Thucydides, who records that he built four ships for the Samians about three hundred years before the end of the Peloponnesian War, that is around 704 BCE. Thucydides cites him in his account of Corinth's leading role in early…

amorgos.s: Amorgos is a Greek island in the south-eastern Cyclades. In antiquity it had three cities, Arcesine, Aegiale and Minoa, the last traditionally settled from Samos, and in 322 BCE its waters saw the defeat of the Athenian fleet by the Macedonians.

aristarchus-of-samos.s: Aristarchus of Samos was a Greek astronomer and mathematician of the third century BCE. He was the first known thinker to propose that the Earth and planets revolve around the Sun, an idea that found little acceptance in antiquity.

alanic-language.s: Alanic was the Eastern Iranian language of the Alans, a nomadic people of the steppes north of the Caucasus in late antiquity and the Middle Ages. It is known only from names, a few words and short texts, among them Alan phrases recorded by the twelfth-century Byzantine writer…

amage.s: Amage was a Sarmatian queen known from the Stratagems of Polyaenus. Taking power from her husband, who was given to drink, she ruled and commanded the army herself.

amazons.s: In Greek mythology the Amazons were a nation of women warriors living on the edges of the known world, often placed near the Black Sea or in Scythia. They fought heroes such as Heracles, Theseus and Achilles in legend, and battles against them were a favourite subject of Greek…

aorsi.s: The Aorsi were a Sarmatian people of the steppes between the Don, the Volga and the Caspian Sea from about the second century BCE. Strabo describes them as rich and powerful, controlling caravan trade in Indian and Babylonian goods carried by camel, and claims that their king…

anahita.s: Anahita is an ancient Iranian goddess of waters, fertility and healing, invoked in the Avesta as Aredvi Sura Anahita. From Artaxerxes II onwards Achaemenid kings named her in their inscriptions, and her cult spread through the Iranian world and Armenia.

adovacrius.s: Adovacrius was a Saxon leader who fought in north-western Gaul in the 460s. According to Gregory of Tours he took hostages from Angers and other places on the lower Loire before the Frankish king Childeric I and Roman forces took the city and defeated the Saxons.

attigny.s: Attigny is a small town on the Aisne in the Ardennes department of north-eastern France. It was a Merovingian and Carolingian royal palace where Frankish kings held assemblies.

antiochus-xiii-asiaticus.s: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus was the last king of the Seleucid dynasty, son of Antiochus X and Cleopatra Selene. After the Roman general Lucullus drove Tigranes of Armenia out of Syria in 69 BCE, he was recognised as king, but his rule was weak and contested.

asharism.s: Ash'arism is a school of Sunni Islamic theology founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari (874–936) in Iraq. It used rational argument to defend traditional doctrines such as God's omnipotence and the uncreated Quran, taking a middle path between the rationalist Mu'tazilites and…

academia-sinica.s: Academia Sinica is the national academy of the Republic of China, founded in Nanjing in 1928 and moved to Taiwan after 1949, where it is based in Taipei. Its Institute of History and Philology carried out the first scientific excavations at Anyang between 1928 and 1937,…

al-mahatta-fort.s: Al Mahatta Fort is a fortified rest house built in Sharjah in 1932 by Imperial Airways for passengers on its air route between Britain and India. The airfield beside it was the first in the Trucial States and was used by civil and military aircraft for decades.

akhsitan-i.s: Akhsitan I was Shirvanshah, ruler of Shirvan in present-day Azerbaijan, in the second half of the twelfth century, succeeding his father Manuchihr III. His court at Shamakhi was a centre of Persian poetry, where Khaqani served, and in 1188 Nizami Ganjavi composed Layla and…

alqas-mirza.s: Alqas Mirza was a Safavid prince, son of Shah Ismail I and brother of Shah Tahmasp I. In 1538 he led the army that annexed Shirvan to the Safavid Empire and became its governor.

agent-orange.s: Agent Orange was a herbicide sprayed by the United States military over forests and crops in South Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia during the Vietnam War, mainly between 1962 and 1971. It was contaminated with the toxic dioxin TCDD, which has been linked to cancers, birth defects…

askia-musa.s: Askia Musa was ruler of the Songhai Empire from 1528 to 1531, a son of Askia Muhammad. He deposed his aged and nearly blind father, sending him into confinement, and ruled harshly, killing several of his brothers and rivals.

abdul-fattah-ismail.s: Abdul Fattah Ismail was a Yemeni Marxist politician, the chief ideologue of the National Liberation Front in South Yemen. Born in North Yemen, he led the party's pro-Soviet wing, founded the Yemeni Socialist Party in 1978 and headed the state from 1978 to 1980, when he was…

aden-emergency.s: The Aden Emergency was an insurgency against British rule in Aden and the Federation of South Arabia, lasting from 1963 to 1967. It began with the National Liberation Front's uprising in the Radfan mountains on 14 October 1963 and grew into urban guerrilla warfare in Aden,…

ali-nasir-muhammad.s: Ali Nasir Muhammad is a Yemeni politician who was prime minister of South Yemen from 1971 to 1985 and head of state and general secretary of the Yemeni Socialist Party from 1980 to 1986. He followed a more pragmatic course, improving relations with Saudi Arabia, Oman and the…

aleksandr-solzhenitsyn.s: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a Russian novelist and historian who spent eight years in Soviet labour camps after criticising Stalin in a private letter. His story One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962) was the first published Soviet account of the camps, and The Gulag…

agiad-dynasty.s: The Agiads were the senior of the two royal houses of Sparta, which was always ruled by two kings at once. They traced their line to Agis I, son of Eurysthenes, and through him to Heracles.

agis-iii.s: Agis III was a Eurypontid king of Sparta from 338 to 331 BCE. While Alexander the Great was campaigning in Asia, he organised a Greek revolt against Macedonian rule with Persian money, gathering allies in the Peloponnese and besieging Megalopolis.

agis-iv.s: Agis IV was a Eurypontid king of Sparta who came to the throne about 245 BCE and tried to restore the shrinking citizen body by cancelling debts and redistributing land among Spartans and selected perioikoi and foreigners. Opposed by wealthy landowners and his co-king Leonidas…

aratus-of-sicyon.s: Aratus of Sicyon was a Greek statesman who freed his city from its tyrant in 251 BCE, brought it into the Achaean League and led the league for over thirty years as its general. He seized Acrocorinth from its Macedonian garrison in 243 BCE and expanded the league across the…

argos.s: Argos is a city in the north-eastern Peloponnese of Greece, one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in Europe. In the Archaic period it dominated the Argolid and was Sparta's chief rival in the Peloponnese, defeating it at Hysiae in the seventh century BCE but losing…

analects.s: The Analects (Lunyu) is a collection of sayings and short dialogues of Confucius and his disciples, compiled by later followers during the Warring States period and fixed in its present form in the Han dynasty. Its twenty books set out the ideals of humaneness, ritual…

alaeddin-mosque.s: The Alaeddin Mosque is the main mosque of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Konya, Turkey, standing on Alaeddin Hill at the heart of the city. Begun in the twelfth century and completed under Kayqubad I around 1220, it has a large hall of reused antique columns and a courtyard…

abaqa-khan.s: Abaqa Khan was the second ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate, reigning from 1265 to 1282 as successor of his father Hulagu. He fought the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate and the Mamluks of Egypt, and sought alliances with Christian Europe.

azim-ud-din-i-of-sulu.s: Azim ud-Din I, also called Alimuddin I, was Sultan of Sulu in the eighteenth century. Seeking Spanish help against his brother Bantilan, who had taken power, he went to Manila and was baptised in 1750, an act that divided his court.

afobaka-dam.s: The Afobaka Dam is a hydroelectric dam on the Suriname River, completed in 1964 to supply power to the aluminium smelter built by Alcoa's subsidiary at Paranam. Its reservoir, the Brokopondo Reservoir, is one of the largest in the world by area and flooded the homes of several…

alcoa.s: Alcoa, the Aluminum Company of America, is an American aluminium producer founded in Pittsburgh in 1888 to exploit Charles Martin Hall's process for refining aluminium. Through its subsidiary Suralco it mined bauxite in Suriname from the early twentieth century, starting at…

aboud-jumbe.s: Aboud Jumbe was a Zanzibari politician who became president of Zanzibar and first vice-president of Tanzania after the assassination of Abeid Karume in 1972. He took the Afro-Shirazi Party into the merger with TANU that created Chama Cha Mapinduzi in 1977 and introduced a…

articles-of-union-1964.s: The Articles of Union were the agreement signed on 22 April 1964 by Julius Nyerere of Tanganyika and Abeid Karume of Zanzibar, uniting the two states as the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar from 26 April 1964, renamed Tanzania later that year. They reserved certain…

arusha.s: Arusha is a city in northern Tanzania at the foot of Mount Meru, a centre of the coffee-growing region and the gateway to the Serengeti and Mount Kilimanjaro. It gave its name to the Arusha Declaration of 1967 and the Arusha Accords of 1993 for Rwanda.

arusha-declaration.s: The Arusha Declaration was a statement of policy issued by Julius Nyerere and the ruling party TANU at Arusha in February 1967. It committed Tanzania to ujamaa, a form of African socialism based on self-reliance and village communities, nationalised banks, major firms and…

abd-al-latif-mirza.s: Abd al-Latif Mirza was a Timurid prince, the son of Ulugh Beg. After quarrelling with his father over the succession, he defeated him in 1449 and had him put to death, then ruled Samarkand for about six months before being assassinated in 1450 by his father's former retainers.

alexis-of-russia.s: Alexis of Russia was the second Romanov tsar, ruling from 1645 to 1676. His reign saw the Salt and Copper Riots, the law code of 1649 that completed the enserfment of the peasantry, the church reforms of Patriarch Nikon that caused the schism with the Old Believers, and the…

apostol-1564.s: The Apostol of 1564 is the first precisely dated book printed in Moscow, produced by Ivan Fyodorov and Pyotr Mstislavets at the Moscow Print Yard and completed on 1 March 1564. A liturgical book containing the Acts and Epistles of the apostles in Church Slavonic, it was…

arkhangelsk.s: Arkhangelsk is a city and port on the Northern Dvina near its mouth on the White Sea, in northern Russia. Founded in 1584 and named after the monastery of the Archangel Michael, it was Russia's chief seaport for trade with western Europe until Peter the Great founded Saint…

avvakum.s: Avvakum Petrov was a Russian archpriest and leader of the Old Believers who opposed the liturgical reforms of Patriarch Nikon. Exiled to Siberia and later imprisoned in an earthen pit at Pustozersk in the far north, he wrote an autobiography, the Life of the Archpriest…

annals-and-antiquities-of-rajasthan.s: Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan is a history of the Rajput states by James Tod, published in two volumes in London in 1829 and 1832. Drawing on bardic chronicles, inscriptions and his years as political agent in western Rajputana, Tod gave pride of place to Mewar and…

acholi.s: The Acholi are a Nilotic, Luo-speaking people of northern Uganda and southern South Sudan. Under British rule many Acholi were recruited into the army and police, and after independence they formed a large part of Milton Obote's armed forces, so Idi Amin purged and killed many…

albertine-rift.s: The Albertine Rift is the western branch of the East African Rift, running from Lake Albert south through Lakes Edward, Kivu and Tanganyika along the borders of the Democratic Republic of the Congo with Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania. Its Ugandan section, the Albertine…

al-walid-ii.s: Al-Walid II was the Umayyad caliph from 743 to 744. A gifted poet known for his wine songs and worldly life, he succeeded his uncle Hisham but quickly alienated powerful members of the family and the Yaman tribal faction through his treatment of rivals and favour to the Qays.

abraham-accords.s: The Abraham Accords are agreements, brokered by the United States, by which Israel established diplomatic relations with Arab states, beginning with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, which signed at the White House on 15 September 2020. Morocco and Sudan followed later in…

abu-dhabi-investment-authority.s: The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority is the sovereign wealth fund of the emirate of Abu Dhabi, founded in 1976 to invest the surplus revenues of its oil exports abroad. It manages a diversified global portfolio of shares, bonds, property, infrastructure and other assets on…
