alan-turing.s: Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. His 1936 paper on computable numbers laid the theoretical foundations of computing, and during the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park, where he led work on breaking German naval Enigma ciphers.

adonijah.s: Adonijah was the fourth son of King David according to the Hebrew Bible. As the eldest surviving son, he claimed the throne in David's old age with the support of the commander Joab and the priest Abiathar, but the prophet Nathan and Bathsheba persuaded David to name Solomon…

amalekites.s: The Amalekites were a nomadic people of the Negev and Sinai described in the Hebrew Bible as descendants of Esau's grandson Amalek and as hereditary enemies of Israel. Saul is said to have fought them and to have been rejected by the prophet Samuel for sparing their king Agag,…

ajmer-merwara.s: Ajmer-Merwara was a small province of British India in Rajputana, formed from the district of Ajmer, ceded by the Marathas to the British in 1818, and the hill tract of Merwara. Ruled directly by a chief commissioner among the princely states, it became the Part C state of…

alexander-hamilton.s: Alexander Hamilton was an American statesman and one of the Founding Fathers of the United States. Born in the West Indies, he served as George Washington's aide in the Revolutionary War, wrote most of The Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution and, as the first…

articles-of-confederation.s: The Articles of Confederation were the first constitution of the United States, adopted by the Continental Congress in 1777 and in force from 1781 to 1789. They created a loose league of sovereign states with a single-chamber Congress that could not levy taxes or regulate…

aga-of-kish.s: Aga of Kish was a king of Kish in Sumer in the Early Dynastic period, around the twenty-seventh century BCE, listed in the Sumerian King List as the last ruler of the First Dynasty of Kish and the son of Enmebaragesi. He is known chiefly from the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and…

aratta.s: Aratta is a distant land rich in precious stones and metals described in Sumerian epic poems, notably Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, in which Enmerkar, king of Uruk, demands that its lord send lapis lazuli and craftsmen to adorn the temples of Uruk. Its location, somewhere…

armada-del-mar-del-sur.s: The Armada del Mar del Sur (South Sea Fleet) was the Spanish naval force based at Callao that guarded the Pacific coast of the Viceroyalty of Peru. From the late sixteenth century it escorted the annual shipments of Potosí silver from Callao to Panama, where the bullion was…

achyuta-deva-raya.s: Achyuta Deva Raya was emperor of Vijayanagara from 1529 to 1542, succeeding his half-brother Krishnadevaraya. He kept most of the empire's territory, campaigning in the south and recovering the Raichur Doab from Bijapur, but faced growing rivalry from Aliya Rama Raya and other…

aliya-rama-raya.s: Aliya Rama Raya was a nobleman of the Aravidu family and son-in-law of Krishnadevaraya who dominated the Vijayanagara Empire as regent for Sadashiva Raya from the 1540s. He played the Deccan sultanates against one another, but his interventions eventually united Bijapur,…

allasani-peddana.s: Allasani Peddana was a sixteenth-century Telugu poet at the court of Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara, the foremost of the eight poets known as the Ashtadiggajas. His Manucharitramu, a long poem on the birth of Svarochisha Manu, is one of the classics of Telugu literature, and…

amuktamalyada.s: The Amuktamalyada is a Telugu epic poem composed by the Vijayanagara emperor Krishnadevaraya in the early sixteenth century. It tells the story of the Tamil saint Andal, devoted to the god Vishnu, and her marriage to the god, and includes a section of advice on statecraft and…

alexander-of-suzdal.s: Alexander of Suzdal (Alexander Vasilyevich) was a Russian prince of Suzdal who in 1328 received from Uzbek Khan of the Golden Horde a share of the grand principality of Vladimir, including the city of Vladimir, while Ivan I Kalita of Moscow held the rest. He had taken part in…

andrei-of-gorodets.s: Andrei of Gorodets (Andrei Alexandrovich) was a son of Alexander Nevsky and grand prince of Vladimir in the early 1280s and from 1294 to 1304. His long feud with his elder brother Dmitry of Pereslavl, each backed by a rival Mongol power, brought repeated Horde armies into…

andrei-ii-of-vladimir.s: Andrei II of Vladimir (Andrei Yaroslavich) was grand prince of Vladimir from 1249 to 1252, a son of Yaroslav II and younger brother of Alexander Nevsky. Appointed by the Mongol court at Karakorum, he tried to act independently of the Golden Horde; in 1252 a Mongol army under…

aristotele-fioravanti.s: Aristotele Fioravanti was an Italian architect and engineer from Bologna who worked for Ivan III of Moscow from 1475. His Cathedral of the Dormition in the Moscow Kremlin, completed in 1479, adapted the plan of the Dormition Cathedral at Vladimir using Renaissance building…

abu-hamid-al-gharnati.s: Abu Hamid al-Gharnati was an Andalusian Muslim traveller born in Granada who journeyed through North Africa, the Middle East and eastern Europe in the twelfth century. He visited Volga Bulgaria and Saqsin on the lower Volga and travelled on to Hungary, and his writings…

alm-s.s: Almış was ruler of Volga Bulgaria in the early tenth century and the first of its kings known to have adopted Islam. In 921 he asked the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir for religious teachers and help in building a mosque and a fortress, and the embassy that arrived in 922,…

adam-asil.s: Adam Asil was sultan of Wadai from 1909 to 1912, a rival of Sultan Muhammad Dud Murra. After the French took the capital Abéché in June 1909 they installed him as a client ruler, but he was suspected of intriguing against them and was deposed in 1912, after which the sultanate…

ajitapurana.s: The Ajitapurana is a Kannada poem by Ranna, completed in 993, telling the life of Ajitanatha, the second Jain tirthankara. Written in the champu style of mixed verse and prose, it was composed under the patronage of Attimabbe, a Jain noblewoman of the Western Chalukya court,…

attimabbe.s: Attimabbe was a Jain noblewoman of the Western Chalukya court in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries, the widow of the general Nagadeva. Celebrated as Danachintamani for her generosity, she had a thousand copies of Ponna's Shantipurana made at her own cost, supported…

ainnurruvar.s: The Five Hundred Lords of Ayyavole (Ainnurruvar) was the most powerful merchant guild of medieval southern India, active from about the ninth to the fourteenth century and named after its home at Aihole in Karnataka. Its members traded across the peninsula and overseas to Sri…

ahmad-fanakati.s: Ahmad Fanakati was a Central Asian Muslim from Banakat who served as chief finance minister of the Yuan dynasty under Kublai Khan for some twenty years. He raised revenue through monopolies and higher taxes and placed his relatives in office, which made him widely hated among…

ayurbarwada-buyantu-khan.s: Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan, known by the temple name Renzong, was emperor of the Yuan dynasty from 1311 to 1320. Educated in Confucian learning, he favoured Chinese-style government, curbed some abuses of his predecessor's reign and in 1315 restored the civil service…

adel-shah.s: Adel Shah, born Ali Qoli Khan, was a nephew of Nader Shah who took part in the conspiracy against him and became shah of the Afsharid Empire after Nader's murder in 1747. He had most of Nader's family killed and ordered the castration of the young Qajar prince Agha Mohammad Khan.

ali-mardan-khan-bakhtiari.s: Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari was a chief of the Bakhtiari tribe who, after the fall of the Afsharids, seized Isfahan in 1750 and with Karim Khan Zand installed the young Safavid prince Ismail III as a puppet shah. The partnership soon broke down, Karim Khan defeated him, and Ali…

anglo-zulu-war.s: The Anglo-Zulu War was fought between Britain and the Zulu Kingdom from January to July 1879, after the high commissioner Sir Bartle Frere demanded that King Cetshwayo disband his army. The Zulu destroyed a British column at Isandlwana, but were defeated at Rorke's Drift,…

aterno-pescara.s: The Aterno-Pescara is the main river of Abruzzo in central Italy, known in its upper course as the Aterno and below Popoli as the Pescara, reaching the Adriatic at the city of Pescara, the ancient Aternum. Its valley linked the mountain peoples of the region, the Vestini,…

ananda-temple.s: The Ananda Temple is a Buddhist temple at Bagan in Myanmar, completed around 1105 under King Kyansittha of the Pagan Kingdom. Built on a cross-shaped plan with four standing Buddha images facing the cardinal points and hundreds of glazed terracotta plaques illustrating the…

anawrahta.s: Anawrahta was king of Pagan from 1044 to 1077 and is regarded as the founder of the first Burmese empire. He conquered the Mon kingdom of Thaton in 1057, brought much of present-day Myanmar under one rule, extended irrigation in the Kyaukse rice lands and promoted Theravada…

ahmad-muadzam-shah-of-pahang.s: Ahmad al-Muadzam Shah, born Wan Ahmad, was ruler of Pahang on the Malay Peninsula. He won the Pahang civil war of 1857–1863 against his brother Tun Mutahir, ruled as bendahara and in 1882 proclaimed himself sultan.

anglo-soviet-invasion-of-iran.s: The Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran took place in August and September 1941, when British and Soviet forces occupied the country to secure its oilfields and a supply route to the Soviet Union during the Second World War. Reza Shah, suspected of German sympathies, was forced to…

arya-pangiri.s: Arya Pangiri was a prince of Demak in Java who seized the throne of Pajang after the death of Sultan Hadiwijaya in 1582. His rule was unpopular, and in 1586 he was deposed by Sutawijaya of Mataram, allied with Hadiwijaya's son Pangeran Benawa, and sent back to Demak.

arthur-evans.s: Sir Arthur Evans was a British archaeologist who excavated the Bronze Age palace at Knossos on Crete from 1900 and partly reconstructed it in concrete. He named the civilisation he uncovered 'Minoan' after the legendary King Minos, devised its chronology and identified the…

anandji-kalyanji-trust.s: The Anandji Kalyanji Trust is a Jain charitable trust based in Ahmedabad, India, which manages many of the most important Shvetambara Jain temples and pilgrimage sites, including Shatrunjaya at Palitana. In the 19th and 20th centuries it was in long legal disputes with the…

aditya-i.s: Aditya I was king of the Chola dynasty of southern India in the late 9th century, the son of Vijayalaya. Around 897 he defeated the Pallava king Aparajita, annexed the Pallava lands of Tondaimandalam and made the Cholas the leading power in the Tamil country.

aparajitavarman.s: Aparajitavarman was the last important king of the Pallava dynasty of Kanchipuram. Around 885, with his Western Ganga ally Prithvipati I and Chola support, he defeated the Pandya king Varaguna II at the Battle of Sripurambiyam.

ahichchhatra.s: Ahichchhatra was an ancient city in Bareilly district of Uttar Pradesh, India, remembered as the capital of northern Panchala. Its extensive ruins near Ramnagar include fortifications and terraced brick temples, and excavations have revealed occupation from the Painted Grey…

arras-culture.s: The Arras culture is an Iron Age culture of East Yorkshire in England, from about the 4th century BCE to the Roman conquest, named after a cemetery at Arras near Market Weighton. It is marked by burials under small square barrows, some containing dismantled two-wheeled…

archilochus.s: Archilochus was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Paros, active in the 7th century BCE and regarded in antiquity as the master of iambic verse. He took part in the Parian colonisation of Thasos, and his surviving fragments speak of war, love and abuse of enemies in a…

arma-people.s: The Arma are the descendants of the Moroccan soldiers who conquered the Songhai Empire in 1591 and of the local women they married. From about 1612 they formed a ruling caste in the Niger bend, electing the pashas of Timbuktu from their own ranks and governing Timbuktu, Djenne…

aurora-de-chile.s: Aurora de Chile was the first newspaper published in Chile, issued weekly in Santiago from February 1812 to April 1813 on a printing press brought from the United States. Edited by the priest Camilo Henríquez under the government of José Miguel Carrera, it spread the ideas of…

apollonius-of-perga.s: Apollonius of Perga was a Greek mathematician and astronomer from Perge in Pamphylia who worked at Alexandria and Pergamon. His treatise Conics, in eight books, gave a systematic theory of the conic sections and introduced the names ellipse, parabola and hyperbola.

artemis-pergaia.s: Artemis Pergaia was the patron goddess of Perge in Pamphylia, a local deity identified with the Greek Artemis and called Wanassa Preiia, the 'Queen of Perge', in the Pamphylian dialect. Her rich temple stood near the city, and her cult image, a decorated conical stone, appears…

arau.s: Arau is the royal town of Perlis, the smallest state of Malaysia, near the Thai border. It is the seat of the state's raja, with the Istana Arau palace and the royal mosque, while the state capital is Kangar nearby.

arco-etrusco.s: The Arco Etrusco is a monumental gate in the Etruscan walls of Perugia in central Italy, built in the 3rd century BCE. After Octavian took and burned the city in 40 BCE, it was restored and inscribed AUGUSTA PERUSIA, and a Renaissance loggia was later added on top.

asopus-peloponnese.s: The Asopus of the Peloponnese is a river of southern Greece that rises in the upland valley of Phlius, south-west of Corinth, and flows north past Sicyon into the Gulf of Corinth. In Greek myth its river god was the father of many nymphs, including Aegina.

asopus-boeotia.s: The Asopus is a river of Boeotia in central Greece, which rises near Mount Cithaeron and flows east past the territories of Plataea and Tanagra to the Euboean Gulf. In 479 BCE the Greek and Persian armies faced each other across it for days before the Battle of Plataea.

alalia.s: Alalia was a Greek colony on the east coast of Corsica, founded by Phocaeans around 565 BCE, on the site of modern Aléria. Refugees from Phocaea reinforced it after the Persian conquest, and around 540 BCE their fleet fought a combined Etruscan and Carthaginian navy off the…

arganthonios.s: Arganthonius was a king of Tartessos in south-western Iberia, known from Herodotus, who says he reigned for 80 years and lived to 120. He welcomed the Phocaean Greeks who traded on his coasts and offered them land to settle; when they declined, he paid for a wall around…

aristonicus.s: Aristonicus was a pretender to the throne of Pergamon who claimed to be a son of Eumenes II and took the royal name Eumenes III. When Attalus III died in 133 BCE leaving his kingdom to Rome, Aristonicus led a revolt that drew support from slaves and the poor of western Anatolia.

abruzzo.s: Abruzzo is a region of central Italy between the Apennines and the Adriatic Sea, with its capital at L'Aquila. Its mountains include the Gran Sasso, the highest peak of the Apennines, and the Majella.

ascoli-piceno.s: Ascoli Piceno is a city in the southern Marche, Italy, on the Tronto river. As Asculum it was the chief town of the Picentes, and its massacre of Roman officials in 91 BCE started the Social War; Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo captured it in 89 BCE.

avalon-peninsula.s: The Avalon Peninsula is a large peninsula in south-eastern Newfoundland, Canada, joined to the rest of the island by a narrow isthmus. It contains St John's, the provincial capital, and was the earliest area of European fishing and settlement in Newfoundland, including Lord…

auktume.s: Auktume was a leader of the Pogesanians, one of the Old Prussian peoples, during the Great Prussian Uprising against the Teutonic Order that began in 1260. Peter of Dusburg's chronicle names him as the Pogesanian commander who led attacks on Elbing and other castles of the Order.

askold-and-dir.s: Askold and Dir were rulers of Kiev in the 9th century, described in the Primary Chronicle as Varangians who took the city from the Khazars' tributaries and led a raid on Constantinople in 860. According to the chronicle, Oleg of Novgorod lured them out of the city in 882 and…

azad-kashmir.s: Azad Kashmir is a self-governing territory administered by Pakistan in the western part of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, with its capital at Muzaffarabad. It was formed in 1947 after a rising in Poonch and the First Kashmir War, and its boundary with…

amilcar-cabral.s: Amílcar Cabral was an agronomist, political thinker and anti-colonial leader from Portuguese Guinea and Cape Verde. He founded the PAIGC in 1956 and from 1963 led its guerrilla war against Portuguese rule, combining military struggle with schools, clinics and people's courts…

alvor-agreement.s: The Alvor Agreement was signed on 15 January 1975 at Alvor in Portugal by the Portuguese government and the three Angolan liberation movements, the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA. It set Angola's independence for 11 November 1975, defined Cabinda as part of Angola, and created a…

axim.s: Axim is a coastal town in the Western Region of Ghana. The Portuguese built Fort São António there around 1515, their second fort on the Gold Coast after Elmina, to trade for gold.

a-famosa.s: A Famosa was the fortress built by the Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque at Malacca after they captured the city in 1511. It enclosed the hill and town by the river and withstood many sieges until the Dutch took it in 1641.

algarve.s: The Algarve is the southernmost region of mainland Portugal, a coastal strip between the Atlantic and the hills of the Serra de Monchique and Serra do Caldeirão. Its name comes from the Arabic al-Gharb, 'the west', from the centuries of Muslim rule, and it was the last part of…

asilah.s: Asilah, historically Arzila, is a fortified town on the Atlantic coast of northern Morocco, south of Tangier. Portugal captured it in 1471 under Afonso V and held it until 1550, and King Sebastian landed there in 1578 before his defeat at Alcácer Quibir.

azemmour.s: Azemmour is a town on the Oum Er-Rbia river near its mouth on the Atlantic coast of Morocco. Portugal took it in 1513 as one of its chain of fortified posts on the coast, but abandoned it in 1541 after the Saadi capture of Agadir.

ang-chan-i.s: Ang Chan I was a king of Cambodia in the 16th century, in the period after the abandonment of Angkor. He fought off Siamese invasions and moved the royal capital to Longvek, near the Tonlé Sap river, which remained the centre of the kingdom until its capture by Siam in 1594.

artabazus-i-of-phrygia.s: Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, was a Persian general and satrap of the 5th century BCE. He commanded the Parthians and Chorasmians in Xerxes' invasion of Greece, took Olynthus and besieged Potidaea in 480–479 BCE, and led the Persian retreat after Plataea.

allah.s: Allah is the Arabic word for God, used by Muslims and also by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews. In pre-Islamic Mecca Allah was recognised as a high creator god alongside lesser deities whose images stood in the Kaaba.

athena-polias.s: Athena Polias, 'Athena of the city', was the form of the goddess Athena worshipped as protector of a Greek city. At Athens her ancient olive-wood statue in the Erechtheion received a new robe at the Panathenaia, and other cities, such as Priene, built temples to her.

adalard-of-corbie.s: Adalard of Corbie was a Frankish abbot and statesman, a cousin of Charlemagne. Abbot of Corbie in Picardy, he served as adviser to Charlemagne's son Pippin in Italy, was exiled by Louis the Pious in 814 and restored in 821.

ansgar.s: Ansgar was a Frankish monk and missionary, known as the Apostle of the North. Trained at Corbie and Corvey, he preached in Denmark and in Sweden, where he founded the first church at Birka.

adalbert-of-hamburg.s: Adalbert was archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen from 1043 to 1072. An ambitious adviser of Emperor Henry III and later dominant at the court of the young Henry IV, he sought to make his see a patriarchate over Scandinavia and the north.

adalbert-of-pomerania.s: Adalbert of Pomerania was the first bishop of Pomerania, appointed in 1140 with his seat at Wolin. A chaplain of Duke Bolesław III of Poland, he had taken part in Otto of Bamberg's missions to convert the Pomeranians in the 1120s.

allgau.s: The Allgäu is a region of southern Germany at the foot of the Alps, mostly in Bavarian Swabia, with smaller parts in Baden-Württemberg and Austria. In the Holy Roman Empire it was divided among the prince-abbey of Kempten, the prince-bishopric of Augsburg, several imperial…

archdiocese-of-freiburg.s: The Archdiocese of Freiburg is a Catholic archdiocese in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, founded in 1821 with its seat at Freiburg im Breisgau. It took over much of the dissolved diocese of Constance and other church territories in Baden, and it is one of the largest dioceses in…

archdiocese-of-munich-and-freising.s: The Archdiocese of Munich and Freising is a Catholic archdiocese in Bavaria, Germany. It continues the diocese of Freising, organised by Saint Boniface in 739, and took its present form in 1821, when the see moved to Munich.

anselm-of-havelberg.s: Anselm of Havelberg was a German churchman and theologian, bishop of Havelberg from 1129 and archbishop of Ravenna from 1155. He served Emperors Lothair III and Frederick Barbarossa as envoy to Constantinople, where he debated with Greek theologians, and he took part in the…

albrechtsburg.s: The Albrechtsburg is a late Gothic castle on the rock above the Elbe at Meissen in Saxony, Germany, built from 1471 for the Wettin brothers Ernest and Albert. Regarded as the first German castle built as a residential palace, it stands beside Meissen Cathedral, and from 1710…

adige.s: The Adige is the second-longest river in Italy, about 410 kilometres long. It rises near the Reschen Pass in the Alps, flows through the Vinschgau, Bolzano, Trento and Verona, and enters the Adriatic south of Venice.

archdiocese-of-trento.s: The Archdiocese of Trento is a Catholic see in northern Italy, traced back to the 4th century, when Saint Vigilius was among its early bishops. From 1027 its bishops were also princes of the Holy Roman Empire, ruling a territory in the Adige valley until secularisation in 1803.

adalbold-ii-of-utrecht.s: Adalbold II was bishop of Utrecht from 1010 to 1026 and one of the learned churchmen of the Ottonian court. A supporter of Emperor Henry II, whose life he wrote, he received counties and royal rights that laid the foundations of the bishops' secular principality.

aller.s: The Aller is a river in northern Germany, about 260 kilometres long, a right tributary of the Weser. It rises near Magdeburg in Saxony-Anhalt and flows north-west through Lower Saxony, past Wolfsburg and Celle, to join the Weser near Verden.

anacopia.s: Anacopia was a hill fortress above the Black Sea coast at present-day New Athos in Abkhazia. In the early Middle Ages it was the seat of the princes of Abasgia, who ruled as clients of the Byzantine Empire.

abkhaz-people.s: The Abkhaz are a people of the north-western Caucasus who live mainly in Abkhazia, on the eastern coast of the Black Sea. They speak Abkhaz, a Northwest Caucasian language.

akova.s: Akova was a castle in the mountains of Arcadia in the central Peloponnese, which the French called Matagrifon. Around 1209 it became the seat of one of the twelve baronies of the crusader Principality of Achaea, granted to Walter of Rosières.

andravida.s: Andravida is a town in Elis in the north-western Peloponnese, Greece. In the 13th century it was the capital of the crusader Principality of Achaea, where the princes held court and the High Court of barons met, and it was known for its French culture.

aschersleben.s: Aschersleben is a town in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, on the northern edge of the Harz. It is one of the oldest towns in the region, and its name in Latin, Ascharia, gave the Ascanian dynasty, the ruling family of Anhalt, Brandenburg and Saxony-Wittenberg, its name.

alexander-karl-duke-of-anhalt-bernburg.s: Alexander Karl was the last Duke of Anhalt-Bernburg, ruling from 1834 until his death. Because of his mental illness the duchy was largely governed by his ministers and by his wife, Duchess Friederike.

assizes-of-antioch.s: The Assizes of Antioch were the law code of the crusader Principality of Antioch, regulating feudal relations, the courts and the rights of burgesses. The original French text is lost, and the code survives only in an Armenian translation made in the 13th century by Smbat the…

anthony-ulrich-duke-of-brunswick-wolfenb.s: Anthony Ulrich was Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, co-ruling with his brother from 1685 and alone from 1704. A rival of the Hanoverian Welfs, he was also a novelist, author of long courtly romances, and an art collector whose collections later formed the Herzog Anton Ulrich…

albert-iii-achilles-elector-of-brandenbu.n: Albert III Achilles, Elector of Brandenburg
albert-iii-achilles-elector-of-brandenbu.s: Albert III Achilles was a Hohenzollern prince, Margrave of Ansbach from 1440 and of Kulmbach from 1464, and Elector of Brandenburg from 1470. A renowned soldier and tournament fighter, he fought long wars against the city of Nuremberg and other neighbours.

aloysius-gonzaga.s: Aloysius Gonzaga was an Italian noble and Jesuit saint. The eldest son of the Marquis of Castiglione, he gave up his rights of succession to his brother to join the Society of Jesus in Rome in 1585.

antonio-da-correggio.s: Antonio Allegri, known as Correggio after his home town, was an Italian painter of the High Renaissance who worked mainly in Parma. His dome frescoes in the church of San Giovanni Evangelista and in Parma Cathedral, with figures soaring upwards into light, anticipated baroque…

anne-marie-louise-dorleans-duchess-of-mo.n: Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier
anne-marie-louise-dorleans-duchess-of-mo.s: Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, known as La Grande Mademoiselle, was a cousin of Louis XIV and the richest heiress in France. During the Fronde she sided with the rebels and in 1652 had the cannon of the Bastille fired on royal troops, for which she was exiled from court.

amalie-zephyrine-of-salm-kyrburg.s: Amalie Zephyrine of Salm-Kyrburg was the wife of Prince Anton Aloys of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. Living apart from her husband in Paris, she befriended Joséphine de Beauharnais, and her influence with Napoleon's circle helped Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen survive the mediatisation…

abazins.s: The Abazins are a north-west Caucasian people closely related to the Abkhaz, living mainly in Karachay-Cherkessia in southern Russia. Their language belongs to the Abkhaz–Adyghe family.

artsakh-historic-province.s: Artsakh is the historical name of a mountainous region of the South Caucasus corresponding largely to Nagorno-Karabakh. A province of the Kingdom of Armenia in antiquity, it passed to Caucasian Albania after the partition of Armenia around 387.

amorbach.s: Amorbach is a small town in the Odenwald in Lower Franconia, Bavaria. It grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in the 8th century, which later belonged to the archbishops of Mainz.

arcangelo-lamberti.s: Arcangelo Lamberti was an Italian Theatine missionary who lived in Mingrelia in western Georgia from the 1630s until about 1649. His account of the country, the Relatione della Colchide hoggi detta Mengrellia, published in Rome in 1654, describes the court of Levan II Dadiani…

antonio-rosetti.s: Antonio Rosetti, born Anton Rösler in Bohemia, was a composer and double-bass player. From 1773 he served in the court orchestra of the princes of Oettingen-Wallerstein, eventually directing it, and in 1789 he moved to Ludwigslust as Kapellmeister to the Duke of…

augustin-calmet.s: Augustin Calmet was a French Benedictine monk and scholar from Lorraine, abbot of Senones from 1728. He wrote a vast literal commentary on the Bible, a dictionary of the Bible and a history of Lorraine, and his treatise on apparitions and vampires of 1746 made him widely known.

ahaus.s: Ahaus is a town in the Borken district of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, close to the Dutch border. Its moated baroque castle was a residence of the prince-bishops of Münster.

afrasiab.s: Afrasiab is the archaeological site of ancient Samarkand, a large mound on the northern edge of the modern city in Uzbekistan. Inhabited from about the 7th century BCE until the Mongol destruction of 1220, it was the Sogdian capital known to the Greeks as Maracanda.

akhaltsikhe.s: Akhaltsikhe is a town in southern Georgia and the centre of the Samtskhe-Javakheti region. It was the seat of the Jaqeli atabegs of Samtskhe and, from 1628, of the Ottoman province of Childir, known for its slave market.

alexander-karadordevic.s: Alexander Karađorđević, son of the rebel leader Karađorđe, was Prince of Serbia from 1842 to 1858. He was raised to the throne by the Constitutionalists after the Obrenović family was driven out, and his reign saw the building of a modern administration and legal code.

ardennes.s: The Ardennes is a region of wooded hills and plateaus spread across south-eastern Belgium, Luxembourg and north-eastern France, with a fringe in Germany. Thinly settled and long a frontier between French and German lands, it held medieval abbeys such as Stavelot and Malmedy.

adygea.s: Adygea is a republic of the Russian Federation in the North Caucasus, surrounded by Krasnodar Krai, with its capital at Maykop. It was created in 1922 as an autonomous region for the Adyghe, the western Circassians, descendants of those who remained after the mass expulsions…

andrey-of-mozhaysk.s: Andrey Dmitriyevich was a son of Dmitry Donskoy of Moscow who received as his appanage Mozhaysk, Vereya and Beloozero. He generally supported his brother Vasily I and nephew Vasily II, and monasteries such as Kirillo-Belozersky flourished in his lands.

aberdyfi.s: Aberdyfi is a village at the mouth of the Dyfi on Cardigan Bay in Gwynedd, Wales. In 1216 Llywelyn the Great held an assembly there at which he divided the lands of Deheubarth among its princes and the other Welsh rulers acknowledged his supremacy, a high point of the native…

aberystwyth.s: Aberystwyth is a town on Cardigan Bay in Ceredigion, Wales. Edward I began its castle in 1277, and Owain Glyndŵr held it from 1404 until English forces recaptured it in 1408.

anthony-ashley-cooper-1st-earl-of-shafte.n: Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury
anthony-ashley-cooper-1st-earl-of-shafte.s: Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, was an English statesman who served Charles II as Chancellor of the Exchequer and Lord Chancellor. One of the eight Lords Proprietors of Carolina, he drafted the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina with his secretary John Locke.

andrew-turnbull.s: Andrew Turnbull was a Scottish physician who founded the colony of New Smyrna in British East Florida in 1768. He brought about 1,400 settlers from Minorca, Greece and Italy to grow indigo on his plantation.

apalachicola-river.s: The Apalachicola River flows south through the Florida Panhandle into the Gulf of Mexico, formed where the Chattahoochee and Flint rivers meet at the Georgia border. In 1763 the British used it as the boundary between their new provinces of East and West Florida.

altamaha-river.s: The Altamaha River in Georgia, United States, is formed by the meeting of the Oconee and Ocmulgee rivers and flows into the Atlantic near Darien. The charter of 1732 set it as the southern limit of the Province of Georgia, facing Spanish Florida, and Scottish Highlanders…

annapolis-maryland.s: Annapolis is the capital of the US state of Maryland, on the Severn River near Chesapeake Bay. Settled by Puritans from Virginia as Providence in 1649, it became the colonial capital in 1694 and was renamed after Princess Anne.

albany-congress.s: The Albany Congress was a meeting of delegates from seven British American colonies held at Albany, New York, in June and July 1754, as war with France loomed. It sought to renew the alliance with the Iroquois Confederacy and adopted Benjamin Franklin's Albany Plan for a union…

adelaide-of-saxe-meiningen.s: Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen was queen consort of the United Kingdom and Hanover from 1830 to 1837 as the wife of William IV. Popular for her piety and charity, she had no surviving children, so the throne passed to the king's niece Victoria.

adelaide-countess-of-vermandois.s: Adelaide was Countess of Vermandois and Valois, heiress of the Herbertian counts of Vermandois, a branch of the Carolingian dynasty. Around 1080 she married Hugh, brother of King Philip I of France, who became count through her and later led a contingent in the First Crusade.

adelaide-of-italy.s: Adelaide of Italy was the daughter of King Rudolf II of Burgundy and became queen of Italy by her first marriage to Lothair II. After his death she was imprisoned by Berengar II, and her rescue led to her marriage in 951 to Otto I, with whom she was crowned empress in 962.

adelaide.s: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, on the plains between Gulf St Vincent and the Mount Lofty Ranges. Founded in 1836 and laid out by Colonel William Light on a grid of streets surrounded by parklands, it was named after Queen Adelaide.

ananus-ben-ananus.s: Ananus ben Ananus was a Jewish high priest who in 62 CE had James, the brother of Jesus, put to death and was deposed after three months. At the start of the First Jewish–Roman War in 66 he became one of the leaders of the provisional government in Jerusalem, favouring a…

acemhoyuk.s: Acemhöyük is a large settlement mound near Aksaray in central Turkey, occupied from the Early Bronze Age. Excavations since 1962 have uncovered two palaces of the 19th and 18th centuries BCE, with clay sealings, ivories and goods linked to the Old Assyrian trade network.

aksaray.s: Aksaray is a city in central Anatolia, Turkey, at the foot of the volcano Hasan Dağı, and capital of the province of the same name. Known in Roman times as Archelais, it flourished under the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, which built great caravanserais such as the Sultan Han on the…

abd-allah-al-uyuni.s: Abd Allah al-Uyuni was the founder of the Uyunid Emirate in eastern Arabia. A chief of the Abd al-Qays tribe, he led a revolt against the Qarmatian state of Bahrain and, with an army sent by the Seljuks, took al-Ahsa in 1077, ending Qarmatian rule.

abu-tahir-al-jannabi.s: Abu Tahir al-Jannabi was ruler of the Qarmatian state of Bahrain in eastern Arabia from 923 until his death in 944. He led raids on Basra, Kufa and the pilgrim caravans, threatened Baghdad, and in January 930 sacked Mecca during the pilgrimage, killing many pilgrims and…

al-mutawakkil-ismail.s: Al-Mutawakkil Isma'il was the Zaydi imam of Yemen from 1644 to 1676 and the most powerful ruler of the Qasimid state. A son of al-Mansur al-Qasim, founder of the dynasty, he extended Zaydi rule over Lower Yemen and took Aden, Lahej and Hadramawt, uniting most of the country…

ash-shihr.s: Ash Shihr is a port town on the Arabian Sea coast of Hadramawt, Yemen, east of Mukalla. For centuries a chief port of Hadramawt for frankincense, horses and Indian Ocean trade, it gave its name to the whole coast in medieval Arabic geography.

awariku.s: Awariku, called Urikki in Assyrian texts, was a king of Que (Hiyawa) on the Cilician plain in the 8th century BCE. He is named in the bilingual Luwian and Phoenician inscriptions of Karatepe, where the local ruler Azatiwada calls himself his protégé, and of Çineköy, which he…

amedee-francois-lamy.s: Amédée-François Lamy was a French army officer who led the military escort of the Foureau–Lamy mission across the Sahara from Algeria to Lake Chad in 1898–1900. Joining the other French columns on the Chari, he attacked Rabih az-Zubayr at Kousseri on 22 April 1900; Rabih's…

aror.s: Aror, also called Alor, was the capital of medieval Sindh, near modern Rohri and Sukkur in Pakistan. It was the seat of the Rai dynasty and of the Brahman dynasty of Chach, and fell to the Arab general Muhammad ibn Qasim in the early 8th century.

arkona.s: Arkona is a chalk cape on the northern tip of the Baltic island of Rügen in Germany, site of a fortified temple of the Slavic Rani. Its sanctuary of the four-headed god Svantevit, described by Saxo Grammaticus, was the last great pagan shrine of the Baltic Slavs until King…

anakena.s: Anakena is a white-sand beach on the north coast of Rapa Nui (Easter Island). Island tradition says that the founding chief Hotu Matuʻa landed there, and excavations show it was among the earliest settled places on the island, from around 1200.

amoghavarsha-i.s: Amoghavarsha I was the longest-reigning Rashtrakuta emperor, ruling the Deccan from 814 to 878. He founded the capital Manyakheta, was a patron of Jain teachers such as Jinasena, and is credited with the Kavirajamarga, the earliest surviving work on Kannada poetics, and the…

al-ashraf-umar-ii.s: Al-Ashraf Umar II was a sultan of the Rasulid dynasty of Yemen who reigned briefly from 1295 to 1296, after his father al-Muzaffar Yusuf I. A noted scholar, he wrote works on astronomy, including a treatise on the astrolabe, as well as on medicine, agriculture, veterinary…

al-muzaffar-yusuf-i.s: Al-Muzaffar Yusuf I was the second sultan of the Rasulid dynasty of Yemen, reigning from 1249 to 1295. He secured the throne after the murder of his father Nur al-Din Umar, extended Rasulid rule over the highlands, conquered Dhofar in 1279 and controlled the rich trade of Aden.

alsace.s: Alsace is a historic region of north-eastern France between the Vosges mountains and the Rhine, with Strasbourg as its main city. Part of the Holy Roman Empire for centuries, it passed largely to France between 1648 and 1681, was annexed by Germany in 1871 as part of…

augusta-raurica.s: Augusta Raurica is a Roman town site at Augst near Basel, Switzerland, on the Rhine. A colony was founded in the land of the Raurici by Lucius Munatius Plancus around 44 BCE, though the town itself grew up under Augustus from about 15 BCE.

alba-iulia.s: Alba Iulia, in Hungarian Gyulafehérvár, is a city in Transylvania, Romania, on the Mureș River, built on the site of the Roman legionary fortress of Apulum. It was the seat of the bishops of Transylvania from the 11th century and the capital of the Principality of Transylvania…

addanki.s: Addanki is a town in Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh, India. Prolaya Vema Reddi, founder of the Reddi Kingdom, made it his first capital in the 1320s before the seat moved to Kondavidu.

amalfi-coast.s: The Amalfi Coast is a stretch of coastline on the southern side of the Sorrento Peninsula, in the province of Salerno in southern Italy. Its steep cliffs, terraced lemon groves and towns such as Amalfi, Positano and Ravello have made it a major tourist destination, and it was…

austrian-peoples-party.s: The Austrian People's Party (ÖVP) is Austria's main Christian democratic and conservative party, founded in April 1945 as the successor of the interwar Christian Social Party. It governed in grand coalitions with the Social Democrats for long periods after 1945 and has…

austrian-state-treaty.s: The Austrian State Treaty, signed in Vienna on 15 May 1955 by the four occupying powers and Austria, restored Austria as a sovereign, independent and democratic state. It ended the Allied occupation that had lasted since 1945, banned union with Germany and protected the rights…

arusha-peace-and-reconciliation-agreemen.n: Arusha Peace and Reconciliation Agreement for Burundi
arusha-peace-and-reconciliation-agreemen.s: The Arusha Peace and Reconciliation Agreement for Burundi was signed in Arusha, Tanzania, on 28 August 2000, after talks mediated first by Julius Nyerere and then by Nelson Mandela. It set out a transition and a system of power-sharing between Hutu and Tutsi in government,…

antofagasta.s: Antofagasta is a port city in northern Chile and capital of the Antofagasta Region, on the edge of the Atacama Desert. Founded under Bolivian rule in 1868 to export nitrates, it was occupied by Chile in February 1879, which opened the War of the Pacific, and it passed to Chile…

amapa.s: Amapá is a state in the far north of Brazil, between the Amazon estuary and French Guiana, with its capital at Macapá. The land between the Oyapock and Araguari rivers was disputed between France and Brazil until Swiss arbitration awarded it to Brazil in 1900.

attack-on-the-moncada-barracks.s: The attack on the Moncada Barracks was an assault on an army post in Santiago de Cuba on 26 July 1953 by about 160 rebels led by Fidel Castro. It failed, and many captured rebels were killed; Castro was tried, gave his speech 'History Will Absolve Me' and was imprisoned until…

antonio-maceo.s: Antonio Maceo was a Cuban general of the wars of independence, nicknamed the 'Bronze Titan'. An Afro-Cuban from Santiago, he rose through the Ten Years' War and rejected the Pact of Zanjón in the Protest of Baraguá in 1878.

altars-of-the-philaeni.s: The Altars of the Philaeni were an ancient landmark on the coast of the Gulf of Sidra in Libya that marked the boundary between the territory of Carthage and Greek Cyrenaica. According to the legend told by Sallust, two Carthaginian brothers, the Philaeni, agreed to be buried…

aristippus-of-cyrene.s: Aristippus of Cyrene was a Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school. He taught that the pleasure of the present moment is the highest good, while urging self-control so as to master pleasure rather than be ruled by it.

abdel-fattah-el-sisi.s: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi is an Egyptian army officer who has been president of Egypt since 2014. As defence minister and head of the armed forces he led the removal of President Mohamed Morsi in July 2013, after which security forces crushed the Muslim Brotherhood, killing…

alessandro-de-medici.s: Alessandro de' Medici was the first Duke of Florence, installed after the imperial and papal siege ended the last Florentine republic in 1530 and made hereditary duke by Emperor Charles V in 1532. He married Charles's illegitimate daughter Margaret and built the Fortezza da…

academy-of-geneva.s: The Academy of Geneva was founded by John Calvin in 1559 to train Reformed pastors and teachers, with Theodore Beza as its first rector. It drew students from France, Scotland, the Netherlands and elsewhere and spread Calvinist teaching across Europe.

andrea-doria.s: Andrea Doria was a Genoese admiral and statesman, the leading naval commander of his age. In 1528 he switched from French to Habsburg service, restored Genoa's independence under a new aristocratic constitution and became its dominant figure for three decades.

ambrogio-spinola.s: Ambrogio Spinola was a Genoese nobleman who became the leading general of Spain's armies in the Low Countries. He took Ostend in 1604 after a three-year siege and Breda in 1625, a victory painted by Velázquez, and in 1620 he occupied the Lower Palatinate early in the Thirty…

ahmed-hassan-al-bakr.s: Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr was an Iraqi army officer and Ba'athist politician who was President of Iraq from 1968 to 1979. Briefly prime minister after the Ba'athist coup of 1963, he led the party back to power in July 1968 and ruled with his relative Saddam Hussein as deputy.

anfal-campaign.s: The Anfal campaign was a genocidal operation by the Iraqi government of Saddam Hussein against the Kurds of northern Iraq, at its height in 1988 during the last phase of the Iran–Iraq War. Commanded by Ali Hassan al-Majid, it destroyed thousands of villages, used chemical…

adam-philippe-comte-de-custine.s: Adam Philippe, Comte de Custine was a French general who served in the American War of Independence and commanded the Army of the Rhine in the French Revolutionary Wars. In autumn 1792 he took Speyer, Worms and Mainz, making possible the short-lived Republic of Mainz, and…

arnulfo-arias.s: Arnulfo Arias was a Panamanian physician and nationalist politician who was elected President of Panama three times and removed by force each time. His first term brought a new constitution in 1941 and measures against foreign minorities before he was deposed later that year;…

andarax.s: The Andarax is a river in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, flowing from the Sierra Nevada and the Alpujarras to the Mediterranean at the city of Almería. Its lower valley, irrigated since Roman and Islamic times, was the site of Pechina (Bajjana), a leading port…

antonio-goncalves-da-cruz.s: Antônio Gonçalves da Cruz, known as Cabugá, was a merchant of Recife and a leader of the Pernambucan revolt of 1817 against Portuguese rule in Brazil. The revolutionary government sent him to the United States to seek recognition and buy arms, the first diplomatic mission of a…

arengo-san-marino.s: The Arengo is the assembly of the heads of families of San Marino, the republic's original governing body in the Middle Ages. It delegated most of its powers to the Great and General Council as the state grew, keeping a largely formal role.

ambrogio-lorenzetti.s: Ambrogio Lorenzetti was a Sienese painter, the younger brother of Pietro Lorenzetti. In 1338–1339 he painted the frescoes of the Allegory of Good and Bad Government in the Palazzo Pubblico of Siena, which include some of the earliest panoramic townscapes and landscapes in…

allegory-of-good-and-bad-government.n: The Allegory of Good and Bad Government
allegory-of-good-and-bad-government.s: The Allegory of Good and Bad Government is a cycle of frescoes painted by Ambrogio Lorenzetti in 1338–1339 in the Palazzo Pubblico of Siena, in the room where the city's governing council of the Nine met. It contrasts the virtues of just republican rule, shown in a prosperous…

antonio-zapata.s: Antonio Zapata was a rancher and federalist military leader from Guerrero, Tamaulipas, who commanded cavalry for the Republic of the Rio Grande, a short-lived breakaway state in northern Mexico in 1840. Captured by centralist forces in March 1840, he was executed and his head…

adnan-menderes.s: Adnan Menderes was a Turkish politician who co-founded the Democrat Party and became prime minister after its victory in the 1950 election, the first peaceful transfer of power in the Turkish Republic. His government encouraged private enterprise and agriculture, brought…

ali-salim-al-beidh.s: Ali Salim al-Beidh is a Yemeni politician who led the Yemeni Socialist Party, the ruling party of South Yemen, from 1986. He negotiated unification with North Yemen and became vice-president of the united Republic of Yemen in 1990.

anaukpetlun.s: Anaukpetlun was king of Burma's Restored Toungoo dynasty from 1605 to 1628. He reunited much of the former kingdom, taking Prome and Toungoo, capturing the Portuguese-held port of Syriam from Filipe de Brito e Nicote in 1613 and reconquering Lan Na in 1615.

abdul-rahman-muazzam-shah.s: Abdul Rahman Muazzam Shah was the last sultan of Riau-Lingga, reigning from 1885 to 1911. Growing friction with the Dutch colonial authorities, who resented his independence, led them to depose him in 1911.

ajdir.s: Ajdir is a village in the Rif region of northern Morocco, near the bay of Al Hoceima. It was the home of Abd el-Krim's family and served as the capital of the Republic of the Rif, which he founded during the war against Spain and France in the 1920s.

alhucemas-landing.s: The Alhucemas landing was an amphibious assault by Spanish forces, supported by France, on the bay of Alhucemas (Al Hoceima) in northern Morocco in September 1925. Landing close to Abd el-Krim's base at Ajdir, the troops broke the Rifian resistance, and the Republic of the Rif…

asta-gudbrandsdatter.s: Åsta Gudbrandsdatter was a Norwegian noblewoman of the late 10th and early 11th centuries, according to the sagas. She was the mother of King Olaf II Haraldsson by her first husband, Harald Grenske, and by her second husband, Sigurd Syr, petty king of Ringerike, the mother of…

alegrete.s: Alegrete is a city in the west of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, on the Ibirapuitã River. During the Ragamuffin War it served for a time as the capital of the Riograndense Republic, and the republic's constituent assembly met there in 1842.

argyll.s: Argyll is a region of western Scotland, made up of sea lochs, peninsulas and islands, including Kintyre, Cowal and Lorn. Its name means 'coast of the Gaels'.

avaldsnes.s: Avaldsnes is a historic site on the island of Karmøy in western Norway, overlooking the Karmsund strait. Its great burial mounds and ship burials show that powerful kings controlled the shipping lane there from the Iron Age, and the sagas make it a royal seat of Harald Fairhair.

aonla.s: Aonla is a town in the Bareilly district of Uttar Pradesh, India. In the first half of the 18th century it was the capital of the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan, whose tomb stands there, before the Rohilla chiefs made Bareilly their main centre.

aures-mountains.s: The Aurès Mountains are a range of the Saharan Atlas in north-eastern Algeria, home of the Chaoui Berbers. Under Rome the legion at Lambaesis guarded their northern edge, and after the Vandal conquest Berber kingdoms held them.

asaba.s: Asaba is a city on the west bank of the Niger River in southern Nigeria, opposite Onitsha, and the capital of Delta State. In the late 19th century it was the administrative headquarters of the Royal Niger Company.

alberta.s: Alberta is a province of western Canada, between British Columbia and Saskatchewan, with Edmonton as its capital and Calgary as its largest city. Once part of Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory, it became a province in 1905.

aleut.s: The Aleut, or Unangan, are the Indigenous people of the Aleutian Islands and the western Alaska Peninsula, skilled sea hunters in skin kayaks. From the 1740s Russian fur traders forced them to hunt sea otters, and violence and disease greatly reduced their numbers.

alutiiq.s: The Alutiiq, or Sugpiaq, are an Indigenous people of south-central Alaska, living on Kodiak Island, the Alaska Peninsula and the coasts of Prince William Sound. In 1784 Grigory Shelikhov's men massacred many of them at Refuge Rock, and under the Russian-American Company they…

aveyron.s: Aveyron is a department in southern France, in the Occitanie region, covering most of the former province of Rouergue. Its capital is Rodez.

amiternum.s: Amiternum was an ancient Sabine town in the upper Aterno valley of central Italy, near modern L'Aquila. It came under Roman control early in the 3rd century BCE and grew into a prosperous Roman town with a theatre and an amphitheatre, whose remains survive.

aniene.s: The Aniene, the ancient Anio, is a river of central Italy that rises in the Simbruini mountains and joins the Tiber just north of Rome. At Tivoli, ancient Tibur, it falls from the hills in waterfalls into the Roman plain.

apennines.s: The Apennines are the mountain range that runs about 1,200 kilometres down the length of the Italian peninsula, from Liguria to Calabria. Their valleys and uplands were home to many ancient Italic peoples, such as the Samnites, Sabines and Umbrians, and their passes linked the…

attus-clausus.s: Attus Clausus was a Sabine leader who, according to Roman tradition, moved to Rome around 504 BCE with a large band of followers. Taking the name Appius Claudius, he was admitted to the patricians and became consul in 495 BCE.

arita.s: Arita is a town in Saga Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, Japan. After Korean potters found porcelain clay nearby around 1616, it became the birthplace of Japanese porcelain under the Nabeshima lords of Saga.

afyonkarahisar.s: Afyonkarahisar is a city in western Turkey, capital of Afyonkarahisar province, beneath a volcanic rock crowned by a castle. In the late 13th century it was held by the family of the Seljuk vizier Sahib Ata, after whom it was long called Karahisar-i Sahib, and it later passed…

argyle-international-airport.s: Argyle International Airport is the main airport of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, on the south-east coast of Saint Vincent. Built over about a decade with help from countries including Cuba and Venezuela, it opened in February 2017, replacing the small E.

appius-claudius-pulcher-consul-143-bce.s: Appius Claudius Pulcher was a Roman statesman of the patrician Claudii. As consul in 143 BCE he attacked the Salassi of the Aosta valley and, after first being defeated, celebrated a triumph without the Senate's approval.

aulus-terentius-varro-murena.s: Aulus Terentius Varro Murena was a Roman general in the early reign of Augustus. In 25 BCE he conquered the Salassi of the Aosta valley, selling about 36,000 of them into slavery, and founded the colony of Augusta Praetoria, modern Aosta, on their land.

aix-en-provence.s: Aix-en-Provence is a city in Provence, southern France, north of Marseille. It was founded in 122 BCE by the Roman consul Gaius Sextius Calvinus as Aquae Sextiae, near the destroyed Salyan stronghold of Entremont, and in 102 BCE Gaius Marius defeated the Teutones nearby.

argive-heraion.s: The Argive Heraion was the chief sanctuary of the goddess Hera in the Argolid in southern Greece, on a hillside between Argos and Mycenae. Controlled by Argos, it had temples from the 7th century BCE, and after a fire in 423 BCE a new temple was built with a gold and ivory…

acoma-pueblo.s: Acoma Pueblo is a Native American pueblo built on a sandstone mesa west of Albuquerque, New Mexico, and is among the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the United States. After its people killed a party of Spanish soldiers in 1598, Juan de Oñate's forces stormed the…

arch-of-germanicus.s: The Arch of Germanicus is a Roman double arch in Saintes, western France, built around 18–19 CE at the entrance to a bridge over the Charente. An inscription records that it was dedicated by Gaius Julius Rufus, a local notable of Santonian descent, to the emperor Tiberius, his…

abna.s: The Abna were the descendants of the Persian soldiers sent by the Sasanian king Khosrow I to Yemen around 570 to drive out its Aksumite rulers. Settling in the country and marrying local women, they formed a distinct ruling elite in Sanaa under Persian governors.

andhra-region.s: Andhra is the historical name of the Telugu-speaking lands of south-eastern India, centred on the lower valleys of the Krishna and Godavari rivers along the Bay of Bengal. The Andhras are mentioned as a people in late Vedic texts and the edicts of Ashoka, and the region was…

ateas.s: Ateas was a king of the Scythians in the 4th century BCE who built a powerful realm north of the Black Sea and extended his rule westwards to the lower Danube. He struck coins in his name at Callatis and at first sought the help of Philip II of Macedon against his enemies, but…

adad-apla-iddina.s: Adad-apla-iddina was king of Babylon from about 1068 to 1047 BCE, during the Second Dynasty of Isin. Later chronicles call him a usurper, and one describes him as of Aramean origin.

admirable-campaign.s: The Admirable Campaign was Simón Bolívar's military campaign of 1813 in which he advanced from New Granada across the Andes into western Venezuela and drove back the royalists in a series of victories. During the march he issued the Decree of War to the Death at Trujillo in June.

abdul-samad-of-selangor.s: Abdul Samad of Selangor was the fourth Sultan of Selangor, reigning from 1857 to 1898. His reign saw the tin rush that drew Chinese miners into the Klang valley and the civil war among Selangor chiefs known as the Klang War.

achaeus-general.s: Achaeus was a Seleucid general and a cousin of Antiochus III who restored Seleucid control of Asia Minor in the 220s BCE. In 220 BCE he proclaimed himself king, and his forces campaigned in Pisidia, besieging Selge in 218 BCE.

al-mustarshid.s: Al-Mustarshid was the Abbasid caliph from 1118 to 1135 who tried to free the caliphate from Seljuk control by raising his own army. He was defeated by Sultan Mas'ud near Hamadan in 1135 and taken prisoner.

andrew-jackson.s: Andrew Jackson was an American general and the seventh President of the United States, serving from 1829 to 1837. He won fame by defeating the British at New Orleans in 1815 and invaded Spanish Florida in the First Seminole War.

allegany-reservation.s: The Allegany Reservation is a territory of the Seneca Nation of Indians along the Allegheny River in western New York. Together with Cattaraugus it formed the Seneca Nation's elected government in 1848.

ager-gallicus.s: The Ager Gallicus was the coastal strip of the Adriatic in northern Marche, Italy, once settled by the Gallic Senones. Rome conquered it in 283 BCE, founded the colony of Sena Gallica, and in 232 BCE divided it among Roman settlers under the land law of Gaius Flaminius.

aleksandar-vucic.s: Aleksandar Vučić is a Serbian politician who has been President of Serbia since 2017 after serving as prime minister from 2014. He was information minister under Slobodan Milošević and in 2008 co-founded the Serbian Progressive Party, which has dominated Serbian politics since…

amadeo-i-of-spain.s: Amadeo I, a son of Victor Emmanuel II of Italy, was elected King of Spain by the Cortes and reigned from 1871 to 1873. His backer Juan Prim was assassinated days before his arrival.

almunecar.s: Almuñécar is a town on the Mediterranean coast of Granada province in southern Spain. Founded by the Phoenicians as Sexi, it grew rich on salted fish and became the Roman town of Firmum Iulium Sexi.

anyang.s: Anyang is a city in northern Henan province, China, near the site of Yin, the last capital of the Shang dynasty. Excavations there since 1928 have uncovered royal tombs, palace foundations and tens of thousands of inscribed oracle bones, the earliest Chinese writing.

anti-atlas.s: The Anti-Atlas is a mountain range in southern Morocco, running north-east from the Atlantic coast towards the Jebel Saghro, south of the High Atlas and the Sous valley. Its dry, terraced valleys are home to Berber villages and fortified granaries.

al-nahyan.s: The Al Nahyan are the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, a branch of the Al Bu Falah section of the Bani Yas tribal confederation. From the Liwa oases they moved their seat to Abu Dhabi island in the 1790s and have ruled the emirate since.

al-naim.s: The Al Na'im are an Arab tribe of the eastern Arabian peninsula, found in the emirate of Ajman, the Buraimi oasis and northern Oman. Their leader Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi seized the fort of Ajman in 1816, and his descendants, the Al Nuaimi family, have ruled Ajman ever…

ahmed-al-fateh.s: Ahmed al-Fateh, Ahmad ibn Muhammad Al Khalifa, was the first Al Khalifa ruler of Bahrain. In 1783 the Al Khalifa and their allies of the Bani Utbah, based at Zubarah in Qatar, crossed to Bahrain and drove out the governor serving the sheikhs of Bushehr, earning him the name…

al-bu-falasah.s: The Al Bu Falasah are a section of the Bani Yas tribal confederation of the southern Gulf coast. In 1833 about 800 of them broke away from Abu Dhabi and settled at Dubai Creek under Maktoum bin Butti and Obaid bin Said, founding the Sheikhdom of Dubai.

al-maktoum.s: The Al Maktoum are the ruling family of Dubai, descended from Maktoum bin Butti, who led the Al Bu Falasah to Dubai Creek in 1833. Under rulers such as Rashid bin Saeed and his sons they turned Dubai from a pearling and trading town into a global commercial hub.

al-qasimi.s: The Al Qasimi, or Qawasim, are an Arab dynasty and tribal confederation of the southern Gulf, centred on Ras al-Khaimah and Sharjah. In the 18th century they built a maritime power on both shores of the Gulf, which Britain attacked in 1809 and 1819 in campaigns against alleged…

anglo-kuwaiti-agreement-of-1899.s: The Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement of 23 January 1899 was a secret treaty between Britain and Mubarak al-Sabah, ruler of Kuwait. Mubarak undertook not to cede territory or receive foreign representatives without British consent, in return for British protection and a subsidy, which…

anglo-qatari-treaty.s: The Anglo-Qatari Treaty of 3 November 1916 was signed by Britain and Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani after the Ottoman garrison left Qatar during the First World War. Qatar joined the Trucial system, giving Britain control of its foreign relations in exchange for protection…

abu-musa.s: Abu Musa is an island in the Persian Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz, long administered by Sharjah. Under a memorandum of understanding of November 1971 Iranian troops were stationed on part of it while Sharjah kept administration of the rest.

al-ali.s: The Al Ali are an Arab tribe of the Trucial Coast, centred on Umm al-Quwain in the United Arab Emirates. Led by the Al Mualla family, they founded a fortified settlement at Umm al-Quwain in 1775, and the Al Mualla have ruled the emirate ever since.

al-mualla.s: The Al Mualla are the ruling family of Umm al-Quwain, leaders of the Al Ali tribe. Rashid bin Majid Al Mualla founded a fortified settlement on the Umm al-Quwain peninsula in 1775, and his descendants signed the British maritime truces of the 19th century.

aghsu.s: Aghsu is a town in central Azerbaijan, on the plain south of Shamakhi. In 1734 Nader Shah destroyed Shamakhi and moved its people to a new town here, known as New Shamakhi.

agnimitra.s: Agnimitra was the second king of the Shunga dynasty of northern India, son of its founder Pushyamitra Shunga, in the 2nd century BCE. Before his accession he governed the region of Vidisha in central India for his father.

abu-salabikh.s: Abu Salabikh is an archaeological site in southern Iraq, about 20 kilometres north-west of Nippur, whose ancient name is uncertain. Excavations found a large archive of cuneiform tablets from about 2600–2500 BCE, including some of the earliest known copies of Sumerian…

agariste-of-sicyon.s: Agariste of Sicyon was the daughter of Cleisthenes, tyrant of Sicyon. Herodotus tells how her father held a year-long contest among suitors from all over Greece, which Megacles of the Athenian Alcmaeonid family won after his rival Hippocleides danced on a table.

apelles.s: Apelles was the most celebrated painter of ancient Greece, active in the 4th century BCE. Born at Colophon, he trained at Ephesus and in the painting school of Sicyon and became court painter to Philip II and Alexander the Great.

aeolis.s: Aeolis was the ancient name of the north-western coast of Anatolia and the island of Lesbos, settled by Aeolian Greeks from the 11th century BCE. Its cities, including Cyme, Myrina and those of Lesbos, formed a league and spoke the Aeolic dialect of Greek.

abdalonymus.s: Abdalonymus was king of Sidon, installed by Alexander the Great in 332 BCE. Ancient writers say he was a poor gardener of royal descent chosen in place of the deposed king Straton.

ahluwalia-misl.s: The Ahluwalia misl was one of the twelve Sikh confederacies of 18th-century Punjab, led by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, who also commanded the Dal Khalsa. It held lands in the Jalandhar Doab and took Kapurthala in the 1770s.

ambarnath.s: Ambarnath is a city in Thane district, Maharashtra, India, in the outer suburbs of Mumbai. It is known for its Shiva temple, completed in 1060 under the Silahara king Mummuni of the North Konkan, one of the finest surviving examples of the Bhumija style of temple architecture…

argun-caucasus.s: The Argun is a river of the North Caucasus that rises in north-eastern Georgia and flows north through Chechnya to join the Sunzha. Its deep gorge was the main route into the Chechen highlands and saw fierce fighting in the Caucasian War of the 19th century and in the Chechen…

akkar.s: Akkar is the northernmost region of Lebanon, a fertile coastal plain and hill country on the border with Syria, now a governorate. The plain lies along the Homs Gap, the route from the Mediterranean coast to the Orontes valley, and was controlled in the Bronze Age by Sumur,…

andrew-doria.s: The Andrew Doria was a brig of the Continental Navy in the American Revolutionary War, named after the Genoese admiral Andrea Doria. On 16 November 1776 the guns of Fort Oranje on Sint Eustatius returned its salute, the first salute given to the flag of the United States by a…

akha.s: The Akha are a Tibeto-Burman hill people living in the mountains of southern Yunnan in China, eastern Myanmar, northern Laos, northern Thailand and Vietnam. Traditionally upland farmers living in villages marked by ceremonial gates and swings, they keep long oral genealogies…

athena.s: Athena was the ancient Greek goddess of wisdom, crafts and war, the virgin daughter of Zeus, said to have sprung fully armed from his head. Patron of Athens, where the Parthenon was her temple, she was worshipped in sanctuaries across the Greek world, at Lindos, Smyrna and…

aristeidis-stergiadis.s: Aristeidis Stergiadis (1861–1949) was a Greek lawyer and administrator, appointed by Eleftherios Venizelos as High Commissioner of the Smyrna zone from 1919 to 1922. Born in Crete, he was known for his stern efforts to treat Muslims and Christians impartially, which made him…

anti-fascist-council-for-the-national-li.n: Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia
anti-fascist-council-for-the-national-li.s: The Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ) was the political assembly of Tito's Partisan movement in the Second World War, first convened at Bihać in November 1942. At its second session at Jajce on 29 November 1943 it declared itself the…

arturo-alessandri.s: Arturo Alessandri (1868–1950) was a Chilean politician who served twice as president, from 1920 to 1925 and from 1932 to 1938. Elected as a reformer backed by the middle and working classes, he clashed with the conservative Congress and, after military interventions, promoted…

african-union.s: The African Union is the continental organisation of the 55 states of Africa, founded in 2002 as the successor to the Organisation of African Unity of 1963. Based in Addis Ababa, it promotes political and economic integration, has a Pan-African Parliament and a Peace and…

african-union-mission-to-somalia.s: The African Union Mission to Somalia (AMISOM) was a peacekeeping force authorised by the African Union and the United Nations in 2007 to support Somalia's transitional government. Made up mainly of troops from Uganda, Burundi, Kenya, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it drove al-Shabaab…

arsames-i.s: Arsames I was a king of Sophene, and possibly of Commagene, in the 3rd century BCE, a member of the Orontid dynasty that had ruled Armenia under the Achaemenids. He is credited with founding the cities of Arsamosata and Arsameia, and he is said to have sheltered the Seleucid…

arsamosata.s: Arsamosata was an ancient city of Sophene in the valley of the Arsanias (Murat) river, a tributary of the Euphrates, east of modern Elazığ in Turkey. Founded by the Orontid king Arsames in the 3rd century BCE, it was a royal seat of Sophene and later a fortress and bishopric…

artanes.s: Artanes was the last king of Sophene, a small Armenian kingdom on the upper Euphrates, descended according to Strabo from the general Zariadres. Around 95 BCE he was deposed by Tigranes the Great of Armenia, who annexed Sophene and united most Armenian lands under the Artaxiad…

avienus.s: Avienus (Rufius Festus Avienius) was a Latin poet of the 4th century CE who adapted Greek works on geography and astronomy into verse. His Ora Maritima, a description of the coasts of which only the part from the Atlantic to Massalia survives, preserves material from a much…

adiatuanus.s: Adiatuanus was king of the Sotiates, an Aquitanian people of south-western Gaul, in 56 BCE. According to Julius Caesar, he defended their stronghold against Caesar's legate Publius Crassus and, after a failed sortie with his six hundred sworn companions, the soldurii,…

arequipa.s: Arequipa is the second-largest city of Peru, in the southern Andes at the foot of the volcano El Misti. Founded by the Spanish in 1540, it is built largely of white volcanic sillar stone, and its historic centre, with the Santa Catalina convent, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

adams-onis-treaty.s: The Adams–Onís Treaty, signed in Washington on 22 February 1819 by the American secretary of state John Quincy Adams and the Spanish minister Luis de Onís, transferred Florida from Spain to the United States. It also fixed the boundary between the United States and New Spain…

antonio-de-ulloa.s: Antonio de Ulloa (1716–1795) was a Spanish naval officer and scientist who took part in the French geodesic mission to Peru from 1735, and whose account of the voyage first described platinum to European science. Appointed the first Spanish governor of Louisiana, he arrived in…

albert-vii-archduke-of-austria.s: Albert VII, Archduke of Austria (1559–1621), a son of Emperor Maximilian II, was a cardinal and viceroy of Portugal before he became governor of the Spanish Netherlands. In 1598 Philip II gave the provinces to his daughter Isabella Clara Eugenia, whom Albert married, and the…

alamo-mission.s: The Alamo Mission, founded in 1718 as Mission San Antonio de Valero, was a Franciscan mission at San Antonio in Spanish Texas that gathered Coahuiltecan peoples. Secularised in 1793, it later housed a Spanish cavalry company and took its name from them.

alonso-de-leon.s: Alonso de León (c. 1639–1691) was a Spanish soldier and governor of Coahuila who led several expeditions into Texas in search of La Salle's French colony.

austin-texas.s: Austin is the capital of the US state of Texas, on the Colorado River. Chosen in 1839 by President Mirabeau Lamar as the permanent capital of the Republic of Texas, it was laid out on the site of the village of Waterloo and named after Stephen F.

amyclae.s: Amyclae was an ancient town in Laconia, a few kilometres south of Sparta in the Eurotas valley. A Mycenaean centre in the Bronze Age, it was absorbed by Sparta, probably in the eighth century BCE, becoming the fifth of its villages.

anura-kumara-dissanayake.s: Anura Kumara Dissanayake (born 1968) is a Sri Lankan politician who became president of Sri Lanka in September 2024. Leader of the left-wing Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna from 2014 and of the National People's Power alliance, he campaigned against corruption after the economic…

arizona.s: Arizona is a state in the south-western United States, with its capital at Phoenix. Home to the Hohokam, Ancestral Puebloan, Navajo, Apache and other peoples, it was a frontier of New Spain and Mexico until most of it passed to the United States in 1848, with the south added…

anastasio-aquino.s: Anastasio Aquino (1792–1833) was an indigenous Nonualco leader who led a rebellion in central El Salvador in 1833 against the seizure of communal lands, harsh labour on indigo estates and forced recruitment into the army. His forces of several thousand defeated government…

appalachian-mountains.s: The Appalachian Mountains are an ancient mountain system of eastern North America, stretching about 2,400 kilometres from Newfoundland to Alabama. For British colonists they formed a barrier to westward settlement, marked by the Proclamation Line of 1763, until settlers…

arab-league.s: The Arab League is a regional organisation of Arab states founded in Cairo on 22 March 1945 by Egypt, Iraq, Transjordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and Syria, with Yemen joining weeks later. It grew to 22 members across the Middle East and North Africa, and works to coordinate the…

antonio-vieira.s: António Vieira (1608–1697) was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary, diplomat and preacher, considered a master of classical Portuguese prose. Raised in Bahia, he served King John IV as an adviser and envoy after 1640, and from 1653 led the Jesuit missions in Maranhão and Grão-Pará,…

al-jazeera.s: Al Jazeera is a television network based in Doha, launched in November 1996 with funding from the emir of Qatar, Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani. As the first major Arabic news channel independent of other Arab governments it transformed the region's media, broadcasting interviews…

ansedonia.s: Ansedonia is a hilltop locality on the coast of southern Tuscany, part of the comune of Orbetello. It occupies the site of Cosa, a Roman colony founded in 273 BCE, whose walls, forum and harbour remains survive.

aisne.s: The Aisne is a river of northern France, about 350 km long, flowing west from the Argonne to join the Oise near Compiègne. Its valley, with Soissons as its chief town, was the land of the Gallic Suessiones.

aden.s: Aden is a port city in southern Yemen, built in the crater of an extinct volcano near the entrance to the Red Sea. For centuries a hub of trade between India, Arabia and Egypt under Yemeni dynasties such as the Zurayids and Rasulids, it was taken by Britain in 1839 and became…

arwa-al-sulayhi.s: Arwa al-Sulayhi was queen of the Sulayhid dynasty of Yemen, who governed for some fifty years, first for her ailing husband Ahmad al-Mukarram and then in her own right, until her death in 1138. She moved the capital to Dhu Jibla, built its great mosque and was given authority…

ahmad-al-mukarram.s: Ahmad al-Mukarram was the second ruler of the Sulayhid dynasty of Yemen, succeeding his father Ali al-Sulayhi after Ali was killed by the Najahids in the 1060s. Afflicted by paralysis, he left much of the government to his wife Arwa, who moved the court to Dhu Jibla.

ali-yusuf-kenadid.s: Ali Yusuf Kenadid was the last sultan of Hobyo in central Somalia, succeeding his father Yusuf Ali Kenadid. In 1925 he refused Italian demands to disarm and accept direct rule, and the forces of governor Cesare Maria De Vecchi occupied the sultanate, which was annexed to…

ahmad-fadl-al-qumandan.s: Ahmad Fadl al-Qumandan was a prince of the Abdali ruling house of the Sultanate of Lahej in southern Arabia, a poet and musician who also commanded the sultanate's forces, from which he took the name al-Qumandan. His songs in the local dialect, set to Lahji melodies, founded a…

ali-ibn-abd-al-karim.s: Ali ibn Abd al-Karim al-Abdali was the sultan of Lahej, the most important of the British-protected states around Aden, from 1952 to 1958. He sympathised with Arab nationalism and was linked to the South Arabian League, which opposed British plans for the region.

abu-bakr-ibn-shaykh-umar.s: Abu Bakr ibn Shaykh Umar was the sultan of Mogadishu when the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited the city in 1331. Ibn Battuta described him as a Somali ruler who spoke both the local language and Arabic, governed with the advice of qadis and notables, and held elaborate…

azzan-ibn-qais.s: Azzan ibn Qais was a member of the Al Bu Said family who, backed by the Ibadi religious leaders of the Omani interior, took Muscat in 1868 and was elected imam. His government tried to restore a strict Ibadi imamate on the coast, but it lacked British support and was…

alanya.s: Alanya is a port city on the Mediterranean coast of southern Turkey. The Byzantine town of Kalonoros was taken in 1221 by the Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I, who renamed it Alaiye and made it a winter residence and naval base, building its citadel walls, the Red Tower and a shipyard.

afgooye.s: Afgooye is a town on the Shabelle river in southern Somalia, about 30 kilometres north-west of Mogadishu. From the early 18th century it was the seat of the Geledi clan and their Gobroon dynasty, who ruled the Sultanate of the Geledi in the fertile lower Shabelle valley.

ahmed-yusuf-of-geledi.s: Ahmed Yusuf was sultan of the Geledi in southern Somalia, son and successor of Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim of the Gobroon dynasty. He ruled from Afgooye over the lower Shabelle valley and its plantations, and dealt with the Sultanate of Zanzibar on the coast.

anglo-zanzibar-war.s: The Anglo-Zanzibar War was a brief conflict on 27 August 1896 between Britain and the Sultanate of Zanzibar. After Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini died, Khalid bin Barghash seized the palace without British approval and refused an ultimatum to stand down.

avungara.s: The Avungara are the ruling aristocratic clan of the Zande people of north-central Africa. From the 18th century Avungara princes led Zande expansion across the watershed of the Nile and Congo basins, founding many small kingdoms in what are now South Sudan, the Central…

avantiputra.s: Avantiputra was a king of Surasena, ruling from Mathura, named in early Buddhist texts. His name means son of the princess of Avanti.

ambikapur.s: Ambikapur is a city in northern Chhattisgarh, India, and the headquarters of Surguja district. It was the capital of the princely state of Surguja under its Maharajas, and takes its name from the goddess Ambika (Mahamaya), whose temple is in the town.

akhund-of-swat.s: The Akhund of Swat, Abdul Ghafur, was a Sufi saint and religious leader of the Swat valley in the north-west of present-day Pakistan. Revered across the Pashtun lands, he helped rally resistance to the British in the Ambela campaign of 1863 and was the dominant figure in Swat…

act-of-union-1815.s: The Act of Union of 1815, Riksakten, was the law adopted by the Norwegian Storting and the Swedish Riksdag that set the terms of the personal union of Sweden and Norway. It confirmed that the two kingdoms shared a king and conducted foreign policy jointly, while each kept its…

archias-of-corinth.s: Archias was a nobleman of the Bacchiad family of Corinth who, according to Greek tradition, led the colonists who founded Syracuse in Sicily in 734 or 733 BCE. Ancient accounts say he left Corinth after a scandal and consulted the oracle at Delphi before sailing.

archimedes.s: Archimedes of Syracuse was the greatest mathematician and engineer of the ancient Greek world. He calculated areas and volumes of curved figures, approximated pi, founded statics and hydrostatics with the principles of the lever and buoyancy, and is credited with the…

ambaris.s: Ambaris was a king of Bit-Burutash in Tabal in south-central Anatolia in the late 8th century BCE. The Assyrian king Sargon II gave him his daughter in marriage and the land of Hilakku, but in 713 BCE accused him of plotting with Mita of Phrygia and Rusa of Urartu, deported…

adrar-des-ifoghas.s: The Adrar des Ifoghas is a sandstone massif in the Kidal region of north-eastern Mali, in the southern Sahara. It is the homeland of the Kel Adagh Tuareg and was the site of the medieval trading town of Tadmekka, at Essouk.

aberdeenshire.s: Aberdeenshire is a council area and historic county of north-east Scotland, lying between the Grampian mountains and the North Sea around the city of Aberdeen. In Roman times it was the land of the Taexali, and it later formed part of the kingdom of the Picts, whose symbol…

abhiraja.s: Abhiraja is the legendary founder of the kingdom of Tagaung in Burmese chronicles. The chronicles say he was a prince of the Sakya clan, the Buddha's kin, who migrated from India and founded Tagaung on the upper Irrawaddy, traditionally in the 9th century BCE, and that his…

amiriya-madrasa.s: The Amiriya Madrasa is a religious school and mosque in Rada'a, Yemen, built by the Tahirid sultan Amir ibn Abd al-Wahhab and completed in 1504. Its white domes and richly painted interiors make it one of the finest Islamic monuments of southern Arabia.

amir-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.s: Amir ibn Abd al-Wahhab was the last major sultan of the Tahirid dynasty of Yemen, reigning from 1489 to 1517. A patron of learning and builder, he founded the Amiriya Madrasa at Rada'a.
