alpuente.s: Alpuente is a small town in the mountains of the north-west of the province of Valencia, Spain, dominated by the ruins of its castle. After the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba it was the seat of a small taifa ruled by the Banu Qasim from about 1009 until the Almoravids took…

abbadid-dynasty.s: The Abbadids were an Arab dynasty that ruled the Taifa of Seville in al-Andalus from 1023 to 1091. Under al-Mutadid and his son al-Mutamid, a celebrated poet, they absorbed neighbouring taifas across the south-west and made Seville the strongest Muslim state in Iberia.

arcos-de-la-frontera.s: Arcos de la Frontera is a hilltop town in the province of Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain, set on a sandstone ridge above the Guadalete river. In the 11th century it was the seat of a small Berber taifa under the Banu Khizrun until the Abbadids of Seville annexed it.

aftasid-dynasty.s: The Aftasid dynasty ruled the Taifa of Badajoz, the largest Muslim kingdom of western al-Andalus, from 1022 to 1094. Founded by Abd Allah ibn al-Aftas, a vizier of Berber descent, it held lands from the Guadiana to the Tagus, including Lisbon and Évora, and its court was known…

andujar.s: Andújar is a town on the Guadalquivir in the province of Jaén, Andalusia, Spain. In the 1220s it passed to Ferdinand III of Castile as one of the castles handed over by his ally, the Almohad prince al-Bayyasi, and it became a Castilian frontier town.

almodovar-del-rio.s: Almodóvar del Río is a town on the Guadalquivir in the province of Córdoba, Spain, dominated by a castle of Muslim origin on a hill above the river; its name comes from the Arabic al-Mudawwar, 'the round one'. The castle changed hands in the wars of the taifa period, and in…

abu-amr-al-dani.s: Abu Amr al-Dani (981–1053) was an Andalusi scholar of the Quran, born in Córdoba, who settled in Dénia under its ruler Mujahid al-Amiri. He wrote more than a hundred works on Quran recitation, orthography and the seven canonical readings, of which al-Taysir became a standard…

ali-iqbal-al-dawla.s: Ali Iqbal al-Dawla was the ruler of the Taifa of Dénia from 1044 to 1076, son and successor of its founder Mujahid al-Amiri. Captured as a boy during his father's Sardinian expedition of 1015–1016, he was held for years by the Christians before returning.

aghmat.s: Aghmat is a town at the foot of the High Atlas south-east of Marrakesh, Morocco. Before Marrakesh was founded around 1070 it was the chief town of the region and an early capital of the Almoravids.

algeciras.s: Algeciras is a port city on the Bay of Gibraltar in the province of Cádiz, Spain. Founded by the Muslim conquerors in the 8th century as al-Jazira al-Khadra, it was the main crossing point to North Africa and the seat of a taifa in the 11th century.

alfonso-iii-of-aragon.s: Alfonso III of Aragon (1265–1291), called the Liberal, was King of Aragon and Count of Barcelona from 1285. Facing the noble Union of Aragon, he granted the Privilege of the Union in 1287, which greatly limited royal power.

aledo.s: Aledo is a small town in the region of Murcia, Spain, on a rocky spur of the Sierra Espuña. Its castle was taken by Castile in 1086 and served García Jiménez as a raiding base deep in Muslim territory.

al-mutamid-ibn-abbad.s: Al-Mutamid ibn Abbad (1040–1095) was the last Abbadid king of the Taifa of Seville, ruling from 1069 to 1091, and one of the finest poets of al-Andalus. He annexed Córdoba and Murcia, with the poet Ibn Ammar as vizier, but paid tribute to Alfonso VI of Castile.

arade.s: The Arade is a river of the western Algarve in southern Portugal, flowing past Silves to the Atlantic at Portimão. In Roman and Islamic times it was navigable up to Silves, which made the town a river port and the chief city of the Algarve.

amirids.s: The Amirids were the family of al-Mansur (Almanzor), the chief minister who ruled the Caliphate of Córdoba in the name of Hisham II from the 970s. His sons Abd al-Malik al-Muzaffar and Abd al-Rahman Sanchuelo succeeded him until Sanchuelo's fall in 1009 set off the civil war…

ahmad-al-muqtadir.s: Ahmad al-Muqtadir (died 1081) was the Hudid king of the Taifa of Zaragoza from 1046 and its most powerful ruler. He removed his brothers from their shares of the kingdom, annexed Tortosa around 1060 and Dénia in 1076, and paid tribute to Castile while fighting Aragon, notably…

ahmad-al-mustain-ii.s: Ahmad al-Mustain II (died 1110) was the Hudid king of the Taifa of Zaragoza from 1085, the last of his line to rule the city. He paid tribute to Castile, lost Huesca to Aragon after the Battle of Alcoraz in 1096, and faced growing Aragonese pressure.

aljaferia.s: The Aljafería is a fortified palace in Zaragoza, Spain, built in the second half of the 11th century for the Hudid king Ahmad al-Muqtadir. Its richly decorated interlaced arches and small oratory make it a key monument of Islamic architecture of the taifa period.

al-mundhir-of-cordoba.s: Al-Mundhir (c. 842–888) was the Umayyad emir of Córdoba from 886 to 888, son of Muhammad I.

arhuaco-people.s: The Arhuaco are an Indigenous people of the southern slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in northern Colombia, speaking a Chibchan language. Regarded as heirs of the Tairona, they keep a traditional spiritual leadership of mamos, who teach that the Sierra is the heart…

angul-district.s: Angul is a district of central Odisha, India, with its headquarters at the town of Angul. Formed in 1993 from part of Dhenkanal district, it includes the former princely states of Talcher, Pal Lahara and Athmallik and the British-ruled area of Angul.

astara.s: Astara is a town on the Caspian coast divided by the Astara river between Azerbaijan and Iran, the two halves forming separate towns. It was the first capital of the Talysh Khanate in the 18th century, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 made the river the border between the…

al-hira.s: Al-Hira was an ancient city in southern Iraq, south of modern Kufa near the Euphrates, capital of the Arab Lakhmid kings from the late 3rd century until 602. A centre of Arab Christianity and early Arabic poetry, it served the Sasanian Empire as a frontier base facing Rome and…

adour.s: The Adour is a river of south-western France, about 300 km long, rising in the Pyrenees near the Tourmalet pass and flowing through Bigorre, the Landes and Dax to the Atlantic at Bayonne. In antiquity its valley was home to Aquitanian peoples such as the Bigerriones and…

aquitani.s: The Aquitani were the ancient peoples of south-western Gaul between the Garonne, the Pyrenees and the Atlantic. Unlike the Celtic Gauls, they spoke a language related to early Basque, known from personal and divine names in Latin inscriptions.

abdul-rahim-khan-i-khanan.s: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan (1556–1627) was a commander and poet at the Mughal court, son of Akbar's guardian Bairam Khan. As one of Akbar's leading generals he conquered Gujarat in 1584 and lower Sindh, receiving the submission of the Tarkhan ruler Mirza Jani Beg in 1591.

ambaghai.s: Ambaghai was a khan of the Khamag Mongol confederation in the 12th century, successor of Khabul Khan and a leader of the Tayichiud clan. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, he was seized by the Tatars while escorting his daughter to her marriage and handed over to…

agron.s: Agron was king of the Ardiaean kingdom of Illyria from about 250 to 231 BCE. He built up a strong fleet and army and extended his power along the eastern Adriatic coast, and in 231 BCE, as an ally of Macedon, his forces defeated the Aetolians at Medion.

alushta.s: Alushta is a resort town on the southern coast of the Crimean peninsula, on the Black Sea between Yalta and Sudak. It grew around the Byzantine fortress of Aluston, built under Justinian I in the 6th century, and later belonged to the Genoese and the Ottomans before the…

andromachus-of-tauromenium.s: Andromachus was the ruler of Tauromenium, modern Taormina, in Sicily in the mid-4th century BCE and the father of the historian Timaeus. In 358 BCE he gathered the survivors of Naxos, destroyed by Dionysius I, and settled them in the new city.

anacreon.s: Anacreon was a Greek lyric poet from Teos in Ionia, famous for short songs about love and wine. When the Persians conquered Ionia he joined the Teians who founded Abdera in Thrace, and later lived at the courts of Polycrates of Samos and of the Peisistratids in Athens.

avenue-of-the-dead.s: The Avenue of the Dead is the main axis of Teotihuacan in central Mexico, a broad ceremonial way more than two kilometres long laid out in the early centuries CE. Running from the Pyramid of the Moon past the Pyramid of the Sun to the Ciudadela, it is oriented about 15.5…

andrew-the-apostle.s: Andrew the Apostle was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, the brother of Simon Peter and a fisherman from Galilee. Tradition holds that he preached around the Black Sea and was crucified at Patras in Greece.

antalya.s: Antalya is a city on the Mediterranean coast of south-western Turkey, on the Gulf of Antalya. Founded as Attalia by Attalus II of Pergamon in the 2nd century BCE, it became a Roman and Byzantine port and was captured by the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in 1207.

ambon.s: Ambon is an island and city in the Maluku Islands of eastern Indonesia and the capital of the province of Maluku. The Portuguese built a fort there in the 1570s, and from 1605 it was a centre of the Dutch East India Company, which concentrated clove growing on Ambon and nearby…

acolhua.s: The Acolhua were a Nahua people of the eastern Valley of Mexico, whose rulers claimed descent from Chichimec migrants led by Xolotl. Their capital, Texcoco, became under Nezahualcoyotl in the 15th century a partner of the Mexica and of Tlacopan in the Aztec Triple Alliance.

akrotiri-prehistoric-city.s: Akrotiri is a Bronze Age settlement on the island of Santorini (Thera) in the Aegean, buried by a volcanic eruption in the 17th or 16th century BCE. Excavated since 1967, its well-preserved multi-storey houses and wall paintings make it one of the most important sites of the…

alexander-romance.s: The Alexander Romance is a legendary account of the life of Alexander the Great, falsely attributed to his historian Callisthenes and compiled in Greek by the 3rd century CE from earlier material. It makes Alexander the son of Nectanebo II, the last native pharaoh of Egypt.

apis.s: Apis was a sacred bull worshipped at Memphis in ancient Egypt as the living manifestation of the god Ptah. A single bull with particular markings was chosen for the role, and on its death it was mummified and buried with great ceremony in the Serapeum at Saqqara.

artaxerxes-iv.s: Artaxerxes IV, known before his accession as Arses, was king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 338 to 336 BCE. The youngest son of Artaxerxes III, he was placed on the throne by the eunuch Bagoas after his father's murder, and was himself poisoned by Bagoas when he tried…

antalo.s: Antalo is a village in the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, south of Mekelle near Hintalo. In the early 19th century it was the seat of Ras Wolde Selassie, the dominant lord of Tigray during the Era of Princes, and British visitors such as Henry Salt met him there.

akapana.s: The Akapana is the largest structure at Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca in Bolivia: a terraced platform mound about 17 metres high, faced with stone and built mainly between about 500 and 950 CE. Its summit held buildings around a sunken court, and an internal drainage system…

aymara.s: The Aymara are an Indigenous people of the Andean altiplano around Lake Titicaca, in Bolivia, Peru and Chile, speaking the Aymara language. After the collapse of Tiwanaku several Aymara kingdoms, such as the Lupaca, Colla and Pacajes, ruled the region until the Inca conquest…

awa-odori.s: Awa Odori is a summer dance festival held in Tokushima, on the Japanese island of Shikoku, during the Obon season in August. Groups of dancers and musicians parade through the streets to a two-beat rhythm of drums, shamisen and flutes.

awaji-island.s: Awaji Island is the largest island of Japan's Inland Sea, lying between Honshu and Shikoku and now part of Hyogo Prefecture. In Japanese mythology it is the first island created by the gods Izanagi and Izanami.

atlantes-of-tula.s: The Atlantes of Tula are four colossal basalt columns carved as Toltec warriors, about 4.6 metres tall, standing on top of Pyramid B at the archaeological site of Tula in Hidalgo, Mexico. Carved around 900–1100 CE, they once supported the roof of the temple, and each wears a…

ashgabat.s: Ashgabat is the capital and largest city of Turkmenistan, on the northern edge of the Kopet Dag mountains. Founded as a Russian fort in 1881, it became the administrative centre of the Transcaspian region and from 1924 the capital of the Turkmen SSR, bearing the name…

akaki-chkhenkeli.s: Akaki Chkhenkeli was a Georgian Menshevik politician who headed the government of the short-lived Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic in April–May 1918 and led its delegation in peace talks with the Ottoman Empire. After the federation dissolved he served as foreign…

addedomarus.s: Addedomarus was a British king known from his coins, who ruled the Trinovantes in what is now Essex in the late 1st century BCE. He was among the first rulers in Britain to put his name on gold coinage, and he may have been buried in the rich Lexden Tumulus at Camulodunum.

agartala.s: Agartala is the capital of the Indian state of Tripura, close to the border with Bangladesh. The Manikya kings moved their capital to the site in the 19th century, and Bir Chandra Manikya (r.

achaeans-achaea.s: The Achaeans of the historical period were the people of Achaea, the strip of the northern Peloponnese along the southern shore of the Gulf of Corinth. Their twelve small cities shared a sanctuary of Zeus Homarios near Aegium and formed the Achaean League, which became a…

abdullahi-issa.s: Abdullahi Issa was a Somali politician of the Somali Youth League. In 1956 he became the first prime minister of the Trust Territory of Somaliland, the former Italian colony administered by Italy under United Nations trusteeship, and he led its government until independence in…

amdo.s: Amdo is the north-eastern region of the Tibetan plateau, now mostly in the Chinese province of Qinghai with parts of Gansu and Sichuan. A frontier of grasslands and farming valleys where Tibetans, Mongols, Chinese and Muslims met, it was home to the 11th-century kingdom of…

ahoeitu.s: ʻAhoʻeitu is the first Tuʻi Tonga, the sacred king of Tonga, in Tongan tradition, usually placed around the 10th century. The story makes him the son of the sky god Tangaloa ʻEitumatupuʻa and a mortal woman, Ilaheva Vaʻepopua.

al-mutadid.s: Al-Mu'tadid was Abbasid caliph from 892 to 902. As the son of the regent al-Muwaffaq he helped his father crush the Zanj rebellion in southern Iraq in the 880s.

al-qatai.s: Al-Qata'i was the capital founded by Ahmad ibn Tulun around 870 north-east of Fustat, on the site of present-day Cairo. Its name, 'the allotments', came from the quarters assigned to his troops and officials.

ain-farah.s: Ain Farah is a ruined hilltop settlement in northern Darfur, in western Sudan. Its red-brick buildings include a palace complex, a structure identified as a mosque and earlier buildings that some scholars compare with the churches of Christian Nubia.

arlanzon-river.s: The Arlanzón is a river of northern Spain in the province of Burgos. It rises in the Sierra de la Demanda and flows west through the city of Burgos before joining the Arlanza, which in turn flows into the Pisuerga, a tributary of the Duero.

abtai-sain-khan.s: Abtai Sain Khan was a Khalkha Mongol prince, a great-grandson of Dayan Khan, who became the leading ruler of central Khalkha in the late 16th century. A champion of Buddhism, he founded the monastery of Erdene Zuu beside the ruins of Karakorum around 1585, and in 1586 he met…

amenirdis-i.s: Amenirdis I was a Kushite princess, daughter of King Kashta and sister of Piye and Shabaka, who served as God's Wife of Amun at Thebes in the late 8th century BCE. She was adopted by Shepenupet I, daughter of Osorkon III, which gave the Kushites a peaceful hold over Thebes.

abimilki.s: Abimilki was king of Tyre in the 14th century BCE, during the Amarna period, when the city was a vassal of Egypt. About ten of his letters to the pharaoh, almost certainly Akhenaten, survive among the Amarna letters.

al-kharj.s: Al-Kharj is a city and agricultural district in central Saudi Arabia, about 80 kilometres south-east of Riyadh. Its springs and groundwater have supported farming since antiquity, and in the 9th century it was the seat of the Ukhaydirid emirate at al-Khidrima.

amelia-umbria.s: Amelia, the ancient Ameria, is a hill town in southern Umbria, Italy. In antiquity it was one of the leading Umbrian communities and later a Roman municipium, and its massive polygonal walls, built of huge fitted stone blocks, still survive.

atiedian-brethren.s: The Atiedian Brethren (Latin fratres Atiedii) were a college of priests at Iguvium, modern Gubbio, in ancient Umbria. Their rituals, including the purification of the city's sacred mount, sacrifices and the reading of bird signs, are recorded in the Iguvine Tablets of the 3rd…

abdel-hakim-amer.s: Abdel Hakim Amer was an Egyptian army officer, a close friend of Gamal Abdel Nasser and a leading member of the Free Officers who seized power in 1952. As commander of the armed forces and field marshal, he served as Nasser's representative in Syria during the United Arab…

act-of-federation-of-the-united-province.n: Act of Federation of the United Provinces of New Granada
act-of-federation-of-the-united-province.s: The Act of Federation of the United Provinces of New Granada was signed on 27 November 1811 by delegates of several provinces of the former Viceroyalty of New Granada, in present-day Colombia. Drafted largely by Camilo Torres, it created a loose confederation of sovereign…

archibald-v-arnold.s: Archibald V. Arnold was a United States Army general who commanded the 7th Infantry Division in the Pacific in the Second World War, including in the Battle of Okinawa.

addu-atoll.s: Addu Atoll is the southernmost atoll of the Maldives, just south of the equator, and home to the country's second city. Britain built an air base on its island of Gan during the Second World War and kept it as RAF Gan until 1976.

amberg.s: Amberg is a town in the Upper Palatinate in Bavaria, Germany. A centre of iron mining and trade from the Middle Ages, it was the seat of government of the Upper Palatinate for the Electors Palatine from the 14th century until 1628, and then under Bavaria until 1810.

abdi-heba.s: Abdi-Heba was the ruler of Jerusalem, called Urusalim, in the mid-14th century BCE, known from six of his letters to the Egyptian pharaoh among the Amarna letters. He presented himself as a loyal vassal installed by Egypt, complained of rival rulers such as Labayu of Shechem…

al-afshin.s: Al-Afshin, born Khaydhar ibn Kawus, was a prince of Ustrushana in Central Asia who became one of the leading generals of the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim. He crushed the revolt of Babak Khorramdin in Azerbaijan in 837 and commanded in the Amorium campaign against Byzantium in 838.

anandavardhana.s: Anandavardhana was a Kashmiri literary theorist of the 9th century, active at the court of King Avantivarman of the Utpala dynasty. In his Dhvanyaloka he argued that the essence of poetry lies in dhvani, suggestion, the meaning a poem conveys beyond its literal sense.

avantipur.s: Avantipur is a town on the Jhelum river in the Kashmir valley, south-east of Srinagar, founded by King Avantivarman of the Utpala dynasty, who reigned from 855 to 883. It preserves the ruins of two great stone temples he built, the Avantiswami temple dedicated to Vishnu and…

andijan.s: Andijan is a city in the eastern Fergana valley of Uzbekistan, one of the oldest towns of the region and the birthplace of Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire. It was a seat of the Timurid rulers of Fergana and later part of the Khanate of Kokand.

akmal-ikramov.s: Akmal Ikramov was an Uzbek communist leader, first secretary of the Communist Party of the Uzbek SSR from 1929 to 1937. He oversaw collectivisation and the expansion of cotton growing in Uzbekistan.

ajanta-caves.s: The Ajanta Caves are about thirty Buddhist rock-cut monasteries and prayer halls in a horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghora river in Maharashtra, India. The earliest were cut around the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE; most of the rest date from the late 5th century, under the…

apostolic-palace.s: The Apostolic Palace is the official residence of the pope in Vatican City, beside St. Peter's Basilica.

alpes-maritimae.s: Alpes Maritimae was a small Roman province in the Maritime Alps between Italy and Gaul, organised under Augustus after the Alpine peoples were subdued, first under a prefect from 14 BCE. Its capital was Cemenelum, now Cimiez in Nice, and in late antiquity Embrun.

apollo-of-veii.s: The Apollo of Veii is a life-size painted terracotta statue of the god Apollo, made around 510–500 BCE for the roof of the Portonaccio temple at Veii. Found in 1916, it shows Apollo striding forward in a contest with Hercules over a sacred deer.

acronauplia.s: Acronauplia is the rocky peninsula and oldest fortified quarter of Nafplio in the Peloponnese, Greece. Walled since antiquity, it was strengthened in turn by the Byzantines, the Franks, the Venetians and the Ottomans, and was the citadel of the town until the larger Palamidi…

antonio-guzman-blanco.s: Antonio Guzmán Blanco was a Venezuelan general and statesman who dominated the country from 1870 to 1888 as president or through allies. A Liberal leader of the Federal War, he made primary education free and compulsory, introduced the bolívar as the currency, curbed the power…

angus.s: Angus is a council area and historic county on the east coast of Scotland, between the Tay estuary and the Grampian mountains, with towns such as Forfar, Arbroath and Montrose. In the early Middle Ages it was a Pictish heartland, rich in carved stones such as those at…

augustobriga-lusitania.s: Augustobriga was a Roman town in Lusitania on the Tagus, at Talavera la Vieja in the modern Spanish province of Cáceres, in the lands of the Vettones. It became a municipium under the early empire.

avila.s: Ávila is a city in Castile and León, Spain, standing at more than 1,100 metres on the northern Meseta west of Madrid. In the Iron Age its district belonged to the Vettones, whose granite boar sculptures (verracos) survive there.

abu-simbel.s: Abu Simbel is a site on the Nile in Lower Nubia, southern Egypt, with two rock-cut temples built by Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE; the larger is fronted by four colossal seated statues of the king. To save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser, both temples were cut…

aniba.s: Aniba, ancient Miam, was a town on the Nile in Lower Nubia, in what is now southern Egypt. A Middle Kingdom fortress there grew into the administrative centre of Wawat under the New Kingdom, the seat of the deputy for Lower Nubia, with a temple of Horus and large cemeteries.

amenhotep-huy.s: Amenhotep, called Huy, was the Egyptian viceroy of Kush, the 'King's Son of Kush', under Tutankhamun in the 14th century BCE. His tomb at Thebes (TT40) is famous for paintings showing Nubian princes bringing gold, ebony, a giraffe and other tribute to the king, one of the key…

aregenua.s: Aregenua was the chief town of the Viducasses in Roman Gaul, at modern Vieux, south-west of Caen in Normandy. It grew in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE into a prosperous civitas capital with baths, a forum, a theatre and rich town houses, and was the home of Titus Sennius…

abdur-razzaq-samarqandi.s: Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi was a Persian historian and envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh. Sent to India in 1442, he visited Calicut and in 1443 the Vijayanagara capital, of which he left a vivid description covering its walls, markets, palaces and the Mahanavami festival.

aravidu-dynasty.s: The Aravidu dynasty was the fourth and last ruling house of the Vijayanagara Empire. Founded by Tirumala Deva Raya, brother of the regent Aliya Rama Raya who fell at Talikota in 1565, it ruled from Penukonda and later Chandragiri and Vellore while the Nayaka governors of…

abbey-of-saint-martial.s: The Abbey of Saint-Martial was a Benedictine monastery in Limoges, central France, built over the tomb of Martial, the city's first bishop. A major pilgrimage church on the road to Compostela, it was famous from the 10th to the 12th centuries for its library, its illuminated…

antonio-da-silva-porto.s: António Francisco Ferreira da Silva Porto was a Portuguese trader and explorer who settled at Belmonte in the Viye (Bié) kingdom of central Angola in the 1840s and led caravans deep into the interior to trade ivory, wax and rubber. In 1890, after King Ndunduma turned against a…

antium.s: Antium was an ancient town on the coast of Latium, at modern Anzio south of Rome. A Volscian port whose ships raided the coast, it resisted Rome until 338 BCE, when its fleet was taken and the bronze prows (rostra) of its ships were set up on the speakers' platform in the…

aventine-hill.s: The Aventine is the southernmost of the seven hills of Rome, beside the Tiber. Outside the sacred boundary of the early city until the reign of Claudius, it was associated with the plebeians and housed temples of Diana, Ceres and Juno Regina, as well as the cult of Vertumnus…

aulus-vibenna.s: Aulus Vibenna (Etruscan Avle Vipinas) was an Etruscan warrior of the 6th century BCE from Vulci, brother of Caelius Vibenna. He appears in the paintings of the François Tomb, and a bucchero vessel dedicated in his name at Veii suggests he was a historical figure.

abenaki.s: The Abenaki are an Algonquian-speaking Indigenous people of northern New England and southern Quebec, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy. Allied with New France against the English colonists in a series of wars from the 1670s to the 1760s, many moved north to mission villages…

arung-matoa.s: Arung Matoa, roughly "chief lord" in Bugis, was the title of the head of the Bugis kingdom of Wajo in South Sulawesi. Unlike most neighbouring rulers, the Arung Matoa did not inherit the office but was elected by a council of nobles, who could also remove him.

amelia-tokagahahau-aliki.s: Amelia Tokagahahau Aliki was queen, or Lavelua, of Uvea (Wallis Island) from 1869 until her death in 1895. A Catholic ruler who governed with strong support from the Marist missionaries, she sought French protection against other powers and in 1886–1887 signed the treaty that…

amarsinhji-of-wankaner.s: Amarsinhji was the ruler, with the title Raj Sahib, of Wankaner, a princely state of the Jhala Rajputs in Kathiawar, western India, from 1881 to 1948. He modernised the state's administration and built the Ranjit Vilas Palace, completed in 1914, which mixes Indian and European…

ayacucho.s: Ayacucho is a city in the central highlands of southern Peru and the capital of the region of the same name. The surrounding basin was the heartland of the Wari Empire, whose capital lies nearby.

akengbuwa.s: Akengbuwa was Olu, or king, of the Itsekiri kingdom of Warri in the western Niger Delta in the early 19th century. After his death in 1848 rival royal houses could not agree on a successor, and the throne remained vacant until 1936.

ankobra-river.s: The Ankobra is a river in the Western Region of Ghana that flows south to the Gulf of Guinea near Axim. Its basin, like that of the neighbouring Pra, is rich in alluvial gold, which sustained the Wassa state and drew European traders to forts on the nearby coast.

anthony-wayne.s: Anthony Wayne (1745–1796) was an American general, nicknamed "Mad Anthony" for his daring, who served in the Revolutionary War and captured Stony Point in 1779. Given command of the Legion of the United States, he defeated the Western Confederacy of Native nations at the…

arthur-st-clair.s: Arthur St. Clair (1737–1818) was a Scottish-born American soldier and politician who served as a general in the Revolutionary War, as president of the Confederation Congress in 1787 and as first governor of the Northwest Territory.

ashina-helu.s: Ashina Helu was the last independent khagan of the Western Turkic Khaganate. Once a Tang vassal, he rebelled in 651 and reunited the Western Turks, but in 657 a Tang army under Su Dingfang defeated him near the Irtysh River.

abraham-crijnssen.s: Abraham Crijnssen was a Dutch naval commander from Zeeland. During the Second Anglo-Dutch War he led a Zeeland squadron to the Caribbean and in February 1667 captured the English colony of Willoughbyland on the Suriname River, renaming its fort Fort Zeelandia.

aphra-behn.s: Aphra Behn (1640–1689) was an English playwright, poet and novelist, one of the first Englishwomen to earn a living by writing. She worked as a spy for Charles II in Antwerp during the Second Anglo-Dutch War and later wrote many successful plays, such as The Rover.

alaksandu.s: Alaksandu was a king of Wilusa in north-western Anatolia in the early 13th century BCE, known from a treaty he made with the Hittite king Muwatalli II around 1280 BCE. The treaty bound him as a Hittite vassal and lists the gods of Wilusa, including one named Appaliuna.

appaliuna.s: Appaliuna was a god of Wilusa in north-western Anatolia, named among the divine witnesses of the treaty between the Hittite king Muwatalli II and Alaksandu of Wilusa around 1280 BCE. Some scholars connect the name with the Greek god Apollo, who in Homer's Iliad is a protector…

aztlan.s: Aztlan is the legendary homeland from which the Mexica (Aztecs) and other Nahua peoples were said to have migrated to central Mexico. Their accounts describe it as an island in a lake somewhere to the north, which the Mexica left in the 12th century, wandering for generations…

afaq-khoja.s: Afaq Khoja (1626–1694), also called Hidayat Allah, was a Naqshbandi Sufi master and leader of the Aqtaghliq (White Mountain) faction of khojas in Kashgaria. Expelled by the khan of Yarkent, he sought help from the Fifth Dalai Lama and the Dzungar ruler Galdan, whose conquest…

amannisa-khan.s: Amannisa Khan (1526–1560) was a poet, musician and queen of the Yarkent Khanate as the wife of Abd al-Rashid Khan. She is credited with collecting and arranging the classical Uyghur Muqam, the great cycle of songs, dances and instrumental pieces, and with writing poetry and…

aqtaghliq.s: The Aqtaghliq, or 'White Mountain' faction, was one of two rival branches of the Naqshbandi khojas who dominated the religious and political life of Kashgaria in the 17th and 18th centuries. Led by Afaq Khoja and his descendants, they contended with the Qarataghliq ('Black…

abd-al-rashid-khan.s: Abd al-Rashid Khan (1508–1560) was the second khan of the Yarkent Khanate, succeeding his father Sultan Said Khan in 1533. He broke the power of the Dughlat amirs, fought the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz over Moghulistan, and made his court at Yarkand a centre of poetry and music, where…

acllahuasi.s: An acllahuasi ('house of the chosen women') was an institution of the Inca Empire housing the aclla, women selected from across the provinces to live in seclusion. They wove fine cloth, brewed chicha and served the cult of the Sun and the Inca state, and some were given as…

armatambo.s: Armatambo is an archaeological complex in Chorrillos, in the south of Lima, Peru, near the Morro Solar headland. It was an important centre of the Ychsma culture of the central coast, with adobe pyramids with ramps, and was later occupied by the Incas.

al-mutahhar-ibn-sharaf-al-din.s: Al-Mutahhar ibn Sharaf al-Din (c. 1503–1572) was a Zaydi leader in Yemen, son of Imam al-Mutawakkil Yahya Sharaf al-Din.

ali-ibn-al-fadl-al-jayshani.s: Ali ibn al-Fadl al-Jayshani (died 915) was an Isma'ili missionary (da'i) in Yemen. Sent with Ibn Hawshab and arriving around 881, he built a following in the south of the country, seized Sanaa in 905 and conquered much of Yemen, but then broke with the future Fatimid caliph…

aquiminzaque.s: Aquiminzaque (died 1540) was the last zaque, ruler of the northern Muisca of Hunza (modern Tunja) in the Colombian highlands. He succeeded Quemuenchatocha, who had been captured by the Spanish under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada in 1537.

annaba.s: Annaba is a port city in north-eastern Algeria, near the ruins of ancient Hippo Regius, the see of Saint Augustine. Known in medieval and early modern times as Bona or Bône, it was a target of European raids, including a sack by the Tuscan Knights of Saint Stephen in 1607.

agaw-people.s: The Agaw are a Cushitic-speaking people of the northern and central highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea, among the oldest inhabitants of the region. An Agaw dynasty, the Zagwe, ruled Ethiopia from Lasta from about the 12th century until 1270 and built the rock-hewn churches of…

avongara.s: The Avongara are the aristocratic ruling clan of the Zande peoples of Central Africa. From the 18th century Avongara rulers led the Ambomu east and south from the Mbomu river, conquering and assimilating many peoples, and each ruler's sons founded kingdoms of their own.

ahvaz.s: Ahvaz is a city on the Karun River in south-western Iran and the capital of Khuzestan province. An important town of the Sasanian and early Islamic periods, it was sacked by the Zanj rebels in the 9th century.

al-mukhtara.s: Al-Mukhtara, "the Chosen", was the fortified capital built by Ali ibn Muhammad, leader of the Zanj Rebellion, among the canals and marshes near Basra in southern Iraq. From it the rebels raided across lower Iraq and Khuzestan for more than a decade.

al-muwaffaq.s: Al-Muwaffaq was an Abbasid prince, son of the caliph al-Mutawakkil, who held real power during the reign of his brother al-Mu'tamid from the 870s until his death in 891. He stopped the Saffarid Ya'qub ibn al-Layth at Dayr al-Aqul in 876 and led the long campaign against the…

al-mutawakkil-yahya-sharaf-al-din.s: Al-Mutawakkil Yahya Sharaf al-Din was Zaydi imam of Yemen from 1506 to 1555. After the fall of the Tahirid sultanate he expanded the imamate from the northern highlands, taking Sanaa and much of the south.

al-hadi-ila-l-haqq-yahya.s: Al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq Yahya ibn al-Husayn was the founder of the Zaydi imamate of Yemen. A descendant of the Prophet's grandson al-Hasan from the Hejaz, he came to Sa'dah in 897 at the invitation of feuding tribes, settled their disputes and set up a state there.

al-mansur-abdallah-ibn-hamza.s: Al-Mansur Abdallah ibn Hamza was Zaydi imam of Yemen from 1187 to 1217 and one of the most prolific Zaydi scholars. He revived the imamate in the northern highlands and fought the Ayyubid rulers of Yemen.

ashir.s: Ashir was a fortified town in the Titteri mountains of central Algeria, founded around 936 by the Sanhaja chief Ziri ibn Manad with the approval of the Fatimid caliph. It was the first seat of the Zirid family, who served the Fatimids from there, and remained a regional centre…

al-muizz-ibn-badis.s: Al-Mu'izz ibn Badis was Zirid emir of Ifriqiya from 1016 to 1062. Kairouan flourished in his early reign, but around 1048 he broke with the Shia Fatimid caliphs and recognised the Sunni Abbasids.

afghan-sikh-wars.s: The Afghan–Sikh Wars were a series of conflicts between the Durrani Afghans and the Sikhs of the Punjab, from the invasions of Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1748 to the Battle of Jamrud in 1837. The Sikhs first resisted as independent misls and later, united under Ranjit Singh, took…

arab-byzantine-wars.s: The Arab–Byzantine wars were fought between the Byzantine Empire and the Arab caliphates and their successor emirates from 629 into the 11th century. In the first decades the Arabs took Syria, Egypt and North Africa and besieged Constantinople, most seriously in 717–718.

argentine-civil-wars.s: The Argentine Civil Wars were the series of conflicts fought from 1814 to 1880 between the Unitarians, who wanted a centralised state led by Buenos Aires, and the Federalists, who defended provincial autonomy. Juan Manuel de Rosas dominated much of the period; his defeat at…

anglo-spanish-war-1585-1604.s: The Anglo-Spanish War of 1585–1604 was an undeclared war between Elizabethan England and Habsburg Spain, provoked by English support for the Dutch Revolt and English privateering against Spanish shipping. Its best-known episode was the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588,…

ahom-mughal-conflicts.s: The Ahom–Mughal conflicts were a series of wars between the Ahom kingdom of Assam and the Mughal Empire from 1615 to 1682. The Mughals under Mir Jumla briefly occupied the Ahom capital in 1662–1663, but the Ahoms under Lachit Borphukan won the river Battle of Saraighat (1671)…

anglo-spanish-war-1796-1808.s: The Anglo-Spanish War of 1796–1808 was fought between Britain and Spain, which had changed sides in the French Revolutionary Wars and allied with France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1796). With a pause after the Peace of Amiens, it included British naval victories at Cape…

austro-russian-turkish-war-1735-1739.s: The Austro-Russian–Turkish War of 1735–1739 was fought between the Ottoman Empire and Russia, joined in 1737 by Austria. The Russians took Azov and Ochakov and won at Stavuchany, but Austria was defeated at Grocka in 1739 and by the Treaty of Belgrade returned northern Serbia,…

anglo-french-war-1627-1629.s: The Anglo-French War of 1627–1629 was fought between England under Charles I and France under Louis XIII, partly in support of the French Huguenots. An English expedition under the Duke of Buckingham to the Île de Ré failed in 1627, and La Rochelle surrendered to Cardinal…

angolan-war-of-independence.s: The Angolan War of Independence was fought from 1961 to 1974 between Portugal and the Angolan nationalist movements, the MPLA, the FNLA and UNITA. The war ended after the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon in April 1974; Angola became independent in November 1975, but the rival…

anglo-french-war-1213-1214.s: The Anglo-French War of 1213–1214 was fought between King John of England, allied with Emperor Otto IV and the counts of Flanders and Boulogne, and Philip II of France. John aimed to recover the lands lost in 1204, but his allies were crushed at Bouvines on 27 July 1214.

acre-war.s: The Acre War was a conflict over the rubber-rich region of Acre in the Amazon, then claimed by Bolivia but settled mainly by Brazilian rubber tappers. Brazilian settlers under José Plácido de Castro rose against Bolivian rule and defeated its forces in 1902–1903.

anglo-persian-war.s: The Anglo-Persian War was fought between Britain and Qajar Persia from November 1856 to April 1857, after Persia occupied Herat in Afghanistan. British and Indian forces landed in the Persian Gulf, took Bushehr and won at Khushab and Mohammerah.
